# Sūrah al-Māʾidah (Chapter 5) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Introduction to the Sūrah

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Sūrah of Last Words**

Sūrah al-Māʾidah, "The Table Spread," is the fifth chapter of the Qur'an in the order of the written muṣḥaf, but among the very last in the order of revelation. It is Madinan in its entirety, and its verses belong, by the near-unanimous testimony of the early authorities, to the period after the conquest of Makkah in the eighth year of the Hijrah — that is, to the final two and a half years of the Prophet's ﷺ life. Several of its passages were revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage of the tenth year, on the plain of ʿArafah itself, and the sūrah is therefore the closest thing the Qur'an contains to a set of parting instructions delivered to a community that had now won its long struggle and was about to lose its Prophet. This is why its tone differs so markedly from the earlier Madinan sūrahs. Al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān speak to a community under siege; al-Māʾidah speaks to a community that has arrived, and whose greatest remaining danger is not the sword of an enemy but the loosening of its own covenant. That is why the sūrah opens with two words that summarize its entire concern: *awfū bi-l-ʿuqūd* — "Fulfill your pacts."

The lateness of the sūrah gave it a special juristic weight in the eyes of the Companions. Because a later revelation can qualify or abrogate an earlier one, but not the reverse, the last sūrahs to descend carry rulings that were never subsequently modified. The Prophet's wife ʿĀʾishah, according to a report transmitted by Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim, therefore instructed the community:

> *"Al-Māʾidah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed; so whatever you find in it made lawful, treat it as lawful, and whatever you find in it made forbidden, treat it as forbidden."* (Aḥmad; al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic)

A similar counsel is ascribed to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and though its chain is weaker, the substance is identical and was acted upon by the earliest jurists. Al-Qurṭubī records the view that not a single ruling in this sūrah was ever abrogated; Ibn Kathīr notes minor exceptions claimed for parts of verse 2 (the protection of idolatrous pilgrims) and verse 106 (the testimony of non-Muslims at a deathbed on a journey), but the general rule stands: al-Māʾidah is legislation in its final, settled form.

**The Descent That Bent a Camel's Back**

The early sources preserve a striking physical detail about the revelation of this sūrah. Aḥmad records from Asmāʾ bint Yazīd, who was holding the halter of the Prophet's she-camel, al-ʿAḍbāʾ, that when al-Māʾidah came down upon him in its entirety, the animal's foreleg nearly broke under the weight, and the Prophet ﷺ was obliged to dismount. A similar report in the collection of Aḥmad describes the camel kneeling until the revelation lifted. Whatever one makes of the metaphysics of such reports, the Companions understood them literally: revelation was a *thiql*, a weight, as God Himself had said — *"Indeed, We will cast upon you a weighty word"* (73:5) — and this particular sūrah, dense with binding law, weighed heavily even on the beast that carried the one who received it. Muslim scholars have always read that detail as a lesson in reverence: what the camel could scarcely carry, the believer is asked to carry in his conduct.

**The Two Great Themes**

Al-Māʾidah has 120 verses arranged around two interwoven concerns. The first is the completion of the community's ritual and legal life. Here the sūrah gathers up, in their definitive form, the laws of lawful and forbidden food (vv. 1, 3–5, 87–88, 96), the sanctities of the pilgrimage (vv. 1–2, 94–97), the ablution and dry ablution (v. 6), the punishments for brigandage and theft (vv. 33–39), the expiation of oaths (v. 89), the final prohibition of wine and gambling (vv. 90–91), the penalty for hunting while in the pilgrim's consecrated state (v. 95), and the procedure for witnesses to a deathbed bequest (vv. 106–108). It is the only sūrah to mention the call to prayer (v. 58), and it contains the verse in which God declares:

> *"This day I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My Blessing upon you, and have approved for you as religion, Submission."* (5:3)

That verse alone secured the sūrah's place in the memory of the community. When a Jewish scholar told ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that had such a verse been revealed to the Jews they would have made its day a festival, ʿUmar answered that he knew precisely the day and the place: a Friday, on the plain of ʿArafah, with the Prophet ﷺ standing at the culmination of his only pilgrimage (al-Bukhārī 45; Muslim 3017).

The second and larger theme is the settling of the Muslim community's relationship with the People of the Book. The sūrah does not treat that relationship as a single thing. It permits Muslims to eat the food of Jews and Christians and to marry their chaste women (v. 5) — the widest social door the Qur'an opens to any non-Muslim community. It recognizes that the Torah and the Gospel each contain "guidance and light" (vv. 44, 46) and lays down the principle that God has given each community "a law and a way" (v. 48). It offers one of the most tender portraits in the whole Qur'an of sincere Christians whose eyes overflow with tears at the recognition of truth (vv. 82–85). At the same time, it rebukes covenant-breaking and the distortion of scripture (vv. 12–14, 41–44), denies with full force the divinity of Jesus and the doctrine of the Trinity (vv. 17, 72–77, 116–118), forbids political alliance with those who make war on the faith (vv. 51–57), and holds up the failure of Israelite scholars to forbid wrong (vv. 62–63, 78–79) as a mirror for Muslim scholars of every age. The sūrah's method is thus neither indiscriminate embrace nor blanket hostility; it is discrimination in the proper sense — the drawing of true lines in the right places.

**Three Narratives as Moral Anchors**

Three stories anchor the sūrah's argument. The first (vv. 20–26) recounts the Israelites' refusal to enter the Holy Land with Moses — "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we shall sit here" — and their forty years of wandering, a lesson about the price of cowardice before a divine command that the Companions applied to themselves on the eve of Badr. The second (vv. 27–32) is the Qur'an's fullest telling of the two sons of Adam, the first murder, and the burial taught by a crow; it culminates in the verse that has become, across the world, the most quoted Qur'anic statement on the value of a single human life: *"whosoever slays a soul ... it is as though he slew mankind altogether."* The third (vv. 110–120) is the story from which the sūrah takes its name: the disciples of Jesus ask for a table spread with food from heaven, Jesus prays, God grants it with a warning, and the sūrah closes with a conversation on the Day of Resurrection between God and Jesus in which Jesus disowns any claim to divinity in words of unsurpassed humility — words the Prophet ﷺ himself once recited, weeping, through an entire night.

**Why the Sūrah Matters for the Modern Reader**

The concerns of al-Māʾidah — how to keep one's word, what to eat, how to treat those of other faiths, how to judge justly even against those one dislikes, how to avoid the intoxicants and games that dissolve societies, how to be a scholar who actually forbids wrong — are not antique. They are the daily material of ethical life in any age. The sūrah's recurring refrain, addressed fifteen times to "O you who believe," assumes an audience that already accepts God and now needs to learn how belief translates into contracts, meals, courts, marriages, and neighborly relations. In that sense, al-Māʾidah is the Qur'an's most sustained lesson in the second half of faith: not the confession of the tongue, but the fidelity of the hand.

What follows is a verse-by-verse expanded commentary. Each of the 120 verses is treated as an independent discourse, drawing upon the Arabic language, the classical commentators — al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī, and others — the authenticated words of the Prophet ﷺ with their collections identified, the reports of the Companions and Successors, and the reasoning that connects a fourteen-hundred-year-old revelation to the actual conditions of the human being who reads it today.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:1

> **O you who believe! Fulfill your pacts. Lawful unto you are grazing cattle, save that which is recited unto you, hunted game being unlawful when you are in the state of pilgrim sanctity. Truly God decrees whatsoever He desires.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Command of the Last Legislation**

It is fitting that a sūrah revealed in the closing months of the Prophet's ﷺ life should open with the command that underwrites every other command: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū awfū bi-l-ʿuqūd* — "O you who believe, fulfill your pacts." Everything the sūrah will go on to legislate — food, purity, pilgrimage, justice, testimony — depends upon the prior willingness to be bound by an agreement. A law that no one feels obliged to keep is not a law but a suggestion. So the Qur'an begins by securing the foundation: the believer is the kind of person who honors what he has committed to. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said, in a report preserved by al-Ṭabarī, that *al-ʿuqūd* here means "the covenants" — what God has made lawful and forbidden, what He has obliged and bound them to in the Qur'an as a whole. Al-Qurṭubī observes that the verse is comprehensive: it covers every binding commitment a person enters, whether with God or with fellow human beings, provided the commitment is not itself sinful.

The address itself, *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū*, deserves attention. Ibn Masʿūd used to say: "When you hear God say, 'O you who believe,' lend it your ear, for it is either a good that He commands you or an evil He forbids you." By addressing the listener through his faith rather than his tribe or name, the Qur'an appeals to the highest thing in him. You are addressed as a believer; therefore act as one. It is the same psychological move a parent makes when saying "you are better than this" — the identity invoked becomes the motive for the conduct required.

**The Word ʿUqūd: Knots That Bind**

The Arabic *ʿuqūd* is the plural of *ʿaqd*, from the root ʿ-q-d, whose primary meaning is to tie a knot, to fasten firmly. From it come *ʿuqdah* (a knot — used in 2:235 and 2:237 for "the knot of marriage") and *iʿtiqād* (creed, a firmly tied conviction). An *ʿaqd* is thus a knot between two parties; to "fulfill" it (*awfā*, from w-f-y, to give something in full measure, to complete) is to keep the knot tight until the agreed purpose is achieved. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that *ʿaqd* is stronger than *ʿahd*: every *ʿaqd* is an *ʿahd*, but an *ʿaqd* is an *ʿahd* that has been *tightened* — mutually confirmed with obligations on both sides. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī distinguished three kinds of *ʿaqd*: the pact between God and His servant (the covenant of faith and obedience), the pact between a person and himself (a vow or oath), and the pact between a person and others (contracts, treaties, marriages). The verse, being unqualified, covers all three.

The commentators fill in these categories concretely. Al-Ṭabarī's preferred view is that the primary reference is to the pacts God has taken upon His servants — the obligations of the religion — because the verse goes on immediately to legislate what is lawful and forbidden in food. Others, cited by al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī, extend the term to the pre-Islamic pacts of mutual protection (*ḥilf*) that the Arabs had sworn among themselves, which Islam upheld insofar as they were for the defense of the oppressed and did not entail sin. The Prophet ﷺ said of such pre-Islamic alliances:

> *"Whatever alliance existed in the Age of Ignorance, Islam only increases it in strength."* (Muslim 2530, from Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim)

And the broadest reading includes commercial sales, leases, marriages, partnerships, and treaties with other communities — all of which are regulated by the Law and none of which may be broken merely because breaking them has become convenient.

**A Letter to the Christians of Najrān**

There is a report of great interest about the earliest circulation of this verse. Al-Qurṭubī records that Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī, the great collector of Hadith of the generation after the Companions, stated that the Prophet ﷺ sent a letter to the Christian community of Najrān in southern Arabia, and that this letter contained the first four verses of this sūrah. If accurate, it shows that the command "fulfill your pacts" was, from the first, understood to extend to the covenanted relationship between the Muslim state and communities of other faiths. The Christians of Najrān had entered into a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ guaranteeing their persons, churches, and property in return for a tribute; the letter would then have functioned as a reminder that covenant-keeping was expected on both sides. This detail also fits the second great theme of the sūrah: the settling of relations with the People of the Book on the basis of mutual, honored agreement.

**Why Covenant-Keeping Is the Foundation of Faith**

The Qur'an repeatedly presents covenant-fidelity as a defining mark of belief. It lists among the righteous "those who keep their covenant when they covenant" (2:177), and it says:

> *"And fulfill the covenant of God when you have covenanted, and do not break oaths after their confirmation, when you have made God a guarantor over you."* (Qur'an 16:91)

> *"And fulfill the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be asked about."* (Qur'an 17:34)

The reason is logical. Faith itself is a covenant: the believer has agreed to worship God and obey Him in return for His guidance and reward. A person who habitually breaks agreements with people will, by that same habit, break the agreement with God. The Prophet ﷺ therefore made breach of promise a sign of the hypocrite:

> *"The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks his promise, and when he is entrusted he betrays."* (al-Bukhārī 33; Muslim 59, from Abū Hurayrah)

And he taught that a broken treaty would be publicly exposed on the Day of Judgment:

> *"For every betrayer there will be a banner on the Day of Resurrection, raised in proportion to his betrayal; and there is no betrayer greater than a leader of the people who betrays."* (al-Bukhārī 3188; Muslim 1738)

Socially, the principle is the glue of civilization. Markets, marriages, states, and friendships all depend on the expectation that words given will be honored. Where that expectation collapses, every transaction must be secured by force or suspicion, and life becomes exhausting. A community in which promises are kept is, quite simply, a community in which people can breathe. The verse's placement at the head of the sūrah of final laws is therefore not merely rhetorical: it identifies the single virtue without which no other law can function.

**Lawful unto You Are Grazing Cattle**

The verse then moves without transition from the general command to a specific area of law: *uḥillat lakum bahīmat al-anʿām* — "Lawful unto you are the beasts of the flocks." *Bahīmah* is any four-footed animal (from b-h-m, connoting something whose speech is unintelligible, i.e., a dumb beast); *al-anʿām* are the livestock specifically — camels, cattle, sheep, and goats, the "eight pairs" enumerated in 6:143–144. The construction *bahīmat al-anʿām* thus means the animals that belong to the category of livestock. Al-Ṭabarī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and others that the phrase includes the young found in the womb of a properly slaughtered mother, whose slaughter suffices for the fetus as well — a ruling the Prophet ﷺ confirmed:

> *"The slaughter of the fetus is the slaughter of its mother."* (Abū Dāwūd 2827; al-Tirmidhī 1476; graded ḥasan)

Some commentators, cited by al-Ṭabarī, extended the term to wild animals resembling livestock, such as gazelles, wild cattle, and wild asses, on the grounds that they are grazing animals. Al-Qurṭubī notes that others treat these under the separate rules of hunted game.

The juxtaposition of "fulfill your pacts" with "lawful unto you are the beasts of the flocks" carries a subtle argument. God, who asks fidelity of His servants, immediately displays His own generosity. He does not demand obedience and then withhold provision; He asks for the knot to be kept and, in the same breath, opens the pastures. Al-Rāzī observes that the command to keep covenants is thereby framed as a reasonable request from a Benefactor who has already given abundantly, not as an arbitrary imposition.

**Save That Which Is Recited unto You**

The permission is qualified: *illā mā yutlā ʿalaykum* — "except what is recited to you." The passive "is recited" points to the Qur'an's own text, and the reference is to the list that will follow two verses later in 5:3: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, what has been consecrated to other than God, and the animals killed by strangling, beating, falling, goring, or predators. It also points backward to 2:173, 6:145, and 16:115, where the same core prohibitions appear. The phrasing teaches a method: the default is permission, and prohibitions are the exceptions that must be stated. This is a foundational legal principle in Islam — *al-aṣl fī al-ashyāʾ al-ibāḥah*, "the default status of things is permissibility" — and it protects the believer from the anxious scrupulosity that invents forbidden things God never forbade (a tendency the sūrah will explicitly rebuke in 5:87 and 5:101–103).

**The Pilgrim's Restraint: Hunting While in Iḥrām**

The second exception is *ghayra muḥillī al-ṣayd wa-antum ḥurum* — "not making game lawful while you are in the consecrated state." The word *ḥurum* is the plural of *ḥarām* in the sense of *muḥrim*, one who has entered *iḥrām*, the state of pilgrim sanctity marked by the seamless garments, the abstention from perfume, sexual relations, cutting hair or nails, and — as here — hunting land animals. The root ḥ-r-m carries the idea of inviolability; the *muḥrim* has made himself inviolable, and in return he must treat the creatures around him as inviolable too. The details of this prohibition, its penalty, and its exception for sea creatures will be given in 5:94–96. The point here is that even a lawful food becomes unlawful under a specific condition, so that the believer learns that lawfulness is not a fixed property of things but a relationship governed by God's command.

There is a moral logic in the restriction. The pilgrim has entered a zone of peace: he may not harm a hair on his own head, let alone a living creature. The Kaʿbah's precinct is a sanctuary where even the plants may not be cut (al-Bukhārī 1834). Training a person to refrain from killing for sport while in this state is a training in the recognition that the whole world belongs to God and that the human license to use it is a delegated, bounded permission — not an absolute right.

**"Truly God Decrees Whatsoever He Desires"**

The verse closes: *inna Allāha yaḥkumu mā yurīd* — "Indeed, God rules as He wills." The verb *yaḥkumu*, from ḥ-k-m, means to judge, to decree, to rule authoritatively; the same root gives *ḥikmah*, wisdom, because a true judgment is one made with wisdom. The sentence answers an unspoken question: why should these particular animals be lawful, those unlawful, and hunting forbidden only at certain times? The answer is that God is the Lawgiver and decrees as He wills — and His will, as the root reminds us, is inseparable from His wisdom.

This is not a demand for blind obedience without reasons. The Qur'an gives reasons abundantly (the prohibition of wine in 5:91, for instance, is explained by its social consequences). It is rather a statement about the source of legal authority. Human beings did not invent the categories of lawful and forbidden; they receive them. The proper response is what Ibn ʿAbbās said about all of God's rulings — that "God has forbidden nothing except that He has placed in it harm, and permitted nothing except that He has placed in it benefit," even where that benefit is hidden from us. Al-Qurṭubī draws attention to the phrase's protective function: it forestalls the objection that these rules are arbitrary, by reminding the believer that the One who decrees them is the One who created the animals, the pilgrim, and the appetite, and knows what befits each.

**Living the Verse Today**

The practical field of this verse is enormous. Every signed lease, every employment contract, every marriage vow, every verbal promise to a child, every online agreement clicked without reading — all fall under *awfū bi-l-ʿuqūd*. The Muslim jurists derived from it the principle that a contract's stipulations are binding unless they contradict the Law: the Prophet ﷺ said, "Muslims are bound by their conditions, except a condition that makes lawful what is forbidden or forbids what is lawful" (al-Tirmidhī 1352; graded ṣaḥīḥ). This means a believer's integrity in business is not a matter of reputation management but of obedience to the first command of a sūrah revealed on the plain of ʿArafah.

The verse also disciplines our relationship to food. The believer eats as one who has been *permitted*, not as one who simply takes. To say *bismillāh* before a meal is to acknowledge that the pasture was opened by Someone. And the pilgrim's abstention from hunting reminds every reader that the right to consume is conditioned by time, place, and state — a lesson that modern debates about the ethical treatment of animals and the limits of consumption have made unexpectedly current. The knot God asks us to keep is thus tied at both ends: fidelity to those we have promised, and restraint before the creation we have been permitted to use.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:2

> **O you who believe! Do not violate the sanctity of the rituals of God, nor the sacred month, nor the offerings, nor the garlands, nor those bound for the Sacred House, seeking the Bounty of their Lord, and [His] Contentment. But when you have left the state of pilgrim sanctity, then hunt for game. And let not hatred for a people who once turned you away from the Sacred Mosque lead you to transgress. Help one another toward piety and reverence; do not help one another toward sin and enmity. And reverence God. Truly God is severe in retribution.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Five Sanctities in a Single Breath**

The second verse of the sūrah takes the general command to keep covenants and applies it to the most visible covenant in Arabian life: the sanctity of the pilgrimage and everything connected to it. In one sentence it names five inviolable things — the rituals of God, the sacred month, the sacrificial offerings, the garlands that mark them, and the pilgrims traveling to the Sacred House. The verb governing all five is *lā tuḥillū* — "do not make lawful," "do not treat as profane" — from the same root as the *ḥalāl* of the previous verse. To "make lawful" a sanctity is to treat as ordinary something God has set apart. The verse thus teaches by negation what reverence is: the refusal to profane.

*Shaʿāʾir Allāh*, "the rituals of God," is the plural of *shaʿīrah*, from sh-ʿ-r, which means to perceive, to be aware, to mark; *shiʿār* is a distinguishing sign or emblem. The *shaʿāʾir* are therefore the visible markers of the religion — its emblems and rites — and the Qur'an uses the term specifically of the pilgrimage: Ṣafā and Marwah are "among the *shaʿāʾir* of God" (2:158), the sacrificial camels are "among the *shaʿāʾir* of God" (22:36), and "whoever honors the *shaʿāʾir* of God, it is from the piety of hearts" (22:32). Al-Ṭabarī reports several understandings: that the *shaʿāʾir* are the rites of the pilgrimage that must not be omitted; that they are the sacred places whose sanctity must not be breached; or, more generally, all the boundaries God has set, whose transgression is forbidden. Ibn ʿAbbās is quoted as understanding the phrase to refer to the sanctities of the pilgrimage in general. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the word's root meaning — perceiving and marking — is apt: these rites are how the community *marks* its devotion outwardly, so that faith becomes visible and shared.

**The Sacred Month and the Peace of Time**

*Al-shahr al-ḥarām*, "the sacred month," is in the singular, but the commentators are largely agreed that it stands for the genus and thus includes all four sacred months: Dhu'l-Qaʿdah, Dhu'l-Ḥijjah, Muḥarram (the three consecutive months surrounding the pilgrimage) and Rajab (standing alone in the middle of the year). The Qur'an affirms their number elsewhere:

> *"Indeed, the number of months with God is twelve months in the Book of God on the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them, four are sacred. That is the upright religion, so do not wrong yourselves during them."* (Qur'an 9:36)

And the Prophet ﷺ named them in his Farewell Sermon:

> *"Time has returned to its original form as it was on the day God created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: three consecutive — Dhu'l-Qaʿdah, Dhu'l-Ḥijjah, and Muḥarram — and Rajab of Muḍar, which lies between Jumādā and Shaʿbān."* (al-Bukhārī 4406; Muslim 1679)

Some commentators, as al-Zamakhsharī notes, take the singular to refer specifically to Dhu'l-Ḥijjah, the month of the pilgrimage, while al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī record opinions favoring Rajab or Dhu'l-Qaʿdah. The broader point is the same in every reading: God has hallowed certain stretches of time, and in them, violence and wrongdoing carry a heavier weight. The pre-Islamic Arabs had observed these months as a truce so that pilgrims and traders could travel safely; the Qur'an did not abolish this institution but confirmed it and purified it of the manipulations (the *nasīʾ*, or postponement, condemned in 9:37) by which the pagans had shifted the months to suit their wars.

Whether the sanctity of these months with respect to fighting remains in force was debated. Some held that 9:5 and 9:36 ("fight the polytheists all together") lifted the prohibition against fighting idolaters in these months; others, including many later jurists, noted that this very verse, along with 5:97 and 9:36, are among the last revealed and reaffirm the sanctity. Ibn Kathīr records the Prophet's ﷺ own reaffirmation in his final sermon and leans toward the view that the sacred months retain their status, though defensive fighting is permitted in them. What is uncontroversial is that sin in these months is more grievous and good deeds in them more rewarded — a principle that governs the believer's calendar to this day.

**Offerings and Garlands: The Marked Animal Is Untouchable**

*Al-hady* is the sacrificial animal that the pilgrim drives to the Sacred House to be slaughtered there (see 2:196: "and whatever *hady* is easy for you"). *Al-qalāʾid*, plural of *qilādah*, are the garlands — originally strips of bark, leather, or sandal — hung around the necks of these animals to announce that they were consecrated. The Prophet ﷺ himself garlanded his sacrificial animals: ʿĀʾishah reported, "I twisted the garlands of the Prophet's sacrificial animals with my own hands, then he garlanded them and marked them and sent them to the House" (al-Bukhārī 1696; Muslim 1321). To "violate" the offerings is to seize them, prevent them from reaching their destination, or slaughter them for one's own use; to "violate" the garlands is to strip them off or to treat a garlanded animal as ordinary property. Al-Qurṭubī records the view that garlanding was an Abrahamic practice that the pagan Arabs had preserved. The garland was a public contract: it told every passerby, "This animal has been promised to God." To respect the garland was to respect a promise made to God by a stranger — a small but telling instance of the covenant-fidelity commanded in verse 1.

**The Pilgrims and the Story of the Stolen Camels**

The fifth sanctity is *āmmīn al-bayt al-ḥarām* — "those bound for the Sacred House" — with the beautiful qualification *yabtaghūna faḍlan min rabbihim wa-riḍwānan*, "seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure." Al-Ṭabarī explains that "bounty" refers to the lawful trade pilgrims conducted along the way, and "good pleasure" to their hope of divine reward; the Qur'an elsewhere confirms that "there is no blame upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord" during the pilgrimage (2:198). The verse therefore commands that pilgrims be allowed safe passage — even, in its original historical context, pagan pilgrims.

The occasion of revelation, preserved by al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Wāḥidī, is instructive. A man named al-Ḥuṭam ibn Hind al-Bakrī came to Madinah, professed some interest in Islam, and then left without accepting it, driving away some camels belonging to the Muslims as he went. The following year, after the conquest of Makkah but before the revelation of Sūrat al-Tawbah barred idolaters from the pilgrimage, the same man was seen approaching Makkah as a pilgrim, driving garlanded camels — the very ones he had stolen. The Muslims wished to intercept him. This verse was revealed forbidding them to do so: the garlanded animals and the pilgrim were sacrosanct, regardless of what the man had done. The Muslims obeyed.

Later, with the revelation of 9:28 ("the polytheists are impure, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs") and the proclamation delivered by ʿAlī at the pilgrimage of the ninth year that "no polytheist shall perform the pilgrimage after this year" (al-Bukhārī 369), the protection of *idolatrous* pilgrims was lifted. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr therefore count this clause as abrogated in its application to idolaters, while the protection of Muslim pilgrims, sacrificial animals, and sacred rites remains fully in force. This is a clear example of *naskh* in which a later ruling qualifies an earlier one without altering its text — and it illustrates an important pattern: God's law was revealed in stages, meeting people where they were and moving them forward.

**"When You Have Left Iḥrām, Then Hunt"**

*Wa-idhā ḥalaltum fa-ṣṭādū* — "and when you have exited the consecrated state, hunt." The grammatical form is an imperative, but the jurists are unanimous that it conveys permission, not obligation: the prohibition of hunting during *iḥrām* has ended, and the pilgrim may now return to what was permitted before. This is a standard rule in the science of legal interpretation — a command that follows a prohibition restores the original permissibility (*al-amr baʿda al-ḥaẓr yufīd al-ibāḥah*). The same structure appears in 62:10: "and when the prayer has ended, disperse in the land." The lesson is that Islamic restraint is temporary and purposeful. The pilgrim does not become an ascetic forever; he learns discipline for a season and then returns, transformed, to ordinary life.

**The Hardest Command: Do Not Let Hatred Make You Unjust**

The verse now turns to its ethical center: *wa-lā yajrimannakum shanaʾānu qawmin an ṣaddūkum ʿan al-masjid al-ḥarām an taʿtadū* — "and let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, drive you to transgress." Every word is weighty. *Yajrimannakum* is from j-r-m, which means to cut, to earn, to commit (a *jarīmah* is a crime); here it means "to drive you into," "to cause you to earn." *Shanaʾān* is intense hatred, loathing; the Qur'an uses the same root of the Prophet's ﷺ enemy in 108:3 ("indeed, your hater is the one cut off"). The people referred to are the Quraysh, who had barred the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque at Ḥudaybiyah in the sixth year, forcing fourteen hundred pilgrims to turn back without completing their ʿumrah — a humiliation the Companions felt deeply, as the Qur'an records in 48:25: "They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque while the offering was detained from reaching its place."

The verse acknowledges the hatred. It does not pretend the grievance is imaginary or that the injury never occurred. It says: you were wronged, you hate them for it, and *still* you may not transgress against them. Al-Qurṭubī explains that the transgression forbidden includes attacking the pagan pilgrims, seizing their animals, or barring them from the House in retaliation for having been barred. The principle is stated as a general rule six verses later: "let not hatred of a people lead you to be unjust; be just, that is nearer to reverence" (5:8).

This is, psychologically, one of the most demanding commands in the Qur'an. Human beings feel that injury justifies retaliation beyond measure — that having been wronged confers a license. The Qur'an denies the license. It permits proportionate response (2:194: "whoever transgresses against you, respond in kind") but forbids the excess that hatred craves. The Prophet's ﷺ conduct at the conquest of Makkah was the living commentary on this verse: standing before the people who had tortured his followers, killed his uncle, and driven him from his home, he said, "Go, for you are free" (recorded by al-Bayhaqī and Ibn Isḥāq). The source text notes his further gesture at Ḥunayn, when he gave the entire spoils to the new Makkan converts to heal any remaining resentment. Justice toward the former enemy was not weakness; it was the strength that ended the cycle.

**Mutual Help in Piety, Not in Sin**

*Wa-taʿāwanū ʿalā al-birr wa-l-taqwā wa-lā taʿāwanū ʿalā al-ithm wa-l-ʿudwān* — "and help one another in righteousness and reverence, and do not help one another in sin and aggression." The verb *taʿāwana* is the reciprocal form of ʿ-w-n, to help: it means to help *each other*, to cooperate. The four nouns are carefully paired. *Birr* is comprehensive goodness, the doing of what is beneficial (defined at length in 2:177); *taqwā* is the guarding of oneself from what God has forbidden. Ibn Taymiyyah, whose treatise on this verse is well known, explains that *birr* concerns the performance of commands and *taqwā* the avoidance of prohibitions — together they constitute the whole of religion. On the negative side, *ithm* is sin in itself (an offense against God), and *ʿudwān* is aggression, an offense against creatures. The verse thus forbids collaboration in both categories of wrong.

The placement of this command directly after the command not to transgress against the Quraysh is significant. The community is told: your energy should go into cooperating in good, not into coordinating revenge. Al-Rāzī notes that the human being is social by nature and cannot achieve much alone; the question is never whether we will cooperate but *toward what*. A society is defined less by its individual virtues than by what its people help each other do. Where people help each other to honesty, charity, and knowledge, a civilization of *birr* arises; where they help each other to fraud, oppression, and vice, a civilization of *ʿudwān*. The Prophet ﷺ expressed the principle through the image of the boat: if those in the lower deck bore a hole to get water, and those above do not stop them, all drown together (al-Bukhārī 2493). Cooperation in good is thus not optional generosity but collective self-preservation.

Ibn Taymiyyah drew from this verse a foundational rule of public ethics: any assistance that enables sin — selling grapes to a winemaker, renting a house for illicit purposes, providing weapons to an aggressor — is itself forbidden, because it is "helping one another in sin and aggression." Conversely, any assistance that enables good acquires the reward of the good. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Whoever guides to something good has a reward like that of the one who does it."* (Muslim 1893)

**The Warning at the End: Severe in Retribution**

The verse closes: *wa-ttaqū Allāha inna Allāha shadīd al-ʿiqāb* — "and reverence God; indeed, God is severe in punishment." After so many commands, the seal is a warning. The commentators note that the ending fits the content: the verse has just forbidden the violation of sanctities and the transgression born of hatred, and these are precisely the sins a victorious community is most tempted to commit. The Muslims had won. They now controlled Makkah. The danger was no longer persecution but the abuse of power. God reminds them that He punishes severely, and the reminder is addressed to the strong, not the weak. *ʿIqāb* is from ʿ-q-b, "to follow after" — a punishment is what *follows* a deed, its consequence. The verse tells the community that the consequences of transgression follow inexorably, even when the transgressor holds the upper hand in this world.

**Applying the Verse Now**

Three lessons are especially urgent in the present age. First, reverence for sanctities: a society that treats nothing as sacred — no time, no place, no promise — becomes a place where everything is negotiable and nothing is safe. Second, the discipline of hatred: online and offline, people who have been wronged routinely feel licensed to inflict wrongs in return, and communities nurse grievances across generations. The verse names the feeling honestly and then forbids letting it govern action. Third, the ethics of cooperation: every professional, commercial, and political association we enter is either help toward *birr* or help toward *ithm*. The believer is asked to audit not only what he does but what he helps others do — a question that reaches into supply chains, investments, votes, and friendships. Al-Māʾidah's second verse is thus a complete program: keep what is sacred sacred, keep your hatred from ruling you, and put your shoulder only to the wheel of good.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:3

> **Forbidden unto you are carrion and blood, the flesh of swine and that which has been offered to other than God, that which has been strangled or beaten to death, that which has been killed by falling or has been gored to death, that which has been mangled by beasts of prey—save that which you may purify—and that which is sacrificed on stone altars, and that which you allot with divining arrows; that is iniquity. This day those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion. So fear them not, but fear Me! This day I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My Blessing upon you, and have approved for you as religion, Submission (Islām). But whosoever is compelled by hunger, without inclining toward sin, then surely God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verse of Law Containing the Announcement of Completion**

This verse is famous throughout the Muslim world for a single sentence in its middle — "This day I have perfected for you your religion" — yet that sentence is set inside a detailed list of forbidden foods and followed by a concession for the starving. The arrangement is deliberate and deeply instructive. The perfection of religion is announced not in a passage of abstract theology but in the midst of ordinary law about what may and may not be eaten. Islam is perfected as a *way of life*, down to the contents of the cooking pot; and the concession at the end reminds us that even the perfected law bends toward mercy where human necessity requires it. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Wāḥidī report from the majority that the verse descended on the Day of ʿArafah, a Friday, during the Farewell Pilgrimage, as the Prophet ﷺ stood on the plain in the tenth year — eighty-one days, by one count, before his death. Mujāhid held the minority view that it was revealed at the conquest of Makkah.

**The Ten Prohibited Categories, One by One**

The verse names ten things, and the classical commentators treat each with care.

*Al-maytah*, carrion, is any animal that has died without lawful slaughter, from disease, age, or accident. The prohibition's wisdom is partly hygienic (the blood is retained and putrefaction begins at once) and partly moral: the believer takes life only deliberately, with God's Name, and does not scavenge what death has left. The Prophet ﷺ exempted two kinds of dead creature: "Two dead things and two bloods have been made lawful for us: the two dead things are fish and locusts, and the two bloods are the liver and the spleen" (Ibn Mājah 3314; Aḥmad; graded ṣaḥīḥ in its content). Of the sea specifically he said, "Its water is pure and its dead are lawful" (Abū Dāwūd 83; al-Tirmidhī 69; graded ṣaḥīḥ).

*Al-dam*, blood, is understood — in light of 6:145, "or blood poured forth" — as flowing blood, not the traces that remain in the meat after slaughter. The pre-Islamic Arabs would draw blood from a living camel and eat it cooked; the Qur'an forbade this.

*Laḥm al-khinzīr*, the flesh of swine, is forbidden absolutely; the mention of "flesh" is understood by the jurists to include its fat, skin, and every part. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the Qur'an singles out the pig by name among all animals, and that its prohibition is one of the few explicitly stated four times (2:173; 5:3; 6:145; 16:115).

*Mā uhilla li-ghayri Allāhi bihi*, "that over which a name other than God's has been invoked," from *ahalla*, to raise the voice — the pagans would cry out the name of their idol at the moment of slaughter. The prohibition concerns the *dedication* of the animal, and it teaches that food is not morally neutral: an animal killed as an act of worship to a false god carries that act with it.

*Al-munkhaniqah*, the strangled, whether by a rope, a snare, or by the animal's own halter; *al-mawqūdhah*, the beaten, from w-q-dh, to strike with a heavy stick until death — a pagan practice, and one that also disqualifies game killed by the blunt side of an arrow, as the Prophet ﷺ told ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim: "If it strikes with its edge, eat; if it strikes with its breadth, it has been beaten to death, so do not eat" (al-Bukhārī 5476; Muslim 1929); *al-mutaraddiyah*, the fallen, from a height or into a well; *al-naṭīḥah*, the gored, killed by the horn of another animal; and *mā akala al-sabuʿ*, that which a predator has partly eaten. Ibn Kathīr explains that the pagans ate all of these, and the Qur'an forbade them because in each case the animal died without the deliberate, invoked act of slaughter that distinguishes human eating from animal predation.

**The Exception That Restores: "Save That Which You Purify"**

*Illā mā dhakkaytum* — "except what you have slaughtered properly." This exception, the commentators agree, applies to the five preceding categories (strangled, beaten, fallen, gored, mauled) and not to carrion, blood, or swine, which are forbidden absolutely. If any of these injured animals is reached while life still remains in it — Ibn ʿAbbās specified "if it moves its tail or blinks its eye or twitches its leg" — and is then slaughtered with God's Name, it becomes lawful. The verb *dhakkā* comes from a root meaning purity, sharpness, and fragrance; *dhakāʾ* is intelligence (sharpness of mind), and *zakāh* — from the related root z-k-w — is purification. Al-Ṭabarī suggests that slaughter is called *tadhkiyah* because it completes and purifies the meat: with the blood drained, the flesh remains fragrant and wholesome.

The ethics of slaughter in Islam, drawn from this verse and the Prophetic sunnah, are exacting. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Indeed God has prescribed excellence (iḥsān) in all things. So when you kill, kill well; and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare suffering to the animal he slaughters."* (Muslim 1955, from Shaddād ibn Aws)

He forbade sharpening the knife in front of the animal (recorded by ʿAbd al-Razzāq and al-Bayhaqī), forbade slaughtering one animal in the sight of another, forbade using an animal as a target, and required that the animal be given water and treated gently. The requirement to mention God's Name, to cut the throat swiftly and cleanly, and to let the blood drain fully was, the source commentary rightly observes, a discipline that removed from the slaughterer any sense of absolute dominion over the creature: the animal is killed *by God's permission*, and the killer says so aloud.

**Stone Altars and Divining Arrows**

*Wa-mā dhubiḥa ʿalā al-nuṣub* — "and what is sacrificed upon the *nuṣub*." The *nuṣub* (singular *nuṣb* or *nuṣbah*) were the stones set up around the Kaʿbah and elsewhere on which the pagans slaughtered to their gods; the word may also mean the idols themselves. This category overlaps with "that dedicated to other than God" but adds the element of place: even an animal slaughtered with no particular invocation but on a pagan altar is forbidden, because participation in the setting is participation in the act.

*Wa-an tastaqsimū bi-l-azlām* — "and that you divide by divining arrows." The *azlām* (singular *zalam*) were featherless arrows kept in the Kaʿbah and in the possession of soothsayers, inscribed "do" and "do not," or blank, and drawn to decide journeys, marriages, and — in the context of this verse — the division of slaughtered meat among gamblers. To "seek division" (*istiqsām*) by them was to seek to know one's allotted share or fate from the arrows. The prohibition is twofold: it forbids consuming meat apportioned by this gambling method, and it forbids the method itself as a form of divination. The Prophet ﷺ, when he entered the Kaʿbah at the conquest and found images of Abraham and Ishmael holding divining arrows, said: "May God fight them! By God, they knew that neither of them ever divided by arrows" (al-Bukhārī 1601). The verse's summation — *dhālikum fisq*, "that is iniquity" — is understood by al-Qurṭubī as referring particularly to divination and more broadly to every violation on the list. *Fisq* is from f-s-q, the splitting of a date's skin as it emerges: to commit *fisq* is to break out of the boundary of obedience.

The modern analogues are not hard to find. Horoscopes, fortune-telling, and every method of "asking the arrows" — attempting to bind one's decisions to a hidden fate read from signs — remain widespread, and the Qur'an classes them not as harmless entertainment but as *fisq*. The believer's alternative, taught by the Prophet ﷺ, is *istikhārah*: the prayer that asks God directly for guidance and then acts, trusting the outcome (al-Bukhārī 1162).

**"This Day the Disbelievers Have Despaired of Your Religion"**

The verse now shifts register entirely: *al-yawma yaʾisa alladhīna kafarū min dīnikum fa-lā takhshawhum wa-khshawn* — "This day those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them; fear Me." The "day" is the Day of ʿArafah; the "despair" is the loss of all hope among the pagans that Islam could be defeated or that the Muslims could be made to abandon their faith. Al-Ṭabarī explains that, with Makkah conquered, the idols destroyed, and the whole Arabian peninsula entering Islam, the disbelievers had given up the project of extinguishing the religion. Ibn Kathīr connects it to the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Satan has despaired of being worshipped in your peninsula, but he is satisfied with what is less than that: with your fighting among yourselves" (Muslim 2812). The enemy without had despaired; the danger now lay within.

"Fear them not, but fear Me" follows naturally. The same phrase appears in 2:150 and 3:175 and again in 5:44. Its logic is that fear is a finite resource that determines allegiance: whomever a person fears most, that one he obeys. When the fear of God dominates, the fear of people loses its power to bend conduct. This is not the abolition of prudence — Muslims still post guards and take precautions — but the removal of fear as the *governor* of decision. A society whose members fear God more than each other is a society in which honesty is possible even when it is dangerous.

**"This Day I Have Perfected for You Your Religion"**

*Al-yawma akmaltu lakum dīnakum wa-atmamtu ʿalaykum niʿmatī wa-raḍītu lakum al-Islāma dīnan* — "This day I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favor upon you, and have approved for you Submission as religion." Three verbs: *akmaltu* (from k-m-l, to be complete, lacking nothing), *atmamtu* (from t-m-m, to bring to fullness, to finish), *raḍītu* (from r-ḍ-y, to be pleased with, to approve). Al-Rāghib noted a subtle difference between the first two: a thing is *kāmil* when it possesses all its parts, and *tāmm* when it has reached its intended end. The religion is thus declared complete in its components and finished in its purpose.

What is the "perfection"? The commentators offer readings that complement rather than exclude each other. First, the completion of the legal revelation: the great obligations — prayer, fasting, alms, pilgrimage — had all been legislated, the pilgrimage last of all, and its rites had just been performed by the Prophet ﷺ himself in the sight of the community. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭūsī, and al-Zamakhsharī record the view that no further ruling of the *ḥalāl* and *ḥarām* was revealed after this day, though al-Qurṭubī notes that some verses (such as 2:281 and the verse of inheritance in 4:176) may have followed. Second, the completion of the religion's *external* victory: idolatry had been driven from the House, and Muslims performed their pilgrimage with no polytheist among them for the first time. Third, and most profoundly, the completion of the *religion as a religion*: the way of life that began with the first word revealed in the cave of Ḥirāʾ had now reached the form in which it would remain until the end of time.

The historical scene is preserved in the Ṣaḥīḥ. A Jew came to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and said:

> *"O Commander of the Faithful, there is a verse in your Book that you recite; had it been revealed to us Jews, we would have taken that day as a festival." ʿUmar asked, "Which verse?" He said, "This day I have perfected for you your religion..." ʿUmar said, "I know the day on which it was revealed and the place where it was revealed: it was revealed to the Messenger of God ﷺ at ʿArafah on a Friday."* (al-Bukhārī 45; Muslim 3017)

ʿUmar's reply is subtle. He did not say that Muslims should take the day as a festival; he said that they already knew it, and by implication that the day was already a festival — it fell on the Day of ʿArafah and on a Friday, both of which are festivals in Islam. The perfection of the religion did not need a new holiday; it was announced within the holidays it had itself established.

It is reported that when this verse was revealed, ʿUmar wept, and when the Prophet ﷺ asked him why, he answered: "Because we were in an increase of our religion; and if it has been perfected, nothing is perfect but that it afterward decreases." The Prophet ﷺ said, "You have spoken the truth." (Reported by Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī; its chain is weak, but the insight was widely accepted by the early community and Ibn Kathīr cites it.) ʿUmar had grasped that perfection is a summit, and after summits come descents; and the Prophet's ﷺ death followed within months. There is a lesson here for every believer: completeness is the moment at which vigilance, not celebration, becomes most necessary.

**The Question of Ghadīr Khumm**

The source commentary notes, and honesty requires mention, that some Twelver Shīʿī traditions place the revelation of this passage at Ghadīr Khumm, a watering-place between Makkah and Madinah, on the return from the Farewell Pilgrimage, where the Prophet ﷺ stood and said, "For whomever I am his *mawlā*, ʿAlī is his *mawlā*" — a saying recorded in Sunni collections as well (al-Tirmidhī 3713; Aḥmad; Ibn Mājah 121) and understood in Shīʿī thought as the designation of ʿAlī's spiritual authority, and hence as the "perfection" the verse announces (so al-Qummī and al-Ṭūsī). Sunni scholarship accepts the ḥadīth of Ghadīr as authentic in its wording — the Prophet ﷺ did say those words — but understands *mawlā* in its sense of "beloved friend and ally," in accord with the context (a dispute among some Companions concerning ʿAlī's conduct in Yemen), and follows the majority of the early reports placing this verse at ʿArafah eight or nine days earlier. The difference of interpretation is well known and is recorded here without polemic. What both communities share is the recognition that this verse marks a closure: the divine work of establishing the religion had reached its end.

**The Meaning of "Islām" Here**

*Raḍītu lakum al-Islāma dīnan* — "I have approved for you Islam as religion." Elsewhere, the Qur'an uses *islām* in its universal sense of submission to God, which was the religion of Abraham and all the prophets (2:131; 3:67). Here, the commentators note, it is also being used in its specific, confessional sense: the completed way of life revealed through Muhammad ﷺ, with its creed, law, and worship. Al-Ṭabarī records a report explaining *islām* in this verse as the full submission of the heart to God's Oneness — a level higher than the verbal profession, the true *islām* that includes *īmān* within it. The two senses converge: the universal religion of submission had now been given its final and complete form. God's "approval" (*riḍā*) of Islam is the counterpart to the human "acceptance" of it; and 3:85 warns what follows from the divine approval: "whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him."

**The Concession for the Starving**

The verse ends where it began, with food — but now with mercy: *fa-man uḍṭurra fī makhmaṣatin ghayra mutajānifin li-ithmin fa-inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — "But whoever is compelled by hunger, not inclining toward sin, then indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful." *Makhmaṣah* is from kh-m-ṣ, the hollowness of the empty belly — literally, the concavity of the abdomen in starvation. *Mutajānif* is from j-n-f, to lean or incline unjustly (the same root as in 2:182). The starving person who eats of the forbidden merely to survive, without exceeding need and without seeking an excuse for sin, incurs no blame. The jurists derived from this the principle *al-ḍarūrāt tubīḥ al-maḥẓūrāt* — "necessities render the prohibited permissible" — and its limit, *al-ḍarūrah tuqaddar bi-qadarihā*, "necessity is measured by its extent." One eats enough to preserve life, not to feast.

The placement of this concession immediately after the announcement of the religion's perfection is the verse's final lesson. The perfect religion is not the religion of maximum severity but the religion of exact proportion: firm where firmness protects, lenient where leniency preserves life. God names Himself *Ghafūr* and *Raḥīm* precisely at the point where a human legislator might be tempted to boast of his law's rigor. A religion that would let a man starve rather than eat carrion would not be perfect; it would be cruel. A religion that permitted carrion at every whim would not be perfect; it would be lax. The perfection lies in the law that forbids in the ordinary case and permits in the extraordinary one — and in the God who is severe in retribution (5:2) and, in the same breath, Forgiving and Merciful.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:4

> **They ask thee what is lawful unto them. Say, "Lawful unto you are all good things." And as for the hunting animals you have taught, teaching them from that which God has taught you, eat of what they catch for you, and mention the Name of God over it. And reverence God; truly God is swift in reckoning!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question Answered with a Principle**

After the long list of prohibitions in the previous verse, a natural question arose in the minds of the Companions: if so much is forbidden, what then is permitted? The verse records the question — *yasʾalūnaka mādhā uḥilla lahum*, "they ask you what has been made lawful for them" — and gives an answer that is not a list but a principle: *qul uḥilla lakum al-ṭayyibāt*, "Say: the good things have been made lawful for you." Al-Ṭabarī explains that the questioners, having heard the ten forbidden categories, wanted a corresponding enumeration of the lawful; God answered by naming a *category*, not a catalogue. This is a deliberate pedagogical choice. A list of the lawful would be endless and would leave anything unmentioned in doubt; a principle covers everything. Lawfulness is the default; wholesomeness is the criterion.

The occasion of revelation, preserved by al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, and Ibn Kathīr, adds a concrete dimension. ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and Zayd ibn al-Muhalhil (known as Zayd al-Khayl, "Zayd of the Horses") came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of God, we are a people who hunt with dogs and falcons, and the dogs of the family of Dhurayḥ catch cattle, wild asses, and gazelles; God has forbidden carrion, so what is lawful for us of this?" This verse came down in answer. Another report connects it to the incident in which the Prophet ﷺ ordered the killing of dogs in Madinah, after which the people asked what was lawful for them regarding the animals they had relied on. The verse thus answers both the general question — what may we eat? — and the specific one — may we still hunt with our trained animals?

**The Meaning of Ṭayyibāt: The Wholesome and the Pure**

*Ṭayyibāt* is the plural of *ṭayyib*, from the root ṭ-y-b, which carries the senses of goodness, pleasantness, purity, and wholesomeness. A *ṭayyib* thing is one that sound human nature finds pleasing and clean; the opposite is *khabīth*, foul or filthy. The Qur'an describes the Prophet's ﷺ mission in exactly these terms:

> *"He makes lawful for them the good things (al-ṭayyibāt) and forbids them the foul things (al-khabāʾith)."* (Qur'an 7:157)

Al-Shāfiʿī and his school made this verse the basis of a legal criterion: whatever the Arabs of sound disposition considered *ṭayyib* is lawful, and whatever they considered *khabīth* is unlawful, unless a text specifies otherwise. Other schools understood *ṭayyib* more directly as "that which God has not forbidden." Al-Qurṭubī notes that both readings converge in practice, since God forbids nothing wholesome and permits nothing foul. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said simply: "The *ṭayyibāt* are the lawful things." The verse thus rejoins the great Qur'anic theme that the human being is invited to enjoy the good of creation, not to flee from it:

> *"O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good."* (Qur'an 2:168)

> *"Eat of the good things We have provided you."* (Qur'an 2:57; 20:81)

The source commentary rightly draws attention to the history behind this permission. The Children of Israel had been given "all food" as lawful before the Torah (3:93); certain foods were then forbidden them as a consequence of their wrongdoing (4:160; 6:146). Jesus came "to make lawful for you part of what was forbidden you" (3:50), partially lifting the burden. And Muhammad ﷺ came to complete that lifting, removing "their burden and the shackles that were upon them" (7:157). The permission of the *ṭayyibāt* in al-Māʾidah is therefore the culmination of a long movement in sacred history from restriction back to the original generosity of God. Correspondingly, those who forbid what God has permitted — whether the pagan Arabs with their *baḥīrah* and *sāʾibah* (5:103) or later ascetics who deem lawful pleasures sinful (5:87) — are reversing the direction of revelation.

**Hunting Animals and the Dignity of Teaching**

The verse then turns to a specific case: *wa-mā ʿallamtum min al-jawāriḥ mukallibīn tuʿallimūnahunna mimmā ʿallamakum Allāh* — "and what you have taught of the hunting creatures, training them, teaching them from what God has taught you." *Jawāriḥ* is the plural of *jāriḥah*, from j-r-ḥ, to wound or to earn; a hunting animal is a "wounder" or an "earner" (the same root gives the verb in 6:60, "He knows what you have earned by day"). The term covers dogs, cheetahs, falcons, hawks, and any other animal that can be trained to hunt. *Mukallibīn* is from *kalb*, dog, and denotes those who train hunting dogs — though the commentators extend it to trainers of all such animals.

The phrase *tuʿallimūnahunna mimmā ʿallamakum Allāh*, "teaching them from what God has taught you," is remarkable. The human capacity to train an animal is itself a gift of divine teaching. The knowledge by which a falconer disciplines a bird or a huntsman conditions a dog is a share in the knowledge God gave Adam when "He taught Adam the names, all of them" (2:31). Al-Rāzī observes that the verse thereby dignifies human craft: even the humble skill of animal training is traced back to God as its ultimate source. This has a humbling and elevating effect at once. Humbling, because no skill is self-generated; elevating, because every skill is a kind of stewardship.

What does the training consist of? Al-Ṭabarī and al-Jalālayn explain that a trained animal is one that goes when sent, stops when called back, and — above all — does not eat from the prey it catches. The last condition is decisive, because it shows the animal caught the prey *for its master*, not for itself. The Prophet ﷺ taught ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim:

> *"When you send your trained dog and mention God's Name over it, then eat of what it catches for you. But if it has eaten from it, do not eat, for I fear it caught it only for itself. And if you find another dog with yours, do not eat, for you mentioned the Name over your dog and not over the other."* (al-Bukhārī 5483; Muslim 1929)

The ḥadīth clarifies every clause of the verse. "Eat of what they catch *for you*" (*mimmā amsakna ʿalaykum*) excludes what the animal catches for itself; "mention God's Name over it" refers to the invocation at the moment of release; and the presence of an untrained or unknown animal disqualifies the catch, because the deliberate, invoked act of hunting has been compromised. Most jurists hold that a bird of prey, unlike a dog, may eat from the catch without disqualifying it, since birds are trained by hunger and cannot be conditioned in the same way — a ruling attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās. Others apply the same rule to all hunting animals. The source commentary adds a further nuance from al-Ṭabarī: if the hunter reaches the prey while it is still alive, he may slaughter it properly under the exception of 5:3, regardless of what the animal has done.

**Why the Verse Matters for the Status of Dogs**

This verse has a quiet importance in Islamic law regarding dogs. The Prophet ﷺ discouraged keeping dogs without need, saying that whoever keeps a dog other than for hunting, herding, or guarding crops loses a portion of his reward each day (al-Bukhārī 5480; Muslim 1574). Yet this very verse explicitly permits the trained hunting dog and treats its catch as lawful food — even though the dog's mouth has touched the prey. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Wāḥidī note that this establishes that the utility of the animal overrides the ordinary caution regarding its impurity, and the jurists extended the principle to dogs used for guarding and other legitimate services. The Mālikī school, in particular, took this verse as evidence that the dog is not intrinsically impure. What the verse teaches, beyond its legal detail, is that the Law is not squeamish for its own sake: the criterion is benefit and cleanliness, not aversion.

**"Mention the Name of God Over It"**

*Wa-dhkurū isma Allāhi ʿalayhi* — "and mention the Name of God over it." The pronoun "it" refers, according to most commentators, to the act of releasing the hunting animal; according to others, to the prey itself when it is reached alive. In either case, the invocation is what turns predation into lawful provision. Without it, the hunt is merely one animal killing another; with it, the human act is consecrated and the life taken is taken under God's permission. The Qur'an is emphatic on this point elsewhere:

> *"And do not eat of that over which the Name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is iniquity."* (Qur'an 6:121)

The psychological effect is considerable. A person who cannot take a life — even the life of a hare — without first pronouncing God's Name is a person who has been trained to remember that life is not his to take by right. The habit reaches beyond hunting. The *bismillāh* before eating, before entering the house, before beginning any task, all derive from the same root discipline: nothing begins without acknowledging its Source.

**"God Is Swift in Reckoning"**

The verse closes: *wa-ttaqū Allāha inna Allāha sarīʿ al-ḥisāb* — "and reverence God; indeed, God is swift in reckoning." The connection to what precedes may seem abrupt, but it is exact. The hunter is alone in the wilderness with his dog and his prey; no one will see whether he mentioned God's Name, whether the dog ate from the catch, whether another dog was involved. Such rulings can be observed only by a person who fears God when no one watches. The reminder of swift reckoning is thus placed precisely where private conscience is the only enforcement. *Sarīʿ al-ḥisāb* also carries a note of hope: the reckoning of the one who observed these rules in secret will be equally swift, and his hidden fidelity will not be forgotten.

**A Lesson About the Shape of the Law**

Verse 4 completes a small trilogy with verses 1 and 3. Verse 1 establishes permission as the default; verse 3 lists the exceptions; verse 4 states the governing principle — the *ṭayyibāt* — and shows that the Law extends its logic even into the field, where a man, a dog, and a gazelle meet. The picture that emerges is of a religion that permits generously, forbids precisely, and consecrates the ordinary. A hunter who lets slip his dog with God's Name on his lips is performing an act of worship. That is what it means to say the religion has been perfected: not that pleasure has been abolished, but that pleasure has been placed within remembrance.
