## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:5

> **This day, all good things are made lawful unto you. The food of those who have been given the Book is lawful unto you, and your food is lawful unto them. And likewise the chaste women of the believers, and the chaste women of those who were given the Book before you, when you have given them their bridewealth as married women, not as fornicators, nor as paramours. And whosoever rejects belief, his deeds have come to naught, and in the Hereafter he shall be among the losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"This Day" — The Third Announcement**

For the third time in three verses, the word *al-yawm*, "this day," opens a sentence. In 5:3 it marked the despair of the disbelievers and the perfection of the religion; here it marks the opening of a social door: *al-yawma uḥilla lakum al-ṭayyibāt* — "This day the good things have been made lawful for you." The repetition binds the three statements together. The religion is complete; the enemies have despaired; and now, from a position of security rather than fear, the community is told how far it may open itself to those who follow other scriptures. Al-Qurṭubī notes the view that "this day" refers not to a single calendar date but to the era of Islam as such — the age in which these permissions are permanently in force. Either way, the tone is one of confident generosity. A frightened minority builds walls; an established community can afford bridges, and this verse builds two of them: the shared table and the shared household.

**The Food of the People of the Book**

*Wa-ṭaʿāmu alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba ḥillun lakum wa-ṭaʿāmukum ḥillun lahum* — "and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them." The word *ṭaʿām* means food generally, but the overwhelming majority of commentators — following Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and others cited by al-Ṭabarī — understand it here to mean specifically the animals slaughtered by Jews and Christians. The reason is contextual: grains, fruits, and vegetables do not become lawful or unlawful by who handles them, so a special permission would be meaningless for them. The permission is meaningful only for meat, which depends on the manner and intention of slaughter. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Their food means their slaughtered animals." The source commentary notes that the early Shīʿī tradition (al-Qummī, al-Ṭūsī) restricted the term to foods not requiring slaughter; the Sunni schools take the broader view.

The significance of this permission is best seen against the preceding verses. Verse 3 had forbidden everything dedicated to other than God and everything slaughtered on pagan altars. A reader might have concluded that Muslims could eat only meat slaughtered by Muslims. This verse draws a sharp line between the idolaters and the People of the Book: the latter, whatever their theological errors, are heirs of a revealed law of slaughter that invokes the One God. Their animals are therefore lawful, as the Prophet ﷺ demonstrated when he accepted the roasted sheep offered him by a Jewish woman at Khaybar (al-Bukhārī 2617) and ate from the food of the Jews of Madinah on more than one occasion.

A qualification was discussed among the Companions. Al-Qurṭubī records that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and ʿĀʾishah held that if one actually hears a Jew or Christian invoke a name other than God's at the moment of slaughter — "in the name of the Messiah," for instance — the meat should not be eaten, on the strength of 6:121. Others, including al-Shaʿbī and ʿAṭāʾ, permitted it regardless, reasoning that God permitted their food while fully knowing what they say. Al-Ṭabarī even records the permission of meat presented to churches. The mainstream position, held by the four Sunni schools, is that the slaughter of the People of the Book is lawful unless it is positively known that a name other than God's was invoked over it. This nuanced position matters today, when Muslims in many countries buy meat from producers of Jewish or Christian background, and the classical debate provides the framework within which contemporary scholars reason about it.

**Reciprocity: "Your Food Is Lawful for Them"**

The verse states the permission in both directions. Muslims may eat the food of the People of the Book, and the People of the Book may eat the food of Muslims. This second clause is not a ruling that binds Jews and Christians — they follow their own law — but it functions as a statement of Islam's openness and of the equality of the table. Muslims are told they may feed their Jewish and Christian neighbors and eat with them. The shared meal is, in every human culture, the most basic act of peace. By making the table common, the verse makes coexistence possible at the level where it actually happens: in kitchens, at weddings, in the hospitality offered to a traveler. Al-Rāzī notes that this reciprocity is the social meaning of the verse's placement after the food laws: the boundaries of *ḥalāl* and *ḥarām* are firm, yet they do not wall the believer off from human fellowship.

**Marriage Across the Line of Scripture**

*Wa-l-muḥṣanātu min al-muʾmināti wa-l-muḥṣanātu min alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba min qablikum* — "and the chaste women of the believers, and the chaste women of those who were given the Book before you." Having permitted the shared table, the verse permits the shared household. Muslim men may marry Jewish and Christian women. The Qur'an had already forbidden marriage with idolaters (2:221: "do not marry the polytheist women until they believe") and, in 60:10, with disbelieving women generally; this verse carves out the People of the Book as an exception, exactly as it did for their food. The parallel is structural: the same communities whose slaughter is accepted are the communities whose women may be married, because both permissions rest on the same ground — a shared belief in the One God and a shared inheritance of revealed law.

The word *muḥṣanāt* is from ḥ-ṣ-n, which means to fortify or protect (a *ḥiṣn* is a fortress). A woman is *muḥṣanah* when she is fortified — by chastity, by marriage, or by free status. Al-Ṭabarī records all three readings. The dominant interpretation takes it as "chaste," meaning women who guard themselves from unlawful relations. He adds a humane point from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: chastity refers to the woman's present state, not her past; a woman who has repented of earlier misconduct is fully *muḥṣanah*, and her past is not to be raised against her when marriage is proposed. Others, as the source notes, understood *muḥṣanāt* as "free women," reasoning that the Qur'an permits marriage to *believing* bondwomen (4:25) but not to bondwomen of the People of the Book. Whichever reading is adopted, the verse's core permission — marriage with chaste Jewish and Christian women — is agreed upon by the Sunni schools, with the Companions ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥah, Ḥudhayfah, and others reported to have married Christian or Jewish women.

**The Conditions: Dower, Marriage, Not Fornication or Secret Liaison**

The permission is fenced by three conditions: *idhā ātaytumūhunna ujūrahunna muḥṣinīna ghayra musāfiḥīna wa-lā muttakhidhī akhdān* — "when you have given them their dowers, taking them in marriage, not as fornicators nor as takers of secret lovers." The *ujūr* (literally "wages," here dowers) must be paid; the man must intend *iḥṣān* — a chaste, protective union; he must not be a *musāfiḥ* (from s-f-ḥ, to pour out — one who pours out desire indiscriminately, an open fornicator); and he must not take an *akhdān* (plural of *khidn*, a secret companion or lover). The pre-Islamic Arabs distinguished between open fornication, which they considered shameful, and the keeping of a discreet lover, which many tolerated. The Qur'an closes both doors. The same triad of conditions appears in 4:24–25 regarding marriage generally, and its repetition here makes an important point: marriage to a woman of another faith is subject to exactly the same standards of dignity as marriage to a Muslim woman. She is entitled to a dower, to a public contract, to the full status of a wife.

This is worth pausing on. The verse does not permit a lesser union with women of other faiths. It permits *marriage*, with all its rights, and it forbids the exploitative alternatives that a powerful community might have been tempted to impose on the women of a minority. The believing man's conduct toward his Christian or Jewish wife is to be governed by the same *iḥṣān* — the same protective chastity — that governs any marriage.

**Why the Permission Runs One Way**

The verse addresses men marrying women of the People of the Book; it does not permit Muslim women to marry Jewish or Christian men. The commentators explain this on the basis of 2:221 ("do not give in marriage to the polytheists until they believe") and 60:10 ("they are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them"), which remain in force for all non-Muslim men. The reasoning offered by the jurists is that a Muslim husband is bound by his own faith to honor the prophets and scriptures of his wife — he believes in Moses and Jesus and the original Torah and Gospel — so her religion is respected in the home. A Jewish or Christian husband does not, by his own faith, recognize the Prophet of his Muslim wife, so the symmetry of respect is absent. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr record this reasoning, and the ruling is a matter of consensus among the classical schools.

**Who Are "Those Given the Book"?**

The phrase applies, by agreement, to Jews and Christians. Whether it extends further was debated. The Zoroastrians (Majūs) were given the legal status of a protected community — the Prophet ﷺ said, "Treat them according to the practice of the People of the Book" (Mālik, *Muwaṭṭaʾ*) — but most jurists did not extend the permissions of food and marriage to them, reading the Prophet's ﷺ instruction as limited to the *jizyah* and protection. The source commentary notes that a minority of scholars adopted a broader definition. The mainstream ruling remains that this verse's permissions apply to Jews and Christians specifically. Most commentators also held that the permission applies to all Jews and Christians, not only to those who observe their religion strictly, though Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have excluded those who had become Christian after the coming of Islam among the Arab tribes.

**The Wisdom of the Permission and Its Prudent Limits**

Why does the Qur'an permit this? Al-Rāzī suggests that the permission serves several ends. It establishes that the People of the Book, though in error on crucial points, stand in a different category from idolaters: their revelation is real, their God is the One God, and marriage with them is not the union of light and darkness that marriage with an idolater would be. It opens a channel through which the Christian or Jewish wife may come to know Islam intimately, in a household of respect — many of the Companions' wives from the People of the Book did embrace Islam. And it knits the communities together at the level of kinship, making enmity harder and understanding easier.

At the same time, the early authorities were not naive. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, hearing that Ḥudhayfah had married a Jewish woman, wrote to him to release her — not because it was unlawful, Ḥudhayfah replied, but, as ʿUmar explained, "I fear that you will marry the prostitutes among them," and that Muslim women would be neglected (al-Ṭabarī; al-Bayhaqī). The permission is thus a permission, not a recommendation. Where the faith of the children is at risk, or where the marriage would leave Muslim women without husbands, the jurists counseled restraint — the source notes the Twelver Shīʿī tradition's general discouragement of such marriages except in necessity. The ruling stands; wisdom governs its use.

**"Whosoever Rejects Belief, His Deeds Have Come to Naught"**

The verse ends with a warning that seems, at first, to break the thread: *wa-man yakfur bi-l-īmāni fa-qad ḥabiṭa ʿamaluhu wa-huwa fī al-ākhirati min al-khāsirīn* — "and whoever disbelieves in faith, his work has come to nothing, and in the Hereafter he is among the losers." The verb *ḥabiṭa* is used of an animal whose belly swells from overeating until it dies — a vivid image of deeds that appear substantial but are hollow and fatal. The commentators offer two connections. First, having opened doors to the People of the Book, God reminds the Muslim that intimacy with them must not lead him to abandon or dilute his own faith: eat with them, marry among them, but do not lose what makes you a believer. Second, and more broadly, the clause reaffirms the Qur'anic principle that deeds without faith have no weight in the Hereafter:

> *"And whoever disbelieves — his work has become worthless, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers."* (Qur'an 39:65, cf. 2:217; 18:105)

Al-Ṭabarī understands "disbelieves in faith" as rejecting what faith requires — God, His messengers, and His Book. The placement of this warning at the close of a verse about interfaith food and marriage is, therefore, a piece of moral realism. Social openness is permitted; theological indifference is not. The Muslim may share a Christian's table and home, and still hold that the way to salvation is faith in God and His final Messenger.

**The Verse in Today's World**

Few verses of the Qur'an speak so directly to contemporary life. Muslims in plural societies eat daily at tables prepared by people of other faiths, form friendships and marriages across religious lines, and must find a way to be both open and rooted. This verse gives the template. It sets the boundary of *ṭayyibāt* — the wholesome — as the standard for food, and makes the slaughter of Jews and Christians lawful within it. It permits marriage with the chaste women of the People of the Book on terms of full dignity. And it closes with the reminder that none of this openness excuses the loss of faith itself. The picture is neither isolation nor dissolution but principled participation: a believer who can break bread with anyone, and who never forgets Whose Name he pronounces before he eats.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:6

> **O you who believe! When you rise to perform the prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and wipe your heads and your feet up to the ankles. If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, then purify yourselves. But if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you has come from satisfying a call of nature, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then resort to clean earth, and wipe therewith your faces and your hands. God desires not to place a burden upon you, but He desires to purify you, and to complete His Blessing upon you, that haply you may give thanks.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse of Ablution and Its Place in the Sūrah**

This is the Qur'an's most complete statement on ritual purification, and it is called by the jurists *āyat al-wuḍūʾ*, "the verse of ablution." Its placement is meaningful. The sūrah has moved from covenants (v. 1) to the sanctities of pilgrimage (v. 2) to food (vv. 3–5); it now turns to the body itself and how it is prepared to stand before God. The logic is cumulative: what a person promises, what he eats, and how he cleanses himself all belong to one integrated life of submission. The verse also deliberately echoes verse 3 in its closing phrase — "to complete His blessing upon you" — signaling that the discipline of purification is not a burden imposed on the community but a component of the perfected favor announced on the Day of ʿArafah.

The occasion of revelation is preserved in the Ṣaḥīḥ. ʿĀʾishah's necklace was lost on a journey, the Prophet ﷺ halted the caravan to search for it in a place with no water, and the people complained to Abū Bakr, who rebuked his daughter. Then the verse of *tayammum* was revealed. Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr said to her: "May God reward you with good, O family of Abū Bakr! By God, no matter befalls you but that God makes for you a way out of it and places in it a blessing for the Muslims" (al-Bukhārī 334; Muslim 367). Some scholars identify that revelation with 4:43 and this verse with a later restatement; others hold this verse itself was the one revealed on that occasion. Either way, the human circumstance is telling: a small inconvenience — a lost necklace — became the door through which a permanent mercy entered the Law.

**"When You Rise to Prayer": The Grammar of Obligation**

*Idhā qumtum ilā al-ṣalāti fa-ghsilū* — "when you rise to the prayer, wash." Taken literally, this would require a fresh ablution before every prayer regardless of one's state. The commentators resolve the matter in several ways. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī record that this was indeed the original practice, later relaxed: Buraydah reported that on the day of the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ prayed all the prayers with a single ablution and wiped over his leather socks, and when ʿUmar remarked that he had done something he had never done before, he replied, "I did it deliberately, O ʿUmar" (Muslim 277). Others understand the verse to carry an implicit condition — "when you rise to prayer *being in a state of minor impurity*" — as Ibn ʿAbbās and most jurists held, so that the verse states the general rule and the Sunnah clarifies its application. The Prophet's ﷺ words settle the practical question: "God does not accept the prayer of one who has broken his ablution until he performs ablution" (al-Bukhārī 135; Muslim 225). Renewing ablution for each prayer while already pure remains a recommended act — the Prophet ﷺ often did so — but it is not required.

**The Four Limbs and Their Meaning**

The verse names four obligatory acts: washing the face; washing the hands (which in Arabic usage includes the forearms) to the elbows; wiping the head; and the feet to the ankles. Each has been examined by the jurists in exhaustive detail, and the Sunnah supplies the additional acts — rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nostrils, wiping the ears, beginning with the right side, washing three times — that the Prophet ﷺ practiced. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān once called for water and performed the ablution in front of the people exactly as he had seen the Prophet ﷺ do it, and then said: "Whoever performs ablution like this ablution of mine, then prays two units without letting his mind wander in them, his past sins are forgiven" (al-Bukhārī 159; Muslim 226).

The word *ilā*, "to," in "to the elbows" and "to the ankles" was understood by the majority as *inclusive*: the elbows and ankles themselves are washed, since the Prophet ﷺ was seen washing them and going beyond them. Abū Hurayrah would wash up to his upper arms and shins, saying that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ say that the believers would be recognized on the Day of Resurrection by the radiance (*ghurrah* and *taḥjīl*, the white markings of a horse's forehead and legs) left by ablution, "so whoever of you can extend his radiance, let him do so" (al-Bukhārī 136; Muslim 246).

**Wash or Wipe the Feet? A Question of Grammar and Sunnah**

The verse presents a well-known grammatical question. In the standard reading, *arjulakum* ("your feet") carries the accusative ending, which links it back to the distant verb "wash" and makes the feet an object of washing, along with the face and hands. In the variant reading transmitted from some Companions, *arjulikum* is in the genitive, which would attach it to the nearer verb "wipe" and make the feet an object of wiping, like the head. Ibn ʿAbbās and a few early figures are reported to have favored wiping, and the Twelver Shīʿī school adopted it; the source commentary records the report from Anas ibn Mālik that "the Qur'an came down with wiping, but the Sunnah is washing."

The four Sunni schools require washing, and the evidence they cite is overwhelming and vivid. The Prophet ﷺ saw people performing ablution hurriedly, leaving their heels dry, and called out at the top of his voice:

> *"Woe to the heels from the Fire! Perform the ablution thoroughly."* (al-Bukhārī 165; Muslim 241)

Had wiping sufficed, a dry heel would have been no fault. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī reconcile the readings by explaining that the genitive can be a case of grammatical attraction to the neighboring word (a known Arabic phenomenon), or that "wiping" the feet here means a light washing, as the Arabs sometimes used the word *masaḥa* for washing sparingly. Ibn Kathīr surveys the evidence and concludes that the Companions' unanimous practice of washing settles the matter. The variant that survives universally is the wiping *over leather socks* (*khuffayn*), a concession the Prophet ﷺ practiced and which more than seventy Companions transmitted; it is not a reading of the verse but a Sunnah rule for the traveler and the cold season.

**Ghusl: The Full Purification**

*Wa-in kuntum junuban fa-ṭṭahharū* — "and if you are in a state of *janābah*, then purify yourselves." *Janābah* is from j-n-b, "side" or "distance": the person in this state is at a remove from prayer and from the recitation of the Qur'an until he bathes. It results from sexual intercourse or seminal emission, and by extension the jurists include the end of menstruation and postnatal bleeding among the causes of obligatory *ghusl*. The command *iṭṭahharū* (from ṭ-h-r, purity) is comprehensive: the whole body is washed. The Prophet's ﷺ method, described by ʿĀʾishah and Maymūnah, was to wash the hands, perform ablution, pour water over the head three times, and then over the entire body (al-Bukhārī 248; Muslim 316). The verse's brevity here — "purify yourselves" — contrasts with the detail of the *wuḍūʾ*, because full washing needs less specification than partial.

**Tayammum: When the Earth Substitutes for Water**

The verse then legislates the third form of purification, for four situations: illness (*marḍā*), journey (*safar*), returning from relieving oneself (*jāʾa aḥadun minkum min al-ghāʾiṭ* — *ghāʾiṭ* being literally a low place in the ground where one would go for privacy), and having "touched women" (*lāmastum al-nisāʾ*). The last phrase was debated: Ibn ʿAbbās understood *lāmastum* as a euphemism for intercourse, while Ibn Masʿūd and ʿUmar understood it literally as touching, and the schools of law divide accordingly on whether skin contact breaks ablution. In all these cases the condition is *fa-lam tajidū māʾan* — "and you do not find water" — whether because none exists or because using it would harm the sick person.

Then: *fa-tayammamū ṣaʿīdan ṭayyiban fa-msaḥū bi-wujūhikum wa-aydīkum minhu* — "then aim for clean earth and wipe your faces and hands from it." *Tayammum* is from a root meaning to intend, to aim at; the worshipper *turns toward* the earth as a substitute. *Ṣaʿīd* is the surface of the earth — soil, sand, or rock — and *ṭayyib* here means pure. The Prophet ﷺ demonstrated the method to ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, who had rolled in the dust thinking that full *janābah* required a full covering: "It would have sufficed you to do this," and he struck the earth once with his palms, blew on them, and wiped his face and the backs of his hands (al-Bukhārī 338; Muslim 368). This is among the distinctive gifts to this community; the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"I have been given five things that no prophet before me was given ... the earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification, so wherever a man of my community is when the time of prayer comes, let him pray."* (al-Bukhārī 335; Muslim 521)

**Why Earth? The Logic of the Substitute**

The choice of earth as substitute for water is not arbitrary. Water cleanses physically; earth cannot. The purpose of *tayammum* is therefore not hygiene but the *ritual* preparation of the worshipper — the act of humbling oneself, of marking a transition from the ordinary to the sacred. The human being was created from earth (*"from it We created you"*, 20:55), and when he cannot reach water, he returns to his origin to prepare for the meeting with his Creator. Al-Rāzī notes that the substitution shows that the essential purpose of purification is the obedience and inward readiness it produces, not the removal of dirt as such; otherwise a dry, dusty hand could never replace a washed one. The symbolic register is clear: the believer places his face — the seat of his dignity — against the dust, and rises clean.

**"God Does Not Desire to Place a Burden Upon You"**

*Mā yurīdu Allāhu li-yajʿala ʿalaykum min ḥarajin wa-lākin yurīdu li-yuṭahhirakum wa-li-yutimma niʿmatahu ʿalaykum laʿallakum tashkurūn* — "God does not want to place upon you any hardship, but He wants to purify you and to complete His favor upon you, that you may be grateful." *Ḥaraj* originally denotes a dense thicket of trees through which one cannot pass; it came to mean constriction, difficulty, and — in legal usage — undue burden. The Qur'an names the removal of *ḥaraj* as a principle of the whole religion:

> *"And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship."* (Qur'an 22:78)

The verse gives the reason for both the rule and its exception. The rule (washing) exists to purify; the exception (*tayammum*) exists because God does not want hardship. The Prophet ﷺ expressed the same balance: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult" (al-Bukhārī 69). The believer who reads this verse learns that the Law's intention is his benefit and that its strictness and its concessions come from the same source. Where a person is genuinely unable, God does not demand; where he is able, the demand is a purification, not a punishment.

**Ablution as Spiritual Cleansing**

The classical commentators, drawing on the Sunnah, insisted that ablution's purpose is not merely ritual. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"When a believing servant performs ablution and washes his face, every sin he looked at with his eyes leaves his face with the water — or with the last drop of water. When he washes his hands, every sin his hands committed leaves with the water — or with the last drop. When he washes his feet, every sin his feet walked toward leaves with the water — or with the last drop — until he emerges purified of sins."* (Muslim 244, from Abū Hurayrah)

And the famous saying: *"Purity is half of faith"* (Muslim 223). Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī, cited in the source, both transmit these reports in their exegesis of the verse. The connection between physical and spiritual cleanliness is not accidental. The person who washes the very limbs with which he sinned — eyes, hands, feet — is performing a bodily act of repentance five times a day. Modern psychology has noted the intimate link between physical washing and the sense of moral renewal; the Prophet ﷺ articulated it fourteen centuries earlier and made it a daily discipline.

**"That You May Be Grateful"**

The verse's final word is *tashkurūn*, gratitude. Al-Rāzī explains the sequence: God purifies the servant and completes His favor upon him so that he will be thankful. Gratitude is thus the intended result of the entire system of purification. This reorients the whole verse. The washing is not a tax the believer pays to be allowed to pray; it is a gift that prepares him for the greatest gift — standing before his Lord. A person who understands this does not experience ablution as an inconvenience but as the first act of the prayer itself, the moment when water on the face begins to wake the heart. The verse thus ends where all worship should: not in the mechanics of the ritual, but in the thankful recognition of the One who made both the water and the earth means of returning to Him.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:7

> **And remember God's Blessing upon you, and His covenant by which He bound you, when you said, "We hear and we obey." And reverence God. Truly God knows what lies within breasts.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Return to Covenant**

The sūrah began with the command "fulfill your pacts." After six verses of specific legislation — pilgrimage, food, marriage, purification — it now returns to that theme and names the greatest pact of all: *wa-dhkurū niʿmata Allāhi ʿalaykum wa-mīthāqahu alladhī wāthaqakum bihi* — "and remember God's favor upon you and His covenant by which He bound you." The structure of the sūrah is thus revealed as circular: the particular laws are set within the frame of a general covenant, and the believer is reminded that every ablution and every dietary choice is an act of keeping faith with a prior agreement. The verse is a hinge. It closes the opening cluster of legal verses and opens the next section (vv. 8–11), in which the community is prepared, by reminders of God's protection, for the long discussion of the covenant-breaking of earlier communities that begins in verse 12.

**The Meaning of Niʿmah and the Discipline of Remembering**

*Niʿmah* is favor, blessing, grace — from n-ʿ-m, the root of softness, ease, and enjoyment. The word appears in verses 3, 6, 7, and 11 of this sūrah, and the repetition is deliberate: God's favor is the recurring theme of the opening section. Al-Rāzī makes a penetrating observation, preserved in the source commentary: the command to "remember" does not imply that the blessing had been forgotten and must now be recalled; it is a command to keep the blessing *perpetually* in mind, lest the ease and success that the community was now enjoying should dull its awareness of where that success came from. This is a real psychological danger. Blessings, once habitual, become invisible. The person who has always had clean water does not think of it as a gift; the community that has always been secure forgets that it was once persecuted. The Qur'an counters this by commanding a discipline of active recollection. "Remember" (*udhkurū*) is in the imperative, a repeated duty, not a one-time act.

The blessing in question is comprehensive: guidance to Islam, the completion of the religion, victory over the idolaters, the unity of hearts that God created among former enemies (3:103: "remember God's favor upon you when you were enemies and He joined your hearts"), and the very fact of being addressed by revelation. Al-Ṭabarī understands it as God's favor in guiding them to the truth and honoring them with the religion of Islam.

**"His Covenant by Which He Bound You"**

*Mīthāq* is from w-th-q, to bind firmly, to trust; *wathīqah* is a binding document, and *mīthāq* is a solemn, binding covenant. The verb *wāthaqakum* — "He bound you," or "He made a binding covenant with you" — is in the intensive form, indicating a mutual and firm obligation. Which covenant is meant? The commentators offer three answers, and the source commentary helpfully surveys them.

The majority — al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī — understand it as the pledges of allegiance (*bayʿah*) made to the Prophet ﷺ: the pledges of ʿAqabah, when the Helpers of Madinah swore before the Hijrah to hear and obey, to protect the Prophet ﷺ as they protected their own families; the Pledge of Riḍwān under the tree at Ḥudaybiyah in the sixth year, when fourteen hundred Companions swore not to flee; and the individual pledges each believer made upon entering Islam. The Qur'an itself identifies such pledges as pledges to God:

> *"Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are pledging allegiance only to God. The Hand of God is over their hands."* (Qur'an 48:10)

And: *"Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God"* (4:80). Thus a covenant made with the Prophet ﷺ is God's covenant, and the phrase "His covenant" is exact.

A second view, associated with Mujāhid and cited by al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī, connects the covenant to the primordial testimony of all human souls before their earthly existence:

> *"And when your Lord took from the children of Adam — from their loins — their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes, we have testified.'"* (Qur'an 7:172)

Al-Rāzī objects that the present verse is addressed to the believers specifically ("O you who believe" governs the whole passage), not to all children of Adam, and al-Ṭabarī notes that verse 12 will contrast this covenant with the one God took from the Children of Israel — a contrast that only makes sense if the covenant here is the specific one made with the Muslim community. The third view, which reconciles the others, holds that the covenant is the general covenant of faith: by accepting Islam, every believer has agreed to hear and obey God in all He commands. The specific pledges are instances of this general agreement.

**"We Hear and We Obey": The Words of the Pledge**

*Idh qultum samiʿnā wa-aṭaʿnā* — "when you said, 'We hear and we obey.'" These were the actual words of the pledge. ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit described the Pledge of ʿAqabah: "We pledged to the Messenger of God ﷺ to hear and obey, in hardship and ease, in what we liked and disliked, and even when others were preferred over us; and not to dispute the authority of those in power; and to speak the truth wherever we were, fearing no one's blame in the cause of God" (al-Bukhārī 7199; Muslim 1709). The same two words close Sūrat al-Baqarah as the believers' response to revelation:

> *"The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and so have the believers ... and they say, 'We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the destination.'"* (Qur'an 2:285)

The phrase is set in deliberate contrast to the Israelites at Sinai, of whom the Qur'an says: *"they said, 'We hear and we disobey'"* (2:93; 4:46). The whole argument of the coming verses — that the Children of Israel broke their covenant and were cursed for it (5:12–13) — is prepared by this reminder that the Muslims made the opposite declaration. The reminder is therefore also a warning: you said "we obey"; do not become like those who said it and then did not.

There is a psychology in the order of the two verbs. Hearing comes before obeying, but only just — there is no gap for objection, delay, or negotiation. The pledge is not "we hear, and we will consider, and we will obey what we find reasonable." It is *samiʿnā wa-aṭaʿnā*. This is not a suppression of the intellect; the Qur'an constantly invites reflection. It is the posture of one who has already been convinced of the trustworthiness of the Speaker and who therefore does not need to re-litigate each command. A patient who trusts his physician does not demand a pharmacology lecture before taking each dose. Al-Rāzī observes that the readiness to obey, once the truth of the Messenger has been established, is the mark of sincere faith.

**"And Reverence God"**

*Wa-ttaqū Allāh* — "and be mindful of God." The command to *taqwā* follows the reminder of the covenant because the covenant is kept by *taqwā*. The root w-q-y means to guard or protect; *taqwā* is the guarding of oneself against what displeases God. A useful image is that of a person walking a narrow path with thorns on both sides, gathering his garments carefully so they are not torn — which is exactly how Ubayy ibn Kaʿb explained *taqwā* to ʿUmar. The person who has said "we obey" and who then guards himself against every breach of that obedience is a person of *taqwā*.

**"God Knows What Lies Within Breasts"**

The verse ends: *inna Allāha ʿalīmun bi-dhāti al-ṣudūr* — "indeed, God is Knowing of what is in the breasts." The phrase *dhāt al-ṣudūr* is literally "the possessor of the breasts" — an idiom for the secret contents of the heart, the intentions and inclinations that a person may hide even from himself. The source notes that this phrase recurs at least a dozen times in the Qur'an (3:119, 154; 8:43; 11:5; 29:10; 31:23; 35:38; 39:7; 42:24; 57:6; 64:4; 67:13). Its placement here is pointed. A covenant can be broken outwardly or inwardly; a person may say "we hear and we obey" with his tongue while his heart withholds consent. Al-Rāzī explains that the closing clause warns against precisely this hidden breach: God knows whether the pledge was sincere and whether it remains so.

This is the difference between a human contract and a divine one. A human counterparty can enforce only what he can observe; hence the need for witnesses, signatures, and courts. God's covenant is enforced at the level of the heart. This is both a warning and a comfort. A warning, because no inner reservation escapes His knowledge. A comfort, because the believer who struggles inwardly to remain faithful — who fights his own doubts and weaknesses to keep his word — is seen and credited for a struggle no human being witnesses.

**The Verse in the Life of a Believer**

Every Muslim renews this covenant in small ways daily. The testimony of faith is its verbal form; the prayer is its bodily form; obedience in the face of temptation is its practical form. The verse asks the believer to do three things: to remember that everything he has is *niʿmah*, favor, not entitlement; to remember that he has already said "we hear and we obey" and is bound by it; and to know that the quality of his fidelity is measured not by appearances but by what lies in the breast. A community that lives this way does not need constant external policing; its members are policed by the knowledge that the Party to their covenant sees into their hearts. That is why, in the verse that follows, the Qur'an can move directly to the most demanding social command — to be just even toward enemies — for only a community that has internalized its covenant can be asked to be fair to those who hate it.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:8

> **O you who believe! Be steadfast for God, bearing witness to justice, and let not hatred for a people lead you to be unjust. Be just; that is nearer to reverence. And reverence God. Surely God is Aware of whatsoever you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Justice as the Highest Form of Standing for God**

Verse 8 is one of the pillars of Qur'anic ethics, and its power lies in the way it joins two things that human beings tend to separate: devotion to God and fairness to people. *Kūnū qawwāmīna li-llāhi shuhadāʾa bi-l-qisṭ* — "Be ever-upright for God, witnesses in justice." The word *qawwām* is an intensive form of *qāʾim*, one who stands; a *qawwām* is one who stands constantly, firmly, and fully — who maintains and upholds. To be a *qawwām li-llāh* is to stand for God without wavering. But the verse immediately defines what standing for God means in practice: bearing witness to *qisṭ*, justice — equity, fair measure, giving each his due. *Qisṭ* is from a root connoting the just portion, the balanced share; a *qisṭās* (17:35) is a balance-scale. Al-Rāzī, cited in the source, explains that to stand for God is to bear witness to His Oneness and Lordship, and that the verse binds this witness inseparably to the witness of justice. One cannot testify to the truth of God while lying about the rights of men.

The Qur'an says almost the same thing in 4:135, but with the two phrases inverted: *"Be ever-upright in justice, witnesses for God."* The source rightly notes the significance of this inversion. In one verse, the believer stands for justice as a witness for God; in the other, he stands for God as a witness to justice. Read together, they say that these are not two acts but one act seen from two sides. Justice is what devotion to God looks like when it meets another human being; and devotion to God is what justice looks like when it is traced to its root. The Qur'an anchors this in God's own being:

> *"God bears witness that there is no god but He, as do the angels and the possessors of knowledge, upholding justice."* (Qur'an 3:18)

God Himself is described as *qāʾiman bi-l-qisṭ*, "upholding justice." To be a *qawwām* in justice is therefore to imitate, at the human level, a divine attribute.

**The Trigger: Hatred of a People**

The verse then names the force most likely to corrupt justice: *wa-lā yajrimannakum shanaʾānu qawmin ʿalā allā taʿdilū* — "and let not the hatred of a people drive you not to be just." The wording repeats verse 2 almost exactly, but with an important extension. In verse 2, the hatred was specified — "because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque" — and the forbidden act was *transgression* (*iʿtidāʾ*). Here the hatred is general — any people, for any reason — and the forbidden act is *injustice* (the failure of *ʿadl*). Verse 2 addressed a specific grievance; verse 8 lays down the universal law.

The Arabic is precise. *Yajrimannakum* uses the emphatic form (*nūn al-tawkīd*): "let it not, under any circumstances, drive you." *Shanaʾān* denotes intense hatred, not mild dislike. And the object of the hatred is *qawm*, a people — a collective. The verse thus addresses the most common form of injustice in human history: the injustice done not to an individual enemy but to a *group* toward which one's community has learned to feel hostility. Tribal hatred, national hatred, sectarian hatred, racial hatred — the verse forbids letting any of these move the hand of judgment.

What does injustice toward a hated people look like? Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī, cited in the source, give examples: killing the women and children of an enemy, breaking treaties with them, mutilating their dead, or exceeding the limits of retaliation. The context of the verse, revealed after the conquest of Makkah, is the community's relationship with those who had persecuted it for twenty years. Even toward *them*, the Qur'an says: be just.

**"Be Just; That Is Nearer to Reverence"**

*Iʿdilū huwa aqrabu li-l-taqwā* — "Be just; it is nearer to *taqwā*." The imperative *iʿdilū* is from ʿ-d-l, the root of balance and straightness; a thing is *ʿadl* when it is even, neither tilted nor crooked. The verse states that justice is *aqrab*, nearer, to *taqwā*. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the comparative here does not imply that injustice is somewhat near to *taqwā*; it is an Arabic idiom meaning that justice is the *closest* path to *taqwā*, or that justice toward one's enemies is even nearer to reverence than justice toward one's friends, because it costs more. The logic is compelling. It is easy to be fair to those we love; fairness there may be mere affection in disguise. It is only when we are fair to those we hate that we know our fairness comes from principle. The person who can judge justly between his own son and a stranger, or between his own tribe and a hostile one, has demonstrated *taqwā* — the guarding of oneself against the pull of one's own inclinations.

There is also a spiritual mechanics implied. Injustice, even against an enemy, damages the one who commits it. It coarsens the conscience, strengthens the ego, and teaches the soul that principles are negotiable when feelings run high. A person who indulges injustice toward his enemies will soon find it easier to be unjust toward his friends. Justice, conversely, disciplines the self; it trains a person to subordinate his feelings to what is right. That is why justice is "nearer to *taqwā*" — it is the very practice by which *taqwā* is built.

**The Prophetic Commentary**

The Prophet ﷺ modeled this verse in cases where the temptation to injustice was strongest. When a woman of the noble clan of Makhzūm stole and her people sought to have the punishment waived through the intercession of Usāmah ibn Zayd, the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Do you intercede concerning one of the punishments of God? ... Those before you were destroyed only because when a noble among them stole, they let him go, and when a weak one among them stole, they applied the punishment. By God, if Fāṭimah the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand."* (al-Bukhārī 3475; Muslim 1688)

He warned against injustice in absolute terms, transmitting from his Lord:

> *"O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and have made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another."* (Muslim 2577, ḥadīth qudsī)

And he taught that justice is required even toward those who commit injustice against us: *"Discharge the trust to him who entrusted you, and do not betray him who betrayed you"* (Abū Dāwūd 3535; al-Tirmidhī 1264; graded ḥasan). The commentators note the treaty of Ḥudaybiyah as a living example: the Prophet ﷺ upheld terms he considered unfavorable, returned Abū Jandal to the Quraysh though he had fled to the Muslims in chains, and did not break the treaty until the Quraysh themselves broke it.

**The Argument from the Lesser to the Greater**

Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī draw a conclusion that the source records and that deserves emphasis: if believers are forbidden injustice even toward disbelievers who hate them, how much more severely must God view injustice toward fellow believers, toward one's own family, employees, neighbors, and dependents? The verse establishes the *outer* boundary of justice — the enemy — precisely so that everything inside that boundary is covered by stronger implication. A person who has learned to be fair to those who wrong him will not struggle to be fair to those who do not.

**Why Justice Is the Foundation of Everything**

Ibn Taymiyyah observed, in a frequently quoted judgment, that "God upholds the just state even if it is unbelieving, and does not uphold the unjust state even if it is Muslim," and that "the world can endure with justice and unbelief, but cannot endure with injustice and Islam." Whatever one makes of the formulation, its point is exact: justice is not a decoration on a good society but the structural condition of any society at all. Where justice fails, trust fails; where trust fails, cooperation fails; where cooperation fails, the society dissolves. The Qur'an declares that the purpose of sending messengers with scriptures and the balance was "that people may uphold justice" (57:25). Verse 8 asks the believer to make that divine purpose his own.

**Justice in the Age of Grievance**

Few verses are more urgently needed today. Modern communication makes it easy to sort humanity into hated groups and to feel that any measure against them is justified by their crimes, real or imagined. Political discourse, ethnic conflict, sectarian strife, and even ordinary online argument run on precisely the mechanism the verse names: *shanaʾān* driving people away from *ʿadl*. The verse's demand is severe: no grievance, however real, licenses unfairness. The believer must report accurately about those he opposes, must not attribute to them what they did not do, must not deny them rights because of what their group did, must judge each case on its merits. This is hard. It is meant to be hard. But it is *aqrab li-l-taqwā* — the nearest road to the reverence that the whole sūrah commands.

**"God Is Aware of What You Do"**

The verse closes: *wa-ttaqū Allāha inna Allāha khabīrun bi-mā taʿmalūn* — "and be mindful of God; indeed God is Aware of what you do." *Khabīr* denotes knowledge of the inner reality of things — the One who knows not only the act but the motive within it. The person who tilts his judgment out of hatred may conceal the tilt from every human observer; he cannot conceal it from God. And the person who forces himself to be fair to one he hates, at a cost no one else sees, is seen by God. The verse thus ends with the assurance that justice is never wasted, even when it goes unrewarded in this world. As the source notes, the closing clause serves as both promise and warning, and the two verses that follow will spell out each: forgiveness and great reward for the just and believing (v. 9), and Hellfire for those who deny (v. 10).

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:9

> **To those who believe and perform righteous deeds, God has promised forgiveness and a great reward.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Promise Following a Command**

After the demanding ethical injunction of verse 8 — to stand for justice even against those one hates — the Qur'an immediately provides the motive that makes such difficulty bearable: *waʿada Allāhu alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti lahum maghfiratun wa-ajrun ʿaẓīm* — "God has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is forgiveness and a great reward." Al-Rāzī, as the source records, explains that the closing phrase of verse 8, "God is aware of what you do," functions simultaneously as a promise to the obedient and a threat to the disobedient; verses 9 and 10 now unfold each side in turn. Verse 9 is the promise. The sequence is pedagogically wise. Human beings are not moved by commands alone; they need to know that obedience leads somewhere. The Qur'an never asks for justice, patience, or sacrifice without also showing the destination.

**The Weight of the Verb "Promised"**

The verse opens with *waʿada*, "He promised." In Arabic usage, *waʿd* is generally a promise of good (as distinct from *waʿīd*, a threat of evil), and the Qur'an is emphatic that God's promise is inviolable:

> *"The promise of God — God does not fail in His promise, but most people do not know."* (Qur'an 30:6)

> *"Indeed, God does not break His promise."* (Qur'an 3:9)

Theologically, this establishes a crucial point. God is under no obligation to reward anyone; the creature has no claim on the Creator. Yet God has *bound Himself* by promise, and His promise, unlike a human one, is backed by perfect knowledge, perfect power, and perfect truthfulness. A human promise can fail because the promiser forgets, becomes unable, or changes his mind. None of these applies to God. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the believer's certainty about the Hereafter rests entirely on this: not on his own merit, but on the reliability of the Promiser. The verse thus offers an assurance that is stronger than any human guarantee ever given.

**The Two Conditions: Faith and Righteous Action**

The promise is made to *alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — "those who believe and do righteous deeds." This pairing occurs more than fifty times in the Qur'an, and its consistency is instructive. Faith without deeds is a claim without evidence; deeds without faith are a body without a soul (the previous verse's warning, in 5:5, was precisely that the deeds of the one who rejects faith "come to naught"). *Ṣāliḥāt* is the plural of *ṣāliḥah*, from ṣ-l-ḥ, the root of soundness, wholeness, and setting right; a righteous deed is one that is sound in itself and that sets things right in the world. Its opposite is *fasād*, corruption, which the sūrah will condemn severely in verses 32–33. Al-Ṭabarī explains that righteous deeds here are those God has commanded and made obligatory, and that the verse promises their doers forgiveness of their past sins.

In the immediate context, the righteous deed the verse has in view is justice — the standing for God and bearing witness in equity commanded in verse 8. The promise thus says: the one who forces himself to be fair to those he hates, who keeps his covenant when breaking it would profit him, who does not let grievance corrupt his judgment — that person has done a *ṣāliḥah*, and God has promised him forgiveness and great reward.

**Forgiveness Before Reward**

The order of the two gifts is significant: *maghfirah* comes first, then *ajr ʿaẓīm*. *Maghfirah* is from gh-f-r, to cover, to shield (a *mighfar* is a helmet, covering the head from harm); God's forgiveness *covers* the servant's sins so that they neither expose him to shame nor to punishment. Why does forgiveness precede reward? Because no human being, however righteous, arrives at the Hereafter without sins to be covered. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said, "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said, "Not even I, unless God envelops me in His mercy."* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816)

Forgiveness is therefore the necessary first gift: it clears away the obstacle. Only then does reward follow. Al-Rāzī notes that this order teaches humility: the righteous person does not approach God claiming payment, but hoping for pardon, and then receiving, beyond pardon, a reward he did not earn. The source commentary points to 4:31 and 25:70 as parallels where forgiveness is promised to those of fundamental righteousness.

**"A Great Reward"**

*Ajr* is a wage, a recompense for work — a word chosen to honor the servant by treating his obedience as labor deserving payment, even though the payment is pure grace. And it is *ʿaẓīm*, great, immense. The Qur'an does not specify its content here; elsewhere it describes gardens, rivers, companions, and, highest of all, the good pleasure of God and the vision of His Face. The indefiniteness of "a great reward" is itself expressive: it is great beyond specification. The Prophet ﷺ transmitted from his Lord:

> *"I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has never occurred to a human heart."* (al-Bukhārī 3244; Muslim 2824)

Note the proportion between deed and reward. Verse 8 asked for justice against one's hatred — a real but finite effort. Verse 9 promises forgiveness and *great* reward — an infinite return. The Qur'an frequently emphasizes this asymmetry (6:160: "whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like"), and the psychology is deliberate: a person will endure a present difficulty if the future gain is disproportionately large. The believer who knows that a moment of costly fairness earns eternal reward finds the cost bearable.

**How the Promise Shapes Conduct**

The practical function of this verse is to make righteousness sustainable. A person who tries to be just, honest, and faithful without any hope of ultimate recompense will eventually tire, especially when injustice seems to prosper. The Qur'an does not ask the believer to be good for nothing; it asks him to be good for God, and it assures him that God does not forget. This is not mercenary. It is realistic about human nature and generous toward it. The reward is not the *reason* justice is right — justice is right because it is God's attribute and His command — but it is the *support* that allows a weak human being to keep doing what is right when everything around him tempts him otherwise.

Consider a person who is wronged by a colleague and later finds himself in a position to evaluate that colleague's work. Verse 8 tells him to be fair. Verse 9 tells him why fairness is worth it: the small satisfaction of revenge is nothing beside forgiveness and a great reward from God. The verse converts every act of costly integrity into an investment whose return is guaranteed by the most reliable Promiser there is.

**Standing Between Hope and Fear**

Finally, verse 9 should be read alongside verse 10, which follows immediately with the opposite promise for those who disbelieve and deny. The two verses form a pair, and Islamic spirituality has always insisted that the believer walk between them — between *rajāʾ*, hope, and *khawf*, fear — like a bird flying with two wings. Verse 9 alone might breed complacency; verse 10 alone might breed despair. Together they produce the balanced heart that hopes in God's promise while never presuming upon it. The believer reads "God has promised forgiveness and a great reward" and takes heart; then he reads the next verse and takes care.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:10

> **And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they shall be the inhabitants of Hellfire.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Other Side of the Balance**

Verse 10 completes the pair begun in verse 9. Where the previous verse promised forgiveness and great reward to those who believe and act righteously, this verse states the consequence for their opposite: *wa-alladhīna kafarū wa-kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā ulāʾika aṣḥābu al-jaḥīm* — "And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Blaze." The Qur'an's habit of pairing promise with warning — *targhīb* and *tarhīb*, encouragement and deterrence — is grounded in an understanding of human motivation that admits both hope and fear as legitimate movers of conduct. Al-Rāzī, cited in the source, reads verses 9 and 10 together as the unfolding of the closing phrase of verse 8: "God is aware of what you do." Awareness of the righteous yields reward; awareness of the deniers yields the Fire.

**Two Verbs: Disbelieving and Denying**

The verse names two acts, not one: *kafarū* and *kadhdhabū*. *Kufr*, from k-f-r, means literally to cover; a farmer is called *kāfir* in Arabic (57:20) because he covers the seed with soil. Disbelief is the covering of a truth one has, at some level, perceived — the deliberate concealment of what the heart knows. *Takdhīb*, from k-dh-b, to lie, in the intensive form means to declare something a lie, to call it false. The two verbs describe a progression: first the inner covering of the truth, then its outer denial. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the deniers here are those who reject the proofs God has sent — the Qur'an, the Prophet ﷺ, and the evidences of His Oneness — and call them false.

This is important for understanding the verse's scope. It does not describe the person who has never heard the message, or the sincere seeker who has not yet arrived, or the one who struggles with doubt while wanting the truth. It describes the one who both covers the truth within and declares it false without — who has met God's signs and pronounced them lies. The Qur'an elsewhere reserves its severest language for exactly this act: *"Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God or denies His signs?"* (6:21).

**"Our Signs" (Āyātinā)**

*Āyāt* is the plural of *āyah*, a sign, a token, a mark that points beyond itself. The word designates the verses of the Qur'an, the miracles of the prophets, and the phenomena of nature — the alternation of night and day, the rain that revives dead earth, the creation of the human being — all of which "point" to their Maker. To deny God's signs is thus to deny a whole system of evidence: the revealed sign in the Book, the historical sign in the Messenger, and the cosmic sign in the world. The person who does this has not merely declined an argument; he has refused to read the language in which everything around him speaks.

**"The Companions of the Blaze"**

*Aṣḥāb al-jaḥīm* — literally "the companions of al-Jaḥīm." *Ṣāḥib* means companion, one who keeps company with another persistently; the Qur'an uses it for the inhabitants of both Paradise (*aṣḥāb al-jannah*) and Hell, and the word implies lasting association. *Al-Jaḥīm* is one of the Qur'an's names for the Fire, from j-ḥ-m, denoting an intensely burning, fiercely blazing fire; it is the term used for the furnace into which Abraham was cast (37:97). To be its "companions" is to be bound to it. The Qur'an's imagery is not arbitrary terror; it is the disclosure of a real consequence, presented in language that a human being can grasp, so that he may avoid it.

The phrase *ulāʾika*, "those," is a demonstrative of distance, and the commentators note its use for emphasis: "those — and no others — are the companions of the Blaze." The verse thus also carries an implicit consolation: it is not the sinner among the believers who is destined to be a permanent companion of the Fire, but the one who disbelieves and denies. The believer who errs and repents remains within the scope of verse 9.

**Why Warning Is a Mercy**

It may seem strange to call a verse about Hell merciful, but that is exactly how the Islamic tradition understands it. The Prophet ﷺ compared himself to a man who sees an enemy army approaching and runs to warn his people, stripped of his garment and crying out, "I have seen the army with my own eyes; I am the naked warner, so save yourselves!" (al-Bukhārī 6482; Muslim 2283). A warning is given because the danger is real and avoidable. To withhold it would be cruelty disguised as kindness. Verse 10 tells human beings, while there is still time, what lies at the end of the road of denial — not to frighten for the sake of fear, but so that no one arrives there and says, "No one told me."

The Qur'an states this purpose explicitly: messengers were sent "as bearers of glad tidings and warners, so that mankind would have no argument against God after the messengers" (4:165). Verse 19 of this very sūrah will repeat the principle to the People of the Book. Verse 10, by stating the consequence plainly, participates in that removal of excuses.

**The Logic of Consequence**

Why should denial lead to the Fire? The commentators offer a reasoning that goes beyond mere decree. A person who covers the truth and calls it false has, by his own choice, cut himself off from the source of light and life. God does not need to *add* punishment to such a person; He need only leave him with what he has chosen. The Fire is, in this sense, the natural terminus of a life oriented away from the Real. Just as a plant that turns from the sun withers by the logic of its own turning, so the soul that turns from God arrives at darkness by the logic of its own denial. Al-Ghazālī and others developed this insight: the punishment of the Hereafter is the unveiling of what the soul made of itself in this world.

This also explains the justice of the verse. God does not punish the ignorant, the unreached, or the sincere doubter; He punishes *takdhīb*, active denial after the signs have come. The person described here had the evidence, understood enough to reject it, and chose rejection. The consequence is proportionate to the act.

**A Mirror for Every Reader**

The verse should not be read only as a description of others. Every believer harbors small acts of *kufr* and *takdhīb* — moments of covering a truth he finds inconvenient, of calling false what he knows to be true because it demands something of him. The commentators warn that the verse is a mirror as well as a window: it describes the destination of a certain orientation, and it invites the reader to examine whether any part of him is turned that way. The believer who reads verse 9 and verse 10 together does what the Qur'an intends — he hopes in God's promise and fears God's threat, and he checks his own heart for the covering and the denial that would place him on the wrong side of the balance.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:11

> **O you who believe! Remember God's Blessing upon you, when a people were prepared to stretch forth their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. Reverence God, and in God let the believers trust.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fourth Reminder of Blessing**

This verse closes the opening section of the sūrah with the fourth mention of God's *niʿmah* — His favor — upon the believers (the others being in verses 3, 6, and 7). Where verse 3 spoke of the blessing of a completed religion, verse 6 of the blessing of purification, and verse 7 of the blessing of the covenant, verse 11 speaks of the most concrete blessing of all: physical survival. *Udhkurū niʿmata Allāhi ʿalaykum idh hamma qawmun an yabsuṭū ilaykum aydiyahum fa-kaffa aydiyahum ʿankum* — "Remember God's favor upon you when a people intended to stretch out their hands against you, and He restrained their hands from you." Before the sūrah turns, in verse 12, to the long history of the Children of Israel and their broken covenant, it pauses to remind the Muslims of what they owe: they are alive, and they are alive because God stopped the hands that would have killed them.

**The Vocabulary of Intended Violence**

The verse's language is vivid and precise. *Hamma* (from h-m-m) means to be on the point of doing something, to be resolved, to have one's mind set — the same verb is used of Joseph and the wife of the ʿAzīz in 12:24 for an intention that approaches action. *Yabsuṭū aydiyahum*, "to stretch out their hands," is the Qur'an's idiom for physical aggression (cf. 5:28, where the righteous son of Adam says "I will not stretch out my hand against you to kill you," and 60:2, "they will stretch out their hands and tongues against you with evil"). *Kaffa* means to hold back, to restrain — the same root gives *kaff*, the palm, the part of the hand that holds. God, the verse says, held back the hands that were already reaching. The picture is of an attack halted in motion: the enemy had decided, had begun, and was stopped.

**Which Attack? The Reports of the Commentators**

The commentators offer several occasions, and the source surveys them faithfully. The first is the well-known incident of the Bedouin and the sword. The Prophet ﷺ was resting under a tree during an expedition, his sword hanging from a branch; a Bedouin (named in some reports as Ghawrath ibn al-Ḥārith, in others as Duʿthūr) crept up, seized the sword, and stood over him saying, "Who will protect you from me?" The Prophet ﷺ answered, "God." The man's hand faltered, the sword fell, the Prophet ﷺ picked it up and asked, "And who will protect *you* from *me*?" — and then, in the version of Jābir preserved by al-Bukhārī (4135) and Muslim (843), let him go. The man returned to his people and said, "I have come to you from the best of people." Al-Rāzī and al-Wāḥidī cite this as an occasion of the verse.

The second occasion, favored by al-Ṭabarī, concerns the Banū al-Naḍīr, a Jewish clan of Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ went to them, with Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿAlī, to ask for help in paying the blood-money for two men of the Banū ʿĀmir who had been killed in error by a Muslim, as the treaty between the two communities required. The Banū al-Naḍīr received him courteously and asked him to sit by a wall while they considered his request; behind the wall, they conspired to drop a millstone on him from the roof. Gabriel informed him of the plot, and he rose and left quietly for Madinah before it could be carried out. The clan's treachery led to their siege and expulsion, recounted in Sūrat al-Ḥashr. Al-Ṭabarī favors this reading because the verse is immediately followed by the discussion of the Israelites' covenant-breaking (5:12–13), which would make the transition natural.

A third view, which the source commentary prefers and which many later scholars endorse, takes the verse in its broadest sense: it refers to the whole history of God's protection of the young community against enemies who were, at the outset, far stronger in numbers and resources. The Quraysh intended to destroy the Muslims at Badr and were stopped; the confederates surrounded Madinah at the Trench and were dispersed by wind and dissension; countless plots against the Prophet's ﷺ life came to nothing. The plural address — "against *you*," "from *you*" — supports this reading, as does the verse's function as the conclusion of a section addressed to the community as a whole. The particular incidents are instances; the verse states the general truth.

These readings are not contradictory. The Qur'an frequently uses a specific occasion to teach a general principle, and each of the incidents exemplifies the same reality: the enemy resolved, the enemy reached, and God restrained.

**The Theology of Restraint**

The verse makes a theological claim that repays reflection. It does not say that the Muslims defended themselves, or that the enemy changed his mind, or that circumstances happened to intervene. It says *fa-kaffa aydiyahum ʿankum* — "He restrained their hands from you." The agent of the restraint is God. This is the Qur'anic doctrine of divine action in history: what appears to human eyes as a fortunate accident, a failure of nerve, or a stroke of luck is, in reality, the hand of God operating through secondary causes. The Qur'an states this explicitly of Badr:

> *"You did not kill them, but God killed them; and you did not throw when you threw, but God threw."* (Qur'an 8:17)

And of Ḥudaybiyah: *"It is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah after He had given you victory over them"* (48:24), using the same verb *kaffa*. The believer is taught to see through the surface of events to the One who governs them. The Bedouin's hand did not slip by chance; the plot of Banū al-Naḍīr was not foiled by mere good fortune; the wind at the Trench was not a coincidence of weather. Behind each stood the restraining hand of God.

This has practical consequences. A person who attributes his survival to his own cleverness becomes proud and, eventually, careless. A person who attributes it to luck becomes anxious, because luck can run out. A person who attributes it to God becomes grateful and calm: grateful, because he has been given what he did not earn; calm, because the One who protected him yesterday is the same today. This is why the verse commands remembrance (*udhkurū*): the community that forgets Who protected it will either grow arrogant in its strength or terrified in its weakness.

**"Reverence God, and in God Let the Believers Trust"**

The verse ends: *wa-ttaqū Allāha wa-ʿalā Allāhi fa-l-yatawakkal al-muʾminūn* — "and be mindful of God, and upon God let the believers rely." The two commands respond to the two ways a person might misuse the memory of divine protection. One might conclude that, since God protects, one need not fear His displeasure — hence "be mindful of God." Or one might conclude that, since the danger was real, one must secure oneself by every means, trusting in walls and alliances rather than in Him — hence "upon God let the believers rely." The word order in the Arabic is emphatic: *ʿalā Allāhi*, "upon God" — upon Him and no other — comes first, before the verb.

*Tawakkul* is from w-k-l, to entrust one's affair to another; a *wakīl* is an agent or guardian. To rely on God is to entrust the outcome of one's efforts to Him while making the efforts. It is not passivity. The Prophet ﷺ told the man who asked whether he should tie his camel or trust in God: "Tie it, and trust in God" (al-Tirmidhī 2517; graded ḥasan). The Prophet ﷺ posted sentries, wore armor, dug a trench — and relied entirely on God. The verse's own occasion illustrates the point: the Prophet ﷺ answered the Bedouin's sword with the single word "God," and the sword fell. His reliance was not a substitute for courage but its source.

The Qur'an makes reliance the very mark of belief: *"and upon God rely, if you are believers"* (5:23, in the words of the two righteous men to the Israelites). The present verse phrases it as a command with a definite subject: "let *the believers* rely." Reliance is what believers do; it is the natural expression of faith in a God who has already demonstrated that He restrains hostile hands.

**The Section's Close and the Turn Ahead**

With this verse, the sūrah completes its address to the Muslim community: covenant (v. 1), sanctities (v. 2), food and the perfection of religion (vv. 3–5), purification (v. 6), covenant renewed (v. 7), justice (v. 8), reward and punishment (vv. 9–10), and protection and reliance (v. 11). The community has been reminded of everything it owes and everything it has promised. Now the sūrah will hold up a mirror: in verses 12 and following it recounts how God took a covenant from the Children of Israel, gave them leaders and promises, and how they broke faith. The placement is a warning by contrast. The Muslims have just been told to remember their blessings and keep their covenant; they are now shown what became of a people who forgot theirs.

**Remembering Protection in Ordinary Life**

Every believer has a personal history of restrained hands — the accident that did not happen, the illness that passed, the enemy whose plan collapsed, the harm that was reaching and was held back. Most of these are forgotten within days. Verse 11 asks for a discipline of remembering them, not as a source of self-congratulation, but as evidence of Who watches over us. The daily supplications the Prophet ﷺ taught — "O God, I ask You for well-being in this world and the next" — are the practical form of this remembrance. A person who begins each day recalling that he is alive because God restrained what could have destroyed him will find it easier to be mindful of Him and to rely on Him — and easier, too, to be just to those who once wished him harm, as the sūrah has already demanded.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:12

> **God had made a covenant with the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve chieftains. And God said, "I am with you!" Surely, if you perform the prayer, and give alms, and believe in My messengers and support them, and lend unto God a goodly loan, I shall surely absolve you of your evil deeds, and shall cause you to enter Gardens with rivers running below. But whosoever among you disbelieves thereafter, surely he has strayed from the right way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Mirror Held Up to the Believers**

Having spent eleven verses reminding the Muslim community of its covenant and God's favor, the sūrah now turns to history. *Wa-laqad akhadha Allāhu mīthāqa Banī Isrāʾīl* — "And certainly God took a covenant from the Children of Israel." The transition is deliberate and, as al-Rāzī observes in the source, cautionary: you have just been told to remember God's blessing and to keep His covenant; here is a people who were given exactly the same, and here is what became of them. The story of Israel in the Qur'an is never told as mere antiquarian history or as sectarian polemic. It is told as a mirror. The Prophet ﷺ himself warned his community: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you, handspan by handspan, cubit by cubit, so that if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would follow them" (al-Bukhārī 7320; Muslim 2669). The purpose of recounting Israel's covenant is to prevent its repetition.

The emphatic opening — *wa-laqad*, "and certainly, indeed" — signals that what follows is well attested and weighty. The covenant with the Children of Israel is one of the Qur'an's recurring themes (2:40, 63, 83, 93; 4:154; 5:70; 7:169), and, as the source notes, its mention is almost always followed by the record of its breach.

**The Twelve Chieftains**

*Wa-baʿathnā minhumu ithnay ʿashara naqīban* — "and We raised among them twelve *naqībs*." The word *naqīb* is from n-q-b, which means to pierce, to examine closely, to search out; a *naqīb* is one who investigates the affairs of his people and stands as their guarantor and representative — a chief who knows his tribe intimately and answers for it. The twelve correspond to the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from the twelve sons of Jacob, into which the Qur'an says God divided the community of Moses (7:160) and for each of which a spring gushed from the rock (2:60). The number twelve recurs at the founding of the Muslim community as well: at the Pledge of ʿAqabah, the Prophet ﷺ chose twelve *nuqabāʾ* from among the Helpers of Madinah and told them, "You are guarantors for your people, as the disciples were guarantors for Jesus son of Mary, and I am guarantor for my people" (Ibn Isḥāq; Aḥmad). The parallel is not accidental; it links the three covenant communities — Moses', Jesus', and Muhammad's — through a shared structure of representative leadership.

The commentators, as the source records, connect these twelve to the episode that will be narrated in verses 21–26. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī transmit that Moses chose one trustworthy man from each tribe and sent them ahead to scout the Holy Land. They returned with reports of the Canaanites' terrifying stature and strength; ten of them, against Moses' instructions, spread fear among the people, and the Israelites refused to enter. Only two — Joshua son of Nun (Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn), of the tribe of Joseph, and Caleb son of Jephunneh (Kālib ibn Yūfannā) — kept faith, and they are the "two men whom God had blessed" of verse 23. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī also mention the possibility that the twelve were righteous kings or judges through whom God guided the Israelites in later generations. The first reading fits the immediate context best, since the sūrah is about to tell that very story.

**"I Am With You"**

*Wa-qāla Allāhu innī maʿakum* — "and God said, 'Indeed, I am with you.'" This is the divine *maʿiyyah*, God's "being-with," a theme of immense consolation in the Qur'an. God says to Moses and Aaron, "Fear not; indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see" (20:46). He tells the Prophet ﷺ in the cave, "Grieve not; indeed, God is with us" (9:40). He is "with those who are patient" (2:153) and "with those who are mindful of Him and those who do good" (16:128). The commentators distinguish the general *maʿiyyah* of knowledge and encompassment, by which God is with all creation (57:4), from the special *maʿiyyah* of support and protection, by which He is with His obedient servants. The covenant with Israel opens with a promise of the second kind: God places Himself, as it were, alongside the twelve and their people — on the condition that follows.

Al-Rāzī suggests that "I am with you" was addressed to the twelve chieftains as they set out on their dangerous mission; al-Ṭabarī takes it as addressed to the whole people. The source rightly proposes that both are intended: the leaders are assured of divine company, and through them, the community. A leader who knows that God is with him can lead through danger; a people who know it can follow.

**The Five Conditions of the Covenant**

The verse then states the covenant's terms with legal precision: *la-in aqamtumu al-ṣalāta wa-ātaytumu al-zakāta wa-āmantum bi-rusulī wa-ʿazzartumūhum wa-aqraḍtumu Allāha qarḍan ḥasanan* — "If you establish the prayer, give the alms, believe in My messengers and support them, and lend God a goodly loan..."

The first two, prayer and alms, are the twin pillars that the Qur'an attributes to every true religious community, not only to Islam. The source lists the many verses in which prayer and *zakāh* are ascribed to the Israelites, to Jesus, to Ishmael, and to the People of the Book generally (2:43, 83; 19:31, 55; 21:73; 98:5). The pairing represents the two directions of religion: prayer is the duty toward God, alms the duty toward creation; a covenant that omitted either would be defective.

The third, *āmantum bi-rusulī*, "believe in My messengers" — in the plural, with no exception — is the clause the Qur'an most often accuses the Israelites of violating. A covenant to believe in *all* God's messengers includes those who come after Moses: it includes Jesus, and it includes Muhammad ﷺ. The Qur'an's critique that the Children of Israel "disbelieve in what came after it" (2:91) and that they killed or rejected prophets (2:87; 5:70) rests on this clause. The commentators observe that this part of the covenant is also the part addressed most directly to the Jews of Madinah, who were being invited to recognize the Prophet ﷺ in fulfillment of their own scripture.

The fourth, *ʿazzartumūhum*, "and support them," is from ʿ-z-r, which means to aid, to strengthen, and also to restrain — the same root gives *taʿzīr*, discretionary punishment, because such punishment restrains the offender and thereby aids him. To *ʿazzara* a prophet is to support him with honor and to defend him against his enemies. The Qur'an uses the same word of the Muslims' duty to the Prophet ﷺ: "that you believe in God and His Messenger, and support him (*tuʿazzirūhu*) and honor him" (48:9). Belief in a messenger is not complete without active loyalty to him.

The fifth, *aqraḍtumu Allāha qarḍan ḥasanan*, "and lend God a goodly loan," is one of the Qur'an's most striking metaphors. God, who owns everything, describes the servant's spending in His cause as a *loan* to Himself — and promises to repay it multiplied:

> *"Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over?"* (Qur'an 2:245)

> *"Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity and lend God a goodly loan — it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward."* (Qur'an 57:18)
