The metaphor honors the giver by casting him as a creditor and the Lord of the worlds as a debtor who never defaults. The word *ḥasan*, "goodly," specifies the manner: the loan must come from lawful wealth, given sincerely, without reproach or reminder (2:264). The source notes the connection with 73:20, where the loan is again paired with prayer and alms. That this clause appears in the covenant with Israel shows that generous spending for God's cause is a universal covenantal duty, not an innovation of Islam.

**The Promise: Absolution and Gardens**

*La-ukaffiranna ʿankum sayyiʾātikum wa-la-udkhilannakum jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār* — "I will surely absolve you of your evil deeds and surely admit you to Gardens beneath which rivers flow." Both verbs carry the emphatic *lām* and *nūn* of oath: God swears to fulfill the promise. *Ukaffir* is from k-f-r, to cover — the same root as *kufr*, but here in the sense of God covering the servant's sins (*kaffārah*, expiation, comes from the same root). The promise thus contains, in a single sentence, the two things every soul needs: the covering of its faults and the granting of its home. The description of Paradise as "Gardens beneath which rivers flow" is the Qur'an's standard image, appearing over thirty times; the image of flowing water beneath shade is the most universal human picture of rest and abundance, and it is presented to Israel exactly as it is presented to the Muslims.

This deserves emphasis. The covenant with Israel was not a covenant of mere earthly reward, nor a covenant of arbitrary demand; it was the same covenant of faith, worship, generosity, and salvation that God offers all people. The Qur'an does not depict a God who dealt harshly with one people and gently with another. It depicts one God, one covenant, one promise — and different human responses.

**"Whosoever Disbelieves Thereafter Has Strayed from the Right Way"**

*Fa-man kafara baʿda dhālika minkum fa-qad ḍalla sawāʾa al-sabīl* — "But whoever of you disbelieves after that has certainly strayed from the even path." *Sawāʾ al-sabīl* is literally "the evenness of the way," the level, straight middle of the road; to stray from it is to wander into the ditches on either side. The phrase "after that" (*baʿda dhālika*) is pointed: after the covenant, after the twelve chieftains, after the promise "I am with you," after the clear conditions and the sworn reward — after all this, disbelief is inexcusable. The person who breaks a covenant of this clarity cannot claim ignorance; he has left the road with his eyes open.

**The Logic of Covenant and Its Lesson**

Why does God bind Himself and His creatures in covenants at all? The commentators reflect that a covenant transforms a relationship of mere command into a relationship of mutual commitment. God does not need the servant's promise, but the servant needs to have promised: a person who has explicitly bound himself feels the weight of his own word, and betrayal becomes not merely disobedience but dishonor. The covenant with Israel, with its named leaders and enumerated terms, gave the people every structural support for fidelity. Their failure, which the next verse recounts, was therefore not a failure of information or of support but of will.

For the Muslim reader, the verse's placement is the lesson. The community had just been told, in verse 7, that it had said "we hear and we obey." Verse 12 shows that the Children of Israel had made the same kind of pledge, with the same conditions — prayer, alms, faith in the messengers, support for them, spending in God's way — and the same promise. What distinguished the two communities was not the covenant but the keeping of it. That is the whole point. A believer who reads this verse should not feel superior to the Children of Israel; he should feel warned. The five conditions are his conditions too, and the "even path" from which they strayed is the path he walks.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:13

> **Then for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and hardened their hearts. They distort the meaning of the Word, and have forgotten part of that whereof they were reminded. Thou wilt not cease to discover their treachery, from all save a few of them. So pardon them, and forbear. Truly God loves the virtuous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consequence Follows the Cause**

The previous verse set out the covenant with its conditions and its promise. This verse records what happened: *fa-bimā naqḍihim mīthāqahum laʿannāhum wa-jaʿalnā qulūbahum qāsiyah* — "Then, because of their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard." The grammatical structure is important. The particle *bi-* ("because of") attached to *mā* ("what," here an intensifier) makes the causal relationship explicit and emphatic: the curse and the hardening were *consequences* of the breach, not arbitrary acts. The verse thus answers in advance any suggestion that God dealt unjustly with a people. They were given a covenant; they broke it; what followed was the result of what they did. The same construction appears in 4:155: "because of their breaking of their covenant and their disbelief in the signs of God and their killing of the prophets without right."

*Naqḍ* is from n-q-ḍ, to unravel, to undo — used of a rope whose strands are untwisted, or a building that is demolished. It is the exact opposite of the *ʿaqd* (knot) of verse 1 and the *mīthāq* (firm binding) of verse 7. The imagery of the sūrah is consistent: God ties, and His covenant-breakers untie. The Qur'an elsewhere uses the vivid image of "the woman who unravels her spun yarn after it was strong" (16:92) to describe those who break their oaths.

**The Curse: Exile from Mercy**

*Laʿannāhum* — "We cursed them." *Laʿnah*, from l-ʿ-n, means to drive away, to banish; al-Zamakhsharī, as the source notes, explains the divine curse as expulsion from the sphere of God's mercy. It is not an emotional outburst but a change of status: the one cursed is placed at a distance. The Qur'an says of the Israelites who broke faith that they were cursed "by the tongue of David and Jesus son of Mary" (5:78), and of those who kill believers deliberately that God "has cursed them" (4:93). The believer should note that the curse is tied to a specific act — covenant-breaking — and to specific persons, not to a people as such. The verse will end by exempting "a few of them," and the sūrah will later praise those among the People of the Book who are upright (5:66, 82–85).

**Hardened Hearts and the Metaphor of Alloyed Metal**

*Wa-jaʿalnā qulūbahum qāsiyah* — "and We made their hearts hard." *Qāsiyah* is from q-s-w, hardness, as of stone; the Qur'an uses the same root in 2:74 of the Israelites after the incident of the cow: "then your hearts hardened after that, and they were like stones or even harder." A hard heart is one that does not respond — to warning, to reminder, to the signs of God. The Qur'an describes the phenomenon in many places (6:43; 39:22; 57:16), and it always presents hardness as both a consequence of sin and a cause of further sin: the heart hardens because it disobeyed, and it disobeys more because it has hardened.

The source preserves a striking interpretive detail from al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, and al-Rāzī. A variant reading of the word is *qasiyyah*, which connects it to *qasiyy* — a debased coin, silver mixed with base metal. Pure gold and silver are soft and workable; alloyed with copper or lead, they become hard and brittle. On this reading, the hardened heart is a heart that is no longer pure — a heart in which belief has been mixed with disbelief, sincerity with hypocrisy — and which has thereby lost its malleability to God's guidance. The metaphor is precise: it is not that the Israelites' hearts had no faith, but that their faith had been corrupted by admixture, and the corruption made them rigid.

How does God "make" hearts hard, and is this compatible with human responsibility? The commentators answer that the hardening is God's *just* response to a person's own choice. A person who repeatedly refuses guidance is left to the consequences of his refusal; God withdraws the softening influence of His grace, and the heart, left to itself, hardens. This is the same doctrine as the "sealing" of hearts in 2:7 and the "turning away" of 61:5: "when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate." The initiative is human; the confirmation is divine. A modern analogy is the calloused hand: a person who repeatedly applies friction develops a thickened skin that no longer feels. He did not will the callus directly, but he willed the acts that produced it. Prevention lies in the softening practice the Prophet ﷺ prescribed: "If you wish to soften your heart, feed the poor and stroke the head of the orphan" (Aḥmad; graded ḥasan).

**Distorting the Word: Taḥrīf**

*Yuḥarrifūna al-kalima ʿan mawāḍiʿihi* — "they distort the words from their places." The verb *ḥarrafa*, from ḥ-r-f (edge, border, letter), means to turn something aside, to tilt it away from its proper position; *taḥrīf* is distortion. The phrase "from their places" (*ʿan mawāḍiʿihi*) describes the technique: taking a word from where God put it and moving it elsewhere. The commentators, as the source records, understood *taḥrīf* in two senses: alteration of the wording itself, and misinterpretation of the meaning while leaving the text intact. Both are attested in the Qur'an's account. Of the first: "woe to those who write the Book with their own hands and then say, 'This is from God'" (2:79). Of the second: "there is a party of them who twist their tongues with the Book so that you would think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book" (3:78). Al-Zamakhsharī notes that *taḥrīf* is the clearest manifestation of a hardened heart: the person whose heart is soft submits to the text; the person whose heart is hard bends the text to himself.

The sūrah will return to this theme in verse 41, where the Jews of Madinah are described as distorting the words concerning the penalty for adultery — the incident in which the Prophet ﷺ called for the Torah, and a rabbi covered the verse of stoning with his hand until ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām told him to lift it (al-Bukhārī 3635; Muslim 1699). The mechanism was exactly what the verse describes: the word was there, in its place, and a hand moved to hide it.

**Forgetting the Reminder**

*Wa-nasū ḥaẓẓan mimmā dhukkirū bihi* — "and they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of." *Ḥaẓẓ* is a share, a portion, a lot. The verse does not accuse them of forgetting everything; it says they forgot *a portion*. This precision is characteristic. The Qur'an does not deny that much of the original revelation remained with the People of the Book — it will say in verses 44 and 46 that the Torah and Gospel contain "guidance and light" — but it charges that part was lost. Al-Ṭabarī understands the forgotten portion as including the covenant to follow Muhammad ﷺ and the laws they neglected. The source observes that forgetting is the oldest human weakness, beginning with Adam — "and We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot" (20:115) — and that the whole institution of prophecy is a system of *dhikr*, reminder, precisely because human beings forget. Forgetting here is not innocent lapse of memory; it is the willful neglect that lets an unwelcome truth slip from attention until it is gone. Every religious community, including the Muslim, is vulnerable to it, and the Qur'an's insistence on *dhikr* — remembrance — is the medicine.

**"You Will Not Cease to Discover Their Treachery"**

*Wa-lā tazālu taṭṭaliʿu ʿalā khāʾinatin minhum illā qalīlan minhum* — "and you will continue to come upon treachery from them, except a few of them." *Khāʾinah* is from kh-w-n, betrayal, breach of trust; the form here may mean "an act of treachery" or "a treacherous party." The Prophet ﷺ is told that he will keep uncovering plots — as indeed he did: the plot of Banū al-Naḍīr to drop a stone on him (which the source connects to verse 11), the breach of the Banū Qurayẓah at the Trench, the poisoning at Khaybar. Al-Ṭabarī reads this clause as a direct reference to the Naḍīr incident, which makes the sequence of the sūrah coherent: verse 11 recalled the hands restrained, verse 12 the covenant, verse 13 its breach and the treachery that followed.

Then the crucial exception: *illā qalīlan minhum*, "except a few of them." The Qur'an never generalizes without qualification. ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Mukhayrīq, and others among the Jews of Madinah kept faith and embraced Islam; the sūrah will later say of the People of the Book that "among them is a moderate community" (5:66) and that some, when they hear the Qur'an, weep in recognition (5:83). The believer who reads this verse is forbidden by the verse itself from treating a whole people as treacherous.

**"So Pardon Them and Forbear"**

*Fa-ʿfu ʿanhum wa-ṣfaḥ* — "so pardon them and overlook." This is the verse's most remarkable turn. After cataloguing curse, hardening, distortion, forgetting, and treachery, God commands not retaliation but forgiveness. *ʿAfw* is from ʿ-f-w, to erase, to efface (a wind that erases footprints in sand is said to *ʿafā*); to pardon is to wipe out the offense. *Ṣafḥ* is from ṣ-f-ḥ, the flat side or page of something; to *ṣafaḥa* is to turn the page, to turn one's face away from a fault as if it were not there. Ṣafḥ is thus a step beyond ʿafw: pardon removes the penalty, forbearance removes even the reproach. The Qur'an pairs the two elsewhere (2:109; 24:22; 64:14), and in 24:22 asks the rhetorical question that gives the reason: "Do you not love that God should forgive you?"

The source records the report from Qatādah that this command was abrogated by 9:29, the verse of fighting the People of the Book until they pay the *jizyah*, and that Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Thaʿlabī transmit this view. It also records the substantial objection: Sūrat al-Tawbah was revealed in the ninth year, and al-Māʾidah — by most accounts including the Farewell Pilgrimage in the tenth — postdates it, so the later verse cannot be abrogated by the earlier. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī offer the reconciliation that the source accepts: the two verses govern different situations. Verse 9:29 concerns those who are at war with the Muslim community; verse 5:13 concerns the treatment of those who have submitted to the covenant of protection, or who have wronged the Muslims in ways that do not amount to war. Once the People of the Book live under treaty, there is no reason their past offenses cannot be pardoned. Indeed, the placement of this command in a sūrah that has just permitted eating their food and marrying their women suggests that its aim is the reestablishment of normal, peaceful relations.

**Why Pardon Is the Right Response**

The command to pardon after such a catalogue of wrongs is not softness; it is strategy and spirituality at once. Strategically, a community that answers every treachery with vengeance becomes indistinguishable from its enemies and locks itself in an endless cycle. Spiritually, pardon is the imitation of God, who is *al-ʿAfuww*, the Pardoner, and who forgives what no human could. The Prophet ﷺ was the living embodiment of this verse. When a Jewish woman poisoned the meat at Khaybar and he was told who did it, he did not have her executed at first (al-Bukhārī 2617). When ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy, the chief of the hypocrites, died after years of plotting, the Prophet ﷺ gave his own shirt for the shroud and prayed over him (al-Bukhārī 1269). Of this disposition, the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Charity does not decrease wealth; God increases a servant in honor through pardon; and no one humbles himself for God's sake but that God raises him."* (Muslim 2588)

**"God Loves the Virtuous"**

*Inna Allāha yuḥibbu al-muḥsinīn* — "indeed, God loves those who do good." The verse ends by naming pardon as an act of *iḥsān*, the highest level of religion, which the Prophet ﷺ defined as "to worship God as though you see Him" (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8). The *muḥsin* is not merely one who does his duty but one who does more than his duty — who gives what he need not give and forgives what he need not forgive. The source notes that this phrase recurs in 2:195; 3:134, 148; and 5:93. In 3:134 it closes a description of those "who restrain their anger and pardon people" — the same virtue as here. To pardon those who have broken faith with you, plotted against you, and distorted God's word is *iḥsān* of the most demanding kind, and God's love is its reward.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse instructs the believer at two levels. At the level of self-examination, it describes the sequence that leads to a hardened heart — breach of covenant, distortion of truth to suit oneself, forgetting what one has been reminded of — and warns that the sequence is universal. Every religious person is tempted to move God's words "from their places" when they demand something inconvenient. At the level of conduct toward others, it forbids the generalization of treachery to a whole people and commands the difficult grace of pardon. A believer who both guards his own heart against hardening and extends forbearance to those whose hearts have hardened has understood this verse. And, the verse promises, he is loved by God.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:14

> **And with those who say, "We are Christians," We made a covenant. Then they forgot part of that whereof they were reminded. So We stirred up enmity and hatred among them, till the Day of Resurrection. God will inform them of what they used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Covenant Community**

The sūrah now turns from the Children of Israel to the Christians: *wa-min alladhīna qālū innā naṣārā akhadhnā mīthāqahum* — "and from those who say, 'We are Christians,' We took their covenant." The structure parallels verse 12 exactly. Both communities received a covenant; both were charged with keeping it; both, the Qur'an says, failed in part. The even-handedness is deliberate. The Qur'an does not single out one People of the Book for criticism while sparing the other; it holds both to the same standard and records the failures of both. Yet, as the source notes, the consequences described are different, and the difference is instructive.

**"Those Who Say, 'We Are Christians'"**

The phrasing is precise and slightly distant: not "the Christians" but "those who *say*, 'We are Christians.'" Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī observe that this construction subtly distinguishes the claim from the reality. The word *naṣārā* is generally derived from Nazareth (*al-Nāṣirah*), the town of Jesus, or from *nuṣrah*, help, in reference to the disciples who said, "We are the helpers (*anṣār*) of God" (3:52; 61:14). If the latter derivation is in view, the verse's phrasing carries an implicit critique: they call themselves "helpers" of God, but a helper who forgets his covenant is a helper in name. The Qur'an uses similar phrasing of the Jews in 5:18 ("the Jews and Christians say, 'We are the children of God and His beloved'") and of the Muslims in 49:14 ("the Bedouins say, 'We believe.' Say: you have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted'"). In each case the self-description is recorded and then measured against conduct.

**The Covenant Taken from the Christians**

What was the covenant? Al-Ṭabarī explains it as the same covenant God took from every prophet's community: to worship God alone, to follow His messenger, to keep His law, and to believe in the messengers who come after. In the case of the Christians, this included the covenant to follow Jesus' teaching of pure monotheism — "worship God, my Lord and your Lord" (5:72, 117) — and to accept the prophet whom Jesus himself foretold: "giving glad tidings of a messenger to come after me whose name is Aḥmad" (61:6). The Gospel, the Qur'an says, contained "guidance and light" (5:46), and the covenant was to live by it.

**"They Forgot a Portion"**

*Fa-nasū ḥaẓẓan mimmā dhukkirū bihi* — "then they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of." The phrase is identical to that used of the Israelites in verse 13. The forgotten portion, in the case of the Christians, is understood by the commentators to include the strict monotheism of Jesus' teaching, which was replaced by doctrines of his divinity and the Trinity (addressed in verses 17, 72–75, and 116–117 of this sūrah), and the foretelling of the final prophet. As with the Israelites, the Qur'an says *a portion*, not the whole. Much remained: the Christians retained the memory of Jesus' teaching on humility, charity, and the love of God, which is why the sūrah can later praise their priests and monks who "are not arrogant" (5:82). The verse is not a blanket condemnation but a diagnosis of partial loss.

The repetition of the word *nasū*, "they forgot," across both verses teaches something about how religious communities decline. It is rarely by explicit rejection. It is by forgetting — by the slow fading of parts of the message that are demanding, inconvenient, or theologically uncomfortable, until what remains is a partial religion that its adherents mistake for the whole. The Qur'an's insistence on itself as *al-Dhikr*, "the Reminder" (15:9), and its promise that God Himself will preserve it, is the answer to this pattern.

**The Consequence: Enmity and Hatred Among Them**

*Fa-aghraynā baynahumu al-ʿadāwata wa-l-baghḍāʾa ilā yawmi al-qiyāmah* — "so We stirred up among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection." *Aghraynā* is from gh-r-w, which means to glue, to stick fast; *ighrāʾ* is to incite, to set one thing upon another so that it clings to it. The image is of enmity *adhering* to the community, becoming part of its fabric. *ʿAdāwah* is active hostility; *baghḍāʾ* is the inner hatred that fuels it. The two together describe a community divided against itself, both in feeling and in act.

Here is the difference from verse 13 that the source highlights. The Israelites' breach led to curse and hardening of hearts — a spiritual punishment affecting their relationship with God. The Christians' forgetting led to enmity and hatred *among themselves* — a social punishment affecting their relationship with each other. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī understand this as a reference to the sectarian divisions of Christianity: the disputes over the nature of Christ that split the church into Nestorians, Jacobites, Melkites, and others, each pronouncing anathema on the rest, with persecutions and wars between them that continued for centuries. Al-Ṭabarī also records the view that the enmity is between Christians and Jews, but, as the source observes, the pronoun "among them" (*baynahum*) most naturally refers to the Christians alone, who are the subject of the verse.

Why is the punishment fitting? The Qur'an implies a logic. The portion the Christians forgot was, above all, the clear doctrine of God's Oneness. A community that loses the unifying center of its faith — the simple, shared confession of the One God — will inevitably fragment, because it has nothing firm enough to agree upon. Every theological complication breeds a new party; every party anathematizes the others. Unity of creed produces unity of community; confusion of creed produces division. The Qur'an makes the same connection for all peoples in 6:65, where God warns that He may "confuse you into sects and make you taste the violence of one another." Division is not merely a misfortune that befalls a community; it is what a community becomes when it forgets what held it together.

**"Until the Day of Resurrection"**

The phrase *ilā yawmi al-qiyāmah* indicates that the division will persist through history. This is not a decree that no Christian may ever be reconciled to another, but a statement about the community as a whole: the fragmentation, once introduced, will not be fully healed in this world. The Qur'an says the same about the Jews (7:167) and about humanity in general — "and they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy" (11:118–119). The persistence of religious division until the end is, in the Qur'an's view, part of the human condition after revelation has been partially forgotten. Only God's final judgment will resolve it.

**"God Will Inform Them of What They Used to Do"**

*Wa-sawfa yunabbiʾuhumu Allāhu bi-mā kānū yaṣnaʿūn* — "and God will inform them of what they used to do." The verb *yunabbiʾu*, from n-b-ʾ, means to inform of something significant (a *nabaʾ* is momentous news; a *nabī*, prophet, is one who brings such news). The verse defers the final accounting to God. This is a consistent Qur'anic pattern, as the source notes with its long list of parallel verses (2:113; 3:55; 5:48; 6:164; 10:93; 16:92, 124; 22:69; 32:25; 39:3, 46): where religious communities differ, the Qur'an states the truth as it sees it, but leaves the final judgment of persons to God on the Day of Resurrection. The word *yaṣnaʿūn*, "they used to do" — more precisely, "they used to craft or manufacture" — may hint at the constructed nature of the doctrines and divisions in question: these were things people *made*, and their makers will be shown what they made.

This closing clause has a restraining effect on the Muslim reader. It tells him that he is not the judge of Christians. He may know, from revelation, that certain doctrines are in error; he may not pronounce on the eternal fate of any individual, and he must leave the accounting where God has placed it. The believer's task is to convey the reminder, not to execute the verdict.

**Lessons for Every Community**

The verse, read together with verse 13, gives a complete diagnosis of how covenanted communities fail: breach, forgetting, distortion, hardening, and division. No community is immune. The Prophet ﷺ predicted that his own community would split into sects (Abū Dāwūd 4596; al-Tirmidhī 2640), and Islamic history bears out the warning. The Muslim who reads verse 14 should ask where his own community has "forgotten a portion" and whether the enmity and hatred among Muslims today are the same consequence the verse describes. The remedy is the one the verse implies by contrast: hold fast to the whole reminder, especially its unifying center — the Oneness of God — and the community will hold together. As the Qur'an says: "And hold fast, all together, to the rope of God, and do not be divided" (3:103).

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:15

> **O People of the Book! Our Messenger has come unto you, making clear to you much of what you once hid of the Book, and pardoning much. There has come unto you, from God, a light and a clear Book,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Direct Address After Diagnosis**

Verses 12–14 diagnosed the condition of the Jews and Christians — broken covenant, forgotten portions, hardened hearts, division. Verse 15 turns from description to invitation: *yā ahla al-kitābi qad jāʾakum rasūlunā* — "O People of the Book! Our Messenger has come to you." The tone changes. The diagnosis was in the third person; the invitation is in the second. God addresses them directly, by an honorific title — "People of the Book" — that acknowledges their possession of prior revelation, and announces that the remedy for their condition has arrived. The verse does not begin with rebuke but with the good news of a messenger. This pattern — critique followed by open invitation — recurs throughout the sūrah and reflects its purpose: not to condemn the People of the Book but to call them.

**"Making Clear Much of What You Hid"**

*Yubayyinu lakum kathīran mimmā kuntum tukhfūna min al-kitāb* — "clarifying for you much of what you used to conceal of the Book." The verb *yubayyinu*, from b-y-n, means to make clear, to distinguish, to reveal what was obscure. The Messenger's first function toward the People of the Book is described not as bringing something new but as *uncovering* what they already had and had hidden. The Qur'an accuses the People of the Book of concealment in many places (2:42, 140, 146, 159, 174; 3:71, 187; 6:91), and the source gives the two classic examples the commentators cite.

The first is the concealment of the prophecies of Muhammad ﷺ. The Qur'an states that the People of the Book "recognize him as they recognize their own sons" (2:146) and that he is "written with them in the Torah and the Gospel" (7:157). The Jewish scholars of Madinah knew the descriptions of the awaited prophet, and ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, who embraced Islam, testified that he recognized the Prophet ﷺ from those descriptions. The Prophet ﷺ made this explicit: "I am the supplication of my father Abraham and the glad tidings of Jesus" (Aḥmad).

The second example is the verse of stoning. When a Jewish man and woman who had committed adultery were brought to the Prophet ﷺ, he asked the Jews what the Torah prescribed. They said: "We disgrace them and they are flogged." ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām said: "You lie; it contains stoning." They brought the Torah and one of them placed his hand over the verse of stoning, reading what was before and after it. Ibn Salām said: "Lift your hand." He lifted it, and there was the verse (al-Bukhārī 3635; Muslim 1699). This incident, which the sūrah will treat at length in verses 41–44, is the perfect illustration of *tukhfūna*, "you conceal": the text was present, and a hand was placed over it. The Messenger's role was to make it clear again.

Al-Jalālayn, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī all cite these examples, and the commentators note the psychological truth they reveal: a community that finds parts of its own scripture inconvenient will conceal them rather than obey them, and this concealment is the practical form that "forgetting a portion" (vv. 13–14) takes.

**"And Pardoning Much"**

*Wa-yaʿfū ʿan kathīr* — "and passing over much." This clause is one of the most gracious in the sūrah. The Messenger is described as making clear *much* — not all — of what they hid, and passing over *much*. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the Prophet ﷺ did not expose every concealment; where exposure served no purpose in guiding them, he let it be. Al-Rāzī observes that this reflects both wisdom and mercy: wisdom, because unnecessary exposure would have provoked hostility without benefit; mercy, because God did not wish to humiliate the People of the Book but to guide them. The Prophet ﷺ practiced this restraint personally. He knew, by revelation, of many secrets — the hypocrites, the plots, the private sins of individuals — and he covered them. He said:

> *"Whoever conceals the fault of a Muslim, God will conceal his fault on the Day of Resurrection."* (al-Bukhārī 2442; Muslim 2580)

The alternative meaning, which al-Zamakhsharī records, is that the verb refers to God pardoning much of their past conduct if they now accept the Messenger. Both readings converge in a portrait of a message brought with clarification where clarification guides, and forbearance where exposure would only wound.

**"There Has Come to You a Light and a Clear Book"**

*Qad jāʾakum mina Allāhi nūrun wa-kitābun mubīn* — "There has come to you from God a light and a clear Book." Two gifts are named. The commentators divide on their identification, and the source records the two views: al-Ṭabarī understands the "light" as the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself and the "clear Book" as the Qur'an; al-Zamakhsharī takes both as descriptions of the Qur'an. The grammatical structure — two nouns joined by "and" — supports the first reading, and it fits the Qur'an's description of the Prophet ﷺ as *sirājan munīran*, "a light-giving lamp" (33:46). But the second reading has its own support in the Qur'an's repeated description of the revelation as light: "We have sent down to you a clear light" (4:174); "follow the light that was sent down with him" (7:157). The two readings are complementary rather than contradictory: the Prophet ﷺ is light because he carries the light of the Book; the Book is light because it came through the lamp of the Prophet ﷺ.

**Why "Light" Is the Perfect Metaphor**

The choice of *nūr* is exact. Light does not force; it reveals. It does not create the objects it illuminates; it makes them visible as they are. The People of the Book had the objects — the Torah, the Gospel, the prophecies — but they were in darkness: concealed, distorted, forgotten. The Messenger and the Qur'an came as light to make them visible again. Light also has the property that it cannot be hidden without hiding oneself: one can close one's eyes to it, but one cannot extinguish it. The Qur'an says of those who try:

> *"They wish to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, but God refuses except to perfect His light, even though the disbelievers hate it."* (Qur'an 9:32; cf. 61:8)

The source connects this verse of extinguishing to the theme of concealment: to hide revelation is to try to blow out God's light with one's breath — a futile and faintly absurd endeavor.

*Mubīn*, "clear," is from the same root as *yubayyinu* earlier in the verse. The Book is clear in itself and makes things clear. The Qur'an calls itself *al-kitāb al-mubīn* in the opening verses of many sūrahs (12:1; 26:2; 27:1; 28:2; 43:2; 44:2). Its clarity is contrasted with the obscurity that concealment had introduced into the earlier scriptures: here is a Book that cannot be hidden under a hand, because God has taken its preservation upon Himself (15:9).

**The Structure of the Invitation**

Verse 15 is incomplete without verse 16, which continues the sentence to describe what God does *through* this light and Book. But even alone, verse 15 establishes the shape of the Qur'an's approach to the People of the Book. It acknowledges what they have ("the Book"); it names what they did with it ("you concealed"); it announces the remedy ("Our Messenger has come, making clear"); it displays mercy in the remedy ("pardoning much"); and it identifies the gift ("a light and a clear Book"). Nothing in this structure is designed to humiliate. Everything is designed to invite. A reader who has been told that his scripture contains truths he has hidden, and that someone has come to show them to him gently while overlooking much, is being offered a way back — not a sentence.

**A Word to the Muslim Reader**

The verse also speaks, by implication, to the Muslim community. The Prophet ﷺ warned that his community would follow the ways of those before it. Muslims too can conceal parts of their Book — by ignoring verses that demand justice toward enemies, or generosity toward the poor, or honesty in trade — while emphasizing the parts that flatter them. The light that came to expose the concealments of the People of the Book is the same light that exposes ours. To recite the Qur'an as a *clear Book* means to let it clarify everything, including the parts we would prefer to keep under our hand.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:16

> **whereby God guides whosoever seeks His Contentment unto the ways of peace, and brings them out of darkness into light, by His Leave, and guides them unto a straight path.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**What the Light Does**

Verse 15 announced that a light and a clear Book had come from God; verse 16 tells what they accomplish: *yahdī bihi Allāhu mani ittabaʿa riḍwānahu subula al-salām* — "by it God guides whoever follows His good pleasure to the ways of peace." The pronoun *bihi*, "by it," refers to the Book (or to the light and Book together), and the subject of the verb is God. The Book is the instrument; God is the Guide. This is a consistent Qur'anic emphasis: no text guides by itself, and no messenger guides by himself ("indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills," 28:56). The Qur'an is the means through which divine guidance operates, and the verse's final phrase — "by His leave" — repeats the point. The believer who understands this reads the Qur'an not as a self-help manual but as an occasion of God's action upon him.

**The Condition: Following God's Good Pleasure**

The guidance is directed to *mani ittabaʿa riḍwānahu* — "whoever follows His good pleasure." *Riḍwān* is from r-ḍ-y, contentment, approval, being well-pleased; God's *riḍwān* is His good pleasure, the highest goal the Qur'an sets before the believer ("and the good pleasure of God is greater," 9:72). To *follow* God's good pleasure is to seek it as one's aim — to orient one's choices by the question "what pleases God?" rather than "what pleases me?" The source notes that the Qur'an consistently identifies the most sincere believers as those who act "seeking the good pleasure of God" (2:207, 265; 4:114; 59:8), and verse 2 of this sūrah described the pilgrims as "seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure."

The condition is significant theologically. Guidance is not arbitrary. God guides those who *want* to be guided — who have oriented themselves toward Him. The light is available to all, but it enters only the eye that is open. Al-Rāzī explains that the verse identifies the disposition that receives guidance: sincerity of aim. A person who reads the Qur'an seeking to confirm his prejudices, to find fault, or to win an argument will not be guided by it, because he is not following God's good pleasure but his own. A person who reads it seeking what pleases God will find the ways of peace opening before him. The Qur'an says of itself that it is "a guidance for the God-conscious" (2:2) — those already inclined toward Him — and this verse states the same principle from another angle.

**"The Ways of Peace"**

*Subul al-salām* — "the ways of peace." *Subul* is the plural of *sabīl*, a path or way; *al-salām* is peace, safety, soundness, wholeness. The phrase can be read in two ways, and both are illuminating. In the first, *al-salām* is peace as such: the Book guides to the paths that lead to peace — inner peace, social peace, and the ultimate peace of Paradise, which the Qur'an calls *dār al-salām*, "the Abode of Peace" (6:127; 10:25). In the second, noted by al-Ṭabarī and preserved in the source, *al-Salām* is one of the Names of God (59:23: "the King, the Holy, the Peace"), and the phrase means "the ways of God" — the paths that lead to Him.

The two readings coincide. God is Peace, and the ways to Him are the ways of peace. This is not a coincidence of vocabulary; it is a theological truth. The person who walks toward God finds his inner conflicts resolving, because his desires and his conscience are no longer at war; he finds his social relations improving, because he is no longer driven by envy, greed, and fear; and he arrives, finally, at the Abode of Peace. The word *Islām* is from the same root as *salām*: to submit to God is to enter the peace of God. The plurality of "ways" is also meaningful. There is not one narrow track but multiple paths — the way of the scholar, the way of the worshipper, the way of the generous, the way of the just — all converging on the same destination. Every believer can find a way suited to his capacity.

**"From Darkness into Light"**

*Wa-yukhrijuhum mina al-ẓulumāti ilā al-nūri bi-idhnihi* — "and He brings them out of the darknesses into the light, by His leave." The source draws attention to a feature of Qur'anic usage that has been much remarked: *ẓulumāt*, "darknesses," is always plural in the Qur'an, and *nūr*, "light," is always singular. The pairing occurs in 2:257, 14:1, 14:5, 33:43, 57:9, and 65:11, always with the same grammatical asymmetry. The commentators drew from this a profound lesson. Falsehood is many; truth is one. There are countless ways to be wrong — idolatry, atheism, superstition, sectarianism, self-worship — and each is a distinct darkness. There is only one way to be right: the light of God's Oneness and His guidance. The multiplicity of darknesses corresponds to the fragmentation of this world; the singularity of light corresponds to the Oneness of God, who is Himself described as "the Light of the heavens and the earth" (24:35).

The verb *yukhriju*, "He brings out," is the language of rescue. The person in darkness cannot see his way out; someone must lead him. The Qur'an describes God as *walī* — guardian and protector — of the believers precisely in these terms: "God is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of the darknesses into the light" (2:257). The imagery is of a person lost in a dark place, his hand taken by One who can see, and led into the day. Every convert to the truth, every sinner who repents, every heart that awakens from heedlessness has experienced this leading out.

**"By His Leave"**

*Bi-idhnihi* — "by His permission." The phrase appears in the middle of the verse, attached to the bringing-out from darkness, and it protects the reader from a subtle error. One might think that the Book, or the Messenger, or one's own effort, produces the emergence into light. The Qur'an says: by God's leave. The Book is His instrument; the Messenger is His envoy; the effort is His gift; but the emergence itself is His act. This preserves the believer from two dangers. The first is pride: the person who thinks he found the light by his own cleverness will look down on those still in darkness. The second is despair: the person who thinks the light depends on his own effort will fear that his effort is insufficient. "By His leave" removes both. The light is God's; He grants it to whom He wills; and the one who has received it should be grateful, not proud, and hopeful, not anxious.

**"And Guides Them to a Straight Path"**

*Wa-yahdīhim ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — "and guides them to a straight path." The verse ends where the Fātiḥah's central petition ends: with the *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm*. *Ṣirāṭ* is a broad, clear road; *mustaqīm* is straight, direct, upright — from q-w-m, to stand. The straight path is the shortest distance between the traveler and his destination; every deviation lengthens the journey. The source lists the path's many appearances (1:6; 2:142; 3:101; 6:87; 43:61; 67:22) and notes its identification with the life lived according to divine guidance.

Observe the sequence of the verse's three verbs. First, God guides to the *ways* (plural) of peace; then He brings out from darknesses to light; then He guides to the *straight path* (singular). Al-Rāzī reads this as a progression. The seeker begins by finding one of the many paths that lead toward God; he is then delivered from the darknesses that surrounded him; and finally he is set upon the one straight road that leads directly to Him. The plural narrows to the singular as the traveler approaches the goal. This matches the experience of the spiritual life: at the start, many roads seem possible; as one advances, the way becomes clearer and more single, until there is only one direction — toward God.

**The Verse's Place in the Argument**

Verses 15–16 form a single sentence, and together they constitute the Qur'an's offer to the People of the Book. Verse 15 said: you concealed, and a Messenger has come to clarify and to pardon, bringing light and a clear Book. Verse 16 says: through that Book, God will do three things for whoever follows His good pleasure — guide to the ways of peace, bring out of darkness into light, and set upon the straight path. The offer is not conditional on ethnicity, history, or prior scripture. It is conditional on one thing: *ittibāʿ riḍwānihi*, following God's good pleasure. Any Jew, any Christian, any human being who genuinely seeks what pleases God is included.

**Living the Verse**

For the reader today, the verse is both a description and a test. It describes what the Qur'an does for those who approach it rightly: it gives peace, it dispels darkness, it straightens the path. And it tests the reader's approach: am I following God's good pleasure, or my own? A person who finds that the Qur'an brings him no peace, dispels no darkness, and straightens nothing should not conclude that the Book has failed; he should examine whether he is reading it seeking *riḍwān*. The light is on. The question is whether the eyes are open toward it.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:17

> **They indeed have disbelieved who say, "God is the Messiah, son of Mary." Say, "Who would have any power over God if He desired to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and those on earth all together?" Unto God belongs sovereignty over the heavens and the earth and whatsoever is between them. He creates whatsoever He will, and God is Powerful over all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Invitation to the Central Doctrinal Error**

Verses 15–16 issued an open invitation to the People of the Book. Verse 17 now names the single most serious obstacle standing between the Christians and that invitation: *laqad kafara alladhīna qālū inna Allāha huwa al-Masīḥu ibnu Maryam* — "Certainly they have disbelieved who say, 'God is the Messiah, son of Mary.'" The verse opens with the strongest possible assertion — *laqad*, "certainly, indeed" — and the verdict *kafara*, "have disbelieved." This is not a matter of minor doctrinal difference. It concerns the very identity of God, and the Qur'an treats it with corresponding seriousness. The same charge will be repeated in verse 72 with identical wording, and related passages address the divinity of Jesus in 4:171, 5:75, 5:116, and 9:31.

The Qur'an's approach here is instructive. It does not begin with insult; it begins with a precise statement of the belief being refuted, and then offers an argument. The argument is not "we say otherwise" but a piece of reasoning that any listener can follow. This is the Qur'anic method in matters of creed: *burhān*, demonstration, not mere assertion.

**"The Messiah, Son of Mary"**

The title *al-Masīḥ* is the Arabic form of the Hebrew *māshīaḥ*, "the anointed one" (Greek *Christos*). The Qur'an uses it eleven times, always of Jesus, and the commentators offer several derivations: from *masaḥa*, to wipe or anoint, because he was anointed with blessing, or because he wiped the sick and they were healed; or from *sāḥa*, to travel, because he journeyed constantly through the land. Whatever the etymology, the Qur'an consistently pairs the title with *ibn Maryam*, "son of Mary." The pairing is deliberate and polemical. In every place where the Qur'an addresses Christian belief about Jesus, it names him by his mother — never "son of God," always "son of Mary." The very form of address is an argument: he had a mother; he was born; he is human.

**The Argument from Power**

*Qul fa-man yamliku mina Allāhi shayʾan in arāda an yuhlika al-Masīḥa ibna Maryama wa-ummahu wa-man fī al-arḍi jamīʿan* — "Say: Then who could have any power against God if He willed to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on earth altogether?" The argument is a *reductio*. If Jesus were God, he could not be destroyed, since God cannot be destroyed. But Jesus is, by the Christians' own account, a being who was born, ate, slept, suffered, and (in their account) died. He is subject to the power of another. Therefore he is not God, but a creature. The verse extends the point by naming his mother and "all who are on the earth": Jesus and Mary belong to the same category as everyone else — beings whose existence depends entirely on the will of God, who can bring them into being and take them out of it.

The source draws attention to the word-play in the Arabic that makes the argument tighter than any translation can convey. *Yamliku*, "has power," is from m-l-k, to own, to possess, to control; and the verse continues immediately with *li-llāhi mulku al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ*, "to God belongs the *mulk*" — the sovereignty, the ownership — "of the heavens and the earth." The question "who *owns* anything against God?" is answered by "God *owns* everything." No one has power over God, because God has power over everyone. The Messiah is within the *mulk*; he is not its owner.

Al-Zamakhsharī draws out the implication the source notes: by grounding the refutation in God's absolute creative power, the verse also implicitly rejects the Nicene formula that Christ is "begotten, not made." Everything other than God is *made*. The verse's closing phrase — *yakhluqu mā yashāʾ*, "He creates whatever He wills" — includes Jesus among the created.

**"He Creates Whatever He Wills"**

This phrase carries a second, subtler function that al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī identify. The Christian argument for the divinity of Jesus rested partly on the manner of his birth: he had no human father, therefore (it was said) his father must be God. The Qur'an answers: *yakhluqu mā yashāʾ* — He creates however He wills. A birth without a father is a sign of God's power, not of Jesus' divinity. The Qur'an makes the comparison explicit elsewhere:

> *"Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with God is as the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust; then He said to him, 'Be,' and he was."* (Qur'an 3:59)

Adam had neither father nor mother, and no one calls Adam divine. Jesus had a mother but no father, and this places him, if anything, closer to ordinary humanity than Adam. The miraculous mode of creation demonstrates that God "creates whatever He wills" — and the One who creates is not the same as what He creates. The same phrase appears in 24:45, 30:54, and 42:49, always in the context of God's freedom to create in any manner and form He chooses.

**The Question of Whether Christians Actually Say This**

The source raises a question that the theologically minded commentators addressed directly. Christian doctrine, as formally stated, says that "the Messiah is God" (the second Person of the Trinity), but it does not typically say that "God is the Messiah" — that is, that the entirety of God is identical with the man Jesus. Does the Qur'an, then, refute a position no Christian holds? Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī answer that the distinction is verbal rather than substantive. If Christ is truly God — possessing divine attributes, receiving worship, exercising creative and ruling authority — then God has been identified with a human being, and the proposition "God is the Messiah" follows logically, even if it is not the formula most Christians use. The Qur'an, on this view, states the belief in its logically consequent form to expose its implication. Moreover, some Christian sects of the time did hold positions close to the literal statement — those who emphasized the divine nature so heavily that the humanity of Christ nearly vanished — and the verse addresses these directly. In either case, the argument from power applies: whoever is subject to destruction is not God, whatever the theological formula.

**Why the Mother Is Mentioned**

The inclusion of "his mother" is not incidental. Verse 116 of this sūrah will record God asking Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as two gods besides God. Some Christian groups of late antiquity venerated Mary in terms approaching worship; the Collyridians, described by Epiphanius, offered her cakes as to a goddess, and the title "Mother of God" (*Theotokos*), affirmed at Ephesus in 431, was capable of misunderstanding among the laity. The Qur'an honors Mary above all women — a whole sūrah bears her name, and 3:42 records the angels telling her that God "has chosen you above the women of the worlds" — and precisely because of that honor, it forecloses her deification. She, like her son, is within the *mulk* of God.

**The Sovereignty That Settles the Matter**

*Wa-li-llāhi mulku al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi wa-mā baynahumā* — "and to God belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth and what is between them." This phrase is the theological bedrock of the sūrah. It appears here, again in verse 18, and forms the sūrah's very last words in verse 120. The refutation of the divinity of Christ thus rests on the same truth that closes the whole chapter: everything belongs to God; nothing else owns anything. Al-Rāzī notes that the phrase "what is between them" extends the sovereignty to every space and every being, so that no room is left for a second divine agent.

**"God Is Powerful over All Things"**

*Wa-Allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "and God is over all things Powerful." The closing formula seals the argument. Power over *all* things includes power over the Messiah and his mother; there is no exception. The verse begins with a specific false claim and ends with a universal true one, and the universal dissolves the particular. Al-Ṭabarī observes that this is the recurring structure of the Qur'an's refutation of *shirk*: it never needs to argue about the particular idol or person deified, because the universal truth of God's sovereignty leaves no space for any such deification.

**The Meaning for the Reader**

This verse teaches Muslims how to think about the central difference between Islam and Christianity. It is not a difference about whether Jesus was great, or virtuous, or born miraculously, or sent by God, or the Messiah — the Qur'an affirms all of these. It is a difference about whether he is *God*. And the Qur'an's answer rests on a principle that any person can examine: whatever is created, born, dependent, and subject to another's power is not the Creator. The believer who grasps this principle holds the key not only to this verse but to the whole doctrine of *tawḥīd*. He also learns the manner of the Qur'an's disagreement: firm in verdict, clear in reasoning, respectful of Jesus and Mary as God's honored servants, and anchored always in the one truth that admits no exception — to God belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:18

> **And the Jews and the Christians say, "We are the children of God, and His beloved ones." Say, "Why then does He punish you for your sins?" Nay, but you are mortals of His creating. He forgives whomsoever He will, and He punishes whomsoever He will, and unto God belongs sovereignty over the heavens and the earth and whatsoever is between them, and unto Him is the journey's end.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Claim of Privilege and Its Examination**

Verse 17 addressed the deification of Christ; verse 18 addresses a subtler and more widespread form of religious self-exaltation: the belief that one's community enjoys a special, guaranteed relationship with God that exempts it from the ordinary consequences of sin. *Wa-qālati al-Yahūdu wa-l-Naṣārā naḥnu abnāʾu Allāhi wa-aḥibbāʾuh* — "And the Jews and the Christians say, 'We are the sons of God and His beloved.'" The Qur'an does not here accuse them of literal divine sonship, as al-Jalālayn and al-Rāzī note; the commentators understood the claim as metaphorical and genealogical. But the verse identifies the *function* of the claim — to secure immunity — and refutes it by an appeal to their own experience.

**The Background of the Claim**

The source usefully surveys the scriptural roots. In the Hebrew Bible, Israel collectively is called God's "firstborn son" (Exodus 4:22), and David and Solomon are addressed as God's "son" (Psalm 2:7; 1 Chronicles 28:6). In the Gospels, the righteous are called "children of God" (Matthew 5:9; Luke 20:36; John 11:52), and Jesus speaks of "my Father and your Father" (John 20:17) — a text Ibn Kathīr cites as a likely source of the Christian usage. Al-Rāzī connects the claim to the Qur'an's other reports of the People of the Book asserting exclusive divine favor: "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian" (2:111); "the Fire will not touch us except for a few days" (2:80; 3:24). The claim to be God's children and beloved is thus the theological root of a whole cluster of claims to exemption.

Ibn ʿAbbās, as transmitted by al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī, gives the occasion: a group of Madinan Jews — Nuʿmān ibn Aḍāʾ, Baḥrī ibn ʿAmr, and Shaʾs ibn ʿAdī are named — came to the Prophet ﷺ, who called them to Islam and warned them of God's punishment. They replied: "You cannot frighten us, Muhammad; we are the children of God and His beloved." The verse came down in answer. The setting matters. The claim was not made in a moment of devotion but as a *shield* against warning — as a reason not to listen. That is the use of the claim the verse targets.

**The Argument from Their Own Experience**

*Qul fa-lima yuʿadhdhibukum bi-dhunūbikum* — "Say: Then why does He punish you for your sins?" The argument is devastating in its simplicity and, as al-Rāzī observes, it operates entirely within premises the listeners accept. A father does not consign his beloved children to torment. Yet the Jews and Christians both acknowledged that God punishes sinners among them: the Jews affirmed the Fire for a limited period (2:80) and knew their own history of exile, defeat, and chastisement recorded in their scriptures; the Christians affirmed eternal punishment for the unrepentant. If they are punished — in this world or the next — then either God is not their loving Father in the sense they claim, or the claim does not confer the immunity they draw from it. Either way, the shield is broken.

The argument has a wider application. Every religious community, including the Muslim, is tempted to convert its relationship with God into a guarantee. The Qur'an's answer applies universally: if you sin and suffer the consequences, your suffering is proof that no label exempts you. The Prophet ﷺ warned his own community in exactly these terms: "Whoever is slowed by his deeds will not be hastened by his lineage" (Muslim 2699). And to his own daughter: "O Fāṭimah, daughter of Muhammad, save yourself from the Fire, for I possess nothing for you from God" (al-Bukhārī 2753; Muslim 206).

**"Nay, You Are Mortals of His Creating"**

*Bal antum basharun mimman khalaq* — "Rather, you are human beings from among those He has created." The word *bashar* denotes the human being in his physical, mortal aspect — from b-sh-r, the skin, the outer surface; the *bashar* is the creature with skin, the visible, vulnerable, perishable human. The Qur'an uses it of the Prophet ﷺ himself: "Say, I am only a *bashar* like you" (18:110). The verse places the Jews and Christians in the category of all humanity: created, mortal, accountable. There is no third category between God and creation for a favored people to occupy.

The source notes that the refutation parallels verse 17's refutation of Christ's divinity: as Jesus and Mary are creatures subject to God's power, so the Jews and Christians are creatures subject to His judgment. The parallel is exact, and it reveals the unity of the two verses. Both puncture a claim to special status by the same instrument — the reminder of creaturehood. Whether the claim is "this man is God" or "we are God's children," the answer is the same: you were made, and what is made belongs to its Maker.

**"He Forgives Whom He Wills and Punishes Whom He Wills"**

*Yaghfiru li-man yashāʾu wa-yuʿadhdhibu man yashāʾ* — "He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills." This clause restores the correct picture of the divine relationship. Forgiveness and punishment are not distributed by lineage or label; they are in God's hands, dispensed according to His will — which the Qur'an elsewhere shows to be a will governed by wisdom and justice: He forgives those who repent and believe and do good (20:82), and He punishes those who persist in wrong. The clause denies the People of the Book any *automatic* claim on forgiveness, but it does not exclude them from it. The door remains open — through the same means it is open to everyone: faith, repentance, and righteous action.

This is a crucial balance. The verse is not saying that God is arbitrary, forgiving and punishing at random. It is saying that the *decision* is His alone, not the community's to presume upon. A person who says "I am forgiven because of who I am" has usurped God's prerogative. A person who says "I hope for His forgiveness because He is Forgiving, and I fear His punishment because I sin" has the correct posture. The verse moves the listener from presumption to this posture.

**The Sovereignty Repeated**

*Wa-li-llāhi mulku al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi wa-mā baynahumā* — "and to God belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth and what is between them." The phrase repeats verse 17 verbatim. Its repetition within two verses is emphatic: whether the error is deifying a man or exalting a community, the corrective is the same. Everything is God's. No one owns a share of His sovereignty that would entitle him to immunity from His judgment. A king's son may presume on his father's palace; but God has no sons, and His kingdom has no heirs by birth.

**"And unto Him Is the Journey's End"**

*Wa-ilayhi al-maṣīr* — "and to Him is the final return." *Maṣīr* is from ṣ-y-r, to become, to end up; the *maṣīr* is the destination toward which a process moves. The clause is both a reminder and a warning. Every human being — Jew, Christian, Muslim, or none — is on a journey whose end is God. At that end, claims will be examined, not accepted. The Prophet ﷺ described the scene in which "a man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection ... and God will say, 'Did I not honor you, and give you a spouse, and subject horses and camels to you?' ... and he will say, 'Yes.' He will say, 'Did you think you would meet Me?' He will say, 'No.' He will say, 'Then today I forget you as you forgot Me'" (Muslim 2968). The end of the journey is where every presumption is tested.

**The Verse as a Universal Warning**

While the verse addresses Jews and Christians by name, the classical commentators were clear that its principle binds Muslims. The Muslim who thinks that his profession of faith guarantees him Paradise regardless of conduct has made the same error under a different name. The Qur'an says to the Muslims: "It is not by your wishful thinking nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it" (4:123). Ibn Kathīr comments that the verse of 4:123 was revealed precisely when Muslims and People of the Book each boasted of their superiority, and God told them all that reward follows deeds, not claims.

The psychological insight is deep. Religious belonging is a genuine good; it provides identity, community, and guidance. But belonging becomes toxic the moment it is used as an excuse — the moment "I am one of God's people" becomes "therefore I need not fear my sins." The verse strikes at that moment. It reminds every believer that the relationship with God is real but not exploitable, that His love is genuine but not a license, and that the journey ends in a reckoning that no title can avert.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:19

> **O People of the Book! Our Messenger has come unto you, making things clear to you, after an interval in [the series] of messengers, lest you should say, "There came unto us no bearer of glad tidings, nor any warner." But there has come unto you a bearer of glad tidings and a warner. And God is Powerful over all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Address and the Removal of Every Excuse**

For the second time in five verses, God addresses the People of the Book directly: *yā ahla al-kitābi qad jāʾakum rasūlunā yubayyinu lakum* — "O People of the Book! Our Messenger has come to you, making things clear to you." Verse 15 used the same opening, and the repetition frames verses 15–19 as a unit: two invitations enclosing two refutations (the divinity of Christ in verse 17, the claim of divine sonship in verse 18). Now the invitation returns, but with a new emphasis. Verse 15 stressed *what* the Messenger clarifies — the concealed portions of their Book. Verse 19 stresses *when* he came — after a long silence — and *why* — so that no one can plead ignorance.

**The Purpose of Prophetic Clarification**

*Yubayyinu lakum*, "making clear to you," repeats the key verb of verse 15. The source observes that the Qur'an consistently presents clarification as a central purpose of prophecy: Muhammad ﷺ is sent "to make clear to them that in which they differ" (16:64), and Jesus said, "I have come to you with wisdom and to make clear to you some of that over which you differ" (43:63). Human religious history is a history of obscuring: revelations are received clearly, then distorted, concealed, forgotten, and overlaid with disputes until the original message can no longer be discerned. The prophet cuts through the accumulated fog. He does not merely add another opinion to the debate; he restores clarity. This is why the Qur'an calls itself *al-Furqān*, the Criterion (25:1), that which separates truth from falsehood.

**The Fatrah: A Silence of Six Centuries**

*ʿAlā fatratin mina al-rusul* — "after an interval in the messengers." *Fatrah* is from f-t-r, to slacken, to abate, to grow weak; a *fatrah* is a lull, a period of cessation or weakening. The Qur'an uses the same root in 21:20 of the angels who glorify God "and do not slacken" (*lā yafturūn*), and the term *fatrat al-waḥy* denotes the pause in revelation to the Prophet ﷺ after the first verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq. Here the *fatrah* is the interval between Jesus and Muhammad ﷺ — by the common reckoning, about six hundred years, which the Prophet ﷺ himself referred to when he said, "I am the closest of people to Jesus son of Mary in this world and the next; the prophets are brothers from one father with different mothers, and there is no prophet between me and him" (al-Bukhārī 3443; Muslim 2365).

The source records the two views on whether any prophets came during this interval. Ibn Kathīr, following the ḥadīth just cited, holds that none did. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Zamakhsharī transmit the report that four minor prophets were sent: three to the Israelites (perhaps the unnamed messengers of 36:13–14, sent to the city usually identified as Antioch) and one to the Arabs, Khālid ibn Sinān al-ʿAbsī, of whom the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said, when his daughter came to him, "That is the daughter of a prophet whose people wasted him." The ḥadīth of "no prophet between me and him" is understood by those who accept these reports as referring to no *major law-giving* prophet in the direct line. What is not in dispute is the essential point: for a long span of time, the world had no clear, living prophetic voice, and into that silence Muhammad ﷺ was sent.

The *fatrah* had consequences. Salmān al-Fārisī's search for the true religion, described in his own long account (Aḥmad; Ibn Isḥāq), took him from Persia through a succession of aging Christian monks, each of whom, dying, told him that the world had fallen into corruption and that a prophet was about to appear in the land of the Arabs. Waraqah ibn Nawfal, the cousin of Khadījah, had studied the scriptures and awaited the coming prophet. The pre-Islamic *ḥanīfs* — men like Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl — rejected idolatry but did not know how to worship. The verse describes the world they inhabited: a world in which the light of the previous revelation had grown dim, and the memory of God's messengers was fading into legend. The coming of the Messenger "after a *fatrah*" answered a need that thoughtful people of that age felt acutely.

**"Lest You Say: No Bearer of Good News Came to Us"**

*An taqūlū mā jāʾanā min bashīrin wa-lā nadhīr* — "lest you should say, 'There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner.'" The verse states the reason for the Messenger's coming in terms of the removal of an excuse. Had the silence continued, the People of the Book could have said on the Day of Judgment: "We had lost the way, but no one came to show us." God forecloses this plea. The Qur'an states the principle repeatedly:

> *"Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against God after the messengers."* (Qur'an 4:165)

> *"And We never punish until We have sent a messenger."* (Qur'an 17:15)

This is a statement about divine justice. God does not hold people accountable for what they had no means of knowing. The sending of a messenger — clearly, in their language, with proofs — is the precondition of accountability. Verse 19 tells the People of the Book that this precondition has been met: the argument they might have made is no longer available. Al-Ṭabarī records from the Companions that the verse was revealed in response to certain Jews of Madinah who claimed that no bearer of good news or warner had been sent after Moses — a claim that both ignored Jesus and, more pertinently, sought to dismiss Muhammad ﷺ in advance. The verse turns their words against them: you say no one came; now one has come.

**Bashīr and Nadhīr: The Two Faces of Prophecy**

*Fa-qad jāʾakum bashīrun wa-nadhīr* — "So there has certainly come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner." The two titles describe the dual function of every prophet. *Bashīr* is from b-sh-r, the root of *bushrā*, good news, and of *bashar*, the human being — because good news shows on the face, in the skin. *Nadhīr* is from n-dh-r, to warn, to make aware of a danger. A prophet who only brought good news would breed complacency; one who only warned would breed despair. The prophet brings both, because reality contains both: a Paradise to be hoped for and a Fire to be avoided. The Qur'an describes Muhammad ﷺ with both titles constantly — "We have sent you as a witness and a bringer of good tidings and a warner" (33:45) — and the source lists further instances (2:213; 6:48; 18:56).

There is wisdom in the order: *bashīr* before *nadhīr*. Good news comes first. The Prophet ﷺ instructed his envoys: "Give glad tidings and do not repel; make things easy and do not make them difficult" (al-Bukhārī 69; Muslim 1734). The warning is real, but it is delivered within a message whose first word is hope.

**"And God Is Powerful over All Things"**

The verse ends: *wa-Allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr*. The formula seems, at first, unconnected to what precedes. The commentators find the connection in two places. First, the sending of a prophet after six centuries of silence, from among an unlettered people, in a land with no prophetic tradition, is itself a demonstration of power: God can raise a messenger wherever and whenever He wills, and the *fatrah* was never a sign that He had abandoned the world. Second, the phrase warns those who now reject the Messenger: the God who was powerful enough to send him is powerful enough to hold accountable those who turn away. The excuse has been removed; the consequence is within His power.

**The Meaning for the Present**

The verse has a personal application beyond its historical setting. Every human being lives through periods of *fatrah* — spiritual lulls in which the voice of guidance seems to have gone quiet, when religion feels like an inherited memory rather than a living call. The verse teaches that such silences are not abandonment. God breaks them, in history by sending messengers, and in individual lives by sending reminders — a verse heard at the right moment, a righteous companion, a crisis that turns the heart. And it teaches that once the reminder has come, the excuse of ignorance is gone. The person who has heard the clear message cannot say, on the Day of Return, "no one told me." The bringer of good tidings and the warner has come — to the People of the Book in the seventh century, and to everyone who has since encountered his message.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:20

> **And when Moses said unto his people, "O my people! Remember God's Blessing upon you, when He appointed prophets among you, and appointed you kings, and gave you that which He gave unto no other in all the worlds.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Beginning of a Cautionary Narrative**

With this verse the sūrah opens the first of its three major narratives: the refusal of the Children of Israel to enter the Holy Land (vv. 20–26). The transition is natural. Verses 12–19 have spoken about the covenant of Israel, its breach, and the coming of the final Messenger. Now the Qur'an illustrates, through a single decisive episode, exactly what covenant-breaking looks like in practice. And it does so by first showing what the Israelites had been given, so that the magnitude of their refusal can be measured against the magnitude of God's favor. *Wa-idh qāla Mūsā li-qawmihi yā qawmi udhkurū niʿmata Allāhi ʿalaykum* — "And when Moses said to his people: O my people, remember God's favor upon you."

The word *idh*, "when," introduces a scene recalled from the past; the Qur'an uses it to summon a moment before the reader's eyes. The scene is the Israelites, freed from Egypt, standing at the border of the land promised to their ancestors. Moses addresses them with tenderness — *yā qawmi*, "O my people," the possessive expressing belonging and care — and his first word is not command but reminder.

**The Rhetoric of Remembered Blessing**

The command "remember God's favor upon you" is the same command addressed to the Muslims in verses 7 and 11 of this sūrah. The source lists further instances addressed to the Israelites (2:231; 14:6; 35:3). The repetition across communities teaches that the technique is universal: before asking a people to undertake something difficult, remind them of what God has already done for them. A person who has forgotten his benefactor's gifts will resent his benefactor's requests; a person who remembers them will regard the request as an opportunity to show gratitude. Moses, about to command his people to march into a land held by a fearsome enemy, first sets before them the record of divine generosity, so that their obedience will spring from thankfulness rather than mere compulsion.

There is also a psychological preparation at work. Fear shrinks the sense of what is possible; gratitude expands it. The Israelites who remembered that God had split the sea for them would find a walled city less terrifying. The Israelites who forgot would see only the giants. Moses' reminder is thus not merely pious preface but strategic encouragement.

**Three Blessings Named**

Moses names three specific favors. *Idh jaʿala fīkum anbiyāʾ* — "when He appointed prophets among you." No other people received so many prophets. From Abraham through Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, and onward through David, Solomon, Elijah, Elisha, Jonah, Zechariah, John, and Jesus, the line of Israel was the principal channel of revelation for many centuries. The commentators note that Moses could say this even in his own generation: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph were their ancestors, and Aaron stood beside him. The Prophet ﷺ described the phenomenon: "The Children of Israel were governed by prophets; whenever a prophet died, another prophet succeeded him" (al-Bukhārī 3455; Muslim 1842). To have God's messengers continually among one's people is a favor beyond price: it means never being without guidance, never being left to guess at God's will.

*Wa-jaʿalakum mulūkan* — "and made you kings." The Israelites addressed by Moses were not literally kings; the monarchy would not arise until Saul, centuries later. The commentators therefore interpret the word in light of the Israelites' condition. Al-Qurṭubī, as the source notes, understands it as sovereignty over their own affairs: they had been slaves in Egypt, owned and commanded by Pharaoh, and God had freed them so that each man was now master of himself, his household, and his goods. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have explained it thus: "whoever has a house, a servant, and a wife is a king." Al-Ṭabarī transmits similar reports from Qatādah and others — that the Israelites were the first people to have servants after the age of Pharaoh's oppression. The word *malik*, king, is from m-l-k, to own and control; a "king" in this sense is anyone who owns and controls his own life. After generations of slavery, this was the most tangible blessing imaginable.

The definition has a lasting relevance. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever among you wakes in the morning secure in his dwelling, healthy in his body, with his day's provision, it is as though the whole world has been gathered for him" (al-Tirmidhī 2346; graded ḥasan). Kingship in the Qur'anic sense is not palaces and crowns; it is freedom, security, and sufficiency. Most people today possess this kingship and do not know it.

*Wa-ātākum mā lam yuʾti aḥadan mina al-ʿālamīn* — "and gave you what He had not given anyone in all the worlds." The commentators offer several referents, and the source records them: the manna and quails that fed them in the desert (2:57; 7:160; 20:80); the cloud that shaded them; the twelve springs from the rock; the parting of the sea; the sheer number of prophets and signs; or, in Ibn Kathīr's summation, an abundance of the goods of this world and the next. The phrase parallels 2:47 and 2:122 — "I favored you over the worlds" — and 45:16, "We gave the Children of Israel the Book and judgment and prophethood, and provided them with good things and favored them over the worlds."

**"In Their Time": The Limit of the Favor**

Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī, as the source notes, add an essential qualification: the favor was "over the worlds *of their time*." The Israelites were the most favored people of their age, not of all ages absolutely. The Qur'an says of the Muslim community, "You are the best community brought forth for mankind" (3:110), and the two statements are reconciled by understanding each as relative to its era and conditional on its conduct. God's favor is not a permanent possession granted to a lineage; it is a trust that rises and falls with fidelity. The Israelites' favor in Moses' time did not survive their refusal in the very next verses, and the Muslims' favor, likewise, depends on their "enjoining right and forbidding wrong and believing in God" — the conditions 3:110 attaches to it.

This qualification protects against two errors. The first is the error verse 18 refuted: treating divine favor as a guarantee. The second is the error of thinking that God's favor to Israel was a mistake or a myth. It was neither. It was real, it was immense, and it was conditional — like every favor God gives.

**Moses as Model of Leadership**

The verse portrays Moses in a role that repays attention. He stands before a people who will, within moments, refuse him, insult him, and condemn themselves to forty years of wandering. He knows their character; he has already endured their calf-worship and their complaints. Yet his address to them is gracious: he calls them "my people," he recalls God's goodness to them, he speaks of blessings before he speaks of demands. This is the prophetic manner of leadership, and it is the manner the Prophet ﷺ practiced when he stood before the Quraysh after the conquest and before the Anṣār after Ḥunayn: reminding, not berating; appealing to gratitude, not to fear alone. A leader — of a nation, a family, a team — who wishes to move people toward a hard task can learn from this verse the sequence: first remind them of what they have received; then ask.

**The Verse for the Reader**

Every believer is addressed by this verse through the Israelites. Each of us has been given "prophets" — access to guidance through the Book and the Sunnah; each has been made a "king" — free, in most cases, over his own affairs; and each has been given favors that, if he considers honestly, are unique to him and were given to no one else in exactly that form. The question the narrative will now pose is: what will you do with this? Will you, when God commands something difficult, remember the favor and advance — or forget it and refuse? Verse 20 sets up that question; verses 21–26 answer it, tragically, for the people to whom Moses spoke.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:21
