> **O my people! Enter the Holy Land, which God has prescribed for you, and do not turn back, or you shall become losers."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command After the Reminder**

Having recalled God's threefold favor in the preceding verse, Moses now issues the command that the favor was preparing them to receive: *yā qawmi udkhulū al-arḍa al-muqaddasata allatī kataba Allāhu lakum* — "O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has prescribed for you." The repetition of the tender address *yā qawmi* binds the two verses: the same Moses who reminded them of God's gifts now asks them to act on the strength of those gifts. The command is simple, direct, and — in its grammatical form — urgent. *Udkhulū*, "enter," is a plain imperative; there is no hedging, no negotiation. God has decreed the land for them; the only thing required is that they walk into it.

**The Holy Land: Meaning and Location**

*Al-arḍ al-muqaddasah* — "the Holy Land," literally "the sanctified land." *Muqaddas* is from q-d-s, purity, holiness, sanctity — the same root as *al-Quddūs*, the Holy, one of God's Names, and *Bayt al-Maqdis*, the Sanctified House, the Arabic name for Jerusalem's sanctuary. To call a land *muqaddasah* is to say that it has been purified and set apart — as al-Zamakhsharī explains, purified from idolatry and made the dwelling of prophets. The source observes, with justice, that the phrase "Holy Land" is now common in Jewish and Christian usage but is rare in the Bible itself; the Qur'an's use of it is thus notable.

Where is this land? The commentators, as the source records, offer a range: the Sinai peninsula, Syria (in the broad classical sense of *al-Shām*, covering Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, and Jordan), Jericho specifically, or the region of Jerusalem's sanctuary. Al-Ṭabarī declines to specify, saying only that it lies between the Euphrates and the Nile — the broad area associated with Abraham's promised inheritance — without encompassing the whole of it. The Qur'an itself describes the region in other verses as blessed: "the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed" (17:1); "the land that We blessed for all peoples," to which Abraham and Lot were delivered (21:71); "the eastern and western parts of the land that We blessed," which the Israelites inherited after Pharaoh (7:137). The precise boundaries matter less than the sacred character: this is the land of Abraham, of the prophets' graves, of the sanctuary toward which the Prophet ﷺ himself first prayed.

**"Which God Has Prescribed for You"**

*Allatī kataba Allāhu lakum* — "which God has written for you." The verb *kataba*, to write, is the Qur'an's term for divine decree: "God has written: I will surely prevail, I and My messengers" (58:21); "your Lord has written mercy upon Himself" (6:54); "fighting has been written upon you" (2:216). Al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī, cited in the source, connect this "writing" to the Preserved Tablet — the repository of divine decree — and to the promise made to Abraham that this land would be an inheritance for his descendants. The source rightly adds that, from the Islamic perspective, Abraham's descendants include his line through Ishmael, so that the Abrahamic promise is not confined to one branch.

The commentators drew an important theological distinction from this verse. God had "written" the land for the Israelites — yet the following verses will show that this generation did not enter it. How can a divine decree fail? The answer is that the decree was *conditional*: the land was written for them on condition of obedience and courage. When they refused to advance, God's decree remained true — their descendants under Joshua did enter — but this generation forfeited its share. Al-Rāzī explains that "written for you" means "made a promise to you, and commanded you to enter," and that a promise conditioned on action lapses when the action is withheld. This is the general pattern of divine promises to communities: they are real, but they require the community to walk through the door that has been opened.

There is a lesson here about the relationship between decree and effort. Some imagine that if God has decreed a thing, human action is superfluous. The Israelites, hearing "God has written this land for you," might have concluded that they need only wait for it to be delivered. Moses' command — *enter!* — corrects the misunderstanding. The decree and the command go together: what God has written for you is what He commands you to strive for. The Companions understood this. When ʿUmar was asked whether fleeing a plague was fleeing from God's decree, he answered, "We flee from God's decree to God's decree" (al-Bukhārī 5729) — meaning that acting prudently is itself part of the decree.

**"Do Not Turn Back"**

*Wa-lā tartaddū ʿalā adbārikum* — "and do not turn back upon your heels." The verb *irtadda* is from r-d-d, to return, to turn back; the same root gives *riddah*, apostasy — the turning back from religion. The phrase "upon your backs" (*ʿalā adbārikum*) is the Qur'an's idiom for retreat, used of soldiers fleeing battle (8:15–16: "whoever turns his back on that day ... has incurred wrath from God") and of apostates abandoning faith (47:25). The source notes both readings for this verse: a command not to retreat from the land without fighting, and a command not to turn away from God's command and Moses' leadership. The two coincide. To refuse the command to enter would be both a military retreat and a spiritual one.

The Qur'an's warning against "turning back" resonates with a verse revealed after Uḥud: "Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? And whoever turns back on his heels will never harm God at all" (3:144). The phrase links the Israelites at the border of Canaan to the Muslims at Uḥud and to every believer at every moment of testing. Faith is a forward motion; to stop advancing is already to begin retreating.

**"Or You Shall Become Losers"**

*Fa-tanqalibū khāsirīn* — "for then you would turn about as losers." The verb *inqalaba* means to be turned over, to be overturned, to revert; it describes a complete reversal of fortune. *Khāsir* is from kh-s-r, loss — the term used in commerce for a trade that ends in deficit. The Qur'an uses it as the most comprehensive word for spiritual failure: "the losers are those who lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection" (39:15). Moses warns that turning back would not be a neutral pause but a catastrophic loss: loss of the land, loss of God's favor, and — as verse 26 will show — loss of forty years of their lives in the wilderness.

The word choice is instructive. Moses does not say "you will be defeated" or "you will be punished." He says "you will become *losers*" — in the sense of one who has thrown away a profit that was in his hand. The land was written for them; it was theirs to take. To refuse it was not merely to fail to gain but to squander what was already given. This is the precise structure of most spiritual failure: not the inability to reach something distant but the refusal to accept something near. The Qur'an says of the Hereafter, "This is Paradise which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do" (43:72) — an inheritance, already assigned, waiting only to be entered.

**The Verse as the Hinge of the Narrative**

Verse 21 is the moment of decision. Everything before it — the reminder of blessings in verse 20 — was preparation; everything after it — the refusal, the two brave men, the insolent reply, Moses' prayer, and the sentence of wandering — is consequence. The verse contains, in miniature, the structure of every divine command: a call (enter), a gift (the land God has written for you), a warning (do not turn back), and a consequence (or you will be losers). It is the same structure that faces every believer at every threshold: the call to prayer, the call to honesty, the call to forgive, the call to give. In each case the land is written; in each case the only question is whether we will enter.

**The Companions' Reading of This Verse**

The Muslims of Madinah knew this narrative well, and it shaped one of the decisive moments of their history. On the eve of the Battle of Badr, when the Prophet ﷺ consulted his Companions about facing the Quraysh, al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad stood and said: "O Messenger of God, go forward with what God has shown you, and we are with you. By God, we will not say to you what the Children of Israel said to Moses, 'Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we shall sit here.' Rather: go, you and your Lord, and fight; we shall fight with you" (al-Bukhārī 3952). The Prophet's ﷺ face shone with joy. The Companions had read verses 21–24 as a warning addressed to themselves, and they resolved to be the people who entered.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:22

> **They said, "O Moses! In this land are a domineering people. We shall not enter it till they leave it. But if they leave it, we shall enter."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Reply: Fear Dressed as Reason**

Moses commanded; the people answered. *Qālū yā Mūsā inna fīhā qawman jabbārīn wa-innā lan nadkhulahā ḥattā yakhrujū minhā fa-in yakhrujū minhā fa-innā dākhilūn* — "They said: O Moses, in it is a people of giants, and we will never enter it until they leave it; but if they leave it, then we will enter." The reply is a masterpiece of self-deception, and the Qur'an records it with precision so that every reader may recognize its structure. It begins with a fact (there are powerful people in the land), proceeds to an absolute refusal (*lan*, "never"), and ends with a condition that makes the refusal look reasonable (if they leave, we will enter). At no point do the speakers say "we are afraid" or "we disobey." They present cowardice as prudence.

**The Reports Behind the Reply**

The commentators fill in the background from the narrative that verse 12 had already alluded to. Al-Ṭabarī transmits that Moses, on God's command, sent twelve chieftains — one from each tribe — to scout the land before the people entered. There they saw the inhabitants: men of enormous stature and strength. Some reports describe a giant who caught the twelve scouts, carried them in his garment, and set them before his king as a curiosity; the king released them so that they would return and frighten their people away. Moses had instructed the scouts to report only to him, lest the people be demoralized. Ten of the twelve broke this instruction and spread the report of the giants through the camp. Only two kept faith — the two men of the next verse. The people's reply in verse 22 is the fruit of the ten scouts' faithlessness: a whole nation infected with the fear of ten men.

The biblical counterpart, Numbers 13–14, tells the same story in greater detail: the scouts return with a cluster of grapes so large it must be carried on a pole between two men, and report that the land "flows with milk and honey" but its people are giants "and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers." The Qur'an's account, characteristically, omits the picturesque details and preserves the moral core: fear of the strong, refusal of the command, and the reasoning by which the refusal was justified.

**Jabbārīn: The Weight of a Word**

The people describe the inhabitants as *jabbārīn*, the plural of *jabbār*. The root j-b-r has two related senses: to set a broken bone, to restore by force; and, by extension, to compel, to overpower, to dominate. A *jabbār* is one who imposes his will by overwhelming force. The source notes the important theological observation of al-Ṭabrisī: *al-Jabbār* is one of the Names of God (59:23) — the One who restores all things and whose will none can resist — and when applied to a human being the word acquires the negative sense of tyrant and oppressor, because such power belongs rightly to God alone. A human *jabbār* is a usurper of a divine prerogative. The Qur'an uses the word of Pharaoh's people (28:19), of those who reject warnings (14:15), and of the arrogant heart (40:35).

The Israelites' use of the word reveals their state of mind. They see the inhabitants as *jabbārīn* — as irresistible powers — because they have forgotten that the only true *Jabbār* is God, and that God has just promised them the land. Verse 20 recalled that God had drowned Pharaoh, the greatest *jabbār* of their experience; verse 22 shows them terrified of lesser ones. The word is thus an index of forgetting. When the memory of God's power fades, human power looms large.

**"We Shall Never Enter It"**

*Lan nadkhulahā* — "we will never enter it." *Lan* is the particle of emphatic future negation: not "we will not" but "we will *never*." The refusal is absolute and final, and it is addressed to a prophet who has just relayed a command from God. Al-Rāzī observes that this is the exact opposite of the Muslims' pledge recalled in verse 7: "we hear and we obey." The Israelites heard and refused. The Qur'an characterizes them elsewhere as those who said "we hear and we disobey" (2:93), and this verse is the narrative demonstration of that character.

The refusal is also an implicit accusation against God. God had said, through Moses, "enter"; the people say, "never." Either God did not know about the giants, or He knew and commanded them into destruction, or His promise of the land was not to be trusted. All three implications are blasphemous, and the people did not state any of them — but their "never" contains them all. This is how disobedience to a clear command always works: it does not announce that God is wrong; it simply acts as though He were.

**The Condition: "If They Leave, We Will Enter"**

*Fa-in yakhrujū minhā fa-innā dākhilūn* — "but if they leave it, then we will surely enter." The conditional is the most revealing part of the reply. It presents the speakers as willing, even eager — "we will surely enter" is emphatic, with *inna* and the active participle — provided that the obstacle removes itself. This is the perennial bargain of the coward and the procrastinator: I will do the right thing as soon as it costs nothing. I will pray when life is calmer. I will give when I am richer. I will speak the truth when it is safe. The Israelites' condition is the ancestor of every such promise.

Al-Zamakhsharī notes the absurdity. God commanded them to enter *in order to* expel the giants; the giants' presence was the very reason the command was given. To say "we will enter after they leave" is to say "we will fight after the battle is won" — to accept the reward while refusing the labor. The condition empties the obedience of all content.

**What They Should Have Said**

The Qur'an's presentation invites the reader to compose the reply the Israelites should have given. They had the material: God's favor recalled in verse 20 — prophets, kingship, gifts given to no other; God's promise in verse 21 — the land written for them. A people who remembered these things would have said: "The One who split the sea for us and drowned Pharaoh is with us; the giants are His creatures as we are; command us, and we advance." That is, in substance, what the two men of the next verse *do* say, and what al-Miqdād said to the Prophet ﷺ before Badr. The Qur'an sets the two replies side by side so that the reader may see that the difference between them is not information — both parties knew about the giants — but faith.

**The Psychology of Collective Fear**

There is a social lesson in the verse as well. The fear did not originate with the people; it originated with ten scouts who broke their prophet's instruction and spread the report. Fear is contagious; a few voices can demoralize a multitude. The Prophet ﷺ was acutely aware of this dynamic. He forbade the spreading of alarming rumors in the community and taught that "the one who says 'the people are ruined' is the most ruined of them" (Muslim 2623). On the eve of the Battle of the Trench, the hypocrites spread exactly this kind of fear — "Muhammad promises us the treasures of Chosroes and Caesar, and none of us can go to relieve himself in safety" — and the Qur'an records that the believers answered, "This is what God and His Messenger promised us, and God and His Messenger spoke the truth" (33:22). The Israelites at the border and the Muslims at the Trench faced the same test; one community was infected by the fearful voices and the other was not.

**Applying the Verse**

The reply of verse 22 is spoken, in some form, by every person who defers obedience until it becomes easy. The verse teaches the reader to hear the structure of his own excuses: the fact (there is a difficulty), the refusal disguised as delay (not now), and the condition that will never be met (when it is convenient). It teaches, too, that the *jabbārīn* — the giants that stand between us and what God has written for us — are always smaller than the *Jabbār* who commands us forward. The land was theirs; they saw only the giants. That is the tragedy the next verses will complete.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:23

> **Two men whom God had blessed among those who feared [Him] said, "Enter upon them by the gate, for once you have entered it, you will be victors. And trust in God, if you are believers."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Voices Against a Multitude**

Against the collective refusal of verse 22, the Qur'an sets two voices: *qāla rajulāni mina alladhīna yakhāfūna anʿama Allāhu ʿalayhimā* — "Two men, from among those who feared, upon whom God had bestowed favor, said..." The dramatic contrast is deliberate. A whole people said "never"; two men said "enter." The Qur'an does not name them, but the commentators — al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Zamakhsharī — identify them, in agreement with the biblical account in Numbers 14, as Joshua son of Nun (Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn), the servant and successor of Moses, and Caleb son of Jephunneh (Kālib ibn Yūfannā). They were two of the twelve scouts, and they alone kept faith with Moses' instruction and with God's promise. The source records a minority report that the two men were inhabitants of the land who had converted to Moses' religion; the majority reading, which fits both the Qur'anic flow and the biblical parallel, is that they were Israelites.

The Qur'an's anonymity is instructive. By not naming them, it universalizes them. They stand for every person who, in a crowd of the fearful, speaks for faith — for the two who advance when the ten retreat.

**"From Among Those Who Feared"**

The phrase *mina alladhīna yakhāfūna*, "from among those who fear," is deliberately ambiguous, and the commentators explored both readings. In the first, the fear is fear of God: the two men were among the God-fearing, and their courage before the giants was the fruit of their fear of Him. This reading rests on a deep principle of Qur'anic psychology: fear is a single capacity, and it is directed either at God or at creatures. The person who fears God most fears people least, because a heart cannot be dominated by two fears at once. The Israelites feared the giants because they did not sufficiently fear God; Joshua and Caleb feared God and therefore did not fear the giants. Verse 3 of this sūrah had stated the principle: "fear them not, but fear Me."

In the second reading, the two men were "from among those who feared" the giants — that is, they were part of the same frightened community, subject to the same fear, and yet they overcame it. On this reading, their courage is not the absence of fear but its mastery. Both readings honor the two men. The first makes them examples of a fear rightly placed; the second makes them examples of a fear rightly conquered.

**"Upon Whom God Had Bestowed Favor"**

*Anʿama Allāhu ʿalayhimā* — "God had bestowed favor upon them." The phrase uses the same root as the *niʿmah*, favor, that Moses recalled in verse 20. The two men had received God's favor and, unlike their people, remembered it; their courage was the practical form of their gratitude. The phrase also connects them to the Fātiḥah's description of the path "of those upon whom You have bestowed favor" (1:7) — the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous (4:69). The favor named here is, above all, the favor of faith and steadfastness, which the Qur'an counts higher than any worldly gift. Al-Rāzī observes that the verse teaches the source of courage: it is a divine favor, not merely a temperament. The person who wishes to be brave should ask God for it.

**The Counsel: "Enter Upon Them by the Gate"**

*Udkhulū ʿalayhimu al-bāb* — "Enter upon them through the gate." The advice is both tactical and symbolic. Tactically, the commentators explain that the two men — who had seen the city as scouts — knew that the inhabitants' strength was in their size, not in their courage or order, and that a bold, direct assault through the city gate would break them. Al-Ṭabarī transmits that the giants, for all their stature, were cowardly, and that the sight of the Israelites entering with resolve would scatter them. Symbolically, "the gate" is the point of decision: the place where one must commit, where there is no more scouting or deliberating, where one either goes in or does not. The Qur'an uses the image of entering "the gate" elsewhere for the Israelites — "enter the gate prostrating" (2:58) — and the gate is always the threshold between hesitation and obedience.

**"Once You Have Entered, You Will Be Victors"**

*Fa-idhā dakhaltumūhu fa-innakum ghālibūn* — "for when you have entered it, you will be victorious." The confidence is grammatically absolute: *fa-innakum*, "then indeed you," with the active participle *ghālibūn*, "overcomers." On what basis? Not on a military calculation — the two men did not deny the giants' size — but on God's promise: He had written the land for them (v. 21). The two men reasoned from the promise to the outcome: God has promised the land; therefore entering it will succeed; therefore the only thing required of us is to enter. Their logic is the logic of faith. It does not ignore the obstacle; it subordinates the obstacle to the promise.

The Qur'an confirms this reasoning as sound in other contexts. Of Ṭālūt's small army facing Goliath, it records those who "were certain they would meet God" saying: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's permission! And God is with the patient" (2:249). The Prophet ﷺ, with three hundred at Badr against a thousand, prayed and then said, "By God, they will be defeated" — and they were. The pattern is constant: victory belongs to those who enter the gate on the strength of God's word.

**"And Trust in God, If You Are Believers"**

*Wa-ʿalā Allāhi fa-tawakkalū in kuntum muʾminīn* — "and upon God rely, if you are believers." The two men close their counsel with the same command that closed verse 11 of this sūrah — *tawakkul*, reliance on God — and with a conditional that is really a challenge: *if* you are believers. The construction is pointed. Reliance on God is the natural expression of belief; a person who claims belief and refuses to rely on God has contradicted himself. The two men are, in effect, telling their people: your refusal is not a tactical judgment; it is a failure of faith. If you believe in the God who promised you this land, act as though you believe.

*Tawakkul* is not passivity; it is the disposition of one who does what is in his power and entrusts the outcome to God. The two men did not say "sit and trust in God to remove the giants" — that was the Israelites' position ("if they leave, we will enter"). They said "enter by the gate, *and* rely on God." The action and the reliance are one act. This is the balance the Prophet ﷺ taught: "Tie your camel and rely on God" (al-Tirmidhī 2517). It is also the balance the Qur'an strikes in describing the believers: "those who, when they are wronged, defend themselves" (42:39) and yet "upon God let the believers rely" (3:160).

**The Loneliness of the Faithful**

There is a human dimension to this verse that the commentators noted. Joshua and Caleb were two against hundreds of thousands. Their counsel would be rejected; the next verse records the people's insolent reply. In the biblical account, the congregation threatened to stone them. The Qur'an does not record the threat, but it records the failure of their appeal, and it records — in verse 26 — that the two were nonetheless vindicated: they alone of their generation entered the land. The verse thus offers consolation to every believer who has spoken the truth to a community unwilling to hear it. The two men's words were not wasted. They were preserved in God's Book to be recited until the end of time, and their speakers were saved when their hearers perished.

The Prophet ﷺ described such people: "Islam began as a stranger, and it will return to being a stranger as it began; so glad tidings to the strangers" (Muslim 145). Joshua and Caleb were the strangers of their day. Their number was two; their reward was the land.

**The Verse for the Reader**

Every believer will stand, at some point, where these two men stood: in a community — a family, a workplace, a nation — that has decided the giants are too large and the gate too dangerous. The verse tells him what to do. Fear God rather than the giants. Remember the favor God has already shown. Point to the gate — the concrete act of obedience that lies immediately ahead. Assert, on the strength of God's promise, that entering will succeed. And rely on God, not as an alternative to action, but as its foundation. Whether the community listens or not, the one who speaks thus has joined the company of the two men "upon whom God bestowed favor."

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:24

> **They said, "O Moses! We shall never enter it, so long as they remain therein. So go forth, thou and thy Lord, and fight! We shall sit here."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reply That Sealed a Generation**

The two men had spoken; the people answered — not the two men, but Moses, and not with reconsideration but with a hardening of their refusal. *Qālū yā Mūsā innā lan nadkhulahā abadan mā dāmū fīhā* — "They said: O Moses, we will never enter it, ever, as long as they are in it." Compare this with their first reply in verse 22: there they said *lan nadkhulahā*, "we will never enter it"; here they say *lan nadkhulahā abadan*, "we will never enter it, *ever*." The addition of *abadan*, "ever, forever," marks the escalation. The counsel of the faithful did not soften them; it provoked them. This is a recognizable pattern in the human heart: when a person has decided on disobedience and is then shown the way of obedience, he often digs deeper rather than turning back, because turning back would mean admitting he was wrong.

**"So Go Forth, Thou and Thy Lord, and Fight"**

*Fa-dhhab anta wa-rabbuka fa-qātilā innā hāhunā qāʿidūn* — "So go, you and your Lord, and fight, both of you; indeed we are sitting right here." This sentence is among the most insolent recorded in the Qur'an, and its offensiveness lies in several layers. The imperative *idhhab*, "go," is addressed by a people to their prophet — the reversal of the proper order, in which the prophet commands and the people obey. The dual verb *qātilā*, "fight, both of you," pairs Moses with God as two combatants, as though God were a warrior who might or might not prevail. And the closing clause, *innā hāhunā qāʿidūn*, "we are sitting right here," with its emphatic *inna* and its demonstrative *hāhunā*, "right here," expresses not merely refusal but a kind of settled, comfortable defiance — the posture of people who have made themselves at ease in their disobedience.

Al-Ṭabarī, as the source notes, records the interpretation that "you and your Lord" means "you, with your Lord's help," since God cannot be said to "go" or "fight" in a physical sense. On this reading the statement is less blasphemous in its literal content, but the commentators are agreed that its *spirit* is contemptuous: whatever the people meant by the words, they were using God's name flippantly to excuse themselves from His command. Al-Zamakhsharī remarks that the phrase reveals a conception of God as an external ally whose success or failure was a matter of indifference to the speakers — a conception incompatible with any real belief in the One who had just delivered them from Pharaoh.

**"Sitting" as the Posture of Refusal**

The word *qāʿidūn*, "sitting," carries weight throughout the Qur'an. In Sūrat al-Tawbah, those who refused to go out with the Prophet ﷺ to Tabūk are called *al-qāʿidūn*, "those who sat" (9:46, 83, 86), and the Qur'an says of them: "they were content to be with those who stayed behind, and their hearts were sealed" (9:87). In Sūrat al-Nisāʾ: "Not equal are those of the believers who sit — except those with a disability — and those who strive in the way of God" (4:95). The Israelites' "we are sitting here" places them at the origin of this type. Sitting is the physical expression of the refusal to move toward what God has commanded. It is not rest after labor; it is the refusal of labor.

**The Contrast the Companions Drew**

This verse became, for the Muslim community, a touchstone of what *not* to say — and the Companions consciously inverted it at the two most dangerous moments of their early history. The source preserves both reports. On the day of Badr, when the Prophet ﷺ consulted his Companions and al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad rose:

> *"O Messenger of God, go forward with what God has shown you, and we are with you. By God, we will not say to you as the Children of Israel said to Moses, 'Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here.' Rather: go, you and your Lord, and fight; we will fight alongside you. By Him who sent you with the truth, if you took us to Bark al-Ghimād [a distant place in Yemen], we would fight with you until you reached it."* (al-Bukhārī 3952; the fuller version in Ibn Isḥāq)

The Prophet's ﷺ face lit up, and he was gladdened. Ibn Kathīr connects the report to Badr; al-Ṭabarī records a version at Ḥudaybiyah. Whether one or both, the point is the same: the Companions knew this verse, understood it as a warning addressed to themselves, and made its inversion the declaration of their loyalty. Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, speaking for the Anṣār on the same occasion, added: "Perhaps you fear that the Anṣār consider themselves obliged to help you only within their own territory. I speak for the Anṣār: go where you wish, join whom you wish, cut off whom you wish, take from our wealth what you wish... By Him who sent you with the truth, if you plunged into the sea, we would plunge into it with you."

The contrast is the most instructive commentary on this verse that could be written. Two communities, two prophets, two commands to face a stronger enemy. One said, "Go, you and your Lord; we sit here." The other said, "Go, and we go with you." The first wandered forty years and died in the wilderness; the second won at Badr and inherited the earth.

**Why the Israelites Spoke This Way**

The commentators asked what produced such insolence in a people who had seen the sea split. Their answers converge on a single theme: the corrosive effect of long humiliation followed by sudden freedom without discipline. Generations of slavery under Pharaoh had taught them to obey force and to fear power; when the force was removed, they had no inner discipline to replace it, and they feared the giants as they had feared Pharaoh. Al-Rāzī notes that they had asked Moses for an idol like the idols of the Egyptians (7:138) and had worshipped the calf within weeks of the sea's parting (20:88); the reply of verse 24 belongs to the same pattern of a people whose bodies were free but whose hearts remained enslaved. This explains, in the commentators' understanding, the wisdom of the forty years' wandering pronounced in verse 26: a generation formed in slavery could not conquer; a new generation, formed in the freedom of the desert under God's provision, could.

**The Danger of Comfort in Disobedience**

The verse's closing phrase — "we are sitting *right here*" — captures a spiritual danger that goes beyond cowardice. The Israelites were not merely afraid; they were comfortable. They had settled into their refusal. The Qur'an's description of the hypocrites at Tabūk uses the same vocabulary: "they were pleased to be with those who stayed behind" (9:87). A person may refuse a command out of fear and be ashamed of his refusal — such a person may yet repent. But a person who refuses and *sits down*, who makes himself at home in the refusal and speaks of it with confidence, has passed to a more dangerous state. The Prophet ﷺ warned of the heart that "is inverted like an overturned vessel, recognizing no good and rejecting no evil, except what is soaked into it of its desires" (Muslim 144). "We are sitting here" is the voice of such a heart.

**The Verse as a Mirror**

The reader should not imagine that this verse describes only ancient Israelites. Its structure is reproduced whenever a believer, called to a demanding act — a public stand for justice, a difficult repentance, a costly generosity, a confrontation with wrong — responds, in effect, "let God handle it; I will stay where I am." The words "go, you and your Lord, and fight" are spoken silently every time a person delegates to God a task God has assigned to him. The Qur'an preserved this reply so that we might recognize its echo in ourselves and answer, as al-Miqdād did, with the opposite.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:25

> **He said, "My Lord! I have no power over anyone save myself and my brother; so separate us from the iniquitous people!"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prophet Turns to His Lord**

The people have spoken their final refusal. Moses does not argue further, does not threaten, does not plead. He turns from the people to God: *qāla rabbi innī lā amliku illā nafsī wa-akhī* — "He said: My Lord, indeed I have no power except over myself and my brother." The turn is itself instructive. When human persuasion has been exhausted, the prophet's recourse is prayer. Moses had reminded the people of God's favor (v. 20), commanded them with clarity (v. 21), and heard the counsel of the two faithful men rejected (vv. 23–24). There was nothing more that speech could do. So he speaks to the only One who can act on hearts.

The address *rabbi*, "my Lord," is the intimate form — not *Allāh* but *rabbī*, "my Sustainer, my Master" — the word a servant uses when he is alone with the One he serves. It is the address of every prophetic supplication in the Qur'an: Noah's (71:26), Abraham's (14:35), Zechariah's (19:4), and Moses' own at the burning bush (20:25). The single possessive suffix carries the whole relationship: I am Yours; You are mine; I bring this to You.

**"I Have No Power Except over Myself and My Brother"**

*Lā amliku illā nafsī wa-akhī* — "I do not control anything except myself and my brother." The verb *amliku* is from m-l-k, the same root as the *mulk* (sovereignty) of verses 17 and 18; Moses is saying that his *mulk* — his dominion, his power to command — extends only to his own person and to Aaron. This is a confession of the limits of prophetic authority, and it teaches a fundamental truth about the relationship between the messenger and the people: the messenger can convey, exhort, warn, and command, but he cannot compel belief or obedience. The Qur'an says to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: "You are not a controller over them" (88:22); "upon you is only the conveying" (42:48). Moses' words are the same acknowledgment in the mouth of an earlier prophet.

Why does he mention Aaron? The commentators offer several answers, and the source preserves al-Zamakhsharī's two. In one reading, Moses names Aaron because Aaron, as a fellow prophet, was the only person whose loyalty he could be certain of in that moment of general defection — and this despite the faithfulness of Joshua and Caleb, whom Moses, in his distress, may not have felt able to count on absolutely. In another reading, "my brother" is not Aaron alone but a generic term for "my brother in religion" — that is, whoever truly follows me — so that Moses is saying, "I control only myself and whoever shares my faith." Al-Ṭabarī takes the plain sense: Aaron. The plain sense also carries a poignancy: of all that vast people, the prophet can vouch for two — himself and his brother. It is the loneliness of leadership stated in its starkest form.

**The Meaning of "Separate Us"**

*Fa-fruq baynanā wa-bayna al-qawmi al-fāsiqīn* — "so make a separation between us and the iniquitous people." The verb *faraqa* is to divide, to distinguish, to part — the root of *Furqān*, the Criterion, and of the "separating" of the sea for these very Israelites (2:50: "when We parted the sea for you"). The commentators, as the source notes, understood the plea in two ways. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī read it as a request for *judgment*: "decide between us and them" — that is, judge between the obedient and the disobedient, as God judges between parties in a dispute. The verb is used in this sense elsewhere ("our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth," 7:89, from Shuʿayb). On this reading, Moses is not asking to be physically removed from his people but asking God to render His verdict on their disobedience.

The other reading takes "separate" more literally: "part us from them," "do not include us in what befalls them." On this reading, Moses is asking that the punishment which must follow such defiance should not fall on himself and Aaron. Both readings are compatible; a judgment between the two parties would naturally distinguish their fates.

**"The Iniquitous People"**

Moses describes his people as *al-qawm al-fāsiqīn*. *Fisq*, from f-s-q, is the splitting of a date's skin as the fruit bursts from it — by extension, the breaking out from the boundaries of obedience. A *fāsiq* is one who has left the bounds of God's command. It is a strong word, and it is the same word God used in verse 3 for divination by arrows ("that is *fisq*"). Moses does not call them disbelievers; they still affirmed God and His prophet. He calls them *fāsiqīn*: people who believe and yet break out of obedience. The distinction is important. The Israelites' sin was not denial of God but refusal to do what God commanded. The Qur'an treats this as a grave matter, and verse 26 will show that God agreed with Moses' characterization, repeating the exact phrase.

**A Prophet's Grief, Not a Prophet's Malice**

The commentators were careful to note that Moses' supplication was not a curse born of anger but a plea born of grief. He had given everything for these people: confronted Pharaoh, led them through the sea, interceded for them after the calf, fasted forty days on the mountain to bring them the Law. Now they told him, "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we sit here." The supplication is the prayer of a leader whose people have rejected the very thing he brought them at such cost. Al-Rāzī observes that the verse's concluding word — "the *iniquitous* people" — shows that Moses was not renouncing his people as such but naming their condition; and the next verse's command to him, "grieve not," shows that his dominant emotion was sorrow, not rage.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ experienced a similar moment at Ṭāʾif, when the people of the city rejected him and set their children to stone him, and he prayed: "O God, to You I complain of my weakness, my lack of resources, and my lowliness before men... If You are not angry with me, I do not care" (Ibn Isḥāq; al-Ṭabarānī). The prophetic response to rejection is to turn to God, to acknowledge one's own limits, and to leave the matter in His hands — not to seek revenge.

**What the Verse Teaches About Responsibility**

Moses' statement "I control only myself and my brother" embodies a principle that the Qur'an states in general terms: "No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" (6:164), and "O you who believe, upon you is yourselves; the one who strays cannot harm you if you are guided" (5:105, later in this sūrah). Each person answers for what is in his power. Moses, having done all that was in his power, is not answerable for the people's refusal. This is liberating for anyone who has tried and failed to guide another: a parent whose child has gone astray, a teacher whose student refuses to learn, a friend whose counsel is ignored. Having conveyed the truth sincerely, one is not accountable for its rejection — and one may say, with Moses, "My Lord, I control only myself."

But the verse also sets a limit on this liberation. Moses does not say "I control only myself" and then walk away. He remains with his people through the forty years (as the next verse's commentary will discuss). Acknowledging the limits of one's power over others is not the same as abandoning them. It is, rather, the correct placement of the burden: the effort is mine; the result is God's.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:26

> **He said, "Then verily it shall be forbidden them for forty years, while they shall wander on the earth. So grieve not for the iniquitous people."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Divine Verdict**

Moses asked for a separation between himself and the iniquitous; God answers with a sentence: *qāla fa-innahā muḥarramatun ʿalayhim arbaʿīna sanatan yatīhūna fī al-arḍ* — "He said: Then indeed it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the earth." The pronoun "it" refers to the Holy Land. The land that God had "written for them" (v. 21) is now "forbidden to them" — *muḥarramah*, from the same root as *ḥarām*. The reversal is exact and terrible. What was theirs to enter has become, by their own refusal, what they may not enter. The Qur'an's vocabulary makes the point that the commentators draw out: God's promises are conditional gifts, and the same divine will that grants can withhold when the condition fails.

**Two Ways to Read the Sentence**

The Arabic admits two readings, and the source records both. In the first, "forty years" modifies "forbidden": the land is forbidden to them for forty years, during which they wander. In the second, "forty years" modifies "wander": the land is forbidden to them (without a stated term), and for forty years they will wander in the earth. Al-Ṭabarī inclines to the second, drawing the implication that the prohibition was, for the disobedient generation, effectively permanent — they would die in the wilderness before it lifted — while the wandering itself lasted forty years. The two readings converge on the same historical outcome: the generation that said "we are sitting here" never entered; their children did.

**The Meaning of Tīh: Wandering Without Arrival**

*Yatīhūna* is from t-y-h, to be lost, to wander bewildered, to be unable to find one's way; the desert of the Sinai came to be called *al-Tīh*, "the Wilderness of Wandering," from this verse. The word describes not merely travel but disoriented travel — movement without arrival. The commentators transmit that the Israelites would journey all day and find themselves, at nightfall, where they had begun. Whether taken literally or as a description of the futility of their years, the image is precise. A people who refused to move forward when commanded were condemned to move endlessly without progress. The punishment fit the sin in kind: they had chosen stasis dressed as movement ("if they leave, we will enter"), and they received movement that was stasis.

There is a profound psychological truth in this. The person who refuses the clear step forward does not remain where he is; he wanders. Having declined the one road that led somewhere, he tries every other road and arrives nowhere. The Qur'an describes the state of those who turn from guidance in exactly these terms: God "leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly" (2:15, using a related verb, *yaʿmahūn*). Refusal is never neutral. It sets a person in motion in the wrong direction.

**Why Forty Years?**

The commentators offer reasons for the specific term. The most compelling, transmitted by al-Ṭabarī and others and consistent with the biblical account (Numbers 14:29–34), is that forty years was the span needed for the generation of slavery to pass away and a new generation to grow up free. Those who had been formed under Pharaoh could not conquer; their fear was too deep, their habits of servility too ingrained. Their children, born in the desert, fed by manna, guided by the pillar of cloud, knowing no master but God, would be different. Under Joshua, they entered. The forty years were thus not merely punitive but formative: God was raising a people fit to receive the promise. Forty is also, in Qur'anic usage, the number of maturity — "until, when he reaches his full strength and reaches forty years" (46:15) — and Moses' own appointment on the mountain lasted forty nights (2:51; 7:142).

There is consolation in this reading. The sentence of forty years was a mercy to the nation, though a severity to the generation. God did not abandon the promise; He postponed it until a people existed who could bear it. When a community fails, God's plan for it is not always cancelled; sometimes it is deferred to those who will be worthy.

**Forbidden by Force or by Devotion?**

Al-Rāzī, cited in the source, raises a subtle question: was the land "forbidden" in the sense that the Israelites were physically prevented from entering it, or in the sense that they were commanded, as a religious prohibition, not to enter? The first reading makes the prohibition a matter of divine decree operating through circumstance; the second makes it a test of obedience — having refused to enter when commanded, they were now commanded not to enter, and obedience to *this* command became their new task. Both readings have force. The second is especially instructive: it suggests that God met their disobedience by giving them a command that matched their inclination — they had wanted not to enter, and now they must not — so that even their reluctance was drawn into the discipline of submission.

**Moses and Aaron in the Wilderness**

The source raises a question the commentators debated: since Moses had asked to be separated from the iniquitous, and since the wandering was their punishment, did Moses and Aaron remain with them? The majority, as al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī record, hold that they did — Moses died in the wilderness, near the Holy Land but not within it, as the biblical account also states, and Aaron died before him. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī add a beautiful comparison: the wandering was no hardship to Moses and Aaron, just as the fire was no hardship to Abraham when he was cast into it — "O fire, be coolness and peace upon Abraham" (21:69). The same circumstance that was punishment for the disobedient was, for the prophets, simply the place where God had put them, and they were at peace in it. This is a general truth about affliction: the same event is a torment to one heart and a trial patiently borne — even a comfort — to another, depending on the heart's relationship with God.

The source also records that God did not withdraw His provision from the Israelites during the wandering. The manna and quails continued; the twelve springs flowed from the rock when Moses struck it (2:60; 7:160); the cloud shaded them. This is characteristic of divine discipline as the Qur'an presents it: even in punishment, mercy persists. God forbade them the land, but He did not let them starve. The punishment was measured to its purpose — the formation of a new generation — and no further.

**"So Grieve Not for the Iniquitous People"**

*Fa-lā taʾsa ʿalā al-qawmi al-fāsiqīn* — "so do not grieve over the iniquitous people." The verb *asiya* denotes deep sorrow, grief over what is lost. The command is addressed to Moses, and its presence tells us something about his state. Al-Rāzī, as the source notes, understands that Moses, upon hearing the severity of the sentence, was dismayed and regretted his supplication; his heart went out to the people he had led for so long. God consoles him: do not grieve. The consolation carries a reason within it — "over the *iniquitous* people" — the same phrase Moses himself had used in verse 25. God confirms Moses' characterization and thereby confirms the justice of the sentence: these people broke the bounds; their fate is the consequence of their own act; your grief, though natural, is not owed to them.

The Qur'an offers the same consolation to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ many times: "So do not let yourself perish in grief over them" (35:8); "perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps if they do not believe in this discourse" (18:6). The prophetic heart is tender; it grieves over the lost. God honors that tenderness but sets a limit to it: the messenger is responsible for conveying, not for the outcome, and grief over the freely chosen ruin of others must not consume him. Every parent, teacher, and counselor who has grieved over someone who would not be helped is included in this consolation.

**The Narrative's Lesson in Full**

The story of verses 20–26 is now complete, and its structure is a lesson in itself. Favor recalled (v. 20). Command given, with promise and warning (v. 21). Refusal dressed as prudence (v. 22). Faithful counsel from two (v. 23). Refusal hardened into insolence (v. 24). The prophet's plea (v. 25). The verdict: the promise deferred, the generation lost, the prophet consoled (v. 26). The Companions read this story as a warning to themselves, and answered it at Badr. The sūrah, which began with "fulfill your pacts," has now shown a people who did not, and what it cost them. Every reader is left with the question the story is designed to raise: when God writes a land for me and commands me to enter, will I enter — or will I sit, and wander?

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:27

> **And recite unto them, with truth, the account of Adam's two sons, when they each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them, though not accepted from the other. One said, "I will surely slay you!" [The other] said, "God accepts only from the reverent.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Narrative and Its Purpose**

Having told the story of a people who refused to fight when God commanded (vv. 20–26), the sūrah now tells the story of a man who killed when God forbade. The two narratives are complementary: the first exposes cowardice before a righteous struggle, the second exposes violence in an unrighteous cause. Between them they map the two ways human beings misuse the capacity for force. *Wa-tlu ʿalayhim nabaʾa ibnay Ādama bi-l-ḥaqq* — "And recite to them the account of the two sons of Adam in truth." The verb *utlu*, "recite," is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ; the audience, "them," is discussed by the commentators, and the source surveys their views: the Jews who plotted against the Prophet ﷺ (v. 11), whose intention to "stretch forth their hands" against him is echoed in the murderer's threat here (v. 28) — so al-Zamakhsharī; the People of the Book generally, whose spiritual envy of the new revelation resembles the first murderer's envy — so al-Rāzī; or all of humanity, since the story concerns the origin of violence among the children of Adam.

Al-Ṭabarī's reading, preserved in the source, deserves emphasis: the story is told so that the Muslims will deal with those who plot against them as Abel dealt with Cain — with restraint, not with the reciprocal raising of hands. He cites the Prophet's ﷺ counsel for times of civil strife:

> *"Indeed, God has set for you the example of the two sons of Adam; so take the better of the two and leave the worse."* (Aḥmad; Abū Dāwūd 4259, in the ḥadīth of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ concerning the trials to come)

**"In Truth": The Qur'anic Manner of Narration**

*Bi-l-ḥaqq*, "with truth," qualifies the recitation. The Qur'an tells this story not as legend or moral fable but as fact, and it tells it stripped of the embellishments that had accumulated around it in oral and written tradition. The biblical account (Genesis 4) names the brothers and describes Abel's blood crying from the ground; later Jewish and Christian retellings added extensive detail. The Qur'an gives no names — the tradition supplies Qābīl and Hābīl — and confines itself to what carries moral weight: the sacrifice, the acceptance, the threat, the reply, the murder, the crow, and the remorse. The phrase "with truth" also implies "for a true purpose": the story is told because it teaches something needed, not for entertainment.

**The Word Nabaʾ: Momentous News**

*Nabaʾ* is not merely "story" (*qiṣṣah*) but momentous tidings — news of consequence, from the same root as *nabī*, prophet, the bringer of such news. The Qur'an uses *nabaʾ* for the great accounts: the *nabaʾ* of Noah (10:71), of Abraham (26:69), of Moses (28:3), and "the great *nabaʾ*" of the Resurrection (78:2). By calling the account of Adam's two sons a *nabaʾ*, the Qur'an signals that this is not a minor incident from the dawn of time but a revelation of something permanent in the human condition.

**The Sacrifice and the Root of Nearness**

*Idh qarrabā qurbānan* — "when they each offered a sacrifice." Both words are from q-r-b, nearness. A *qurbān* is literally a "means of drawing near"; to *qarraba* is to bring something near, to offer it as a means of approach to God. The source rightly stresses this etymology: sacrifice in the Qur'anic conception is not appeasement of an angry deity but the offering by which the servant approaches his Lord. This root will resurface later in the sūrah, in verse 35: "seek the means (*wasīlah*) of nearness to Him."

The commentators fill in the circumstances from tradition. Al-Ṭabarī transmits that God commanded the two brothers to offer sacrifices; al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī also record the widely circulated account that the sacrifice was a means of settling a dispute over marriage — that each son of Adam was born with a twin sister, that the sons were to marry each other's twins, and that Cain refused because his own twin was more beautiful, so that Adam proposed a sacrifice to decide the matter. The source notes al-Ṭabarī's reservation: the word *qurbān* implies that both brothers sought nearness to God, which sits uneasily with a merely competitive motive. Whatever the occasion, the essential content is the same: Abel, a herdsman, offered the best of his flock — a fat, prized ram; Cain, a farmer, offered the poorest of his produce. Fire descended and consumed Abel's offering, the ancient sign of acceptance (cf. 3:183), and left Cain's untouched.

**Accepted from One, Not from the Other**

*Fa-tuqubbila min aḥadihimā wa-lam yutaqabbal mina al-ākhar* — "and it was accepted from one of them and not accepted from the other." The passive voice conceals the agent and thereby focuses attention on the fact of acceptance rather than on its mechanics. The Qur'an, like Genesis, does not state the reason at this point; it lets Abel state it in his reply. The commentators note that the difference in the offerings — best versus worst — was itself the symptom of the difference in the hearts, and it is the heart that God regards. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed God does not look at your bodies or your forms, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds" (Muslim 2564). And the Qur'an says of the pilgrimage sacrifices, in a verse the source cites:

> *"Neither their flesh nor their blood reaches God, but what reaches Him is the reverence (taqwā) from you."* (Qur'an 22:37)

**The Threat: "I Will Surely Kill You"**

*Qāla la-aqtulannak* — "He said: I will surely kill you." The sentence is a single word in Arabic, with the emphatic *lām* and *nūn*: "I-will-most-certainly-kill-you." Its brevity is chilling. Cain does not argue, complain to God, or ask why his offering failed. He moves directly from rejection to murder. The commentators identify the mechanism: *ḥasad*, envy — the resentment of another's blessing that wishes it removed. Envy was the sin of Iblīs against Adam (his refusal to prostrate because "I am better than he," 7:12), and now it is the sin of Adam's son against Adam's son. The Prophet ﷺ warned: "Beware of envy, for envy devours good deeds as fire devours wood" (Abū Dāwūd 4903). The first murder was the child of the first envy. Al-Rāzī draws the connection to the sūrah's context: the People of the Book who opposed the Prophet ﷺ did so, the Qur'an says elsewhere, "out of envy from their own souls" (2:109), and the story of Cain warns them where envy leads.

**Abel's Reply: "God Accepts Only from the Reverent"**

*Qāla innamā yataqabbalu Allāhu mina al-muttaqīn* — "He said: God accepts only from the God-conscious." This is one of the most quoted sentences in the Qur'an, and it functions on two levels. As a reply to Cain, it is both explanation and gentle rebuke: the fault is not in me but in the manner of your offering; had you offered with *taqwā*, it would have been accepted; so the remedy is not to kill me but to reform yourself. As a universal principle, it states the condition of all worship: acts are accepted according to the state of the heart that performs them. The restrictive particle *innamā*, "only," excludes every other ground of acceptance — not lineage, not quantity, not display, but reverence alone.

The source records al-Ṭabarī's observation that the sacrifice of earlier communities corresponds to charity, prayer, and fasting in Islam, and that Abel's principle therefore governs all these: they are accepted only from the reverent. The Companions felt the weight of this. ʿĀʾishah asked the Prophet ﷺ about the verse "those who give what they give while their hearts tremble" (23:60): is it the one who steals and drinks? He said: "No, daughter of al-Ṣiddīq; it is the one who fasts and prays and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him" (al-Tirmidhī 3175). ʿAlī is reported to have said: "Be more concerned with the acceptance of the deed than with the deed itself; have you not heard God say, 'God accepts only from the reverent'?"

**Sacrifice in Islam: The Continuation of the Principle**

The source connects the story to the living practice of Muslims. The pilgrimage culminates in the sacrifice that commemorates Abraham's readiness to offer his son and God's provision of a ram in his place, and the ʿĪd al-Aḍḥā — also called ʿĪd al-Qurbān in many Muslim lands — repeats it annually. The meat is distributed to the poor. In this practice, Abel's principle and al-Ṭabarī's observation meet: the sacrifice is a means of nearness, its acceptance depends on *taqwā*, and its practical fruit is charity. The believer who slaughters on ʿĪd is re-enacting, with the right intention, what Abel did — and is reminded, by this verse, that the animal is nothing and the reverence is everything.

**The Verse's Opening of the Narrative**

Verse 27 sets the stage with economy: two brothers, two offerings, one acceptance, one threat, one reply. Everything that follows — Abel's refusal to retaliate (v. 28), his reasoning (v. 29), the murder (v. 30), the crow and the remorse (v. 31), and the universal law derived from it (v. 32) — flows from this scene. The reader is meant to feel the shock of Cain's *la-aqtulannak* and the calm of Abel's *innamā yataqabbalu Allāhu mina al-muttaqīn*: the voice of envy and the voice of reverence, set side by side at the very beginning of human history, and echoing in every human heart since.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:28

> **Even if you stretch forth your hand against me to slay me, I shall not stretch forth my hand against you to slay you. Truly I fear God, Lord of the worlds.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reply of the Reverent**

Abel's reply continues. Having stated the principle — God accepts only from the reverent — he now demonstrates what reverence looks like when one's own life is threatened: *la-in basaṭta ilayya yadaka li-taqtulanī mā anā bi-bāsiṭin yadiya ilayka li-aqtulak* — "If you stretch out your hand toward me to kill me, I am not one to stretch out my hand toward you to kill you." The symmetry of the Arabic is exact and deliberate: your hand toward me to kill me / my hand toward you to kill you. Abel takes his brother's threatened act and mirrors it precisely, only to refuse it. The construction *mā anā bi-bāsiṭin* — with the negating *mā* and the emphatic *bi-* — is stronger than a simple "I will not"; it means "I am not the kind of person who would." It describes not a decision made in the moment but a settled character.

The phrase *basaṭa yadahu*, "stretched out his hand," is the Qur'an's idiom for aggression, and the source notes its appearance in verse 11 of this sūrah, where God restrained the hands of those who "were prepared to stretch forth their hands" against the believers. The verbal echo links the primordial murder to the plots against the Prophet ﷺ and, through him, to every act of violence against the innocent.

**Why Did Abel Not Defend Himself?**

This question exercised the commentators, and the source records their answers. The question is a real one, because Islamic law permits — and in some cases requires — self-defense; the Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr; whoever is killed defending his life is a martyr" (Abū Dāwūd 4772; al-Tirmidhī 1421). Why, then, is Abel praised for declining to raise his hand?

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī offer the historical answer: at that early stage of human history, self-defense had not yet been legislated; killing, even in defense, was simply forbidden. On this view, Abel was obeying the law of his time. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī also suggest that the Qur'an presents Abel's restraint to magnify the enormity of Cain's crime: the victim was not a combatant but a man who had explicitly renounced violence, so the murder was of the purest innocence.

Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī propose a more precise reading, which the source preserves: Abel's words are not a renunciation of *defense* but a renunciation of *killing*. He says, "I will not stretch out my hand to *kill* you" — not "I will not resist you." On this reading, Abel refuses to become a murderer, whether preemptively or in the heat of struggle, but does not necessarily forgo repelling the attack by other means. The distinction matters in Islamic law, which permits repelling an attacker with the least force necessary and treats the taking of life as a last resort.

There is also the report, transmitted by al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī, that Cain killed Abel while he slept, so that the question of defense never practically arose. And al-Rāzī allows a further possibility: that Abel judged it better to be killed than to kill, even in self-defense, when the attacker was his own brother and a fellow monotheist. This last reading connects to the Prophet's ﷺ guidance for times of civil strife among Muslims.

**The Verse in the Crisis of the Early Community**

The source records an application of this verse that reveals its power. During the First Civil War (36–40 AH), when Muslims fought Muslims after the murder of ʿUthmān, a number of eminent Companions — ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Muḥammad ibn Maslamah, Usāmah ibn Zayd — refused to take up arms on either side. Al-Qurṭubī notes that they cited Abel as their model. Their reasoning was that when both parties are believers, the one who refuses to kill is on the safer side, whatever the outcome. The Prophet ﷺ had foreseen this and had given guidance in exactly Abel's terms:

> *"There will be trials in which the one sitting is better than the one standing, the one standing better than the one walking, and the one walking better than the one running... So if you are able to be the servant of God who is killed rather than the one who kills, then be so."* (Aḥmad; Abū Dāwūd 4259, from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ; a similar text in al-Bukhārī 3601 and Muslim 2886)

And in the version that names our verse's protagonist directly: *"Be like the better of the two sons of Adam."* (Abū Dāwūd 4257; al-Tirmidhī 2194)

The believer thus receives from Abel a rule for the hardest case — not the case of an external enemy, against whom defense is plainly lawful, but the case of a brother in faith who has become an aggressor. In that case, Abel's way — to refuse to become a killer — is the way the Prophet ﷺ commended.

**"Truly I Fear God, Lord of the Worlds"**

*Innī akhāfu Allāha rabba al-ʿālamīn* — "Indeed, I fear God, the Lord of the worlds." Here is the reason for Abel's restraint, and it is the same reason that explains his acceptance: *taqwā*, reverent fear of God. Cain feared nothing but the loss of status; Abel feared God, and that fear made him incapable of murder. The verse thus completes the thought of verse 27: God accepts only from the reverent, and here is what the reverent do — they refuse to kill even when threatened with death.

The choice of the divine title *Rabb al-ʿālamīn*, "Lord of the worlds," is meaningful. Abel does not say merely "I fear God"; he names God by the title that emphasizes His universal Lordship — over both brothers, over the sacrifice, over life and death. The One who accepted my offering is the Lord of both of us, and He will judge between us; I need not take judgment into my own hands. The title also appears in the second verse of the Fātiḥah, and Abel's use of it places him among the first worshippers who understood God as Lord of all that exists.

The psychological content of this fear deserves attention. It is not terror; it is the awareness that God sees, that He will call to account, and that the taking of an innocent life is something one could never justify before Him. This awareness restrains the hand more effectively than any law. Laws can be evaded when no one is watching; the fear of God operates precisely when no one is watching. Abel and Cain were alone; there was no witness, no court, no police. What stood between Abel and violence was *innī akhāfu Allāh*.

**The Strength in Refusal**

It would be easy to read Abel's stance as weakness. The Qur'an presents it as strength. The person who can be threatened with death and reply, calmly, "I will not kill you, for I fear God," has mastered the most powerful instinct there is — the instinct of self-preservation by any means. Cain, by contrast, is the weak one: enslaved by envy, unable to bear his brother's success, incapable of the self-examination that would have shown him the fault in his own offering. The Prophet ﷺ defined the matter: "The strong man is not the one who overcomes others in wrestling; the strong man is the one who controls himself when angry" (al-Bukhārī 6114; Muslim 2609). By this definition, Abel is the strong brother and Cain the weak one, and the verse inverts the world's estimate of strength.

**The Verse for the Reader**

Verse 28 teaches a discipline of the hand rooted in the fear of God. It does not abolish self-defense, which the Law establishes elsewhere; it establishes a ceiling above which the believer will not go — he will not become a killer of the innocent, and among believers in conflict he will lean toward the side that suffers rather than the side that inflicts. In an age when provocation is constant and retaliation is celebrated, Abel's reply is a standing rebuke and a standing invitation: to be the one who, when hands are raised against him, keeps his own hand down, and says why.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:29

> **I desire that you should be burdened with my sin and your sin and so become one of the inhabitants of the Fire. Such is the recompense of the wrongdoers."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Conclusion of Abel's Speech**

Abel's reply, begun in verse 27 and continued in verse 28, closes here with a statement that has troubled some readers and illuminated others: *innī urīdu an tabūʾa bi-ithmī wa-ithmika fa-takūna min aṣḥābi al-nāri wa-dhālika jazāʾu al-ẓālimīn* — "Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin and so be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers." The sentence completes Abel's reasoning. He has said he will not kill (v. 28) and given the reason — fear of God. Now he explains the consequence of his choice: if one of us must bear the sin of murder, let it be you, not me.

**The Verb "Bear": Returning with a Burden**

*Tabūʾa* is from b-w-ʾ, which means to return to a place, to settle, to come back bearing something; the Qur'an uses it of those who "return with wrath from God" (2:61, 90; 3:112; 8:16). The image is of a person returning home laden — here, laden with sin. Abel is saying: I would rather you return to God carrying the burden than that I do. The Qur'an elsewhere uses the same verb of the one who confesses: "I return to You with Your favor upon me, and I return with my sin" (the ḥadīth of *Sayyid al-Istighfār*, al-Bukhārī 6306, uses *abūʾu*). To "return with" sin is to arrive at the reckoning bearing it.

**"My Sin and Your Sin": What Is Meant**

The phrase *bi-ithmī wa-ithmika*, "my sin and your sin," requires careful reading, and the source presents the commentators' resolution. Taken literally, it might suggest that Cain would bear the burden of Abel's own sins — a transfer of moral responsibility that the Qur'an categorically rejects: "No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another" (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38). Al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī therefore explain that "my sin" means "the sin of killing me" (*ithm qatlī*) — the word "killing" being elided by a common Arabic ellipsis — and "your sin" means the sins Cain had already committed, including the defective sacrifice and the envy that followed it. On this reading, Abel says: you will bear the sin of murdering me, on top of your own prior sins.

Another reading, also transmitted by the commentators and grounded in an authentic ḥadīth, takes "my sin" in a more specific sense. The Prophet ﷺ said of the wronged party on the Day of Judgment: "The bankrupt of my community is he who comes on the Day of Resurrection with prayer, fasting, and charity, but has insulted this one, slandered that one, consumed the wealth of this one, shed the blood of that one, and struck this one; so this one is given of his good deeds and that one of his good deeds, and if his good deeds are exhausted before what is owed is paid, their sins are taken and cast upon him, and he is thrown into the Fire" (Muslim 2581). On this basis, some understood Abel to mean: on the Day of Judgment, you will be made to carry the sins I would otherwise have carried, as compensation for the wrong you did me. The murderer does, in this sense, come to "bear the sin" of his victim — not by an unjust transfer, but by the just settlement of accounts.

Both readings preserve the principle of individual responsibility. In neither does Abel wish that Cain be punished for what Cain did not do; in both, Cain bears what his own act brings upon him.

**Did Abel "Desire" His Brother's Damnation?**

The verb *urīdu*, "I want," raises a further question: is it fitting for a righteous man to *want* his brother in the Fire? The commentators answer that Abel's statement is not a wish but a preference between two alternatives, and the alternatives were set by Cain, not by Abel. Given that Cain has resolved on murder, and given that Abel will not kill, one of two things must happen: either Cain kills Abel and bears the sin, or Abel kills Cain and bears it. Abel "wants" the first only in the sense that he prefers it to the second — he prefers to be the wronged rather than the wrongdoer. Al-Rāzī puts it thus: Abel does not desire his brother's sin as such; he desires that, if there must be a sin, it be his brother's and not his own. This is the exact meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ counsel to "be the servant of God who is killed rather than the one who kills."

There is also a rhetorical dimension. Abel's statement is a final warning to Cain. By naming the consequence — "you will be among the companions of the Fire" — Abel gives his brother one last chance to see where his intention leads. Al-Qushayrī, cited in the source's discussion of the next verse, observes that once the soul has resolved on evil, warnings become muted; but the warning must still be given. Abel gives it. Cain does not hear.

**"And That Is the Recompense of the Wrongdoers"**

*Wa-dhālika jazāʾu al-ẓālimīn* — "and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers." *Ẓulm*, wrongdoing, is literally to place something where it does not belong — to put darkness where light should be, to give a thing other than its due. Murder is the ultimate *ẓulm*: it places death where God placed life. The closing formula generalizes the case. What is true of Cain is true of every wrongdoer: the recompense of *ẓulm* is the Fire. The phrase appears throughout the Qur'an (e.g., 59:17) and functions here to lift the story from the particular to the universal. The reader is not merely watching two ancient brothers; he is learning the law of consequence that governs his own acts.

**The Wisdom of Preferring to Be Wronged**

The stance Abel takes in this verse is among the most spiritually advanced in the Qur'an, and it deserves to be understood correctly. It is not passivity in the face of injustice generally; the Qur'an commands resistance to oppression and defense of the weak. It is a specific choice in a specific situation: when the only alternatives are to kill a brother or to be killed by him, the reverent person chooses to be the victim rather than the criminal. The reasoning is that the victim loses this life, which he will lose anyway; the criminal loses the next, which is everlasting. The Prophet ﷺ described those who make this choice in times of civil strife: "The one killed will be in Paradise, and the killer in the Fire" — and when asked about the one killed, who also wished to kill his companion, he said, "He was eager to kill his companion," meaning that both had become killers in intent (al-Bukhārī 31; Muslim 2888). Abel's distinction is that he had *no* such intent, and the verse records his innocence in his own words.

**A Theology of Loss and Gain**

Verse 29 quietly inverts the ordinary calculation of loss and gain. In the world's reckoning, Abel lost everything and Cain won. In the Qur'an's reckoning, Abel — who died with no sin of violence on his soul and with his sacrifice accepted — is the victor, and Cain — who lived on with the burden of the first murder — is "among the losers," as the next verse will say. The Qur'an's consistent use of commercial vocabulary (*khusr*, loss; *ribḥ*, profit; *tijārah*, trade) for spiritual outcomes reflects this inversion: the true ledger is kept elsewhere, and the person who preserves his soul at the cost of his life has made the better trade. The believer who understands this is freed from the fear that makes people do terrible things to survive.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:30

> **Then his soul prompted him to slay his brother, and he slew him, and thus came to be among the losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Deed and Its Anatomy**

After Abel's long reply — the principle, the refusal, the warning — the Qur'an narrates the murder in a single verse of stark economy: *fa-ṭawwaʿat lahu nafsuhu qatla akhīhi fa-qatalahu fa-aṣbaḥa mina al-khāsirīn* — "Then his soul made easy for him the killing of his brother, so he killed him, and became among the losers." Three clauses, three stages: the inward consent, the outward act, the lasting consequence. The Qur'an does not describe the method, the place, or the moment; the commentators supply from tradition that Cain crushed his brother's head with a stone, most say while he slept, and some say that Satan showed him the method by killing a bird before his eyes (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The Qur'an's silence on these details focuses the reader on what matters: how a human being comes to kill his brother.

**"His Soul Made It Easy for Him"**

The verb *ṭawwaʿat* is the key to the verse. It is from ṭ-w-ʿ, obedience, willingness (the same root as *ṭāʿah*, obedience, and *taṭawwuʿ*, voluntary devotion). In its intensive form here, it means to make something compliant, to render it easy, to bring it within reach of the will. The source records the commentators' glosses: the soul "led him," "encouraged him," "made it easy for him," "made it seem good to him," "emboldened him" (al-Ājurrī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The murder had seemed monstrous even to Cain; his soul worked on the monstrousness until it became doable. This is the precise psychology of grave sin. No one begins by finding murder easy. The soul must first be brought to consent — by rehearsing the grievance, by inflating the injury, by diminishing the victim, by imagining the relief that the act will bring — until what was unthinkable becomes, step by step, merely difficult, and then possible, and then done.

Al-Qushayrī's remark, cited in the source, penetrates further: once the soul has formed an intention toward evil — as Cain's had when he said "I will surely kill you" in verse 27 — subsequent calls to righteousness lose their force. This explains why Abel's reply, for all its wisdom, had no effect. Cain was no longer listening. The intention had closed his ears. The lesson is that the decisive battle is fought at the level of intention, before the act; once the soul has been made compliant, the act follows almost of itself.

**The Nafs That Commands Evil**

The word *nafs*, soul, here denotes the lower self, the seat of appetite and passion. The source connects it to Joseph's confession: "I do not absolve my own soul; indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except that on which my Lord has mercy" (12:53). Islamic spiritual psychology, developed by al-Ghazālī and others from these verses, distinguishes the *nafs al-ammārah bi-l-sūʾ* (the soul commanding evil), the *nafs al-lawwāmah* (the reproaching soul, 75:2), and the *nafs al-muṭmaʾinnah* (the soul at peace, 89:27). Cain's soul, in verse 30, is the first; in verse 31, when remorse overtakes him, it becomes the second — too late. The verse thus teaches that the soul is not a fixed thing but a field of struggle, and that the outcome depends on which of its tendencies a person feeds.

The Prophet ﷺ described the mechanism of temptation in similar terms: "Satan flows in the son of Adam as blood flows" (al-Bukhārī 2039; Muslim 2175), and the Qur'an says that on the Day of Judgment Satan will disown those he misled: "I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me; so do not blame me, but blame yourselves" (14:22). Whatever Satan's role in showing Cain the method, the verse places responsibility squarely in Cain's own *nafs*: *his* soul made it easy for *him*. This is the Qur'anic refusal to let the sinner externalize his sin.

**"So He Killed Him"**

*Fa-qatalahu* — "so he killed him." Two words. The Qur'an does not linger. The brevity conveys the terrible simplicity of the act once the soul has consented: after all the inner work of making it easy, the deed itself takes a moment. The word *akhīhi*, "his brother," in the preceding clause, is repeated by implication; the Qur'an does not let the reader forget that the victim was not a stranger, not an enemy, but the killer's own brother, born of the same parents, who had just declared that he would not raise his hand against him. The first murder in human history was fratricide, and every murder since has been, in the Qur'an's understanding, a killing of a brother in Adam.
