The tradition, transmitted by al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī, adds that Adam lived many years after this but never laughed again. Whatever the historicity of that detail, it expresses a truth: the first murder introduced into the human family a grief that has never left it.

**"And He Became Among the Losers"**

*Fa-aṣbaḥa mina al-khāsirīn* — "and he became among the losers." The verb *aṣbaḥa*, literally "he entered the morning," is used in Arabic for a change of state — "he came to be." The murder did not merely add a sin to Cain's account; it changed what he *was*. He became a *khāsir*, one who has lost. The same word closed the story of the Israelites in verse 21 ("or you will become losers") and will describe the state of all who reject faith (5:5). The Qur'an's commercial vocabulary is exact: Cain had a brother, a family, a place among the children of Adam, a relationship with God, and the possibility of an accepted sacrifice. He traded all of it for the momentary satisfaction of envy. No trade in history has been worse.

The Prophet ﷺ made Cain's loss permanent and cumulative in a way the verse implies: "No soul is killed unjustly but that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to institute killing" (al-Bukhārī 3335; Muslim 1677). Every murder since Abel's adds to Cain's burden, because he opened the door. This is the principle the Prophet ﷺ stated generally: "Whoever institutes an evil practice in Islam bears its sin and the sin of everyone who acts on it after him, without their sins being diminished" (Muslim 1017). The "loss" of verse 30 is therefore not a single loss but an ever-growing one, as long as human beings kill.

**The Verse as a Warning About Process**

The greatest value of this verse is its exposure of process. Sin is presented not as a lightning strike but as a sequence: envy (v. 27), threat (v. 27), the closing of the ears to counsel (vv. 28–29), the soul's gradual consent (v. 30), the act (v. 30), and the loss (v. 30). Every stage before the act was an opportunity to stop. Cain could have examined his sacrifice, could have heeded his brother's principle, could have feared the Fire his brother named, could have refused his soul's easing. He did none of these. The verse is a warning to intervene early — at the level of envy, before it becomes threat; at the level of threat, before the soul begins its work; at the level of the soul's work, before the hand moves. The Prophet ﷺ taught: "Do not be angry" (al-Bukhārī 6116) — not "do not kill," which is too late, but "do not be angry," which is where killing begins.

**The Verse for Today**

Every reader has a *nafs* capable of *taṭwīʿ* — of making the forbidden seem possible. The forbidden thing may not be murder; it may be a betrayal, a theft, a lie, a cruelty. The process is the same. The verse asks the reader to notice the moment when his soul begins to make a wrong thing "easy" — to hear the inner rehearsal of justifications — and to recognize it for what it is: the same voice that spoke in Cain before he killed his brother. The one who catches that voice early can silence it. The one who lets it finish its work will find, like Cain, that the act itself takes only a moment, and the loss lasts forever.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:31

> **Then God sent a crow, scratching the earth, to show him how he might conceal his brother's nakedness. He said, "Oh, woe unto me! Am I not able to be even as this crow and conceal my brother's nakedness?" And he came to be among the remorseful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Corpse and the Ignorance of the Killer**

The murder is done. Now the Qur'an shows its aftermath, and it does so through an image found in no other scripture: *fa-baʿatha Allāhu ghurāban yabḥathu fī al-arḍi li-yuriyahu kayfa yuwārī sawʾata akhīh* — "Then God sent a crow, scratching in the earth, to show him how to hide his brother's corpse." The commentators explain the situation the verse presupposes. Abel was, according to al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī, the first human being to die — or at least the first to be killed — and Cain did not know what to do with a dead body. Burial had not yet been taught. He is reported to have carried the body on his back for days, not knowing where to put it, while it began to decay and the beasts and birds gathered. The man who had known how to kill did not know how to bury. The verse captures a terrible incongruity: the capacity for destruction outran the capacity for care.

**The Crow as Teacher**

*Ghurāb*, crow or raven, is the bird the Qur'an chooses, and the choice repays reflection. The crow is a scavenger, associated in most cultures with death and ill omen; the Arabs derived words for separation and misfortune from its name. Yet here God makes it the instrument of the first lesson in human dignity. The verb *yabḥathu* means to dig, to search by scratching — the root of *baḥth*, research, investigation. The crow, according to the most widely transmitted account (al-Ṭabarī), was one of two crows that fought until one killed the other; the survivor then dug in the earth with its beak and claws and buried the dead one. Al-Rāzī records alternative versions: that the crow was digging to bury some other thing and gave Cain the idea, or that the crow began covering Abel's body itself.

Whatever the version, the structure is the same. A bird — a creature without revelation, without law, without the intellect that distinguishes the human being — performs an act of concealment and respect toward its dead that the son of Adam had not thought to perform. The Qur'an says God *sent* the crow (*baʿatha*, the verb used for sending prophets and raising the dead); the bird was on a mission. The source rightly draws the inference: the rite of burial was taught to humanity by God, through the humblest of teachers.

**"To Conceal His Brother's Nakedness"**

*Sawʾah* is a word of shame. From s-w-ʾ, evil, badness, it denotes what is shameful to expose — used in the Qur'an for the private parts of Adam and Eve that became visible after the fall (7:20, 22, 27). The source notes the two readings: al-Zamakhsharī takes it as the shame of Abel's exposed, decomposing body; al-Ṭabarī glosses it simply as "corpse." Both are contained in the word. A dead human body left uncovered is a *sawʾah* — an exposure that offends the dignity of the person who inhabited it. The verb *yuwārī*, from w-r-y, to hide behind something, to cover, is the same verb the Qur'an uses of the garments given to clothe the *sawʾah* of Adam's children (7:26). The parallel is exact: as clothing covers the shame of the living, burial covers the shame of the dead. Both are acts of *satr*, of covering, which Islam ranks among the highest human duties.

From this verse the jurists derived the obligation of burial. It is a communal duty (*farḍ kifāyah*) to wash, shroud, pray over, and bury the dead, and the Prophet ﷺ commanded haste in it: "Hasten with the funeral" (al-Bukhārī 1315; Muslim 944). He forbade the mutilation of corpses even in war and instructed that the dead of the enemy at Badr be buried. The dignity that a crow taught Cain became, in the Law, a right owed to every human body.

**The Cry of Regret**

*Qāla yā waylatā a-ʿajaztu an akūna mithla hādhā al-ghurābi fa-uwāriya sawʾata akhī* — "He said: O woe is me! Was I unable to be like this crow and hide my brother's corpse?" The exclamation *yā waylatā*, "O my woe," is the Qur'an's cry of realized ruin; the source lists its occurrences (18:49; 21:14, 47, 97; 25:28; 36:52; 37:20; 68:31), most of them on the Day of Judgment when the wrongdoers see their record. Cain utters it in this life, at the sight of a bird. The question *a-ʿajaztu*, "was I incapable?", is one of self-contempt: a crow could do what I could not. The killer who had considered himself strong enough to take a life discovers that he is weaker, in the things that matter, than a scavenging bird.

Notice what triggers the regret. It is not Abel's warning about the Fire (v. 29) — that had no effect. It is the sight of the crow's decency. Cain is shamed not by argument but by example. This is a profound observation about the human heart: exhortation can be resisted; the silent witness of a good act cannot be so easily dismissed. The crow did not preach. It buried its dead, and the murderer wept. The Prophet ﷺ taught by the same method; his Companions learned more from watching him than from any sermon, and the Qur'an says of him: "You have in the Messenger of God a beautiful example" (33:21).

**"And He Became Among the Remorseful"**

*Fa-aṣbaḥa mina al-nādimīn* — "and he came to be among the regretful." The verb *aṣbaḥa* echoes the end of verse 30 — "he came to be among the losers" — and the two endings frame Cain's state: loser and regretter. *Nadam*, regret, is from n-d-m, and it is the root of the word the Prophet ﷺ used to define repentance: "Regret is repentance" (*al-nadam tawbah*, Ibn Mājah 4252; Aḥmad; graded ṣaḥīḥ). Was Cain's regret, then, repentance?

The commentators say no, and their reasoning is instructive. Cain regretted, but what did he regret? The commentators — al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī — observe that the text presents his regret as arising from his inability to bury the body, his shame before the crow, his fear of his parents' reaction, and the burden of carrying a corpse — not from the recognition that he had wronged God and murdered his brother. Regret over the *consequences* of a sin is not repentance; repentance is regret over the *sin itself*, combined with the resolve never to return to it and the effort to make amends. The Qur'an nowhere records Cain's turning to God, seeking forgiveness, or acknowledging Abel's right. His *nadam* remained at the level of self-pity — "woe is me" — and self-pity is not contrition. The ḥadīth cited above confirms that Cain's burden continued to grow with every subsequent murder; had he truly repented, the tradition would not have recorded this.

This distinction is among the most practically important in the spiritual life. Many people regret their sins in Cain's manner: they regret being caught, regret the damage to their reputation, regret the loss they suffered, regret how they now feel. Such regret may be sincere as an emotion and yet fall short of repentance, because its object is the self, not the wrong. True repentance turns outward and upward: toward the one wronged, and toward God. The test is simple: does the regret produce a change of conduct and a seeking of forgiveness, or only a lament?

**The Verse's Place in the Story**

Verse 31 is the story's turn from crime to consequence, and it prepares the universal law of verse 32. Cain has learned, from a crow, what he should have known from his own heart: that a human being is worthy of care even in death. This knowledge, arriving too late, is his punishment in this world — the punishment of understanding what one has destroyed only after destroying it. And it is the Qur'an's way of establishing, before stating the law of the sanctity of life, that even the murderer cannot escape the recognition of that sanctity. The crow taught Cain that a body must be honored. The next verse will teach all humanity that a life must be preserved.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:32

> **For this reason, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whosoever slays a soul—unless it be for another soul or working corruption upon the earth—it is as though he slew mankind altogether, and whosoever saves the life of one, it is as though he saved the life of mankind altogether. Our messengers have certainly come unto them with clear proofs. Yet even after that, many of them are prodigal on the earth.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Law Drawn from the Story**

The narrative of the two sons of Adam has been told; now its moral is codified. *Min ajli dhālika katabnā ʿalā Banī Isrāʾīla* — "For this reason, We prescribed for the Children of Israel..." The phrase *min ajli dhālika*, "because of that," binds the law to the story: because one man killed his brother out of envy, and because that act opened the door to all subsequent killing, God laid down a principle that would fix in human consciousness the true weight of a single life. The verb *katabnā*, "We wrote, We prescribed," is the language of binding legislation (2:183: "fasting is prescribed for you"). What follows is not a sentiment but a law.

This verse has become, in the modern world, the most widely quoted sentence of the Qur'an. It appears on monuments, in charters, in the speeches of statesmen, in the mission statements of humanitarian organizations. Its fame is deserved, and the commentators' careful reading of it reveals that its depth exceeds even its reputation.

**Why the Children of Israel?**

The verse says the law was prescribed for the Children of Israel, and the source records the commentators' reflections on this. Al-Qurṭubī notes that they were the first religious community to be explicitly threatened with eternal punishment for murder, in the Torah's commandment. Al-Rāzī connects the specification to the sūrah's context: certain Jews of Madinah had plotted to kill the Prophet ﷺ (v. 11), and the verse reminds them that their own Law contains this principle. The source also notes that the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 4:5) preserves a closely parallel statement — that whoever destroys a single life is regarded as if he destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves a single life as if he saved a whole world — and that Jewish tradition, like the Qur'an, connects this teaching to the story of Cain and Abel. The Qur'an here confirms a truth the People of the Book already possessed and calls them to live by it.

But the commentators are unanimous — Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī — that the principle binds Muslims equally. The Qur'an states the same sanctity of life for this community in other terms: "Do not kill the soul which God has made sacred, except by right" (6:151; 17:33); and the Prophet ﷺ declared in his Farewell Sermon: "Your blood, your property, and your honor are sacred to one another, as the sacredness of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours" (al-Bukhārī 67; Muslim 1679). The law was prescribed for Israel; it is affirmed for all.

**"Whosoever Slays a Soul"**

*Man qatala nafsan* — "whoever kills a soul." The word *nafs*, soul or person, is unqualified: not "a believing soul," not "an Israelite soul," but *a soul*. The sanctity extends to every human being. The Qur'an's choice of the indefinite is deliberate; the jurists derived from it, together with 6:151 and 17:33, that the life of every human being is protected by default, and that only a specific, lawful cause can remove that protection.

**The Two Exceptions**

*Bi-ghayri nafsin aw fasādin fī al-arḍ* — "other than for a soul or for corruption in the earth." The verse names two grounds on which the taking of life is not the crime it describes. The first is *qiṣāṣ*, retribution for murder: "a soul for a soul" (5:45), the lawful execution, by due process, of one who has unlawfully killed. The second is *fasād fī al-arḍ*, "corruption in the earth," which the next verse (5:33) will define in terms of armed brigandage and warfare against the community, and which the commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) explain as including idolatrous aggression, waging war on the Muslims, and terrorizing the roads. Al-Rāzī extends the first exception to any crime for which the Law prescribes capital punishment.

The exceptions are essential to the verse's coherence. A law that forbade all killing without exception would make justice impossible: it would protect the murderer from the consequence of his murder and the brigand from the consequence of his terror. The Qur'an's principle is not that life may never be taken, but that it may be taken only *by right* — by lawful authority, after due process, for a cause the Law recognizes. The person who kills outside these bounds — the murderer, the terrorist, the vigilante, the one who kills for revenge, for gain, for envy like Cain — has done what the verse describes.

**"As Though He Slew Mankind Altogether"**

*Fa-ka-annamā qatala al-nāsa jamīʿan* — "it is as if he had killed all of mankind." The commentators labored to explain this equivalence, and the source presents their explanations, each of which illuminates a facet of the truth.

Some, as al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī record, understood it of the killing of a person of special sanctity — a prophet or a just leader — whose death is a catastrophe for all. Others understood it *from the victim's point of view*: to the one killed, his death is the end of the whole world; he loses everything, as if all humanity had perished. Others understood it from the perspective of the *offense to God*: the one who kills a single innocent has violated the sanctity God placed on human life as such, and that violation is the same in kind whether the victims are one or many — he has declared, by his act, that human life is his to take, and that declaration is an assault on all life. Mujāhid, as the source notes, understood it of the punishment: the murderer of one incurs the Fire, and the murderer of many can incur no worse; the Hereafter's penalty for the crime does not scale with the count.

Ibn ʿAbbās offered a reading that the tradition has treasured: whoever kills a soul is like one who killed all mankind because he has *violated the sanctity of all of them*; and whoever saves a soul has *honored the sanctity of all of them*. On this reading, the verse is about the principle at stake, not the number of bodies. The murderer's act says: "Human life may be taken by private will." If that principle stood, no human being would be safe. The one who saves a life says the opposite: "Human life is inviolable." If that principle stands, all human beings are safe. Each act is thus, in its logic, an act toward all of humanity.

A modern reader may add another consideration. Each human being is a unique, unrepeatable world: a consciousness, a history, a web of relationships, a set of descendants who will now never exist. To extinguish one is to extinguish an entire world that will never come again. The verse's "as though" is not hyperbole; it is a description of what a single death actually is when seen truly.

**"And Whosoever Saves a Life"**

*Wa-man aḥyāhā fa-ka-annamā aḥyā al-nāsa jamīʿan* — "and whoever gives it life, it is as if he gave life to all of mankind." The positive half of the principle is as important as the negative, and the commentators were expansive in defining what "giving life" includes. The source records: the next of kin who forgoes retaliation and accepts blood-money or forgives outright (2:178), thereby sparing a life that the law would have permitted him to take; the one who rescues a person from drowning, fire, or starvation; and, in the broader reading recorded by al-Qummī and others, the one who lifts a person from poverty or from spiritual ruin. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī extended the meaning to the one who refrains from killing when he could have killed: by not killing, he has "given life."

The verb *aḥyā*, "to give life," is used in the Qur'an primarily of God; that the verse uses it of a human act elevates that act to a participation in a divine attribute. The physician who saves a patient, the rescuer who pulls a child from the water, the donor whose gift feeds a famine victim, the mediator who prevents a war, the teacher who turns a young person from a ruinous path — each has "given life," and each, the verse says, has done something whose value is measured against the whole of humanity. The Prophet ﷺ gave the principle a daily form: "In every living creature there is reward" for the one who gives it drink (al-Bukhārī 2363; Muslim 2244).

**"Our Messengers Came to Them with Clear Proofs"**

*Wa-laqad jāʾathum rusulunā bi-l-bayyināt* — "And Our messengers certainly came to them with clear proofs." Having stated the law, the verse records that it was delivered with evidence: not merely inscribed but explained, demonstrated, confirmed by messengers with signs. The Children of Israel — and, through them, all who received the message — cannot plead that the sanctity of life was obscure. It was among the clearest of all teachings.

**"Yet Even After That, Many of Them Are Prodigal on the Earth"**

*Thumma inna kathīran minhum baʿda dhālika fī al-arḍi la-musrifūn* — "then indeed, many of them, after that, are extravagant in the earth." *Isrāf* is excess, extravagance, the transgression of proper limits — used in the Qur'an of wasteful spending (7:31), of Pharaoh's tyranny (10:83), and of the taking of life beyond right (17:33: "let him not exceed (*lā yusrif*) in killing"). The verse ends on a note of realism: the law was given, the proofs were shown, and *many* — not all — still killed beyond every limit. The word "many" (*kathīr*) again preserves the Qur'an's refusal to condemn a whole people; the sūrah will speak in verse 66 of "a moderate community" among them.

The sadness of this ending is deliberate. The most beautiful statement of the sanctity of life in any scripture is followed immediately by the acknowledgment that it has been, and will be, ignored. This is the human record. Cain's regret did not stop the killing; the law given to Israel did not stop it; the Qur'an's restatement has not stopped it. The verse does not despair, but it does not pretend. It states the law with full clarity, so that those who will hear may hear, and it names the fact that many will not. The reader who takes the verse to heart joins the minority the verse implicitly honors: those who, "after that," were *not* prodigal, who held a single life to be worth the whole world, and lived accordingly.

**The Verse's Enduring Charge**

Verse 32 is the Qur'an's answer to the question that the story of the two sons of Adam poses: what is a human life worth? The answer is: everything. Not the life of one's own tribe, faith, or nation — *a soul*. Not only in the refraining from killing but in the active saving. The verse confers on every human being an infinite value and on every believer an infinite responsibility. The Muslim who reads it cannot regard any killing outside the bounds of law as small, and cannot regard any act of saving as small. In a world where death is counted in statistics, the verse insists on the arithmetic of heaven, in which one equals all.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:33

> **Verily the recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger, and endeavor to work corruption upon the earth is that they be killed or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be banished from the land. That is their disgrace in this world, and in the Hereafter theirs shall be a great punishment,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Sanctity of Life to the Defense of Society**

The previous verse established that the killing of one soul is like the killing of all mankind, and it named two exceptions: retribution for a soul, and "corruption in the earth." This verse defines the second exception and prescribes its penalty. The sequence is coherent: a law that sanctifies life must also provide for the punishment of those who make life unsafe for everyone. *Innamā jazāʾu alladhīna yuḥāribūna Allāha wa-rasūlahu wa-yasʿawna fī al-arḍi fasādan* — "The recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive in the earth to spread corruption is only that..." This is the verse of *ḥirābah*, one of the five *ḥudūd* — the fixed penalties for crimes the Qur'an itself names (the others being theft, in verse 38; adultery and slander, in Sūrat al-Nūr; and the penalty for murder through *qiṣāṣ*).

**"Waging War Against God and His Messenger"**

The phrase *yuḥāribūna Allāha wa-rasūlahu* is, as al-Qurṭubī notes in the source, a figure: one cannot literally make war on God. The meaning is that they make war on His servants, His law, and the order He has established, and this is described as war on Him and His Messenger because the community's security is His right and His Messenger's charge. The Qur'an uses similar language in 2:279, where those who persist in usury are told to "take notice of a war from God and His Messenger." The crimes covered are collectively called *ḥirābah*, from ḥ-r-b, war; the perpetrators are *muḥāribūn*, "warriors" against the public peace. The jurists defined *ḥirābah* as taking up arms to rob, kill, rape, or terrorize openly, so that the victims cannot seek help — classically on the highways, but, as the source notes, also in towns and settled areas according to most schools. The hallmark that distinguishes *ḥirābah* from ordinary theft or assault is the use of weapons and terror: it is crime that attacks not merely an individual but the general sense of safety on which communal life depends.

**"Striving in the Earth to Spread Corruption"**

*Yasʿawna fī al-arḍi fasādan* — "and they strive in the land for corruption." *Fasād* is the opposite of *ṣalāḥ*, soundness; it is spoilage, rot, the disordering of what should be ordered. The source rightly observes that the phrase is broad in its other Qur'anic uses — spiritual corruption (2:11–12), the wickedness of nations (7:74, 85–86), the tyranny of Pharaoh (28:4) — and that in 2:30 the angels linked "working corruption" directly to "shedding blood," anticipating the story of Cain that has just been told. But in this verse, the major commentators — al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī — limit its legal application to the armed crimes just described. The word *yasʿawna*, "they strive, they run about," indicates active, deliberate effort: not a single lapse but a campaign of corruption. The verse is thus aimed at those who make violence their occupation.

**The Occasion: The Men of ʿUkl and ʿUraynah**

The source preserves the most widely attested occasion of revelation, recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ. A group of men from the tribes of ʿUkl and ʿUraynah came to Madinah and professed Islam. The climate disagreed with them and they fell ill. The Prophet ﷺ, with characteristic care, sent them out to the pasture where the community's camels grazed and told them to drink the camels' milk and urine (a remedy of that age) until they recovered. They recovered — and then they murdered the herdsman, gouged out his eyes, drove off the camels, and fled. The Prophet ﷺ sent men in pursuit; they were captured and brought back, and he ordered that their hands and feet be cut off and their eyes put out, and they were left in the sun until they died (al-Bukhārī 233, 3018; Muslim 1671). This verse was then revealed.

The commentators, as the source records, disagreed on the verse's relationship to the Prophet's ﷺ action. Some, cited by al-Ṭabarī, held that the verse confirmed and clarified what he had done. Others, cited by al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī, held that it qualified the punishment: the verse names execution, crucifixion, cross-amputation, and banishment, but not the gouging of eyes or exposure until death, and the Prophet ﷺ is not known to have repeated those measures afterward. Anas ibn Mālik himself, the narrator, is reported to have said that the Prophet ﷺ subsequently forbade mutilation. Al-Qurṭubī records the reading that the verse thus implicitly bans torture. A third group reconciled the accounts: the gouging of the eyes was *qiṣāṣ*, exact retribution for what the criminals had done to the herdsman, whose eyes they had put out — and retribution in kind is a separate principle (2:178; 5:45). What is agreed is that after this verse, the penalty for *ḥirābah* is confined to what it names, and that the Prophet ﷺ prohibited torture and mutilation in every other context: "The most restrained of people in killing are the people of faith" (Abū Dāwūd 2666).

**The Four Penalties and Their Correlation to the Crime**

The verse lists four punishments joined by "or": *an yuqattalū aw yuṣallabū aw tuqaṭṭaʿa aydīhim wa-arjuluhum min khilāfin aw yunfaw mina al-arḍ* — "that they be killed, or crucified, or their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or exiled from the land." The source records the two juristic interpretations. Mālik and some others, as al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī note, held that the ruler chooses among the four according to the gravity and circumstances of the case — the "or" being an "or" of option. Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah, and the majority held that the "or" is an "or" of distribution: the penalties correspond to degrees of the crime. Those who killed but did not rob are executed; those who robbed but did not kill suffer cross-amputation (right hand and left foot); those who both killed and robbed are executed and then exposed (crucified); and those who terrorized the roads without killing or robbing are exiled. This correlation, transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, makes the penalty proportionate: each act receives its measure.

The source details the procedural care the jurists took. Crucifixion (*ṣalb*) was understood as public exposure of the body *after* execution, as deterrence, not as a means of killing; those who permitted exposure before death required that death follow almost immediately, lest the exposure become torture, which the Law forbids. Banishment (*nafy*) was understood by some early authorities as relentless pursuit until the criminal left Muslim lands; by most, as exile from his home region; and by Abū Ḥanīfah and others, as imprisonment — which "banishes" the criminal from society while keeping him within reach of justice. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the source notes, is credited with first using imprisonment for this purpose, holding offenders until they repented.

**Why Such Severity?**

A modern reader may recoil at the penalties, and the Qur'an does not hide their severity — it calls them "disgrace in this world." The reasoning of the Law deserves a fair hearing. The crime is not ordinary crime. *Ḥirābah* is organized terror: the robbery and murder of travelers, the rape of the defenseless, the making of roads and markets unsafe, the destruction of the elementary trust that allows people to leave their homes. Such crimes do not injure one victim; they injure everyone, because everyone now lives in fear. The verse's preceding sentence, that killing one soul is like killing all, applies here in its full weight: the *muḥārib* has attacked all of society. The penalty is correspondingly grave, and it is meant to be — the source notes that the *ḥudūd* are understood as deterrents whose severity is designed to keep the incidence of such crimes very low. Al-Rāzī observes that a state which cannot protect its people from armed terror has failed in its first duty, and that the mercy owed to the innocent traveler is greater than the mercy owed to the one who lies in wait for him.

At the same time, the Law surrounds these penalties with safeguards. The standard of proof is the highest; doubt averts the *ḥadd* ("avert the *ḥudūd* by doubts," a principle transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions); the penalties may be applied only by legitimate authority after due process, never by private persons; and, as the next verse will show, repentance before capture removes them entirely. The verse is thus not a license for brutality but a boundary: it names the maximum, and the surrounding law ensures that the maximum is reached rarely and only with certainty.

**The Question of Apostasy**

Because the men of ʿUraynah had professed Islam and then renounced it by their deeds, a small minority, as al-Ṭabarī records and the source notes, applied the verse to apostates generally. The great majority rejected this: the verse's own wording speaks of *ḥirābah* and *fasād* — armed violence and corruption — not of change of belief, and the penalties are graduated according to the acts committed, which would make no sense for a crime of belief. The verse applies, the source concludes, to those who commit brazen, violent, terrorizing crimes against the innocent.

**"Disgrace in This World and a Great Punishment in the Hereafter"**

*Dhālika lahum khizyun fī al-dunyā wa-lahum fī al-ākhirati ʿadhābun ʿaẓīm* — "That is for them a disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment." *Khizy* is humiliation, public shame; the penalty is not only pain but exposure, because the crime was public and the deterrent must be public. And the worldly penalty does not exhaust the matter: a great punishment awaits in the Hereafter, because the sin is against God as well as against society. The source notes the parallel in 2:114, 9:74, and 13:33–34. But the jurists also held — on the strength of the ḥadīth of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit (al-Bukhārī 18; Muslim 1709) — that one who undergoes the *ḥadd* in this world and repents is thereby purified, and the worldly penalty becomes an expiation rather than a prelude to the Fire. The verse thus warns the unrepentant of a double punishment while leaving open, as the next verse will make explicit, the door of return.

**Reading the Verse Today**

The crime this verse addresses has not vanished. Armed robbery, kidnapping for ransom, the terrorizing of civilians, the massacre of the defenseless in markets and places of worship — all are *ḥirābah* in the classical sense, and contemporary Muslim jurists have applied the term precisely to terrorism, holding that those who commit such acts, whatever they claim as their cause, "wage war against God and His Messenger and spread corruption in the earth." The verse thus stands as the Qur'an's own condemnation of terror, delivered in the strongest terms the Law possesses. The believer who reads it understands that the sanctity of life established in verse 32 is protected, in verse 33, by the state's duty to punish those who violate it most flagrantly — and that both verses flow from a single conviction: that the safety of human beings on God's earth is among the things He holds most sacred.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:34

> **save those who repent before you overpower them. And know that God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Door Left Open**

Immediately after the severest penalties in the Qur'an, the text turns to mercy: *illā alladhīna tābū min qabli an taqdirū ʿalayhim* — "except those who repent before you gain power over them." The exception is grammatically attached to the preceding verse, so that the two form a single legal statement: the recompense of those who wage war and spread corruption is such-and-such — *except* those who repent before capture. The structure teaches that in the Qur'anic law, even the gravest crime is framed by the possibility of return. The penalties of verse 33 are not the last word; repentance is.

**The Meaning and Timing of the Repentance**

*Tābū* is from t-w-b, to return; repentance (*tawbah*) is the turning back of the sinner to God, and God's *tawbah* upon him (the same root: *tāba ʿalayhi*) is His turning back toward the sinner in acceptance. The condition is *min qabli an taqdirū ʿalayhim*, "before you have power over them" — before they are captured, subdued, or brought before the authorities. The source explains the logic: repentance under the shadow of the sword is of doubtful sincerity, because it may be a mere attempt to escape punishment; repentance offered freely, while the criminal still has the power to continue his crimes, is evidence of a true change of heart. The Law rewards the second with immunity from the *ḥadd* and does not extend that immunity to the first.

The parallel the source draws is exact: the Qur'an states the same principle for repentance before death. "Repentance is not accepted of those who do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, 'Indeed, I have repented now'" (4:18). Just as the deathbed convert who has seen the angels can no longer be said to believe in the unseen, so the brigand in chains can no longer be said to have chosen goodness. The moment of choice must precede the moment of compulsion.

This does not mean that the captured criminal's repentance is worthless before God. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī, as the source notes, hold that the *ḥadd* must be applied once the case reaches the authorities — the penalty is God's right and cannot be waived by the judge — but the criminal's sincere repentance may still avail him in the Hereafter, and the ḥadīth of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit teaches that a *ḥadd* borne in this world is an expiation. The verse's exception concerns the worldly penalty specifically.

**What Repentance Removes and What It Does Not**

The jurists drew a careful distinction that the source preserves. Repentance before capture removes the *ḥadd* — the fixed penalty that is God's right: execution, crucifixion, cross-amputation, exile. It does not remove the rights of the victims, which are human rights and belong to the injured parties. The repentant brigand must still return stolen property or pay its value, and if he killed, the heirs of the victim retain their right to *qiṣāṣ* (retribution) or blood-money, or may forgive. God's right may be forgiven by God upon repentance; the human right remains with the human being to whom it is owed. This distinction is one of the most just features of Islamic criminal law: it prevents the criminal from using repentance to evade restitution, while allowing repentance to spare him the state's severest penalty.

The source adds a further point: in most schools, if a victim forgives the perpetrator and does not bring the matter to the authorities, the *ḥadd* need not be applied at all. The Prophet ﷺ encouraged such private forgiveness before matters reached him: "Forgive the *ḥudūd* among yourselves; whatever *ḥadd* reaches me, its application becomes obligatory" (Abū Dāwūd 4376). Once the case is before the judge, mercy is no longer his to grant; before that point, it is the victim's to give.

**"And Know That God Is Forgiving, Merciful"**

*Fa-ʿlamū anna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — "and know that God is Forgiving, Merciful." The verse ends with the two Names that the Qur'an pairs more often than any others. The imperative *iʿlamū*, "know," is addressed to the community — to those who would apply the penalties and to those who might incur them. To the authorities it says: do not be so zealous in punishment that you forget the God who forgives; when the criminal repents before capture, let him go. To the criminal it says: the God whose law prescribes such severity is the same God who is Forgiving and Merciful; turn back before it is too late, and you will find Him so.

The two Names carry a graduated meaning that the commentators noted. *Ghafūr* is the One who covers sins — who hides them, protects the sinner from their consequences, and does not expose him. *Raḥīm* is the One whose mercy is active and continuous — who not only covers the sin but bestows good upon the one who has turned back. Forgiveness removes the debt; mercy adds the gift. The repentant brigand is promised both: his crime covered, and God's mercy upon him.

**Why This Mercy Is Wise**

The exception in this verse is not merely compassionate; it is wise, and the commentators explained its wisdom. A law that offered no exit to the criminal would give him no reason to stop: having committed one crime and facing certain death, he would commit more, since nothing could worsen his position. The exception gives him a reason to stop *now*. It tells the outlaw on the highway: lay down your arms today, of your own accord, and the state will not pursue you for the *ḥadd*. This incentive has, historically, brought many such men back into society. The Umayyad and Abbasid chronicles record bands of highwaymen who, on hearing this verse recited, surrendered and became upright — and the classical jurists composed treatises on how to receive them.

The verse also reveals the purpose of the penalties of verse 33. Their purpose is not vengeance; it is the protection of society and the reform of the criminal. When the criminal reforms himself before he is forced to, the purpose is achieved without the penalty, and the penalty becomes unnecessary. A law aimed at vengeance would punish regardless; a law aimed at reform welcomes the reform when it comes. Verse 34 thus tells us what verse 33 is *for*.

**The Spiritual Merit of the Victim's Forgiveness**

The source draws attention to a further dimension: the victim who forgives and declines to denounce the perpetrator, thereby sparing him the *ḥadd*, participates in the divine attributes invoked at the verse's end. Just as God is Forgiving and Merciful toward the repentant, the human being may be forgiving and merciful toward the one who wronged him. The Qur'an says of retribution generally: "The recompense of an evil is an evil like it; but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with God" (42:40). Justice is the victim's right; forgiveness is his opportunity for a higher reward. The Prophet ﷺ himself, when a woman was brought to him who had confessed to a crime carrying the *ḥadd*, said, "Had you covered her with your garment, it would have been better for you" (Abū Dāwūd 4377) — to the man who brought her. The Law prefers, wherever the rights of society permit, that sins be covered and sinners be given the chance to return.

**The Verse for the Reader**

Verse 34 addresses every person who has done wrong and fears that the wrong is beyond forgiveness. If the Qur'an opens the door of repentance to those who "wage war against God and His Messenger" — to murderers, robbers, and terrorists — it opens it to everyone. The only condition is that the turning be real and that it come before compulsion forces it: before the arrest, before the exposure, before death. The believer learns from this verse to repent early and freely, and learns, too, how to treat those who have repented: not with perpetual suspicion, but with the recognition that God Himself has said of them, "*Forgiving, Merciful*."

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:35

> **O you who believe! Reverence God, and seek the means to approach Him, and strive in His way, that haply you may prosper.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Turn from Law to the Inner Life**

After the penal verses on brigandage and the exception for the repentant, the sūrah addresses the believers with a command that is purely spiritual: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū ittaqū Allāha wa-btaghū ilayhi al-wasīlata wa-jāhidū fī sabīlihi laʿallakum tufliḥūn* — "O you who believe, be mindful of God, seek the means to Him, and strive in His way, that you may succeed." The placement is deliberate. Verses 33–34 dealt with those who distanced themselves from God by the gravest crimes and were offered a way back through repentance; verse 35 speaks to the believers about the positive movement toward God — not merely returning from sin but actively drawing near. The source suggests that the "means of approach" may allude to the repentance of the sinner or to the forgiveness offered by the victim, both of which draw a person close to God. The verse thus generalizes: after the law has done its work of restraint, the believer's task is approach.

**Three Commands in Ascending Order**

The verse contains three imperatives, and the commentators saw in them a progression. *Ittaqū Allāha*, "be mindful of God," is the foundation: the guarding of oneself from what displeases Him. *Ibtaghū ilayhi al-wasīlah*, "seek the means to Him," is the building: the active pursuit of what pleases Him. *Jāhidū fī sabīlihi*, "strive in His way," is the summit: the expenditure of one's utmost effort for His cause. The first is avoidance, the second is approach, the third is exertion. Together they describe the complete religious life: leaving what is forbidden, doing what is commanded, and going beyond the required to the heroic.

**Taqwā as the Foundation**

*Taqwā* has already appeared repeatedly in this sūrah (vv. 2, 4, 7, 8, 11), and its recurrence here reminds the reader that it underlies everything. The root w-q-y means to guard; *taqwā* is the guarding of oneself against divine displeasure by staying within the bounds God has set. The most useful image, as the source's guidance suggests, is that of walking carefully along a dangerous path — through thorns, along a cliff edge, through traffic — where awareness prevents avoidable harm. The person of *taqwā* is not paralyzed by fear; he moves with attentiveness. He knows where the dangers are and steps around them. Without this foundation, seeking nearness to God is incoherent: one cannot approach while walking away.

**The Wasīlah: The Means of Approach**

*Al-wasīlah* is from w-s-l, to draw near, to connect; a *wasīlah* is that by which one attains nearness to something or someone — the means, the bridge, the connection. The Qur'an uses the word twice, here and in 17:57, where it describes the righteous who "seek the means to their Lord, which of them is nearest." The commentators — Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Mujāhid, as transmitted by al-Ṭabarī — explain it as nearness (*qurbah*) achieved through obedience and righteous deeds. Al-Ṭabarī summarizes: "Seek nearness to Him by acting in what pleases Him." Ibn Kathīr confirms this consensus and cites the ḥadīth qudsī that the source references:

> *"Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war upon him. My servant draws near to Me with nothing more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. And My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary works until I love him; and when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. Were he to ask Me, I would surely give him; and were he to seek refuge in Me, I would surely grant him refuge."* (al-Bukhārī 6502, from Abū Hurayrah)

This ḥadīth is the fullest commentary on the *wasīlah*. It establishes a hierarchy of means: first the obligatory acts — prayer, fasting, alms, pilgrimage, honesty, justice — which are the most beloved to God and the primary bridge; then the voluntary acts — extra prayers, charity, remembrance, fasting — which build upon the obligatory and draw the servant into God's love. And it describes the destination of the approach: a state in which the servant's faculties are so aligned with God's will that God describes Himself as their guide and strength.

The source notes the Sufi commentators' emphasis on the inner virtues — patience, contentment, sincerity — as means of approach, and Ibn ʿAjībah's insistence that a spiritually accomplished guide is among the *wasāʾil*. These readings extend rather than contradict the classical one: the acts of obedience are the road, and the virtues and the guide are the provisions and companion for the road. What all the commentators agree upon is what the *wasīlah* is *not*: it is not the intercession of false deities or the invocation of intermediaries in place of God. The Qur'an rebukes those who say of their idols, "We worship them only that they may bring us near to God" (39:3); the source cites this and 46:28. The means of approach is obedience to God, sought from God, directed to God.

**Nearness as the Goal of Existence**

Why is nearness the goal? The Qur'an presents the highest rank of the blessed as *al-muqarrabūn*, "those brought near" (56:11, 88; 83:21, 28), and the source notes this. The spiritual life is conceived as a journey of approach, whose end is proximity to the Divine Presence. The Prophet ﷺ described the nearest a servant comes to his Lord as the moment of prostration: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating, so make abundant supplication" (Muslim 482). Every act of obedience shortens the distance; every sin lengthens it. To "seek the *wasīlah*" is to spend one's life closing the gap.

There is a psychological reality here that everyone can verify. Human beings feel the distance from God as restlessness, emptiness, and anxiety, however they name it. The Qur'an says: "Whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a constricted life" (20:124). And it says of the remedy: "Truly, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest" (13:28). The *wasīlah* is the practical answer to this restlessness — not a technique of relaxation but a real movement toward the One in whose nearness alone the heart is at peace.

**"And Strive in His Way"**

*Wa-jāhidū fī sabīlihi* — "and struggle in His way." *Jihād* is from j-h-d, to exert effort, to strive to one's utmost. The source lists the command's frequent occurrence (2:218; 4:95; 8:72, 74; 9:20; 49:15). Its primary reference in many verses is to the armed defense of the community; its broader meaning, which the Prophet ﷺ affirmed, encompasses every form of striving for God: "The *mujāhid* is the one who strives against his own soul in obedience to God" (al-Tirmidhī 1621; graded ṣaḥīḥ). In the context of this verse — following "seek the means" and preceding "that you may prosper" — the striving is the effort that seeking nearness requires. The *wasīlah* is not attained by wishing. It demands *jihād*: the struggle against laziness in prayer, against greed in giving, against pride in humility, against the whole weight of the lower self that resists approach.

The order of the three commands is instructive here. One does not begin with *jihād*; one begins with *taqwā*, guards oneself, then seeks the means, then, strengthened by these, strives. The person who attempts heroic exertion without the foundation of *taqwā* and the practice of obedience builds on sand.

**"That You May Prosper"**

*Laʿallakum tufliḥūn* — "that you may prosper, succeed." *Falāḥ* is from f-l-ḥ, to cleave, to split — the farmer (*fallāḥ*) is one who splits the earth; *falāḥ* is the success that comes from cultivation, the harvest that follows labor. The word is the Qur'an's term for ultimate success, and it is the word the muezzin calls five times a day: *ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ*, "come to success." The verse promises that *taqwā*, the seeking of the *wasīlah*, and striving lead to *falāḥ* — the harvest of a cultivated life. The word *laʿalla*, "perhaps, that haply," does not express doubt on God's part but hope on the servant's: it invites him to do these things *in hope* of success, without presumption.

**The Verse in Practice**

Verse 35 is a program for a life. It asks the believer to do three things every day: to guard himself against what displeases God (*taqwā*), to perform the acts — obligatory first, voluntary second — that bring him nearer (*wasīlah*), and to put real effort into it (*jihād*). The Prophet's ﷺ daily practice embodied all three: he avoided the doubtful, he prayed until his feet swelled, and he exerted himself in every cause of God. The ordinary believer will not match him, but the direction is the same. And the verse promises what every person most deeply wants: not merely to be forgiven, which verse 34 offered even to the brigand, but to be *near* — to be among those brought close.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:36

> **Truly those who disbelieve, were they to possess all that is on the earth and the like of it besides with which to ransom themselves from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them. And theirs shall be a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Contrast with Nearness**

Verse 35 described those who seek the means of approach to God; verse 36 describes those who, on the Day of Resurrection, will seek a means of escape from Him and find none. *Inna alladhīna kafarū law anna lahum mā fī al-arḍi jamīʿan wa-mithlahu maʿahu li-yaftadū bihi min ʿadhābi yawmi al-qiyāmati mā tuqubbila minhum* — "Indeed, those who disbelieve, if they possessed all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them." The contrast is precise. The believer's *wasīlah* — his obedience — is accepted, and it brings him near. The disbeliever's proposed ransom — the whole earth twice over — is refused, and he remains in the punishment. What God accepts is not wealth but *taqwā*, as Abel said in verse 27: "God accepts only from the reverent." The verb *tuqubbila*, "accepted," in this verse deliberately echoes that earlier statement.

**The Rhetoric of the Impossible Ransom**

The verse constructs a hypothetical that no human being could ever satisfy: *all* that is on the earth — every mine, every field, every treasury, every city — *and the like of it besides*, a second earth's worth. Even this, offered as a ransom (*fidyah*, from f-d-y, to redeem, to buy back), would be refused. The purpose of the hyperbole is to close every avenue of hope for those who imagine that the Hereafter operates like this world, where wealth can purchase escape from consequences. The source lists the many places where the Qur'an makes this point (2:48, 123; 3:91; 10:54; 13:18; 39:47; 57:15; 70:11), and the repetition is itself significant: the Qur'an returns to this theme because the illusion it corrects is so deeply rooted.

Sūrat al-Maʿārij paints the scene: "The criminal will wish that he could be ransomed from the punishment of that Day by his children, and his wife and his brother, and his nearest kindred who shelter him, and all who are on the earth — so that it might save him. No!" (70:11–15). And Sūrat Āl ʿImrān specifies the substance: "Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers — never would the earth full of gold be accepted from one of them if he sought to ransom himself with it" (3:91). The Prophet ﷺ described the exchange directly:

> *"It will be said to the inhabitant of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection: 'If you had all that is on the earth, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say, 'Yes.' God will say: 'I asked of you what was far less than that — when you were in the loins of Adam — that you not associate anything with Me; but you refused anything but association.'"* (al-Bukhārī 3334; Muslim 2805)

This ḥadīth reveals the terrible irony the verse contains. What God asked in this world was small — belief, the refusal of *shirk*. What the disbeliever would offer in the next is immense — the whole earth. But the small thing was asked when it could be given, and the immense thing is offered when it can no longer be accepted. The exchange rate of the Hereafter is not a matter of quantity but of time: the currency of faith is valid only before death.

**Why Wealth Cannot Ransom**

The commentators explained why the ransom is refused, and their explanations expose the logic of the Hereafter. First, the wealth is not the disbeliever's to offer. Everything on earth belongs to God — the sūrah has said so twice already (vv. 17, 18) and will say so again in its final verse. To offer God His own property as a ransom is like a thief offering to pay his fine with the goods he stole. Second, the Day of Resurrection is precisely the day on which the worldly means of influence cease: "the Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped" (2:48). Wealth, connections, bribes, pleading — all the ways human beings evade consequences here — are abolished there. Third, and most deeply, the punishment is not an external penalty that could in principle be paid off; it is the consequence of what the person has become. A soul that has spent its life covering the truth cannot buy its way into the light, because the problem is not a debt but a condition.

**"And Theirs Shall Be a Painful Punishment"**

*Wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīm* — "and for them is a painful punishment." The phrase is one of the Qur'an's standard closings for warnings, and its adjective *alīm* — from a-l-m, pain — indicates that the punishment is felt, not merely imposed. The verse that follows will add that it is lasting. The two verses together describe a punishment from which there is no ransom (v. 36), no exit (v. 37), and no end (v. 37). The Qur'an does not present these facts to frighten for the sake of fear; it presents them, as verse 19 explained, so that no one may say "no warner came to us." The believer who reads them is meant to feel the weight of the Day and to act accordingly — now, while the small thing God asks can still be given.

**The Verse as a Corrective to a Worldly Mind**

The deepest function of this verse is to correct a habit of mind that this world instills in everyone. Here, almost everything is negotiable. Fines can be paid, judgments appealed, penalties reduced, officials persuaded. The wealthy live in a world where consequences are soft, and even the poor learn to believe that if only they had enough, they too could escape. The Qur'an says: not there. The Day of Resurrection is the one place where wealth is worth exactly nothing, where "neither wealth nor children will benefit anyone, except one who comes to God with a sound heart" (26:88–89). The person who internalizes this stops trusting in his accumulation and starts investing in his heart.

There is a positive corollary that the commentators drew out. If all the earth's wealth cannot ransom a disbeliever, then the smallest act of faith is worth more than all the earth's wealth. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Two units of prayer before dawn are better than the world and all it contains" (Muslim 725). The scales of the Hereafter invert the scales of the world: what is cheap here — a prostration, a kind word, a dirham given in secret — is priceless there, and what is priceless here — the earth and the like of it — is worthless there. Verse 36 teaches the believer which currency to accumulate.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:37

> **They will wish to come forth from the Fire, but they shall not come forth from it. And theirs shall be a lasting punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Completion of the Warning**

Verse 36 stated that no ransom would be accepted; verse 37 states that no exit will be found. *Yurīdūna an yakhrujū mina al-nāri wa-mā hum bi-khārijīna minhā wa-lahum ʿadhābun muqīm* — "They will want to get out of the Fire, but they will not get out of it; and for them is an enduring punishment." The two verses together form a complete picture: the disbelievers will have neither the means to purchase release (v. 36) nor the ability to effect it (v. 37), and the punishment will not end of itself (v. 37). Every route of escape — payment, force, and time — is closed.

**The Grammar of Hopelessness**

The verse's structure is worth attending to. *Yurīdūna*, "they want," is in the imperfect tense, indicating continuous, repeated desire: they will keep wanting to leave. *Wa-mā hum bi-khārijīna minhā*, "and they are not ones who will leave it," uses the emphatic negation with *bi-* and the active participle, a construction stronger than a simple verbal negation; it denies not merely the act but the very possibility — they are not "leavers" of it. The Qur'an uses a similar construction of the same situation in 32:20: "Every time they want to get out of it, they will be returned to it, and it will be said to them, 'Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.'" The image is of repeated attempts, repeated failures. Al-Rāzī observes that the verse depicts a will that persists and a barrier that does not yield — the most painful of all conditions, since the desire for escape never dies and is never satisfied.

**"An Enduring Punishment"**

*ʿAdhāb muqīm* — "a lasting punishment." *Muqīm* is from q-w-m, to stand; the active participle means "standing, remaining, abiding, resident." It is the word for a person who has settled in a place, as opposed to a traveler. The punishment is thus described as one that has taken up residence — it does not pass through; it stays. The Qur'an uses the same root in *dār al-muqāmah*, "the Abode of Permanent Residence" (35:35), for Paradise; the two destinations are equally permanent, and this verse's *muqīm* answers the Paradise-dweller's *muqāmah*. The choice made in this life settles into an eternal dwelling.

**Why Permanence?**

The permanence of punishment for disbelief is among the most difficult teachings of revelation, and the classical scholars addressed it with seriousness. Their reasoning takes several forms.

First, the punishment corresponds to the state of the soul, not merely to a finite quantity of deeds. The disbeliever did not merely commit a certain number of sins; he chose a fundamental orientation — the covering of the truth of his Creator — and persisted in it until death fixed it. The Qur'an says of the people of the Fire: "if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden" (6:28). Their disbelief is not a phase that would end if given time; it is what they are, as they made themselves. A permanent condition receives a permanent consequence.

Second, the offense is against the Infinite. Al-Ghazālī and others reasoned that the gravity of a wrong is measured partly by the one wronged, and that the rejection of the Lord of the worlds — the One who created, sustained, guided, and warned — is a wrong of unlimited gravity, incommensurable with any finite penalty.

Third, the Qur'an is emphatic that no one enters this punishment without having been warned clearly and having chosen freely. Verse 19 of this sūrah said that the Messenger came "lest you should say, 'There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner.'" The permanence of the punishment is presented alongside the completeness of the warning; the one is just because the other was given.

The scholars also insisted on what the verse does *not* say. It speaks of "those who disbelieve" (v. 36) — those who rejected faith and died upon that rejection. It does not speak of believers who sinned. The Qur'an and the Sunnah are clear that believers who enter the Fire for their sins will eventually be brought out; the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever says 'there is no god but God' and has in his heart the weight of a grain of barley of good will come out of the Fire" (al-Bukhārī 44; Muslim 193). The permanence of verse 37 belongs to disbelief, not to sin as such. The believer who reads it should fear for his faith, not despair of his forgiveness.

**The Mercy Within the Warning**

It may seem strange to speak of mercy in connection with this verse, but the commentators did. The warning is given *now*, in this world, where it can still be acted upon. Every human being who reads or hears this verse is, by that very fact, not yet in the situation it describes; he is in the situation where the small thing God asks — faith — can still be given, and where repentance still avails. The verse's severity is the measure of the urgency: God tells us the worst so that we will avoid it. The Prophet ﷺ compared himself to a man who lights a fire, and when moths and insects begin falling into it, he tries to drive them away: "I am seizing you by your waists to keep you from the Fire, and you are plunging into it" (al-Bukhārī 6483; Muslim 2284). Verse 37 is one of his hands on our waists.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Argument**

Verses 36–37 occupy a specific place in the sūrah's flow. The preceding verses dealt with law — the sanctity of life, the penalty for brigandage, the door of repentance, and the seeking of nearness to God. These two verses set the whole matter against its ultimate horizon: the Day of Resurrection, where ransom fails and exit is barred. The legal penalties of this world, severe as they are, are temporary, and repentance averts them; the penalty of the Hereafter for disbelief is permanent, and only faith averts it. The sequence teaches the believer to keep the proportions right: to fear the *ḥadd* less than the Fire, and to value the *wasīlah* — the means of approach — more than any escape from earthly punishment. The next verse will return to law, with the penalty for theft; but it will do so in the shadow of this reminder that all human justice is provisional, and that the final justice belongs to God.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:38

> **As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, as an exemplary punishment from God. Truly God is Mighty, Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Ḥadd of the Sūrah**

After the horizon of the Hereafter in verses 36–37, the sūrah returns to the law of this world with the penalty for theft: *wa-l-sāriqu wa-l-sāriqatu fa-qṭaʿū aydiyahumā jazāʾan bi-mā kasabā nakālan mina Allāh* — "And the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, an exemplary punishment from God." This is the second of the *ḥudūd* named in this sūrah (the first being *ḥirābah* in verse 33), and it is among the most discussed verses in Islamic law. The commentators note the logic of the sequence: verse 33 addressed the armed robber who takes property by terror; verse 38 addresses the thief who takes it by stealth. Both violate the security of property on which social life depends; the penalty is graduated to the crime.

**The Word Sāriq: Theft by Stealth**

*Sariqa* means to take something secretly, by stealth, from a place where it is kept safe. The jurists built the definition of legally punishable theft from this root meaning and the Prophet's ﷺ practice, and their definition is precise. It is not every taking of another's property. The *ḥadd* applies to the taking of property (1) secretly, not openly — the open snatcher, the embezzler, and the one who betrays a trust are punished by discretionary penalties, not amputation, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no cutting for the treacherous, the plunderer, or the snatcher" (Abū Dāwūd 4391; al-Tirmidhī 1448; graded ṣaḥīḥ); (2) from a place of safekeeping (*ḥirz*) — property left unguarded in the open does not qualify; (3) reaching a minimum value (*niṣāb*); and (4) by a sane adult who has no doubt of ownership or claim to the property. The source records the *niṣāb*: three dirhams according to Mālik, a quarter of a dīnār according to al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad, ten dirhams according to Abū Ḥanīfah — and notes the ḥadīth on which the majority rests: "The hand of the thief is not cut except for a quarter of a dīnār or more" (al-Bukhārī 6789; Muslim 1684). Some early figures, as al-Qurṭubī notes, applied the penalty to any theft; the Prophet's ﷺ practice excluded this. Below the minimum, the penalty is restitution and discretionary punishment.

**The Explicit Inclusion of the Woman**

*Al-sāriqu wa-l-sāriqatu* — "the male thief and the female thief." The Qur'an names both, as it does for adultery (24:2), and the source notes that the *ḥudūd* are understood to apply equally to both sexes. The explicit mention is not redundant. In many legal systems of the ancient world, women were either exempt from certain penalties or subjected to different ones, and the Qur'an's insistence on equality before the criminal law was a statement of principle. The most famous application concerned a woman. When a woman of the noble Makhzūm clan stole and her people sought to have the penalty waived through the intercession of Usāmah ibn Zayd, the Prophet's ﷺ beloved, he refused in words that Ibn Kathīr cites here:

> *"Those before you were destroyed only because when a noble among them stole, they let him go, and when a weak one among them stole, they applied the penalty. By God, if Fāṭimah the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand."* (al-Bukhārī 3475; Muslim 1688)

The ḥadīth teaches two things at once: that the penalty applies to women, and that it applies to the powerful. The corruption of earlier communities, the Prophet ﷺ said, lay precisely in a two-tier justice — leniency for the strong and severity for the weak — and the Law's equality is its protection against that corruption.

**"Cut Off Their Hands"**

*Fa-qṭaʿū aydiyahumā* — "then cut off their hands." The verb is in the plural imperative addressed to the community — in practice, to its legitimate authority; no private person may carry out a *ḥadd*. The Sunnah specified that the right hand is cut at the wrist for a first offense; the jurists debated the penalty for repeat offenses. The source notes the essential humane provisions: the penalty is meant to disable, not to kill; the wound must be cauterized and treated to prevent death; and the *ḥadd* is averted by any reasonable doubt, per the principle transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions, "avert the *ḥudūd* by doubts as much as you can" (al-Tirmidhī 1424; al-Ḥākim). ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb suspended the penalty during the Year of Famine, reasoning that hunger created a doubt about the thief's culpability — a precedent that the jurists took as establishing that the *ḥadd* does not apply where the thief was driven by necessity.

The exacting conditions and the doubt-principle together explain why, in the classical Islamic societies where the penalty was law, its actual application was rare. The *ḥadd* stood as a deterrent whose severity communicated the sanctity of property; its execution was hedged about with requirements that made it a last resort. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the pre-Islamic Arabs already amputated for theft, so that the verse was not introducing a novel cruelty but regulating and limiting an existing practice.

**"As a Recompense for What They Have Earned"**

*Jazāʾan bi-mā kasabā* — "as a recompense for what they have earned." The word *kasabā*, "they earned," is pointed. The thief sought to *earn* by taking what he had not earned; the Law names his penalty as his true "earning." The Qur'an consistently describes consequences as what the soul has *kasabat*, earned (2:286), and the thief's amputation is thus framed not as arbitrary infliction but as the return of his own deed upon him. The hand that took is the hand that is taken.

**"An Exemplary Punishment from God"**

*Nakālan mina Allāh* — "an exemplary punishment from God." *Nakāl* is from n-k-l, to restrain, to deter; a *nakāl* is a punishment that serves as a warning to others, the same word used of Pharaoh's fate (79:25) and of the Sabbath-breakers (2:66: "We made it a *nakāl* for those before it and after it"). The word names the penalty's purpose: deterrence. The source explains that the *ḥudūd* are understood as God's rights against crimes that destabilize society as a whole, and that they serve not only as recompense but as example, to keep the incidence of such crimes very low. A penalty that is severe, certain (when proven), and public deters in a way that a mild, uncertain, hidden one does not.

The phrase "from God" is also significant. The penalty is not the invention of a ruler or a jurist; it is God's. This protects it in two directions: from those who would abolish it out of misplaced softness, and from those who would exceed it out of cruelty. The ruler may not substitute a lighter penalty for a proven, unrepented theft that meets all conditions; nor may he add torture, mutilation beyond the hand, or humiliation beyond what the Law specifies.

**"Truly God Is Mighty, Wise"**

*Wa-Allāhu ʿazīzun ḥakīm* — "And God is Mighty, Wise." The two Names are chosen with care, and al-Rāzī drew attention to their pairing. *ʿAzīz* — Mighty, Invincible — corresponds to the severity of the penalty: God has the power to impose it and the authority that none can question. *Ḥakīm* — Wise — corresponds to its proportion and purpose: the penalty is not the act of a tyrant but of One who knows what preserves society and what corrupts it. A famous anecdote, transmitted by al-Aṣmaʿī, captures the point: a Bedouin heard a reciter conclude the verse with "and God is Forgiving, Merciful" (a slip of the tongue) and objected, "That is not the speech of God"; when the reciter corrected himself to "Mighty, Wise," the Bedouin said, "Yes — He was Mighty, so He decreed; and Wise, so He cut. Had He been Forgiving and Merciful here, He would not have cut." The anecdote, whatever its historicity, expresses the commentators' sensitivity to the fit between the Names and the ruling.

**The Rationale of the Law**

Why does theft carry such a penalty? The scholars answered from several angles. Theft attacks the foundation of economic life: if property is not secure, no one will labor, save, or trade, and society collapses into predation. It attacks the security of the home: the thief by stealth violates the space in which people must be able to rest. And it is a crime of choice, not of passion: the thief plans, waits, and acts deliberately, so that the deterrent operates upon a calculating mind. The penalty's severity is calibrated to the ease of the crime and the difficulty of detection: because theft is easy and often undiscovered, the penalty when discovered must be heavy enough to outweigh the temptation. Al-Rāzī also observes the moral symbolism: the hand is the instrument of both earning and taking, and its loss marks the thief publicly as one who chose the second over the first.

At the same time, the classical jurists were unanimous that the *ḥadd* presupposes a society in which the poor are provided for. ʿUmar's suspension of the penalty during famine expresses a principle: the state that has not fulfilled its duty to feed the hungry cannot amputate the hand of one who stole to eat. The penalty and the welfare obligation are two halves of a single system, and the second is the precondition of the first.

**The Verse and the Modern Reader**

Contemporary readers, formed in societies with different penal philosophies, often find this verse difficult. The tradition's response is not to apologize for the verse but to present it whole: the penalty is real and severe; it applies only to theft by stealth, from safekeeping, above a minimum, by one with no claim or necessity, proven beyond doubt, by legitimate authority, in a society that provides for its poor; it is averted by repentance before conviction (as the next verse will indicate) and by the victim's forgiveness before the matter reaches the court; and it is accompanied by the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to seek doubts that avert it. A person who considers the whole system — deterrence, safeguards, welfare, and mercy together — sees a law aimed at making theft rare, not at multiplying amputations. And a person who considers the alternative — societies in which theft is common because its punishment is trivial — may find the Qur'an's wisdom less foreign than it first appeared.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:39

> **But whosoever repents after his wrongdoing, and makes amends, God will relent unto him. Truly God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mercy Following Severity, Again**

For the second time in this sūrah, a verse prescribing a severe penalty is followed immediately by a verse opening the door of repentance. Verse 33 was followed by verse 34; verse 38 is followed by verse 39: *fa-man tāba min baʿdi ẓulmihi wa-aṣlaḥa fa-inna Allāha yatūbu ʿalayhi inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm* — "But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and sets things right, indeed God will turn to him; indeed, God is Forgiving, Merciful." The pattern is not accidental. The Qur'an never leaves a *ḥadd* standing alone; it always places beside it the possibility of return. The law protects society; the repentance verse protects the sinner's hope. A believer who reads the two together understands that the same God who cuts the thief's hand desires the thief's salvation.

**The Word Ẓulm for Theft**

The verse calls the thief's act *ẓulm*, wrongdoing — literally, placing something where it does not belong. Theft is the paradigm of *ẓulm* in this sense: it takes property from the place God assigned it and puts it where it does not belong. The word also connects theft to the whole moral universe of the Qur'an, in which *ẓulm* is the root category of sin — against God (*shirk*, "a great *ẓulm*," 31:13), against others (as here), and against oneself (7:23). The thief has wronged his victim, wronged society, and wronged himself, and his repentance must address all three.

**Two Conditions: Repentance and Setting Right**

The verse names two things: *tāba*, "he repented," and *aṣlaḥa*, "he set right, he made amends." The pairing is characteristic — the Qur'an rarely mentions repentance without reform (2:160; 4:146; 6:54; 16:119; 24:5) — and it establishes that repentance is not a feeling but a transaction with two parts. The inward part is regret and the turning of the heart back to God. The outward part is *iṣlāḥ*: the correction of what was corrupted. For the thief, this means, first and unavoidably, the return of the stolen property or its value to its owner. Al-Qurṭubī, as the source notes, understands *aṣlaḥa* more broadly as repenting of all disobedience — a comprehensive reform of life — but the return of the property is its minimum. The Prophet ﷺ made restitution the condition of forgiveness for wrongs against people: "Whoever has wronged his brother in his honor or anything else, let him seek his pardon today, before there is neither dinar nor dirham; if he has good deeds, they will be taken from him in the measure of his wrong, and if he has no good deeds, the sins of his victim will be taken and cast upon him" (al-Bukhārī 2449). A "repentance" that keeps the stolen goods is not repentance.

The root ṣ-l-ḥ, soundness, is the opposite of the f-s-d, corruption, of verse 33. The brigand and the thief spread *fasād*; the repentant sets things back in order, *ṣalāḥ*. The verse thus asks the wrongdoer to undo, as far as he can, the disorder he introduced.

**"God Will Turn to Him"**

*Fa-inna Allāha yatūbu ʿalayhi* — "then indeed God turns to him." The same root — t-w-b — is used for the servant's act and God's response. The servant *tāba* (turned back); God *yatūbu ʿalayhi* (turns toward him). The Qur'an presents repentance as a mutual turning: the servant turns from his sin to God, and God turns from His displeasure to the servant. The Qur'an even reverses the order in one verse — "then He turned to them, that they might turn" (9:118) — indicating that God's turning toward the servant precedes and enables the servant's own turning. The door is opened from the inside before the sinner knocks. This is the theology of *tawbah*: it is never a human achievement alone but a divine gift met by human response.

The Prophet ﷺ described God's joy at this turning:

> *"God is more joyful at the repentance of His servant than one of you would be, who was on his riding camel in a barren wasteland, and it escaped from him with his food and drink on it, and he despaired of it, and came to a tree and lay down in its shade in despair of his camel — and while he was thus, there it was, standing beside him; and he seized its halter and said, in the intensity of his joy, 'O God, You are my servant and I am Your Lord' — erring from the intensity of his joy."* (Muslim 2747)

**Does Repentance Avert the Ḥadd?**

The source records the juristic debate. Some held that the thief's repentance averts the amputation, by analogy with verse 34, where the brigand's repentance before capture averts his penalty. The majority — including Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī, as al-Jalālayn and al-Zamakhsharī record — held that the *ḥadd* for theft, once the case is proven before the authorities, must be applied regardless of repentance, and that God's "turning" in this verse pertains to the sinner's standing in the Hereafter. The difference between the two cases is that verse 34 contains the explicit temporal condition — "before you have power over them" — while verse 39 does not, so that the majority understood the thief's repentance to avail him with God, whether or not the earthly penalty is applied.
