Where the majority agreed with the minority is that the *ḥadd* is averted if the victim forgives the thief and the matter never reaches the court — the source cites this consensus — and that the Prophet ﷺ encouraged such private settlement.

**The Ḥadd as Purification**

A further teaching, preserved in the source and in Ibn Kathīr's commentary, transforms the meaning of the penalty for the repentant thief. The Prophet ﷺ assured those who underwent the *ḥadd* and repented that they were forgiven and purified. When a thief's hand was cut, the Prophet ﷺ said to him, "Say: I seek God's forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance," and the man said it, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "O God, turn to him" (Abū Dāwūd 4380). And the general principle, from the ḥadīth of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit: "Whoever commits any of these [sins] and is punished for it in this world, it is an expiation for him" (al-Bukhārī 18; Muslim 1709). For the believer, the *ḥadd* is not merely a penalty but a cleansing: he leaves the court having paid his debt to society and to God, with nothing further held against him in the Hereafter. This is a radically different conception of criminal punishment from one that stigmatizes the offender permanently. The Islamic conception says: the penalty is paid, the repentance is accepted, the matter is closed, and the person is restored.

**"Forgiving, Merciful"**

The verse ends, as verse 34 did, with *ghafūr raḥīm*. The repetition of this pair after each *ḥadd* is the sūrah's way of insisting that the Lawgiver's fundamental disposition is mercy. The penalties are real; they protect the innocent; but they are set within a frame of forgiveness that is wider than they are. Al-Rāzī observes that the verse's placement teaches the community's attitude toward the punished: not contempt, but the recognition that a repentant thief has been forgiven by God, and that no one has the right to hold against him what God has erased. The Prophet ﷺ rebuked those who cursed a man punished for drinking: "Do not help Satan against your brother" (al-Bukhārī 6781).

**The Verse Beyond the Thief**

Though revealed about the thief, the verse's principle is universal. Every wrongdoing (*ẓulm*) can be followed by repentance (*tawbah*) and amends (*iṣlāḥ*), and God turns to whoever does both. The verse gives the structure of every genuine return: acknowledge the wrong, turn back to God in regret, and — this is the part most often neglected — *set right* what was damaged: return the property, restore the reputation, repair the relationship, correct the lie. The person who does these three things is promised the turning of the Forgiving and Merciful toward him. That promise, given even to the thief whose hand the Law has taken, is given to everyone.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:40

> **Dost thou not know that unto God belongs sovereignty over the heavens and the earth? He punishes whomsoever He will, and He forgives whomsoever He will. And God is Powerful over all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Seal on the Section of Penalties**

Verses 32–39 have set out the sanctity of life, the penalty for brigandage, the penalty for theft, and — after each penalty — the door of repentance. Verse 40 closes the section by stating the principle that underlies all of it: *a-lam taʿlam anna Allāha lahu mulku al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi yuʿadhdhibu man yashāʾu wa-yaghfiru li-man yashāʾu wa-Allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "Do you not know that to God belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and God is over all things Powerful." The source rightly describes the verse as a reminder that God is the ultimate judge and the true dispenser of both punishment and forgiveness. Human courts apply the *ḥudūd*; human victims forgive or demand their rights; but behind every human judgment stands the One whose judgment is final.

**The Rhetorical Question**

*A-lam taʿlam*, "Do you not know?", is addressed in the singular — to the Prophet ﷺ, and through him to every reader. The question is not one of ignorance; it is a rhetorical device that summons a known truth to attention. Of course the Prophet ﷺ knew that God owns the heavens and the earth. The question asks him to *bring that knowledge to bear* on what has just been legislated. Al-Rāzī explains the connection: the penalties of verses 33 and 38 might provoke the question "by what right?" — by what right is a hand cut or a life taken? — and the answer is: by the right of the One who owns the hand and the life. The Creator has the authority to legislate for His creation, and His legislation is not subject to appeal to any higher standard, because there is no higher standard than the One who is Himself the source of justice.

**The Sovereignty Motif Recurring**

This is the fourth occurrence in the sūrah of the phrase "to God belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth" (after verses 17 and 18, and anticipating 120). Its repetition is structural. In verse 17 it refuted the divinity of Christ; in verse 18 it refuted the claim of a favored people to immunity; here it grounds the authority of divine law and the divine prerogative of punishment and forgiveness; in verse 120 it closes the entire sūrah. The single truth — God owns everything — answers questions of theology, of communal identity, of law, and of ultimate destiny. The reader who grasps this one sentence has the key to the whole chapter.

**"He Punishes Whom He Wills and Forgives Whom He Wills"**

The order of the verbs here — punishment first, forgiveness second — reverses the order in verse 18 ("He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills"). The commentators noted the fit with context: verse 18 followed a claim of divine favor and put forgiveness first to affirm that it is real but not owed; verse 40 follows the prescription of penalties and puts punishment first to affirm that it is just, before restoring forgiveness as the complement.

The source records al-Rāzī's use of this verse to support the Ashʿarī position that God's prerogative to punish some and forgive others rests on His absolute *mulk* — His ownership — of all things, and is therefore beyond human objection even where it seems, to human reason, arbitrary. The point deserves careful statement. The Ashʿarī school did not hold that God acts capriciously; it held that God is not *obligated* by anything external to Himself, since nothing is external to His ownership. He forgives by grace, not because anyone has earned it; He punishes by justice, and none can say He has wronged them, since He has taken nothing that was not His. The Māturīdī and other schools placed greater emphasis on the wisdom (*ḥikmah*) that governs God's will, holding that He never acts without wisdom even when the wisdom is hidden. Both agree on what the verse insists upon: the decision is His, and His alone. No human being — not the judge, not the victim, not the criminal, not the Prophet ﷺ himself — determines who is finally punished or forgiven. The human court decides the *ḥadd*; God decides the soul.

This distinction is liberating for the believer. The judge who applies the *ḥadd* is not condemning the criminal to Hell; that is not his to decide. The victim who forgives is not thereby guaranteeing the offender's salvation; that too is not his. And the criminal who suffers the penalty is not thereby excluded from God's mercy; the ḥadīth of ʿUbādah teaches the opposite. Each human actor does his part within his sphere, and leaves the final matter to the Sovereign.

**The Combination of Punishment and Forgiveness in One Sentence**

There is theological depth in the fact that the verse names both divine acts together and attributes both to a single will. Human beings tend to imagine that punishment and forgiveness are opposed — that a merciful being would not punish, and a punishing being is not merciful. The Qur'an denies the opposition. The same God, in the same sentence, punishes and forgives, and both flow from His sovereignty and both express His perfection. Justice without mercy would be tyranny; mercy without justice would be chaos. God's *mulk* includes both, held in a balance no creature could maintain. The Prophet ﷺ transmitted from his Lord: "My mercy prevails over My wrath" (al-Bukhārī 7404; Muslim 2751) — establishing the priority within the balance while confirming that both are real.

**"And God Is Powerful over All Things"**

*Wa-Allāhu ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — "and God is over all things Powerful." The closing formula appears for the third time in this sūrah (after verses 17 and 19). Here it completes the argument: God owns all things (*mulk*), decides their fate (punishment and forgiveness), and has the power to execute His decision (*qudrah*). The three together constitute sovereignty in its full sense: title, judgment, and enforcement. A king who owned a realm but could not enforce his will, or could enforce it but had no rightful title, would be sovereign in name only. God's sovereignty lacks nothing.

**The Verse's Function for the Reader**

Verse 40 teaches the believer how to hold the law of God in his mind. He is to accept it as coming from the One who has the right to legislate, not to evaluate it as though he were a peer of the Lawgiver. He is to apply it — where he has authority — within its limits, without arrogating to himself the final judgment on any soul. He is to hope for forgiveness and fear punishment, knowing that both are in the hands of One who is not obliged to him and who nonetheless describes Himself as Forgiving and Merciful. And he is to rest in the knowledge that the world's injustices — the criminals who escape, the innocent who suffer — are not the last word, because the One who owns the heavens and the earth will punish whom He wills and forgive whom He wills, and nothing escapes His power.

The verse also serves as a bridge. The section of penalties is complete; the next verses (41–50) will turn to the People of the Book and their relationship to divine law — the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an as successive revelations of the one Sovereign's judgment. Verse 40's reminder that judgment belongs to God prepares the ground for the central question of those verses: who judges by what God has sent down, and who does not?

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:41

> **O Messenger! Let them not grieve thee, those who hasten unto disbelief, those who say, "We believe" with their mouths, while their hearts believe not, and those who are Jews, who listen to lies and to others who have not come to thee. They distort the meaning of the word, saying, "If you are given this, then take it, but if you are not given this, then beware!" For whomsoever God desires that he be tried, thou hast no power to avail him aught against God. They are those whose hearts God desired not to purify. Theirs is disgrace in this world, and in the Hereafter they shall have a great punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Address "O Messenger"**

Only twice in the Qur'an is the Prophet ﷺ addressed by the title *yā ayyuhā al-rasūl*, "O Messenger" — here and in verse 67 of this same sūrah. Elsewhere he is "O Prophet" (*yā ayyuhā al-nabī*) or, in the early revelations, "O you wrapped in garments." The choice is significant. *Rasūl* emphasizes the office of conveying a message from a sender; and the two verses in which the title appears both concern the burden of that office — here, the grief of seeing the message rejected and distorted; in verse 67, the command to convey it fully regardless. The verse opens with consolation: *lā yaḥzunka alladhīna yusāriʿūna fī al-kufr* — "let them not grieve you, those who race into disbelief." The Prophet's ﷺ grief at rejection was real and deep; the Qur'an addresses it repeatedly (3:176; 6:33; 10:65; 16:127; 31:23; 36:76, as the source lists), and each time the consolation takes the same form: the rejection is theirs, not yours; their loss is theirs, not yours.

**"Those Who Race into Disbelief"**

*Yusāriʿūna fī al-kufr* — "they hasten, they race, into disbelief." The verb is the same one the Qur'an uses for the believers who "race to forgiveness from their Lord" (3:133) and for those who "hasten to good deeds" (3:114; 21:90). The choice creates a bitter irony: the same human energy that the righteous direct toward God, these direct toward its opposite. And the preposition *fī*, "in," rather than *ilā*, "to," suggests that they are already inside disbelief and racing *deeper* into it — from one degree to the next. The verse then names two groups who do this.

**The Two Groups: Hypocrites and Certain Jews**

The first group is *alladhīna qālū āmannā bi-afwāhihim wa-lam tuʾmin qulūbuhum* — "those who say 'we believe' with their mouths while their hearts do not believe." These are the hypocrites of Madinah, whose profile the Qur'an drew at length in the opening of Sūrat al-Baqarah. The phrase "with their mouths" (*bi-afwāhihim*) is the Qur'an's recurring marker of speech without substance (3:167; 9:8; 48:11). The second group is *mina alladhīna hādū* — "of those who are Jews" — with the partitive *min*, "of," marking, as always in the Qur'an, that it is *some* of them, not all. The source notes al-Rāzī's and al-Zamakhsharī's observation that the two groups may be read as distinct clauses, so that the descriptions that follow — listening to lies, distorting the word — apply to the second group specifically.

**"Listeners to Lies, Listeners for Others Who Have Not Come to You"**

*Sammāʿūna li-l-kadhibi sammāʿūna li-qawmin ākharīna lam yaʾtūk* — "listeners to falsehood, listeners on behalf of another people who have not come to you." The intensive form *sammāʿ* means one who listens much, eagerly, habitually. The commentators offer two readings, both preserved in the source. In the first, they listen to and accept the lies their leaders tell them — the misrepresentations of the Torah's rulings. In the second, they listen to the Prophet ﷺ *in order to* lie about what he says, or as spies on behalf of others — the "other people who have not come to you" being the Jews of Khaybar (or Fadak), who would not come to the Prophet ﷺ themselves but sent the Madinan Jews to sound him out and report back. The preposition *li-* can bear both senses: listening *to* lies, and listening *for* others.

**The Occasion: The Case of the Two Adulterers**

The source preserves the most widely reported context, and it is essential to understanding verses 41–47. Two Jews from Khaybar (or, in some accounts, Fadak) — a man and a woman of high standing — committed adultery. The Torah's penalty was stoning. The Jewish leaders, reluctant to apply it to persons of rank, had long since substituted a lesser penalty: flogging, blackening the face, and parading on a donkey. They now sought to make the substitution respectable by obtaining the Prophet's ﷺ ruling. They sent the case to the Jews of Madinah with instructions: "Ask Muhammad. If he rules flogging and blackening, accept it — he is a king, and it will give you cover; but if he rules stoning, beware of him." This is the exact content of the verse: *in ūtītum hādhā fa-khudhūhu wa-in lam tuʾtawhu fa-ḥdharū* — "if you are given this, take it; and if you are not given it, beware."

The Prophet ﷺ, when the case was brought, asked, "What do you find in the Torah concerning stoning?" They said, "We disgrace them and they are flogged." ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām said, "You lie; it contains stoning." The Torah was brought; a rabbi covered the verse of stoning with his hand, reading what was before and after it. Ibn Salām said, "Lift your hand." He lifted it, and there was the verse of stoning. In another account, the young rabbi Ibn Ṣūriyā, adjured by God who revealed the Torah to Moses, admitted that the penalty was stoning and explained how it had been abandoned: "Adultery became common among our nobles; we would apply the penalty to the weak and leave the noble; so we agreed on a penalty that could be applied to noble and lowly alike." The Prophet ﷺ ordered the two to be stoned, saying, "O God, I am the first to revive Your command after they had killed it" (al-Bukhārī 3635, 6841; Muslim 1699; and the fuller narratives in Abū Dāwūd 4450 and al-Ṭabarī). The source also notes a minority report connecting the verses to a dispute between the Banū Naḍīr and the Banū Qurayẓah over unequal blood-money, which verse 45 will address.

**"They Distort the Word from After Its Places"**

*Yuḥarrifūna al-kalima min baʿdi mawāḍiʿihi* — "they distort the word from after its places." The phrase is nearly identical to verse 13's *ʿan mawāḍiʿihi*, "from its places," but with a subtle change: *min baʿdi*, "from after." The commentators noted that this may indicate distortion *after* the word had been correctly placed and understood — a knowing alteration, not an innocent error. Al-Jalālayn suggests, as the source records, that the leaders literally removed the stoning passage from its context. Whether the distortion was textual or interpretive, the incident shows its mechanism precisely: a hand placed over a verse, a penalty quietly replaced, a false account given to one who asks. The Qur'an's charge of *taḥrīf* (2:75; 4:46; 5:13) is illustrated here by an event witnessed by many.

The mechanism is not confined to any one people. Any community whose scholars, out of fear or favor, "cover" the inconvenient parts of their scripture and substitute more comfortable rulings is engaged in *taḥrīf*. The Prophet ﷺ warned of his own community's scholars who would do this, and verses 62–63 of this sūrah will rebuke religious authorities who fail to forbid wrong.

**"Whomsoever God Wills to Try, You Cannot Avail Him Against God"**

*Wa-man yuridi Allāhu fitnatahu fa-lan tamlika lahu mina Allāhi shayʾan* — "and whoever God intends to try, you will never possess for him anything against God." *Fitnah* is trial, test, temptation — originally the smelting of gold to separate it from dross. The source notes that in this negative context, major commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī) understand it as God's leaving a person in error as the consequence of his own choices. The verse's message to the Prophet ﷺ is the same as that to Moses in verse 25: your power extends to conveying, not to converting. The Qur'an states it flatly elsewhere: "Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills" (28:56). This is not fatalism; it is a description of the limits of one person's agency over another's heart. The Prophet ﷺ was consoled, not excused from effort — he continued to call the Jews of Madinah until his death.

**"Those Whose Hearts God Did Not Will to Purify"**

*Ulāʾika alladhīna lam yuridi Allāhu an yuṭahhira qulūbahum* — "those are the ones whose hearts God did not will to purify." Al-Rāzī, as the source records, offers two readings: God declined to aid them spiritually as a consequence of their evil deeds, or God declined to purify them of the passions — envy, greed, fear of losing status — that led them to conceal the Torah's ruling. The verse presents purification of the heart as a divine act that responds to human disposition. The heart that wants purity is purified; the heart that clings to its impurities — that prefers a comfortable falsehood to a demanding truth — is left with what it chose. The Qur'an says of the opposite type: "God loves those who purify themselves" (2:222; 9:108). The choice comes first; the divine confirmation follows.

**"Disgrace in This World and Great Punishment in the Hereafter"**

The verse closes with the same pairing that closed verse 33. The *khizy*, disgrace, of the Jewish leaders in this incident was public: their concealment was exposed before the Prophet ﷺ and the community; their own scripture testified against them; and the young rabbi's confession revealed that they had known all along. This is the natural consequence of *taḥrīf*: sooner or later the covered verse is uncovered, and the coverer is shamed. The greater punishment awaits in the Hereafter for those who die unrepentant.

**The Verse for the Reader**

Verse 41 speaks first to the Prophet ﷺ, comforting him; but it speaks to every believer who has taught the truth and seen it twisted. It teaches that grief over such twisting is natural but must not overwhelm; that the twister's fate is in God's hands, not the teacher's; and that the essential crime — covering the demanding parts of God's word to spare the powerful — is a temptation for every religious community. The Muslim who reads it should look at his own community's handling of its own Book: which verses are read aloud and which are quietly passed over? Whose conduct is exempted from rulings applied to others? The rabbi's hand over the verse of stoning is an image that every scholar and every community should keep before its eyes.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:42

> **Those who listen to lies, and consume what is unlawful—if they come to thee, then judge between them, or turn away from them. If thou turnest away from them, they will not harm thee in the least. But if thou judgest, judge between them with justice. Truly God loves the just.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Continuation of the Portrait**

Verse 42 picks up the description begun in verse 41 — *sammāʿūna li-l-kadhib*, "listeners to lies" — and adds a second trait: *akkālūna li-l-suḥt*, "devourers of the unlawful." Then it turns from description to instruction: what should the Prophet ﷺ do when such people bring their disputes to him? The verse is thus both a continuation of the indictment and the beginning of the Qur'an's legislation on the judicial relationship between the Muslim authority and non-Muslim communities.

**Suḥt: The Gain That Destroys**

*Suḥt* is a striking word. It comes from s-ḥ-t, to uproot, to exterminate, to destroy utterly; the Qur'an uses the verb in 20:61, where Moses warns Pharaoh's sorcerers that God will "exterminate" (*yusḥitakum*) them with punishment. *Suḥt*, as a noun, is unlawful gain — so called, the linguists explain, because it destroys the blessing of wealth and, ultimately, the one who consumes it. The source records the commentators' identification: it does not refer to food but to illicit financial gain, and specifically — per al-Ṭabarī and al-Jalālayn — to bribery. In the context of the incident of the two adulterers, the reference is to the payments the Jewish leaders took to soften the Torah's penalties for the wealthy. Verses 62–63 of this sūrah will repeat the charge. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Every flesh that grows from *suḥt*, the Fire has more right to it" (al-Tirmidhī 614; graded ṣaḥīḥ), and he cursed "the one who bribes and the one who takes the bribe" (Abū Dāwūd 3580; al-Tirmidhī 1337).

The pairing of "listening to lies" and "devouring the unlawful" is diagnostic. The two go together: the scholar who takes bribes must lie to justify the rulings he sells, and the community that wants comfortable rulings must listen to the lies. Corruption of judgment and corruption of income feed each other, and both spring from the same root — the preference of this world over the next.

**"If They Come to You, Judge Between Them or Turn Away"**

*Fa-in jāʾūka fa-ḥkum baynahum aw aʿriḍ ʿanhum* — "So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them." The verse gives the Prophet ﷺ a choice. He may adjudicate the dispute the Jews bring to him, or he may decline and leave it to their own courts. The source records the juristic development of this option. Al-Shāfiʿī and Mālik held, on the basis of this verse, that when non-Muslims living under Muslim rule bring a dispute among themselves to the Muslim judge, the judge may choose to hear it or to refer it back to their own community's authorities. This became the foundation of the juridical autonomy that Jewish and Christian communities enjoyed under Islamic rule for centuries: they maintained their own courts, applied their own law in matters of personal status and internal disputes, and came before the Muslim judge only by their own choice or when a Muslim was party to the case. The source notes that when a Muslim is involved, the schools agree that the Muslim judge must hear the case; and that once a case is heard, it is decided according to Islamic law.

Some commentators, as al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī record, held that this option was abrogated by verse 48 or 49, which command the Prophet ﷺ to "judge between them by what God has sent down." Others held that the verses are compatible: verse 42 gives the option to hear or decline; verse 48 governs the standard of judgment *when* the case is heard. The latter reading has been the operative one in Islamic legal history, since the autonomy of non-Muslim courts persisted throughout.

**"If You Turn Away, They Will Not Harm You at All"**

*Wa-in tuʿriḍ ʿanhum fa-lan yaḍurrūka shayʾan* — "and if you turn away from them, they will never harm you at all." The reassurance addresses a practical fear. The Jews had come with a hidden agenda — "if you are given this, take it; if not, beware" — and declining to rule might have seemed to expose the Prophet ﷺ to their hostility or their propaganda. God tells him that no harm will come from declining. The verse frees the judge from the pressure of litigants who come in bad faith; he need not fear that refusing to be used will cost him. The Prophet ﷺ, in the actual incident, chose to judge — and judged by the Torah's own ruling — but the freedom not to judge was his.

**"But If You Judge, Judge with Justice"**

*Wa-in ḥakamta fa-ḥkum baynahum bi-l-qisṭ* — "and if you judge, judge between them with equity." This is the verse's heart, and it lays down a principle of immense consequence. The litigants are described, in this very verse, as listeners to lies and devourers of bribes; they came with a scheme to manipulate the Prophet ﷺ; they are not Muslims. And yet the command is: if you judge them, judge *justly*. The character of the parties does not affect the standard of judgment. The judge does not tilt against the dishonest litigant because he is dishonest, or against the non-Muslim because he is not a Muslim. *Qisṭ* — equity, fair measure — is owed to everyone who comes before the court.

This is the judicial application of verse 8: "let not the hatred of a people lead you to be unjust; be just, that is nearer to *taqwā*." The Qur'an commands justice toward enemies in verse 8, and here commands it toward litigants of bad faith. The Prophet ﷺ embodied the command. He judged for a Jew against a Muslim when the evidence favored the Jew, and Sūrat al-Nisāʾ (4:105–113) was revealed to confirm a similar judgment in which a Jew had been falsely accused by Muslims. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, as caliph, appeared before the judge Shurayḥ in a dispute with a Jew over a coat of armor, and when Shurayḥ ruled for the Jew for want of admissible evidence on ʿAlī's side, the Jew, astonished that the ruler had submitted to the ruling, embraced Islam.

The source directs the reader to 4:58 — "when you judge between people, judge with justice" — and to 4:135. The Qur'an's insistence on this point is so consistent that the classical jurists made judicial impartiality a condition of the judge's validity: a judge known to favor one party over another on grounds other than evidence is disqualified.

**"Truly God Loves the Just"**

*Inna Allāha yuḥibbu al-muqsiṭīn* — "indeed, God loves the equitable." The verse ends not with a threat but with love. The source notes the repetition in 60:8, where God permits kindness and justice toward non-Muslims who do not fight the believers, and again says, "indeed God loves the just." The *muqsiṭ* — the one who gives fair measure — is among the categories of people the Qur'an explicitly names as beloved of God, alongside the God-conscious, the patient, the doers of good, and those who purify themselves. The Prophet ﷺ described the reward:

> *"The just will be with God upon pulpits of light, on the right of the Most Merciful — and both His hands are right — those who are just in their judgment, their families, and what they are put in charge of."* (Muslim 1827)

Note the ḥadīth's range: justice in judgment, justice in one's family, justice in every trust. The judicial verse opens onto the whole of life.

**The Verse in a Plural Society**

Verse 42 is among the Qur'anic foundations of coexistence. It presumes that non-Muslims live within the Muslim polity, that they have their own law and courts, that they may choose to come before the Muslim judge, and that when they do, they must receive exactly the justice a Muslim would receive. It presumes, too, that some of them will come in bad faith — and it does not permit that bad faith to alter the standard. For a Muslim living today in a plural society, whether as a majority or a minority, the verse's principle governs every position of authority he holds: the manager evaluating employees of different faiths, the teacher grading students, the official processing applications, the arbitrator settling a dispute. The identity and even the character of the person before him do not alter what he owes: *qisṭ*. And the reward for giving it is not merely a clear conscience but the love of God.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:43

> **And how is it that they come to thee for judgment, when they have the Torah, wherein is God's Judgment? Yet even after that, they turn their backs, and they are not believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question That Exposes a Motive**

The verse opens with an expression of astonishment: *wa-kayfa yuḥakkimūnaka wa-ʿindahumu al-Tawrātu fīhā ḥukmu Allāh* — "And how do they make you judge, when they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God?" The question is not a request for information; it is an exposure. The Jews who brought the case of the two adulterers to the Prophet ﷺ had, in their own possession, a scripture that already contained God's ruling on the matter — stoning for the married adulterer. Why, then, come to him? The source records al-Ṭabarī's answer: because they hoped for a lighter ruling. They were not seeking God's judgment; they were shopping for a more comfortable one. The question *kayfa*, "how?", lays bare the disingenuousness: a person who has God's ruling in his hand and goes looking for another is not seeking truth but escape.

**The Recognition of the Torah's Authority**

The verse contains a statement of great significance for the Qur'an's view of earlier scripture: *wa-ʿindahumu al-Tawrātu fīhā ḥukmu Allāh* — "they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God." The Qur'an here affirms that the Torah in the possession of the Jews of Madinah contained God's judgment — not merely that it once did, but that it does, *fīhā*, "in it." The source draws the correct inference, which the following verses (44–47) will develop: the Torah and the Gospel remain valid sources of moral and legal guidance for Jews and Christians respectively, even after the coming of the Prophet ﷺ and even in his presence. The Prophet ﷺ himself acted on this in the incident: he did not rule by a new revelation but sent for the Torah and applied what he found there, saying, "I judge by what is in the Torah."

This must be held together with the Qur'an's charge of *taḥrīf*. The Qur'an does not say that the Torah is entirely corrupt; it says that some of its people distort some of its words and conceal some of its rulings (5:13, 15, 41). The text still contained the verse of stoning — the rabbi had to cover it with his hand. The distortion was primarily in handling and interpretation, and where the text remained, its authority remained. The Qur'an's own position, as the next verse will say, is that it was "sent down" containing "guidance and light," and that its faithful custodians judged by it.

**"Then They Turn Away After That"**

*Thumma yatawallawna min baʿdi dhālik* — "then they turn away after that." The sequence is damning. They have the Torah; it contains God's judgment; they come to the Prophet ﷺ seeking something else; and when he gives them God's judgment — the very one their Torah contains — they turn away from it. Their scheme had been, as verse 41 recorded, "if you are given this, take it; if not, beware." When the Prophet ﷺ ruled stoning, they were not "given this," and they turned away. The verb *tawallā* means to turn one's back, to walk away — and the phrase "after that" (*min baʿdi dhālik*) marks the turning as one made with full knowledge. They turned away not from ignorance but from a ruling they knew to be God's, delivered from their own Book, by a Prophet whose judgment they had themselves invoked.

**"And They Are Not Believers"**

*Wa-mā ulāʾika bi-l-muʾminīn* — "and those are not believers." The construction is emphatic: *mā ... bi-*, the strong negation. The commentators drew out what this verdict is based upon. It is not based on their being Jews; the Qur'an praises believing Jews elsewhere (3:113–115; 5:66). It is based on their conduct in this matter: a person who possesses God's judgment, seeks another, and then turns from God's judgment when it is delivered has shown that he does not believe *in that judgment* — neither in his own Torah, which he evaded, nor in the Prophet ﷺ, whom he invoked only as a possible source of leniency. Faith is demonstrated by submission to God's ruling when it is known. Its absence is demonstrated by evasion. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the verse describes a state of unbelief in the *practical* sense: whatever these people professed, their behavior showed that they did not hold God's law to be binding upon them.

**The Universal Principle: Forum-Shopping in Religion**

The verse names a phenomenon that exists in every religious community, and the commentators applied it beyond its occasion. It is the search for a ruling one prefers, from a source one does not otherwise respect, in order to escape a ruling one already knows. A Muslim who knows the clear ruling of the Qur'an and the Sunnah on a matter and goes from scholar to scholar seeking a more lenient opinion — not out of genuine uncertainty but out of a desire for permission — is doing what the Jews of this verse did. The jurists named this practice *tatabbuʿ al-rukhaṣ*, "hunting for concessions," and condemned it. The Prophet ﷺ described the person of sound faith as one who "consults his heart" and recognizes that "righteousness is what the soul is at ease with, and sin is what wavers in the breast, even if people give you rulings" (Aḥmad; al-Dārimī). The person who knows God's judgment and seeks another has already turned away, whatever ruling he finally obtains.

**The Verse's Place in the Argument of 41–50**

Verse 43 is a pivot. Verses 41–42 described the Jews who came to the Prophet ﷺ and instructed him on how to receive them. Verse 43 asks *why* they came, given that they had the Torah, and answers by exposing their motive. Verses 44–47 will then establish the authority of the Torah and the Gospel as God's revelations, each with its faithful custodians, and will state three times the principle that whoever does not judge by what God sent down is a disbeliever, a wrongdoer, an iniquitous person. Verses 48–50 will place the Qur'an as the final revelation, confirming and guarding the earlier ones, and will command the Prophet ﷺ to judge by it. The whole passage is a meditation on the relationship between revelation and judgment: God has sent down His law in successive scriptures; each community is bound by what it received; and the mark of belief is submission to that law, not evasion of it.

**The Lesson for the Reader**

The astonished *kayfa*, "how?", of this verse should be heard by every believer who has God's judgment in his possession. The Muslim has the Qur'an and the Sunnah, "in which is the judgment of God." When he knows the ruling and seeks another, when he consults the Book only to find what he wants and turns away when it says what he does not want, the verse's question is addressed to him: *how* do you seek judgment elsewhere, when you have it here? And its verdict is a warning: the one who turns away from God's known judgment, however he names himself, is not, in that act, a believer.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:44

> **Truly We sent down the Torah, wherein is a guidance and a light, by which the prophets who submitted [unto God] judged those who are Jews, as did the sages and the rabbis, in accordance with such of God's Book as they were bidden to preserve and to which they were witnesses. So fear not mankind, but fear Me! And sell not My signs for a paltry price. Whosoever judges not by that which God has sent down—it is they who are disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Qur'an's Testimony to the Torah**

Few verses in the Qur'an speak of an earlier scripture with such honor. *Innā anzalnā al-Tawrāta fīhā hudan wa-nūr* — "Indeed, We sent down the Torah; in it is guidance and light." The verb *anzalnā*, "We sent down," is the same verb used of the Qur'an itself; the Torah is placed, by this word, in the category of true revelation. And it is described with the two terms — *hudā* (guidance) and *nūr* (light) — that the Qur'an uses of itself (5:15–16). The source notes the parallel in 6:91: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought as a light and a guidance for the people?" The Qur'an does not merely tolerate the Torah; it affirms it as God's own sending-down, luminous and guiding.

This affirmation is the foundation of the verse's argument. Because the Torah is God's light, those who possess it are bound to judge by it; because it contains guidance, evading it is culpable; and because it was preserved and witnessed by faithful custodians for centuries, the failure of some later custodians to uphold it is a betrayal of their own tradition. The verse thus honors the Torah in order to hold its people to it.

**Three Ranks of Custodians**

The verse names those who judged by the Torah: *yaḥkumu bihā al-nabiyyūna alladhīna aslamū li-lladhīna hādū wa-l-rabbāniyyūna wa-l-aḥbār* — "the prophets who submitted judged by it for those who are Jews, and the *rabbāniyyūn* and the *aḥbār*."

First, *al-nabiyyūna alladhīna aslamū*, "the prophets who submitted." The description of the Israelite prophets as those who "submitted" — who were *muslimūn* in the universal sense — is the Qur'an's consistent teaching: every prophet was a submitter to God, and Islam in this sense is the religion of all of them. The source records two identifications: some (al-Ṭabarī) took the phrase to include the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who did indeed judge the Jews by the Torah in the incident of the adulterers; most (al-Zamakhsharī) took it to refer to the prophets of Israel between Moses and Jesus — David, Solomon, and the others — who ruled their people by the Torah. Both are compatible: the line of submitting prophets who upheld the Torah's law culminates in the final Prophet ﷺ, who applied it when it was brought before him. The phrase also carries a quiet rebuke: the prophets themselves submitted to the Torah's rulings; who are their followers to evade them?

Second, *al-rabbāniyyūn*. The source records the range of interpretations: the legal and political authorities of the Jews (al-Ṭabarī); the devout ascetics among Aaron's descendants, hence something like "priests" (al-Zamakhsharī); or the most authoritative scholars, comparable to the *mujtahid* jurists of Islam, qualified to issue decisive rulings (al-Rāzī). The word is from *rabb*, Lord; a *rabbānī* is one devoted to the Lord, one who teaches and trains others in the Lord's way. The Qur'an uses it in 3:79 for what a prophet's followers should become: "be *rabbāniyyūn*, because you teach the Book and study it." Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that the *rabbānī* is one who nurtures people with the small matters of knowledge before the great.

Third, *al-aḥbār*, the plural of *ḥibr* or *ḥabr*, a learned man, a scholar — the word the source notes was usually glossed as the *ʿulamāʾ* of the Jews. The three ranks together describe a complete chain of religious authority — prophets, devoted teachers, and learned scholars — all of whom judged by the Torah. The verse thereby establishes that the Torah's law was not an abstraction but a living system, upheld across generations by every level of leadership.

**"By What They Were Entrusted to Preserve, and They Were Witnesses to It"**

*Bi-mā stuḥfiẓū min kitābi Allāhi wa-kānū ʿalayhi shuhadāʾ* — "by what they were entrusted to preserve of God's Book, and they were witnesses over it." The verb *istuḥfiẓū* is the passive of the tenth form of ḥ-f-ẓ, to guard, to memorize: "they were asked to preserve," "preservation was entrusted to them." The construction is significant. The Torah's preservation was *entrusted* to its custodians; it was their responsibility, and the Qur'an implies that the responsibility was not fully discharged — which is why *taḥrīf* was possible. By contrast, of the Qur'an God says: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its Guardian" (15:9). The commentators drew the contrast explicitly: the earlier scriptures were preserved by human custodians, who could fail; the final scripture is preserved by God, who cannot.

"And they were witnesses over it" — they testified to its authenticity and its rulings, and were bound to testify truly. The rabbi who covered the verse of stoning with his hand was a witness who bore false witness against the Book entrusted to him.

**"Fear Not Mankind, but Fear Me"**

*Fa-lā takhshawu al-nāsa wa-khshawn* — "so do not fear people, but fear Me." The command is addressed to the custodians of the Torah, and it diagnoses precisely what had gone wrong. Why had the Jewish leaders abandoned the penalty of stoning? By Ibn Ṣūriyā's own confession: because it fell upon nobles, and they feared the nobles' displeasure. Fear of people had overridden fear of God, and the ruling was changed. The verse's remedy is to restore the right order of fear. The source notes the recurrence of the command in verse 3 of this sūrah, and in 2:150 and 3:175. Every scholar of every community faces this test: the powerful want rulings that suit them, and the scholar who fears them will supply such rulings; the scholar who fears God will not. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The best *jihād* is a word of truth before a tyrannical ruler" (Abū Dāwūd 4344; al-Tirmidhī 2174).

**"And Sell Not My Signs for a Paltry Price"**

*Wa-lā tashtarū bi-āyātī thamanan qalīlan* — "and do not purchase with My signs a small price." The Qur'an's recurring metaphor of the bad bargain, which the source traces through 2:41, 79, 174; 3:77, 187, 199; 9:9; 16:95, is here applied to the specific corruption of verse 42: taking bribes to alter rulings. Note the construction: it is not "do not sell My signs for a price" but "do not *buy* a small price *with* My signs" — the signs are the currency, and what is purchased with them is a paltry sum. The image inverts the usual order to stress the absurdity: one trades eternal, infinitely valuable guidance to acquire something trivial. Every price is paltry beside God's signs; the phrase "small price" does not mean that a large enough bribe would be acceptable, but that any worldly gain is small by comparison.

The two commands together — fear not people, sell not My signs — name the two motives that corrupt religious scholarship: fear and greed. The scholar bends the ruling because he fears the powerful, or because he wants their money. Both were present in the incident of the adulterers; both are present wherever a scripture's custodians betray it.

**"Whosoever Judges Not by What God Has Sent Down — They Are the Disbelievers"**

*Wa-man lam yaḥkum bi-mā anzala Allāhu fa-ulāʾika humu al-kāfirūn* — "and whoever does not judge by what God has sent down, those are the disbelievers." This is the first of three nearly identical statements (the others in verses 45 and 47, ending "wrongdoers" and "iniquitous" respectively), and it is among the most discussed sentences in the history of Islamic thought. The source presents the classical framework.

First, the verse's occasion is the Jews' abandonment of the Torah's ruling, and al-Ṭabarī notes that *kāfirūn* here may carry its root sense of "coverers" — those who hide the ruling — rather than absolute unbelief. Second, the interpretation attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, which al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn Kathīr transmit, distinguishes degrees: the one who *rejects* God's judgment — who denies that it is binding, or holds another law to be superior — is a disbeliever in the full sense; the one who acknowledges God's judgment as binding but fails to apply it out of weakness, desire, or fear is a wrongdoer (v. 45) and an iniquitous person (v. 47) — a sinner, not an apostate. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said of this verse: "It is not the disbelief they mean; it is a disbelief less than disbelief" (*kufr dūna kufr*). Ṭāwūs and ʿAṭāʾ transmitted the same distinction.

This distinction became the mainstream Sunni position and has enormous practical consequence. It prevents the verse from being used to declare every sinning ruler or judge an apostate — a misuse that the Khārijites made in the first century and that extremist movements have made since. It preserves the verse's full force: to reject God's law, to deny its authority, to prefer another law as better, is disbelief. And it preserves the Qur'an's own distinction between the disbeliever and the disobedient believer. The three verses, read together with their three different verdicts, support the graded reading: the same failure — not judging by what God sent down — is *kufr* when it springs from rejection, *ẓulm* when it wrongs others, and *fisq* when it breaks the bounds of obedience.

**The Verse's Standing Charge**

Verse 44 establishes that every community that has received God's revelation is bound to judge by it, and that its custodians — prophets, teachers, scholars — hold it in trust. It names the two corruptions that destroy that trust — fear of people and love of gain — and it declares that the abandonment of God's judgment is, at its root, a form of disbelief. The verse honors the Torah in the strongest terms and holds its people to it; and by the same logic it holds the Muslims to the Qur'an. The scholar who reads it is warned; the judge who reads it is warned; the ordinary believer who reads it learns why the sūrah began with "fulfill your pacts": the greatest pact is the one that binds a people to the Book God sent them.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:45

> **And therein We prescribed for them: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds, retribution. But whosoever forgoes it out of charity, it shall be an expiation for him. Whosoever judges not by that which God has sent down—it is they who are wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Example from the Torah**

Verse 44 affirmed that the Torah contains guidance and light and was judged by faithfully for generations. Verse 45 gives a specific example of its contents: *wa-katabnā ʿalayhim fīhā anna al-nafsa bi-l-nafsi wa-l-ʿayna bi-l-ʿayni wa-l-anfa bi-l-anfi wa-l-udhuna bi-l-udhuni wa-l-sinna bi-l-sinni wa-l-jurūḥa qiṣāṣ* — "And We prescribed for them in it: the life for the life, the eye for the eye, the nose for the nose, the ear for the ear, the tooth for the tooth, and wounds are retribution." The source notes the biblical parallels — Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20, Deuteronomy 19:21 — and observes that the Qur'an here accurately represents the Torah's law of retribution. Al-Rāzī, cited in the source, explains the verse's purpose: to remind the Jews of Madinah of a Torah ruling they had also been neglecting.

**The Occasion: Unequal Blood Among the Tribes**

The source preserves the historical background. The Banū al-Naḍīr and the Banū Qurayẓah, the two principal Jewish tribes of Madinah, had established an unequal system of retribution based on tribal standing. The Naḍīr held themselves superior. If a man of the Naḍīr killed a man of the Qurayẓah, he was not executed but paid a reduced blood-money; if a man of the Qurayẓah killed a man of the Naḍīr, he was executed, or made to pay double. When the Qurayẓah appealed to the Prophet ﷺ, he ruled that the blood of the two tribes was equal — "a life for a life" — and this verse confirmed the ruling. The incident illustrates exactly the corruption verse 44 named: a ruling of God's Book set aside to accommodate social hierarchy, out of fear of the powerful. The Torah said "a life for a life," without qualification by rank; the Naḍīr had rewritten it.

The verse's structure enforces the equality it describes. Each pair is exactly symmetrical: life for life, eye for eye, nose for nose, ear for ear, tooth for tooth. There is no "a noble's life for a commoner's life plus compensation." The repetition of the definite article — *the* life, *the* eye — universalizes: any life, any eye. The Prophet ﷺ confirmed the principle for his own community in his Farewell Sermon: "The blood of the Muslims is equal" (Abū Dāwūd 2751; al-Nasāʾī).

**Qiṣāṣ: The Meaning of Retribution**

*Qiṣāṣ* is from q-ṣ-ṣ, to follow a track, to trace footsteps (a *qiṣṣah*, story, follows the track of events); *qiṣāṣ* is the following of an injury with its exact equivalent — no more, no less. The word itself contains the principle of proportion. It is not vengeance (*thaʾr*), which the pre-Islamic Arabs practiced without limit, killing several for one, or a noble for a slave; it is measured equivalence. The Qur'an calls this a source of life: "In retribution there is life for you, O possessors of intellect" (2:179) — because the certainty of exact retribution deters the crime and, when a crime occurs, closes the matter without the endless escalation of blood-feud. The verse's phrase "and wounds are retribution" extends the principle to non-fatal injuries, which the jurists developed in detail: an injury inflicted deliberately may be requited by an equivalent injury where exact equivalence is possible, and by compensation (*arsh*) where it is not.

**"But Whosoever Forgoes It Out of Charity, It Is an Expiation for Him"**

*Fa-man taṣaddaqa bihi fa-huwa kaffāratun lah* — "but whoever gives it up as charity, it is an expiation for him." Here the verse introduces an element that the source notes is absent from the biblical passages: the option of forgiveness, described as *ṣadaqah*, charity. The victim (or the victim's heirs) may forgo retribution, and this forgoing is framed as a gift — not to the offender only, but to God, from whom the giver receives *kaffārah*, expiation.

The source records the commentators' debate over whose sins are expiated. Al-Ṭabarī argues that the expiation is for the *forgiver*: he cites the ḥadīth, "No man is injured in his body and forgives it but that God raises him a degree and removes from him a sin" (al-Tirmidhī 1393; Ibn Mājah 2693), and notes that the offender's expiation comes, by other texts, through undergoing the penalty. Others held that the expiation is for the *offender*, whose crime is covered by the victim's forgiveness. Al-Rāzī reconciles them with 42:40 — "whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with God" — suggesting that the forgiver receives a reward and the offender an expiation, or that the expiation is the forgiver's and the reward is additional. The mainstream reading, following al-Ṭabarī and the ḥadīth, is that the forgiver's own sins are expiated in proportion to what he forgoes. This is a remarkable incentive: a person injured in body or bereaved of kin, who has every right to exact equivalent harm, is told that if he lets it go for God's sake, God will let go of his sins.

**The Islamic Development of the Principle**

The source notes an important difference between the Torah's law as this verse describes it and the Qur'an's law for the Muslims. The verse presents the Torah as allowing only retribution or outright forgiveness, with no middle option. The Qur'an, in 2:178, adds a third: blood-money (*diyah*), which the victim's heirs may accept in place of retribution — "but whoever is pardoned somewhat by his brother, then let there be a following in fairness and payment to him in kindness; that is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy." Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī, as the source records, understood this as an easing granted to the Muslim community: three options instead of two. The Qur'an thus confirms the Torah's principle — proportionate retribution with the option of forgiveness — while extending its mercy.

**The Ethics of Retribution and Forgiveness Together**

The verse holds two things in balance that modern moral thinking often separates: the right to justice and the virtue of mercy. The right is real. The victim is not commanded to forgive; he is *permitted* to demand exact retribution, and the state must provide it. This protects the weak, who in every society are the ones injured with impunity when justice is optional. But the virtue is also real, and it is set above the right: forgiveness is *ṣadaqah*, and its reward is *kaffārah*. The Prophet ﷺ, whenever a case of retribution was brought to him, would counsel forgiveness before ruling (Abū Dāwūd 4497; al-Nasāʾī). He never forced it; he always encouraged it. The Law thus builds a society in which justice is guaranteed and mercy is honored — where no one is forced to forgive and everyone is invited to.

**"Whosoever Judges Not by What God Has Sent Down — They Are the Wrongdoers"**

*Wa-man lam yaḥkum bi-mā anzala Allāhu fa-ulāʾika humu al-ẓālimūn* — "and whoever does not judge by what God has sent down, those are the wrongdoers." The refrain of verse 44 returns with a different ending. There it was *al-kāfirūn*, the disbelievers; here it is *al-ẓālimūn*, the wrongdoers. The source records the reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās: the three verdicts correspond to three failures. Rejecting God's judgment is disbelief; applying it unequally, so that some are wronged, is *ẓulm*; and breaking out of its bounds is *fisq* (v. 47). The fit with this verse's content is exact. The Naḍīr's unequal retribution did not deny the Torah's law; it *wronged* the Qurayẓah by applying it unequally. To judge partially is *ẓulm* — placing things where they do not belong, giving one party more than his due and another less.

The word *ẓālim* also points to the injured. Wherever God's judgment is not applied, someone is wronged: the Qurayẓah under the Naḍīr's system; the weak under any system that exempts the strong. The refrain thus reminds the judge that his failure is not an abstract dereliction but a concrete injustice done to a concrete person.

**The Verse for the Reader**

Verse 45 teaches the equal value of every human life and limb before the law, the proportion that must govern all response to injury, and the mercy that lies above proportion. It condemns every system that measures blood by status — and such systems are not confined to seventh-century Madinah; every society has its Naḍīr and its Qurayẓah, its lives that count more and lives that count less. And it offers the injured a choice whose consequence reaches into eternity: to take what is owed, or to give it as charity and receive expiation. The believer who has been wronged should know both that his right is real and that his forgiveness is precious; and the believer who judges should know that to weigh lives unequally is *ẓulm*, whatever custom or power may say.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:46

> **And in their footsteps, We sent Jesus son of Mary, confirming the Torah that had come before him, and We gave him the Gospel, wherein is a guidance and a light, confirming the Torah that had come before him, as a guidance and an exhortation to the reverent.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**"In Their Footsteps"**

*Wa-qaffaynā ʿalā āthārihim bi-ʿĪsā ibni Maryam* — "And We sent following in their footsteps Jesus son of Mary." The verb *qaffā* comes from *qafā*, the nape of the neck, and means to follow directly behind, to come at the heels of; the Qur'an uses it of the succession of messengers to Israel: "We gave Moses the Book and followed him with the messengers" (2:87). The phrase *ʿalā āthārihim*, "upon their traces," places Jesus in the exact line of the prophets named in verse 44 — "the prophets who submitted" — who judged by the Torah. The source records al-Rāzī's and al-Zamakhsharī's reading: Jesus came in the footsteps of the prophets, walking the same path, sent by the same God, upholding the same law. This is the Qur'an's consistent picture of Jesus: not a founder of a new religion but a link in the chain of Israelite prophethood, sent, as he says in the Gospel, "to the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and, as the Qur'an says, "a messenger to the Children of Israel" (3:49).

The name "Jesus son of Mary" (*ʿĪsā ibn Maryam*) is itself doctrinal. Naming a man by his mother is unusual in Arabic and in Semitic naming generally; the Qur'an does it with Jesus consistently, and the reason is twofold: to affirm the virgin birth — he has no human father to be named by — and to affirm his humanity against those who would call him the son of God. He is Mary's son; he is God's messenger; he is not God's son. Verses 17, 72–75, and 116–117 of this sūrah will press the point.

**"Confirming the Torah That Was Before Him"**

*Muṣaddiqan li-mā bayna yadayhi mina al-Tawrāh* — "confirming what was before him of the Torah." The phrase occurs twice in this verse, once of Jesus himself and once of the Gospel, and the repetition is emphatic. The source cites the parallels: 3:50, where Jesus says, "confirming what was before me of the Torah, and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you"; 61:6, where he says, "I am the messenger of God to you, confirming what was before me of the Torah"; and 3:39, where John (Yaḥyā) is described as "confirming a word from God" — that is, Jesus. The verb *ṣaddaqa* means to declare true, to verify, to endorse. Jesus did not come to abolish the Torah but to confirm it — and al-Ṭabarī, as the source notes, draws the legal implication: Jesus upheld the Torah's rulings, and those not abrogated by the Gospel remained binding on his followers. The Gospel's own record agrees: "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil" (Matthew 5:17).

The point matters for the argument of verses 41–50. The Qur'an is building a picture of successive revelations, each confirming the one before. The Torah was sent down with guidance and light (v. 44); Jesus came confirming it, and the Gospel was given confirming it (v. 46); and the Qur'an comes confirming both and guarding over them (v. 48). No revelation contradicts the essential message of its predecessors; each reaffirms the one God, the one moral law, and the one accountability. What changes is the detailed legislation suited to each community and age — and even that changes by the authority of the same God.

**"And We Gave Him the Gospel, Wherein Is Guidance and Light"**

*Wa-ātaynāhu al-Injīla fīhi hudan wa-nūr* — "and We gave him the Gospel; in it is guidance and light." The Qur'an describes the Gospel with the very words it used for the Torah in verse 44 and for itself in verse 15. The source lists the Qur'an's self-descriptions as light — 5:15; 7:157; 64:8 — and observes that the same terms are here applied to the Gospel. Three scriptures, one description: guidance and light. The *Injīl* (from the Greek *euangelion*, "good news," through Syriac or Ethiopic) is in the Qur'an's usage the revelation given to Jesus — the message he preached — of which the four canonical Gospels are the community's records. The Qur'an affirms that the revelation to Jesus was God's guidance and light, and it holds Christians to it, as verse 47 will say: "Let the people of the Gospel judge by what God sent down in it."

Note the verb: *ātaynāhu*, "We gave him." The Gospel is described as something given to Jesus, as the Torah was given to Moses — placing Jesus firmly in the position of a recipient of revelation, a prophet, not its author or source. The doctrinal implication is the same as the naming "son of Mary": the one who receives the Book from God is God's servant.

**"A Guidance and an Exhortation to the Reverent"**

*Wa-hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan li-l-muttaqīn* — "and a guidance and an admonition for the God-fearing." The verse ends with a second *hudā*, guidance, and adds *mawʿiẓah*, exhortation, admonition — the kind of speech that softens the heart and moves it to right action. The Gospel is preeminently a book of *mawʿiẓah*: the Sermon on the Mount, the parables, the calls to mercy, humility, and love of God and neighbor are exhortation in the fullest sense. The Qur'an elsewhere praises the Christians' "compassion and mercy" (57:27) and will, in verses 82–85 of this sūrah, praise those among them whose eyes overflow with tears at the truth.

But the guidance and exhortation are "for the *muttaqīn*" — the God-fearing, those who guard themselves against God's displeasure. The same restriction governs the Qur'an: "a guidance for the *muttaqīn*" (2:2). A scripture guides those who approach it with reverence and the will to obey; those who approach it to evade, distort, or exploit — like the Jews of verses 41–43 — are not guided by it, however much light it contains. The Gospel's light, like the Torah's and the Qur'an's, illuminates the path only for those who want to walk it.

**The Qur'an's Honor for Jesus and the Gospel**

The verse should be read with attention to how a Muslim is required to regard Jesus and his Book. He is God's messenger, sent in the footsteps of the prophets; he confirmed the Torah; he received the Gospel from God; the Gospel is guidance and light. A Muslim who denies any of this has departed from the Qur'an. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the nearest of people to Jesus son of Mary in this world and the next; the prophets are brothers from one father with different mothers, and their religion is one" (al-Bukhārī 3443; Muslim 2365). The Qur'an's disagreement with Christianity is not about the honor due to Jesus but about the claims made *beyond* what he taught — divinity, sonship, trinity — which the Qur'an holds to be later developments that Jesus himself will disavow (5:116–117). The distinction between the message and its later interpretation is exactly the distinction the sūrah has drawn in the case of the Torah: the revelation is light; the distortion is human.

**The Verse in the Argument of 41–50**

Verse 46 completes the second stage of the sūrah's account of successive revelation. Verse 44: the Torah, with its prophets, teachers, and scholars. Verse 46: Jesus and the Gospel, confirming the Torah. Verse 47 will draw the conclusion for Christians — judge by the Gospel — and verse 48 will introduce the Qur'an as the confirmer and guardian of both. The reader who follows the sequence sees the Qur'an's theology of revelation unfold: one God, one line of prophets each walking in the footsteps of the last, one light passed from Book to Book, each community bound to the Book it received, and a final Book that confirms and completes. Jesus stands in that line, honored and human, and his Gospel shines with the same light as the Torah before it and the Qur'an after.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:47

> **Let the people of the Gospel judge by what God has sent down therein. Whosoever judges not by that which God has sent down—it is they who are iniquitous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Command Addressed to Christians**

*Wa-l-yaḥkum ahlu al-Injīli bi-mā anzala Allāhu fīh* — "And let the people of the Gospel judge by what God has sent down in it." The verse is grammatically a command — the *lām* of command (*lām al-amr*) prefixed to the jussive verb — and it is addressed not to Muslims but to "the people of the Gospel," the Christians. This is remarkable. The Qur'an, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, here instructs the Christian community to judge by its own scripture. The phrase *ahl al-Injīl*, "the people of the Gospel," occurs only here in the Qur'an, and it names the Christians by their Book, as the Jews are named by theirs — a designation that dignifies them as the recipients of a revelation and, at the same time, binds them to it.

There is a variant reading (*qirāʾah*) attributed to Ḥamzah in which the verb is read *wa-li-yaḥkuma*, "and so that they might judge," making the clause depend on the previous verse: "We gave him the Gospel ... so that the people of the Gospel might judge by what God sent down in it." Both readings yield the same meaning: the Gospel was given to be judged by.

**What Does the Gospel Contain to Judge By?**

The source records an important discussion among the commentators. The Gospel, as al-Zamakhsharī observes, contains teachings and exhortations but relatively few legal rulings — it is, as verse 46 said, "a guidance and an exhortation" (*mawʿiẓah*). What, then, does it mean to "judge by what God sent down in it"? Ibn Kathīr's answer, preserved in the source, is that judging by the Gospel means, in most matters, following the Torah's rulings, since Jesus lived largely according to the Torah and confirmed it (v. 46), and the Gospel abrogated only some specific rulings — "to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you" (3:50). The Christians were thus bound to the law of Moses as Jesus confirmed and modified it, together with the Gospel's own moral and spiritual teaching.

Among the Gospel's contents that bear directly on this sūrah's argument is its testimony to Jesus' own status. The source's discussion of verses 17 and 72–75 and the Qur'an's insistence that Jesus is God's servant and messenger find their claimed anchor here: to "judge by the Gospel" includes taking seriously what the Gospel records of Jesus' own words — his worship of the Father, his prayers, his declaration that "the Lord our God is one Lord" (Mark 12:29), and his statement, "I can of mine own self do nothing" (John 5:30). The Qur'an's claim, pressed in verses 116–117, is that Jesus taught what the Gospel records him teaching, and that the Christians who deified him departed from their own Book.

**Does the Gospel Remain Valid?**

The source presents the central interpretive question directly. Some commentators (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī) held that the command to judge by the Gospel refers to the period before the Qur'an's revelation: the Christians *should have* judged by the Gospel, and after the coming of the Prophet ﷺ they are bound to follow the Qur'an, which abrogates the earlier scriptures. On this reading the verse is a historical statement, not a present command.

The source argues, and the weight of the passage supports, that this reading sits uneasily with the surrounding verses. Verse 43 asked in astonishment why the Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ for judgment "when they have the Torah, in which is God's judgment" — implying that, even in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, their recourse to their own scripture was sufficient. Verse 44 commanded the Torah's custodians to judge by it and not to sell God's signs. Verse 68 will say to the People of the Book, "You stand on nothing until you observe the Torah and the Gospel and what has been sent down to you from your Lord." And in the incident of the adulterers, the Prophet ﷺ judged by the Torah and said, "O God, I am the first to revive Your command after they had killed it" — reviving, and thereby legitimating, the Torah's ruling for the Jews.

The reconciling position, which many hold, is this. The Qur'an calls all people, including Jews and Christians, to believe in the final Prophet ﷺ — verses 15, 19, and 68 of this sūrah make that call explicit, and 3:85 states that a religion other than submission to God will not be accepted. But so long as a community of the Book remains a community of the Book — has not accepted the Qur'an — its members are bound by the law God gave them, and it is better that they judge by their own scripture faithfully than that they abandon it for "the judgment of the Age of Ignorance" (v. 50). The Torah and the Gospel are still God's sending-down, still "guidance and light"; their light has not gone out because a greater light has come. The Islamic legal tradition acted on this: Christians under Muslim rule were left to their own law in their own affairs, and the Muslim judge was to respect it.

**"Whosoever Judges Not by What God Has Sent Down — They Are the Iniquitous"**

*Wa-man lam yaḥkum bi-mā anzala Allāhu fa-ulāʾika humu al-fāsiqūn* — "and whoever does not judge by what God has sent down, those are the *fāsiqūn*." The refrain completes its third variation. Verse 44: *al-kāfirūn*, the disbelievers. Verse 45: *al-ẓālimūn*, the wrongdoers. Verse 47: *al-fāsiqūn*, the iniquitous. The word *fisq* is from f-s-q, used of a date bursting out of its skin: the *fāsiq* is one who has broken out of the bounds of obedience, who has left the path while perhaps still professing to walk it. The commentary on verse 44 presented Ibn ʿAbbās's graded reading: rejection of God's judgment is *kufr*; unequal application is *ẓulm*; breach of its bounds is *fisq*.

The three verses may also be read, as some commentators proposed, as three descriptions of the same act from three angles. The one who abandons God's judgment covers the truth (*kufr*), wrongs those who deserved justice (*ẓulm*), and breaks out of obedience (*fisq*). Each verse ends with the epithet most fitting to its content: verse 44, on concealment of the Torah's ruling — concealment being the root meaning of *kufr*; verse 45, on unequal retribution — inequality being *ẓulm*; and verse 47, on the Christians' departure from the Gospel — departure being *fisq*. Both readings serve the passage's purpose: to establish that the abandonment of revealed judgment is a grave sin however it is described, and that each community stands accountable to the Book it was given.

**The Standing Principle: Each Community Is Judged by Its Book**

Verses 44, 45, and 47 together lay down a principle that the next verse will crown. God sent the Torah; those who received it are judged by it. God sent the Gospel; those who received it are judged by it. God sent the Qur'an; those who receive it are judged by it — and, as verse 48 will say, the Qur'an is also the guardian and criterion over the earlier Books. No community is judged by a Book it never received, and no community may abandon the Book it did receive. The Qur'an says of the Day of Judgment: "Every community will be called to its Book" (45:28).

**A Word to the Muslim Reader**

The Muslim who reads a verse addressed to Christians should not read it as though it concerned only them. The principle is universal, and the Qur'an, by stating it of the Torah and the Gospel before stating it of itself, teaches the Muslims that they are not exempt. If it is *fisq* for the people of the Gospel to abandon the Gospel's judgment, it is *fisq* for the people of the Qur'an to abandon the Qur'an's. The Prophet ﷺ foretold that his community would follow the ways of those before them "span by span and cubit by cubit" (al-Bukhārī 3456; Muslim 2669) — and the way of abandoning one's Book while professing it is the way this sūrah has been describing since verse 13. The verse's honor for the Gospel is real, and its warning is for everyone.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:48

> **And We have sent down unto thee the Book in truth, confirming the Book that came before it, and as a protector over it. So judge between them in accordance with what God has sent down, and follow not their caprices away from the truth that has come unto thee. For each among you We have appointed a law and a way. And had God willed, He would have made you one community, but [He willed otherwise], that He might try you in that which He has given you. So vie with one another in good deeds. Unto God shall be your return all together, and He will inform you of that wherein you differ.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Culmination of the Sequence**

Verses 44 and 46 described the Torah and the Gospel, each "sent down" with "guidance and light." Verse 48 completes the sequence: *wa-anzalnā ilayka al-kitāba bi-l-ḥaqq* — "And We have sent down to you the Book with the truth." The Prophet ﷺ is addressed directly; the Qur'an is placed as the third and final revelation in the chain. Three further descriptions follow, and then the verse opens into one of the most important statements in the entire Qur'an about the existence of different religious communities. This is among the densest verses in the sūrah, and it must be read slowly.

**"Confirming the Book Before It"**

*Muṣaddiqan li-mā bayna yadayhi mina al-kitāb* — "confirming what is before it of the Book." The source lists the many places where the Qur'an describes itself as confirming the earlier scriptures: 2:41, 89, 91, 97, 101; 3:3, 81; 6:92; 35:31; 46:30. The Qur'an does for the Torah and the Gospel what verse 46 said the Gospel did for the Torah: it verifies them, endorses their essential message, and testifies that they came from God. "The Book" (*al-kitāb*), in the singular, is used generically for revealed scripture as a category; the Qur'an confirms *the Book* — all of God's sending-down before it. The confirmation is of the message: one God, prophets, accountability, the moral law. It is not a confirmation of every reading, interpretation, or textual state of the earlier scriptures as held by their communities — as the sūrah's charge of *taḥrīf* makes clear.

**"And as a Guardian over It" — Muhaymin**

*Wa-muhayminan ʿalayh* — "and as a *muhaymin* over it." The word is rich and rare. The source records al-Ṭabarī's and al-Zamakhsharī's glosses: the Qur'an is the witness (*shāhid*) to the earlier scriptures, their trustee (*amīn*), their keeper and guardian (*raqīb*, *ḥāfiẓ*). The root h-y-m-n is related to *amina*, to be secure, to be trustworthy; a *muhaymin* is one who watches over something and guarantees it. The source notes that *al-Muhaymin* is one of God's Names in 59:23 — the Guardian, the Overseer. The Qur'an is thus the standard by which the earlier scriptures are measured: what agrees with it is confirmed; what conflicts with it is exposed as distortion; what it neither confirms nor denies is left as it stands. The Prophet ﷺ taught the Muslims exactly this attitude toward the People of the Book's reports: "Neither believe the People of the Book nor disbelieve them; say, 'We believe in God and what was sent down to us'" (al-Bukhārī 4485) — that is, neither accept everything nor reject everything, but measure by the Qur'an.

The source connects *muhaymin* to the incidents of verses 41 and 45: the Prophet ﷺ restored the Torah's ruling on stoning and its rule of equal retribution, acting as the guardian of the earlier revelation against those who had abandoned it. This is *hayminah* in action: the final revelation protecting the integrity of the earlier ones from their own custodians' neglect.

**"So Judge Between Them by What God Has Sent Down"**

*Fa-ḥkum baynahum bi-mā anzala Allāh* — "so judge between them by what God has sent down." The source presents the two readings. Most commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī) understood "what God has sent down" as the Qur'an: when the Prophet ﷺ judges the People of the Book, he judges by what was revealed to him. Others noted that the phrase could mean what God sent down *to them* — their own scriptures — which is what the Prophet ﷺ actually did in the incident of the adulterers. The two readings converge, because the Qur'an, as *muhaymin*, confirms the true rulings of the earlier scriptures; to judge the Jews by the Torah's genuine ruling on stoning was to judge by what God sent down in both senses.

*Wa-lā tattabiʿ ahwāʾahum ʿammā jāʾaka mina al-ḥaqq* — "and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you." *Ahwāʾ* (sing. *hawā*) is caprice, whim, desire uncontrolled by knowledge; the Qur'an uses it as the opposite of guidance (28:50). The source gives two applications: do not rule according to their departures from their own law (al-Ṭabarī), or do not comply with their wish that you alter or neglect what has come to you (al-Bayḍāwī). The Qur'an repeats the warning in the next verse and in 2:120, 145; 42:15. The one who judges must be immune to the pressure of the litigants' preferences — which was precisely the pressure the Jews of verse 41 tried to apply.

**"For Each of You We Have Appointed a Law and a Way"**

*Li-kullin jaʿalnā minkum shirʿatan wa-minhājā* — "for each of you We have appointed a *shirʿah* and a *minhāj*." Here the verse widens from the Prophet's ﷺ judicial task to a universal statement. The source explains the terms. *Shirʿah* is from sh-r-ʿ, the root of *sharīʿah*: originally the path to a watering place, then a revealed law — the way to the water of life. *Minhāj* is from n-h-j: a clear, open, well-trodden road (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). Together they describe the specific legal and ritual form God appointed for each community: its prescribed worship, its regulations, its practices.

The source records the classical consensus that different religious communities have different laws and ways specifically appointed by God, each independent of the others' laws, even while the essential truths and principles are one (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī). The Prophet ﷺ expressed the same thing: "The prophets are brothers from one father with different mothers; their religion is one" (al-Bukhārī 3443) — one father (the *dīn*, the essential religion of submission to God), different mothers (the *sharāʾiʿ*, the specific laws). The Torah's Sabbath, the Gospel's modifications, the Qur'an's Friday and its five prayers: different ways to the same water.

The source also records the divergent readings. Some commentators (al-Bayḍāwī, al-Zamakhsharī) held that the different laws were valid successively, each for its era, and that the Qur'an's law now governs. Mujāhid's minority opinion read "a law and a way" as a reference to Islam alone. Ibn Kathīr proposed that "the Qur'an" was implied — "for each of you We have appointed [the Qur'an] as a law and a way." The source judges these exclusivist readings difficult to square with the verse's next clause, which grounds the plurality of laws in the divine will itself, and with al-Ṭabarī's own reading of that clause.

**"Had God Willed, He Would Have Made You One Community"**

*Wa-law shāʾa Allāhu la-jaʿalakum ummatan wāḥidatan wa-lākin li-yabluwakum fī mā ātākum* — "And had God willed, He would have made you one community, but [He willed otherwise] in order to test you in what He has given you." The source notes the grammar: the counterfactual conditional (*law*) states that humanity does *not* exist as one community *because* God did not will it. The plurality of communities is not an accident that God failed to prevent; it is a state that God chose not to abolish, for a stated purpose. The Qur'an says the same in 2:213; 10:19; 11:118; 16:93; 42:8 — and in 11:118–119: "Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community; but they will not cease to differ, except those on whom your Lord has mercy — and for that He created them."

The purpose is *li-yabluwakum fī mā ātākum*, "to test you in what He has given you" — al-Ṭabarī: to test your obedience. Each community is tested by its faithfulness to what it was given. The source draws the parallel with 49:13, where the differentiation of humanity into peoples and tribes is a matter of divine wisdom, and with 2:143–145, where the change of *qiblah* is explicitly a test "that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels."
