Diversity of religious form is thus a field of trial, as diversity of wealth, gender, and status are. The source notes that the commentators who read the laws as successive understood the "trial" as distinguishing those who accept the law of their own era from those who cling to an abrogated one (al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr).

**"So Vie with One Another in Good Deeds"**

*Fa-stabiqū al-khayrāt* — "so race one another to good things." The source's observation is precise: this command, addressed most plausibly to human beings as a whole (al-Ṭabarī), presupposes the *contemporaneous* existence of different communities competing in virtue — one does not race against a competitor who has left the field. The Qur'an uses the same command in 2:148, immediately after stating that "each has a direction to which he turns," and in 3:114 in praise of the righteous among the People of the Book. The competition is in *khayrāt*, good deeds — on the practical, not the theological, level. The verse does not ask the communities to resolve their doctrinal differences by argument; it asks them to outdo one another in goodness. And it reserves the resolution of the differences to God.

**"To God Is Your Return All Together, and He Will Inform You of That Wherein You Differed"**

*Ilā Allāhi marjiʿukum jamīʿan fa-yunabbiʾukum bi-mā kuntum fīhi takhtalifūn* — "to God is your return, all together, and He will inform you of what you used to differ about." All communities return to the same Lord. He, not any human tribunal, will settle the disputes among them. The verse does not say that the differences are unreal or unimportant — the Qur'an argues strenuously against the Trinity in this very sūrah — but it places their final adjudication in God's hands and in the Hereafter. In this world, the task is to be faithful to what one has been given and to race in good deeds.

**The Verse's Importance and Its Balance**

The source rightly calls this verse one of enormous importance for the question of religious pluralism in Islamic thought. It has been central to contemporary Muslim reflection on how to live among other faiths. A balanced reading holds several things at once. First, the Qur'an is the final revelation, confirming and guarding the earlier ones, and its call is universal; the sūrah itself calls the People of the Book to believe in the Prophet ﷺ (vv. 15, 19, 68). Second, the earlier scriptures are God's light, and their communities are bound by them; their existence as distinct communities is within God's will and serves His purpose of testing. Third, the believer's task toward other communities is not coercion but competition in goodness, and the final judgment of their differences belongs to God alone. Fourth, none of this relieves the Muslim of his own test: he has been given the Qur'an, and he will be asked about *that*.

The verse thus grounds a distinctive posture: conviction without coercion, a universal call without contempt for those who have not yet answered it, and a confidence that leaves the last word to God. The Muslim who has absorbed it can hold his faith with full certainty and still meet the Jew and the Christian as fellow runners in a race whose Judge is watching all of them — and who will, at the finish, explain everything.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:49

> **And judge between them in accordance with what God has sent down, and follow not their caprices. And beware of them, lest they tempt thee away from some part of that which God has sent down unto thee. And if they turn away, know that God desires to smite them for some sin of theirs, and surely many among mankind are iniquitous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Repetition with Intensification**

Verse 49 repeats the two commands of verse 48 — *wa-ani ḥkum baynahum bi-mā anzala Allāhu wa-lā tattabiʿ ahwāʾahum*, "and judge between them by what God has sent down, and do not follow their desires" — and then adds a third that verse 48 did not contain: *wa-ḥdharhum an yaftinūka ʿan baʿḍi mā anzala Allāhu ilayk*, "and beware of them, lest they tempt you away from *some* of what God has sent down to you." The repetition is not redundant. In the Qur'an's rhetoric, a repeated command signals urgency and permanence, and here the second statement sharpens the first. Verse 48 warned against following their desires away from the truth as a whole; verse 49 warns against being drawn away from *some part* of it — *baʿḍ*. The danger is not that the Prophet ﷺ would abandon revelation wholesale but that he might be induced to yield on a single point.

The source records that many major commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) took the "what God has sent down" of this verse to mean specifically the Qur'an — the Islamic scripture alone — by which the Prophet ﷺ should judge. Whether the standard is the Qur'an itself or the Qur'an confirming the genuine rulings of the earlier Books, the demand is the same: the source of judgment is revelation, not the litigants' wishes.

**The Occasion: The Offer of Conversion for a Ruling**

The source preserves Ibn ʿAbbās's report of the occasion, transmitted by Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī. A group of Jewish leaders of Madinah — among them Ibn Ṣūriyā, already encountered in the incident of the adulterers (v. 41), and Kaʿb ibn Asad, ʿAbdullāh ibn Ṣūriyā, and Shās ibn Qays — came to the Prophet ﷺ with a proposal. They said, in effect: "Muhammad, you know that we are the rabbis and nobles of the Jews. If we follow you, the Jews will follow us and will not oppose us. There is a dispute between us and some of our people. Rule in our favor, and we will believe in you and confirm you." The Prophet ﷺ refused, and this verse was revealed.

The temptation was subtle and, from a purely worldly calculation, powerful. The conversion of the Jewish leadership would have brought the whole Jewish community of Madinah with it — an immense strengthening of the young Muslim state, an end to internal opposition, a vindication of the Prophet's ﷺ mission before the Arabs. And the price seemed small: a favorable ruling in a single dispute. The verse names this precisely as *fitnah* — the smelting-fire of trial, the seduction away from the truth — and it forbids the bargain absolutely. The truth of a ruling cannot be traded, not even for the conversion of a nation. A faith purchased by injustice would be worthless, and a Prophet who bent the law for gain would have ceased to be trustworthy.

**"Beware of Them" and the Question of Prophetic Infallibility**

The command *iḥdharhum*, "beware of them," raised a theological question for the commentators, and the source records it. If the Prophet ﷺ is protected from sin, why warn him against temptation? Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī drew from the verse the position that, while prophets never sin deliberately, they may be subject to lapses of judgment or error in matters not yet revealed to them — and that the warning is a protection from such error. Others held that the warning concerns not a real susceptibility of the Prophet ﷺ but the character of the Jews: the verse describes *them* as people who would attempt such a seduction, and it instructs the Prophet ﷺ as an example to every judge after him. Al-Ṭabrisī, as the source notes, suggested a more specific reading: the Jews might mislead the Prophet ﷺ not by tempting him but by *lying* to him about the content of the Torah and its penalties — as the rabbi who covered the stoning verse attempted — and the warning is to be on guard against their misrepresentations.

These readings are not exclusive. The verse fits the broader concern of verses 41–47: that the Jews should follow the Torah's rulings as revealed, without alteration, and that the Prophet ﷺ should not be drawn into confirming their alterations. The warning is also, and permanently, addressed to every Muslim in a position of judgment: litigants will lie, they will flatter, they will offer inducements, and the judge must *beware* — the imperative is active vigilance, not passive innocence.

**"And If They Turn Away, Know That God Wills to Afflict Them for Some of Their Sins"**

*Fa-in tawallaw fa-ʿlam annamā yurīdu Allāhu an yuṣībahum bi-baʿḍi dhunūbihim* — "and if they turn away, then know that God only wills to afflict them for some of their sins." The Jews did turn away; they did not accept the Prophet's ﷺ refusal to be bought. The verse consoles him — as verse 41 consoled him — by placing their turning away within God's purpose: it is the means by which God brings upon them the consequence of *some* of their sins. The source notes al-Rāzī's inference that all good and evil come about through God's will for some ultimate purpose. The word *baʿḍ*, "some," should be noticed: God does not punish for all sins in this world, but for some, as a warning — "and He pardons much" (42:30). The affliction that followed — the expulsion of the Naḍīr, the fate of the Qurayẓah, the loss of Khaybar — the commentators saw as the worldly instance of what this verse foretold.

The verse also frames rejection as itself a symptom. When people turn away from a just ruling because it does not favor them, the turning away is not a failure of the ruling but a revelation of their state — the accumulated effect of prior sins that have hardened the heart. The Qur'an's law of the heart, stated in 83:14 — "rather, what they used to earn has rusted upon their hearts" — operates here: past sins produce present blindness.

**"And Surely Many of Mankind Are Iniquitous"**

*Wa-inna kathīran mina al-nāsi la-fāsiqūn* — "and indeed many of mankind are *fāsiqūn*." The verse ends with a generalization that lifts it out of its immediate context. It is not only these Jewish leaders; it is *many people*, of every community, who break out of the bounds of God's law when it costs them something. The word *fāsiqūn* echoes the close of verse 47. And the statement guards the Prophet ﷺ — and every teacher after him — against a false expectation: that truth, clearly presented, will be widely accepted. It will not. Many will turn away. This is not a reason to soften the truth to gain their acceptance — the verse has just forbidden that — but a reason to expect rejection calmly and to measure success by fidelity, not by numbers.

**The Principle: The Ruling Is Not for Sale, Whatever the Price**

The abiding lesson of verse 49 is the absolute incorruptibility required of the one who judges by revelation. The temptation refused here was not a bribe of money — that would have been crude — but a bribe of *religious success*: the conversion of a community, the strengthening of the faith, the vindication of the mission. Even that price was refused. The principle extends to every believer who holds any authority. The scholar who softens a ruling to keep his following; the leader who bends a principle to win an ally; the parent who overlooks an injustice among his children to keep the peace; the preacher who omits what his audience does not want to hear in order to draw them closer — each is being tempted "away from some of what God has sent down," and each is offered, as the Jews offered the Prophet ﷺ, a seemingly good end as the reason. The verse's answer is: *beware*. God's law is not a means to any end, however good; it is the end that all means must serve. And those who turn away when it is upheld are not to be pursued by concession but left to God, who "wills to afflict them for some of their sins" — and who "pardons much."

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:50

> **Is it the judgment of the Age of Ignorance that they seek? And who is fairer in judgment than God, for a people who are certain.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Closing Question of the Passage**

Verses 41–49 have moved through the incident of the adulterers, the affirmation of the Torah and the Gospel, the threefold refrain about judging by what God sent down, the placing of the Qur'an as confirmer and guardian, and the warning against being tempted from any part of it. Verse 50 closes the passage with two rhetorical questions that reduce the whole matter to its essence. *A-fa-ḥukma al-jāhiliyyati yabghūn?* — "Is it, then, the judgment of the Age of Ignorance that they seek?" *Wa-man aḥsanu mina Allāhi ḥukman li-qawmin yūqinūn?* — "And who is better than God in judgment, for a people who have certainty?" The first question exposes what the alternative to God's judgment actually is; the second asks whether anyone could seriously prefer it.

**Jāhiliyyah: What the Word Means**

*Al-jāhiliyyah* is from j-h-l, ignorance — but the word does not mean mere lack of information. In pre-Islamic Arabic, *jahl* was the opposite not only of *ʿilm* (knowledge) but of *ḥilm* (forbearance, self-mastery, reasoned restraint); the *jāhil* was the man of impulse, rashness, and unrestrained passion, who acted on pride and anger rather than on principle. *Jāhiliyyah* thus names a *condition*: the state of a society governed by impulse, tribal pride, and human opinion rather than by revealed law and self-restraint. The source explains that the Qur'an uses the term (also in 3:154; 33:33; 48:26) for the era of Arabia before Islam — an era marked by idolatry and a culpable ignorance of true religion — and that "the judgment of *jāhiliyyah*," unguided by any religious law, was governed solely by human opinion and caprice (Ibn Kathīr).

Note that the verse does not say the era is over in the sense that its judgment can no longer be sought. It asks whether *they* — people living in the Prophet's ﷺ own time, possessors of a revealed scripture — are *seeking* it. *Jāhiliyyah* is not simply a period; it is a way of judging that any people, in any age, may return to. Ibn Kathīr, commenting on this verse, extended it to every system of law devised by human caprice in preference to God's law; and the later scholars made "the judgment of *jāhiliyyah*" a standing category for any adjudication that sets aside revelation for custom, status, or whim.

**What the Judgment of Jāhiliyyah Looked Like**

The source notes that the reference may pertain specifically to the differential penalties among the Jewish clans according to the status of killer and killed (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī; see verse 45). This was exactly the tribal system of pre-Islamic Arabia: a noble's blood was worth more than a commoner's; a strong tribe demanded two lives for one; a weak tribe accepted less. The Naḍīr's treatment of the Qurayẓah replicated the Arab *jāhiliyyah* precisely, and the Qur'an calls it by that name. The point is sharp: these were People of the Book, possessors of the Torah with its "life for life," and in practice they had reverted to the pagan Arab standard. Possessing a revealed law did not prevent them from judging by *jāhiliyyah*; abandoning the law in practice while holding it in theory is the very thing verses 41–47 have been describing.

The Prophet ﷺ abolished the tribal system of unequal blood in his Farewell Sermon — "Every claim of blood from the *jāhiliyyah* is under my feet, abolished" (Muslim 1218) — and the Qur'an's law of equal retribution (2:178; 5:45) replaced it. The verse's rhetorical question invites the Jews of Madinah to see what they were actually seeking when they sought a lighter ruling from the Prophet ﷺ: not God's judgment, not even the Torah's, but the standard of the idolaters around them.

**The Marks of Jāhilī Judgment**

From the passage as a whole, one can identify the features that distinguish the judgment of *jāhiliyyah* from the judgment of God — features that recur wherever the former displaces the latter. It weighs persons by status rather than treating them equally (v. 45). It is moved by fear of the powerful (v. 44). It is purchased with bribes (v. 42). It follows the desires of the litigants (vv. 48–49). It conceals the inconvenient rule (v. 41). And it calls itself by pious names while doing all these things. God's judgment, by contrast, is equal, fearless, incorruptible, indifferent to the litigants' wishes, and open. The believer who wants to know whether a given adjudication — in a court, an institution, a family — is God's or *jāhiliyyah*'s may apply these tests.

**"Who Is Better Than God in Judgment?"**

*Wa-man aḥsanu mina Allāhi ḥukman* — "and who is better than God in judgment?" The second question is not merely rhetorical assertion; it is grounded in the nature of the Judge. The source describes God's law as possessing "ultimate justice, benefit, and mercy" (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī), and each term deserves its reason. God's judgment is *just* because He has no interest in the case, no tribe, no fear, no need; human judgment is always shadowed by the judge's own position. God's judgment is *beneficial* because He knows the full consequences of every ruling for every party, in this world and the next; human judgment sees a fraction. And God's judgment is *merciful* because He is "the Most Merciful of the merciful" (7:151) and legislates for creatures He loves; human judgment is often harsh where it should be gentle and lax where it should be firm. The Qur'an asks the same question in 6:114: "Shall I seek a judge other than God, when it is He who sent down to you the Book explained in detail?"

**"For a People Who Are Certain"**

*Li-qawmin yūqinūn* — "for a people who have certainty." The verse's final phrase is the key to its logic. The superiority of God's judgment is evident *to those who are certain* — those who possess *yaqīn*, settled conviction about God's existence, knowledge, and goodness. To such people the question answers itself: of course God's judgment is better; how could the judgment of the ignorant compete with the judgment of the All-Knowing? The one who prefers *jāhiliyyah*'s judgment reveals, by that preference, a deficiency of certainty: at some level he does not fully believe that God's rule is truly best for him, or he would not seek to evade it. The source notes that the verse serves as a chastisement to those who would reject the Prophet's ﷺ judgment because it did not accord with their wishes. Their rejection was a symptom of doubt.

This connects preference to faith in a way that is both diagnostic and demanding. It is diagnostic because a person can measure his own certainty by his reaction to God's rulings: does he receive them with ease, or does he look for a way around them? And it is demanding because it implies that growth in certainty will show itself in growth of submission — the more one knows God, the more one prefers His judgment, not as a burden but as the obvious choice of a mind that sees clearly.

**Closing the Passage and Opening the Next**

Verse 50 completes the unit that began at verse 41 and lays a foundation for the one that follows. Verses 51–57 will address the Muslims' alliances with Jews and Christians, and the connection is not accidental: a community that has just been told to prefer God's judgment over *jāhiliyyah*'s is now told where its protective loyalties must lie. The link is loyalty. To seek *jāhiliyyah*'s judgment is a form of disloyalty to God; to seek protection from those who oppose God's religion, at the expense of the community of believers, is another. The sūrah moves from the integrity of judgment to the integrity of allegiance.

**The Verse for the Reader**

Every believer should hear this verse's first question as addressed to himself whenever he is tempted to settle a matter by custom, family pride, social status, or personal advantage rather than by what God has revealed: "Is it the judgment of *jāhiliyyah* you seek?" And every believer should hear its second question as an invitation to certainty: "Who is better than God in judgment?" The one who can answer that question from the heart — not merely with the tongue — has found the certainty the verse describes, and will find that submission to God's rulings ceases to feel like constraint and begins to feel like relief.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:51

> **O you who believe! Take not Jews and Christians as protectors. They are the protectors of one another. And whosoever takes them as protectors, surely he is of them. Truly God guides not wrongdoing people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verse That Demands Careful Reading**

Few verses in the Qur'an have been more often quoted out of context, by hostile readers and by careless believers alike, than this one. Read in isolation and with the key word translated as "friends," it appears to forbid Muslims from having any friendly relations with Jews and Christians. Read in its language, its historical setting, and the wider Qur'an, it says something quite different and quite precise. The classical commentators — al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī — were careful readers, and this commentary follows them.

**The Word Awliyāʾ: Protectors, Patrons, Allies**

The verse forbids taking Jews and Christians as *awliyāʾ* (singular *walī*). The root w-l-y means to be near, to be adjacent; from it come *walī*, *mawlā*, *wilāyah*, and *walāyah*, a cluster of terms describing a relationship of closeness that carries obligations: guardianship, patronage, protection, alliance, and — in its most intimate sense — friendship and love. God is *al-Walī*, the Protector of the believers (2:257). The guardian of a bride is her *walī*. The pre-Islamic Arab who sought the protection of a stronger tribe entered its *walāʾ*. The source's analysis is precise: while *awliyāʾ* can mean "friends" or "allies" (see 3:28; 4:139), here it more likely denotes those to whom one turns as *protectors* or dominant authorities, and the term describes the bonds of loyalty, mutual protection, and allegiance that ideally mark the relationship among members of the same religious community (8:72; 9:71).

The Qur'an itself defines the term in this sense in 8:72: the Emigrants and Helpers "are *awliyāʾ* of one another," while believers who did not emigrate "have no *walāyah* with you until they emigrate" — where *walāyah* plainly means the political bond of mutual defense, not friendship, since the non-emigrant believers were beloved fellow Muslims. Verse 51's phrase "they are *awliyāʾ* of one another" carries the same sense: the Jews and Christians form their own communities of mutual protection.

**The Occasion of Revelation**

The source records the reports. The verse concerned certain Madinan Muslims who had treaties of mutual protection with the Jewish clans, dating from before Islam. ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, of the Anṣār, came to the Prophet ﷺ and renounced his alliance with the Jews of Qaynuqāʿ, declaring that he took as his *walī* only God, His Messenger, and the believers (which verse 55 will echo). ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites, came declaring the opposite — that he feared "changes of fortune" and must keep his Jewish allies (verse 52 will quote him). The verse came down in response (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī). Another report places the verse after Uḥud, when some Muslims, feeling vulnerable, sought alliances with Jewish clans as insurance against the Muslim community's defeat (al-Ṭabarī).

In every version the situation is the same: Madinah was a fragile polity in which the Muslims, the Jewish tribes, and the pagan Arabs were bound by overlapping tribal pacts; some of the Jewish tribes were, at that very time, in active treaty violation and conspiring with the Makkans (the Naḍīr's plot of verse 11; the Qurayẓah's treachery during the Trench). A Muslim who retained a protective alliance with such a tribe had divided loyalties in a state of war — and, in a crisis, might side with his protectors against his fellow believers. This is what the verse forbids.

**"They Are Protectors of One Another"**

*Baʿḍuhum awliyāʾu baʿḍ* — "some of them are *awliyāʾ* of others." The clause is a statement of fact and a reason. The Jews form a community of mutual protection; the Christians form another; each looks after its own. The Muslim who enters their protective structure enters a system whose loyalties are not his. The source notes that in verses 80–81 the People of the Book are themselves criticized for taking disbelievers as *awliyāʾ* — the same principle applied to them: a religious community's bond of protection belongs within the community of faith.

**"Whoever Takes Them as Protectors Is of Them"**

*Wa-man yatawallahum minkum fa-innahu minhum* — "and whoever among you takes them as protectors, he is of them." The source explains: to enter an alliance of mutual protection with another religious community is to identify oneself with it, since *walāyah* is part of what defines membership in a community. Some (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭūsī) took this to mean that such a person acquires the legal and theological status of the community he joins; others took it as a statement of practical consequence — he will share their fate and be treated as one of them — or of moral affinity: in the crisis, he will stand where they stand. The source also notes the connection some commentators drew with inheritance: since the root of *walī* relates to inheritance as well, the alliance would nullify the inheritance bond between such a person and the Muslim community (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabrisī).

The verse's end, *inna Allāha lā yahdī al-qawma al-ẓālimīn*, "indeed God does not guide the wrongdoing people," names the act as *ẓulm* — placing loyalty where it does not belong.

**What the Verse Does Not Forbid**

The source is emphatic on this point, and it must be stated plainly. The verse does not forbid friendly, kind, just, or even intimate personal relations with Jews and Christians. The proof is within this very sūrah. Verse 5 permits a Muslim man to marry a Jewish or Christian woman — the most intimate relationship two people can have; a man does not take as wife, and mother of his children, a woman he is forbidden to befriend. Verse 5 also permits sharing food with the People of the Book — the basic act of social fellowship. And 60:8–9 states the governing principle for all non-Muslims: "God does not forbid you from those who have not fought you on account of religion nor driven you from your homes — that you be kind to them and deal justly with them; indeed, God loves the just. God only forbids you from those who fought you on account of religion, drove you from your homes, and aided in your expulsion — that you take them as *awliyāʾ*." The word forbidden in 60:9 is exactly the word of 5:51 — *tawallaw* — and it is forbidden specifically toward those at war with the believers, while kindness and justice toward the peaceful are explicitly permitted and loved by God.

The Prophet's ﷺ own practice confirms the reading. He accepted the protection of the Christian king of Abyssinia for the first emigrants; he visited his sick Jewish neighbor; he stood for a Jewish funeral procession (al-Bukhārī 1312); he borrowed from a Jew and died with his armor pledged to him (al-Bukhārī 2916); he accepted gifts from and gave gifts to Jews and Christians. The source records the anecdote of ʿUmar objecting to Abū Mūsā's Christian scribe on the basis of this verse — and notes that Abū Mūsā was not persuaded, and that the issue there was placing a non-Muslim in a position of authority over Muslim affairs, not personal relations. The source also notes that Islamic law, once the state was established, allowed treaties of mutual protection with non-Muslim states — the very alliances the verse's occasion involved, once the emergency of Madinah had passed and such treaties no longer meant divided loyalty within a war.

**The Principle: Where the Believer's Protective Loyalty Lies**

The verse's enduring principle is about *walāyah* in its strong sense: the bond of protection, allegiance, and ultimate loyalty. That bond belongs to God, His Messenger, and the community of believers, as verse 55 will say. A Muslim may love, befriend, marry, trade with, and defend the rights of Jews and Christians; what he may not do is make a hostile community his patron and protector against his own, such that in the decisive moment his loyalty stands with them. The verse addresses the fear that drove the hypocrites — "we fear a change of fortune" — and answers it: your security is in God and the believers, not in hedging your bets with those who oppose the faith.

**The Verse for the Reader Today**

A Muslim living in a plural society, whether as a majority or a minority, should hold two things together. First, the verse binds his ultimate loyalty to God and the believers; he does not join those who fight the faith, and he does not make the faith's enemies his protectors. Second, the verse leaves entirely intact — indeed the Qur'an commands — kindness, justice, honesty, neighborliness, and friendship toward Jews, Christians, and all who do not fight him for his religion. The one who uses this verse to justify hostility toward peaceful neighbors has both mistranslated its key word and ignored verse 5 of the same sūrah and 60:8. And the one who uses it to justify abandoning fellow believers for the patronage of the faith's enemies has understood its meaning exactly, and stands condemned by it.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:52

> **Yet thou seest those in whose hearts is a disease hastening to them, saying, "We fear lest a change of fortune should befall us." It may be that God will grant victory, or a command from Him. And then they shall be remorseful for that which they secretly harbored in their souls.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ones Who Hasten to Them**

Verse 51 prohibited taking Jews and Christians as *awliyāʾ*. Verse 52 describes those who nonetheless do it, and lays bare their motive. *Fa-tarā alladhīna fī qulūbihim maraḍun yusāriʿūna fīhim* — "So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening into them." The verb *yusāriʿūna*, "they race," is the same used in verse 41 of those who "race into disbelief"; here they race *fīhim*, "into them" — into the ranks and protection of the other communities. The preposition *fī*, "in," rather than *ilā*, "to," conveys immersion: they rush not merely toward these alliances but into them, embedding themselves.

**"Those in Whose Hearts Is a Disease"**

*Maraḍ*, disease, sickness, is the Qur'an's standard diagnosis of hypocrisy. The source lists the occurrences: 2:8–11, where the hypocrites' "disease" is increased by God; 24:47–50; 33:12, 32, 60; 47:20, 29; 74:31. The image is medical and exact. A diseased heart is not a dead one — the hypocrite is not an open disbeliever — but it is impaired: it cannot fully trust, cannot fully commit, cannot rest in faith. The disease shows itself as doubt about God's promise, and doubt shows itself as hedging. The source identifies the persons: perhaps ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy specifically, mentioned in the occasion of verse 51, or more likely the hypocrites generally (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī).

The Qur'an's choice of *maraḍ* over *kufr* is deliberate and instructive. Disbelief is a settled state; disease is a condition that can worsen or be cured. The hypocrite of verse 52 is not yet lost; the verse's ending — remorse when God's victory comes — leaves open the possibility that the remorse becomes repentance. But left untreated, the disease progresses.

**"We Fear a Change of Fortune"**

*Yaqūlūna nakhshā an tuṣībanā dāʾirah* — "they say, 'We fear that a turn [of fortune] will strike us.'" *Dāʾirah* is from d-w-r, to turn, to revolve; it is a turn of the wheel, a reversal, a calamity that comes round — the Qur'an uses it also in 9:98 of the hypocrites who "await turns of fortune against you." The hypocrites' reasoning is entirely worldly. The Muslims might be defeated; the Jews or the Makkans might prevail; if so, those who had alliances with the winners would be protected, and those who had none would be destroyed. Therefore keep the alliances as insurance. This is exactly what ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy is reported to have said: "I am a man who fears changes of fortune; I will not renounce my allies."

The verse quotes the reasoning without immediately refuting it — it lets the reader see it plainly — and then answers it with a single sentence about what God may do. The hypocrites' error is not that they think about the future; it is that they calculate the future without God in the calculation. They weigh the Muslims' strength against the Jews' and the Makkans', as though the outcome depended on those weights alone. The believer weighs differently: he knows that "if God helps you, none can overcome you" (3:160), and he places his security in God rather than in a balanced portfolio of alliances.

**"Perhaps God Will Bring Victory, or a Command from Him"**

*Fa-ʿasā Allāhu an yaʾtiya bi-l-fatḥi aw amrin min ʿindih* — "but perhaps God will bring the victory, or some command from Him." The source records al-Rāzī's observation that *ʿasā*, "perhaps," when used by God, indicates a promised certainty, not a mere possibility — for God does not speak of what He does not know; the tentative form is a courtesy to human expectation, or a way of keeping the believers in hope and the hypocrites in fear. And the promise was fulfilled.

*Al-fatḥ*, "the opening," "the victory": the source records its identification with the conquest of Makkah in 8/630 (al-Ṭabarī) or, more broadly, with the Muslim triumph over their religious opponents (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī). The source also notes that *fatḥ* can mean "judgment" or "decision" — the Qur'an uses *al-Fattāḥ* for God as the Judge who decides (34:26) — and that many commentators reconcile the two senses: the conquest of Makkah *was* God's judgment in favor of the believers over the idolaters. When the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah with ten thousand, the hypocrites' calculation was overturned in a day. The power they had feared was gone; the power they had hedged against was supreme; and their hedging was exposed as folly.

*Aw amrin min ʿindih*, "or a command from Him": the source lists the commentators' suggestions — the imposition of the *jizyah* on the non-Muslim residents of the state (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī; see 9:29); the later removal of the Jewish and Christian communities from the central regions of Arabia under ʿUmar (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī); or a sudden exposure of the hypocrites' intentions (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The common thread is that events would make the hypocrites' insurance worthless: the communities they had relied on would themselves come under Muslim authority, and the protection they had bought would protect nothing.

**"Then They Will Become Remorseful for What They Concealed in Their Souls"**

*Fa-yuṣbiḥū ʿalā mā asarrū fī anfusihim nādimīn* — "then they will become, over what they hid within themselves, regretful." *Asarrū*, "they concealed": the hypocrites' hedging was a secret; outwardly they professed faith, inwardly they doubted and prepared for the faith's defeat. When God's victory comes, the secret is not only exposed but becomes a source of *nadam*, remorse. The remorse has two faces. Before the world, the hypocrite is humiliated: he had bet against the winning side. Before God, he is shamed: he had doubted the promise, and the promise came true. The Qur'an's psychology is acute: nothing produces sharper regret than having hedged against an outcome that then arrives — the person feels both the loss of the reward he could have had and the shame of the doubt he harbored.

**The Psychology of Hedging in Faith**

The verse describes a permanent spiritual type. The hedger is not an unbeliever; he prays with the community, professes the creed, and would say sincerely that he hopes for Islam's success. But his heart contains a reserve: a private calculation that the promise might fail, and a private arrangement to survive if it does. The arrangement may be an alliance, a compromised position, a friendship kept warm with the faith's opponents "just in case," a refusal to commit publicly, a reluctance to give or sacrifice because "one never knows." The Qur'an calls this a disease because it is a partial failure of the organ of trust. And it warns that the reserve, when God's promise is fulfilled — as it always is — becomes the source of the sharpest regret.

The believer's alternative is not recklessness. The Prophet ﷺ made treaties, wore armor, posted guards, and took every prudent measure. The difference lies in where trust is *finally* placed. The believer takes his precautions and rests his heart on God; the hypocrite takes his precautions and rests his heart on them. The one says, "We have done what we can; the outcome is God's"; the other says, "We have covered ourselves whatever happens." The first is *tawakkul*; the second is the disease of this verse.

**The Verse in the Passage**

Verse 52 gives the motive behind the alliances verse 51 forbade: not affection for the Jews and Christians but fear for oneself. This confirms the reading of verse 51: the issue is not friendship but *protection* sought from fear. Verse 53 will show the believers' reaction when the hedgers are exposed, and verses 54–56 will describe the true community of loyalty — those whom God loves and who love Him, who take God, His Messenger, and the believers as their *awliyāʾ*. The sūrah is drawing a sharp contrast between two kinds of heart: the diseased heart that hedges, and the loving heart that commits.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:53

> **And those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore by God with their most solemn oaths that they were with you?" Their deeds have come to naught, and they have become losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Moment of Exposure**

Verse 52 ended with the hypocrites' regret when God brings the victory or a command from Him. Verse 53 shows the same moment from the believers' side: *wa-yaqūlu alladhīna āmanū a-hāʾulāʾi alladhīna aqsamū bi-Allāhi jahda aymānihim innahum la-maʿakum* — "And those who believe will say, 'Are these the ones who swore by God their most solemn oaths that they were surely with you?'" The believers, seeing the hypocrites exposed, ask a question of astonishment. These are the same men who swore — by God, and with their utmost oaths — that they stood with the believers; and now their secret alliances and their private calculations are laid bare.

*Jahda aymānihim* — "the utmost of their oaths," the strongest formula, the most emphatic swearing. The phrase occurs elsewhere for the same type: 6:109; 16:38; 24:53; 35:42. The hypocrite compensates for his lack of real commitment with excess of verbal commitment. He swears too much because he means too little. The Prophet ﷺ described the hypocrite's marks: "When he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; when he is trusted, he betrays" (al-Bukhārī 33; Muslim 59) — and the solemn oath is the lie's dress uniform.

**Two Readings of the Question**

The source presents two ways of construing to whom the believers speak. In the first (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī), the believers speak among themselves, or to the Prophet ﷺ, expressing surprise at the hypocrisy of those who had sworn they were "with you" — with the believers — and gratitude for God's granting success to the sincere. On this reading the "command" of verse 52 is understood as the sudden exposure of the hypocrites' insincerity, and verse 53 is the believers' reaction to it.

In the second reading, which al-Zamakhsharī records, the believers address the Jews with whom the hypocrites had sought alliance: "Are *these* the ones who swore to *you* that they were with *you*?" — that is, the hypocrites had sworn loyalty to their Jewish protectors, and when the crisis came they abandoned them too. The source points to 59:11, where the hypocrites are quoted promising the Banū Naḍīr: "If you are expelled, we will go out with you, and we will never obey anyone against you; and if you are fought, we will surely help you" — and 59:12 continues: "If they are expelled, they will not go out with them, and if they are fought, they will not help them." The hypocrites broke their oaths to both sides. This is the nature of the hedger: having no real loyalty, he swears loyalty to everyone, and in the end is loyal to no one. The Jews of the Naḍīr learned this when the promised help never came; the Muslims learned it when the professed brotherhood proved hollow.

The two readings are complementary rather than competing. The hypocrite's oaths to the believers and his oaths to the Jews were both false, and both were exposed by the same events. The question "are these the ones who swore?" could be asked, with equal astonishment, by either party.

**"Their Deeds Have Come to Nothing"**

*Ḥabiṭat aʿmāluhum* — "their deeds have fallen void," "have come to nothing." *Ḥabiṭa* originally describes an animal that swells from overeating on rich pasture and dies; it came to mean the collapse and nullification of what seemed substantial. The hypocrites had *deeds*: they prayed, fasted, gave, fought in some campaigns, swore oaths. The verse declares all of it void. The source explains the theological principle, which the Qur'an states repeatedly (2:217; 5:5; 6:88; 7:147; 9:17; 18:105; 33:19; 39:65; 47:32): works in the absence of true faith have no salvific value and merit no reward (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The hypocrite's prayer was a performance, his charity a purchase of reputation, his oath a tactic. The deeds were real as actions and void as worship, because the faith that alone gives a deed its worth before God was absent.

**Faith and Works: The Principle Stated**

The source uses this verse to state the Islamic teaching on faith and works with care, and the statement deserves repetition. The Qur'an requires both belief and good deeds for salvation — "those who believe *and* do righteous deeds" is its constant formula (2:25; 3:57; 4:57). Schools of theology differed over whether one who has faith but neglects works may eventually be saved: the mainstream Sunni position is that such a person, if he dies a believer, will ultimately enter Paradise after whatever punishment his sins deserve, since faith is the root and works are its fruit; the Muʿtazilah and Khārijites held stricter views. But *all* schools agree, on the basis of this and similar verses, that works without faith are void — that a good deed done by one who denies God, or done by a hypocrite whose profession is a lie, will be weightless on the Day of Judgment. The Qur'an says of the disbelievers' works: "like ashes on which the wind blows hard on a stormy day; they have no power over anything of what they earned" (14:18), and "like a mirage in a desert, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing" (24:39).

The source adds a deeper point: what one calls a "good deed" is not truly good unless it is joined to faith, because the goodness of a deed lies in its orientation toward God. A deed done for show, for advantage, for insurance, is not a good deed that happens to lack faith; it is a different kind of act altogether — an act of self-service wearing the costume of worship. This is why the hypocrite's deeds come to *nothing*: they were never what they appeared to be.

**"And They Have Become Losers"**

*Fa-aṣbaḥū khāsirīn* — "so they have become losers." The commercial metaphor that runs through the Qur'an closes the verse. The hypocrite thought he was investing wisely — keeping his position among the believers while insuring himself among their opponents. The verse shows the result of the investment: total loss. He lost the believers' trust when exposed; he lost the Jews' protection when they were themselves overcome; and he lost the Hereafter, because his deeds were void. The hedger who tried to hold both sides ends by holding neither. The Qur'an describes the same type in 4:143: "wavering between this and that, neither to these nor to those." The source notes al-Ṭabarī's gloss: they will perish for lack of faith despite their deeds. The word *aṣbaḥū*, "they became," "they found themselves in the morning," carries the image of dawn revealing what the night hid: the hypocrite wakes to find that everything he built is gone.

**The Verse for the Believer**

The believer reading this verse should first ask about his own oaths. The Prophet ﷺ was sparing with oaths and taught his community to be so (2:224; 5:89); the person who swears often and emphatically, who reinforces every commitment with "by God," should ask whether his oaths are compensating for a weakness of intention. Second, he should ask about his own deeds — not whether they are many, but whether they are rooted in faith and sincerity, since only that root makes them count. And third, he should take from the verse the believers' reaction as a model: astonishment at hypocrisy, gratitude for God's exposure of it, and no triumphalism — for the believers in the verse do not gloat; they marvel, and the Qur'an, not they, pronounces the verdict.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:54

> **O you who believe! Whosoever among you should renounce his religion, God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, stern toward the disbelievers, striving in the way of God, and fearing not the blame of any blamer. That is the Bounty of God, which He gives to whomsoever He will. And God is All-Encompassing, Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse of Mutual Love**

This is one of the most beloved verses in the Qur'an, and it stands at a hinge in the sūrah. Verses 51–53 described those whose diseased hearts led them to seek protection outside the community of faith, and whose deeds came to nothing. Verse 54 turns from the hedgers to the lovers. It opens with a warning — those who renounce their religion do God no harm — and unfolds into a portrait of the people God will raise in their place: a people bound to God by mutual love, humble to believers, firm against disbelievers, striving in God's way, unmoved by any blamer's blame. Every phrase repays attention.

**"Whosoever Among You Renounces His Religion"**

*Man yartadda minkum ʿan dīnihi* — "whoever among you turns back from his religion." The verb *irtadda* is from r-d-d, to turn back, to return; *riddah* and *irtidād*, apostasy, are the turning back from faith to disbelief. The source notes the placement: immediately after verses 51–53, the verse implies that the improper alliances just condemned can, in some cases, amount to apostasy (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī) — taking the enemies of the faith as one's protectors against the faithful is a step on the road back out of it. The source is careful to add that this must not be read absolutely: the Prophet ﷺ and the early Muslims made treaties with non-Muslim powers, and the Christian king of Abyssinia sheltered the first emigrants. The problem is alliance that entails betrayal or division of the Muslim community in favor of its enemies.

The source records that many commentators (al-Jalālayn, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī) read the verse as foretelling the apostasy of some Arab tribes late in the Prophet's ﷺ life and, more extensively, after his death — the *riddah* wars, when tribes across Arabia renounced their allegiance, refused the *zakāh*, and followed false prophets. The verse's promise that God would "bring a people" was fulfilled, on this reading, in those who fought and reversed the apostasy.

**"God Will Bring a People"**

*Fa-sawfa yaʾtī Allāhu bi-qawmin* — "then God will bring a people." The source cites the parallel verses in which God declares that He can remove a people and bring others (4:133; 6:133; 14:19; 35:16; 47:38). The message is the sovereignty of God over His religion: the religion does not depend on any individual or tribe; those who leave it harm only themselves; God will always raise up others. The Prophet ﷺ said: "This religion will remain established; a group of my community will fight for it, victorious, until the Hour comes" (Muslim 1922) — the promise of this verse in ḥadīth form.

The source presents the commentators' discussion of who these people were. Many identified them with Abū Bakr and those who fought the apostate tribes with him (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī) — for it was Abū Bakr's unshaken firmness, when the Companions themselves hesitated, that preserved the community; ʿUmar said, "By God, it was as if I saw that God had opened Abū Bakr's breast to fighting, and I knew it was the truth." Many others cited the ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ, when this verse was revealed, pointed to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī and said, "They are this man's people" — the tribes of Yemen, who bore a major part in the conquests under ʿUmar (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The Prophet ﷺ had praised the Yemenis: "The people of Yemen have come to you; they are the tenderest of heart and softest of soul; faith is Yemeni and wisdom is Yemeni" (al-Bukhārī 4388; Muslim 52). Less widely reported identifications include the Anṣār (al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭūsī) and the Persians, on the basis of the ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ placed his hand on Salmān al-Fārsī and said that if faith were at the Pleiades, men of his people would reach it (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Zamakhsharī; the ḥadīth is in al-Bukhārī 4897 and Muslim 2546, on 62:3).

The source also records the identification with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, on the strength of the Prophet's ﷺ words on the eve of Khaybar: "Tomorrow I shall give the standard to a man who loves God and His Messenger, and whom God and His Messenger love" (al-Bukhārī 3702; Muslim 2406) — words that echo this verse's "whom He loves and who love Him" (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Ṭūsī). The source notes that the verse thus became a site of Sunni–Shiite debate over the relative merits of Abū Bakr and ʿAlī, each side arguing that its figure best exemplified the verse's qualities, and that some Shiite commentators read "those who renounce their religion" as those who rebelled against ʿAlī's caliphate, or extended the verse to the awaited Mahdī (al-Qummī, al-Ṭabrisī). Al-Rāzī used the verse in the opposite direction: since God promises to *replace* those who apostatize, and the Companions who supported Abū Bakr were not replaced but went on to spread Islam across the earth, the verse refutes the extreme early claim that they had apostatized — a claim the source notes was later rejected by most Imāmī authorities themselves.

The source's conclusion is the sound one: the reference is general as well as historical. God's promise is not exhausted by any one group; it is that He will never lack sincere servants. Abū Bakr and the Companions, the Yemenis, the Persians, the Anṣār, ʿAlī and his household — all of these, and every generation of the faithful since, are instances of the "people" God brings.

**"Whom He Loves and Who Love Him"**

*Yuḥibbuhum wa-yuḥibbūnah* — "He loves them and they love Him." Here is the verse's heart, and the source gives it extended treatment. The Qur'an speaks often of whom God loves (the just, the patient, the doers of good, those who purify themselves) and whom He does not (the transgressors, the proud, the corrupt); and it speaks of the believers' love of God — "those who believe are stronger in love for God" (2:165). But this verse is distinctive: it joins the two in a single reciprocal phrase, and it places God's love *first*. He loves them; they love Him.

The source records the discomfort of some theologians with the idea of love between the incommensurable God and the creature. Al-Ṭūsī and al-Zamakhsharī glossed "they love Him" as "they obey Him and seek His pleasure" and "He loves them" as "He rewards them." But the source points out — following al-Rāzī and al-Ghazālī — that this reverses the verse's order. If love meant obedience and God's love meant reward, then the servant's love would have to come first (obedience precedes reward), whereas the verse puts God's love first. The verse says something more than obedience-and-reward: it says that God's love for a person *precedes and produces* the person's love for God. Ibn ʿAjībah, as the source notes, connects this to the truth that the human turning toward God is the result of God's having first turned toward the human; al-Qushayrī, that God's love necessarily engenders human love. This is the Qur'an's teaching in 9:118: "He turned to them so that they might turn to Him" — God's *tawbah* precedes the servant's *tawbah*. The ḥadīth qudsī says: "When My servant draws near to Me a hand-span, I draw near to him an arm's length; when he comes to Me walking, I come to him running" (al-Bukhārī 7405; Muslim 2675) — and the verse adds that even the servant's first hand-span was set in motion by God's prior love.

The source records al-Ghazālī's further reflection (*Iḥyāʾ*, IV): that God's love for anything is ultimately His love for His own manifestation, since nothing exists outside His being; and that human love for God is God's unveiling of Himself in the heart of the seeker, whose very seeking He determined. And Rūmī's, in the *Mathnawī* (V, 2184–90): that love is an attribute belonging to God alone, in which human beings participate derivatively. Al-Qushayrī distinguishes God's love from His mercy: mercy embraces all creatures; love is a more particular and ennobling relationship with certain servants. And he describes the servant's love as a "subtle state" of delight in the divine presence, an "intoxication from which one never recovers, an illness for which no cure is sought." These are the Sufis' articulations; the mainstream tradition, affirming the plain sense of the verse against those who would reduce it, holds that God truly loves His servants in a manner befitting His majesty, and that they truly love Him — and that this mutual love is the deepest reality of faith. Ibn al-Qayyim wrote that love of God is "the station over which the seekers compete and toward which the strivers race; it is the spirit of faith and of works."

**"Humble Toward the Believers, Stern Toward the Disbelievers"**

*Adhillatin ʿalā al-muʾminīna aʿizzatin ʿalā al-kāfirīn* — "lowly toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers." The source explains that *adhillah* (from *dhull*, lowliness) means not only humility but sympathy, mercy, and tenderness (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭūsī, al-Zamakhsharī): they are gentle and yielding with their fellow believers. *Aʿizzah* (from *ʿizz*, might, honor) means firm, unyielding, showing strength against those who oppose the faith. The source cites the parallel in 48:29: "harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves." The pairing corrects a common inversion. Many people are harsh with those closest to them and deferential to those who hold power over them; the people God loves are the reverse — soft where softness is owed, firm where firmness is owed. The order of the words is also instructive: *adhillah* comes first. The lover of God is defined first by his tenderness to the believers; his firmness toward the faith's enemies is secondary and defensive, not the leading trait. The "sternness" is not cruelty or aggression — the same sūrah commands justice toward enemies (v. 8) — but a refusal to be intimidated, bought, or made to compromise, in direct contrast to the hypocrites who bent before their non-Muslim protectors out of fear.

**"Striving in the Way of God, Fearing Not the Blame of Any Blamer"**

*Yujāhidūna fī sabīli Allāhi wa-lā yakhāfūna lawmata lāʾim* — "they strive in God's way and do not fear the blame of any blamer." The source notes that many commentators connected the striving with the fight against the apostate tribes, and that al-Qushayrī and the Sufi tradition read it as the inner struggle to maintain obedience, detach from the world, and witness God at every moment. Both are true; *jihād* in the Qur'an comprises every form of exertion for God's sake, from the battlefield to the struggle against one's own soul. The phrase "the blame of any blamer" is the verse's answer to the hypocrites' fear. The indefinite construction — *lawmata lāʾim*, "a blame of a blamer," any blame from anyone — is comprehensive. The lovers of God are not moved by criticism, mockery, social pressure, or the disapproval of the powerful. Abū Dharr reported that the Prophet ﷺ commanded him "to speak the truth even if it is bitter, and not to fear, for God's sake, the blame of any blamer" (Aḥmad; Ibn Ḥibbān). The person who loves God has an audience of One, and the opinions of others lose their power to govern him. This is exactly what the hypocrites lacked: they feared "a change of fortune" and the disapproval of their allies; the people God loves fear neither.

**"That Is the Bounty of God, Which He Gives to Whom He Will"**

*Dhālika faḍlu Allāhi yuʾtīhi man yashāʾ* — "that is the bounty of God; He gives it to whom He wills." The source records al-Rāzī's inference: the spiritual qualities just described — love, humility, firmness, striving, fearlessness — are God's *faḍl*, His gift; all good, including the righteous acts of human beings, comes from Him. Others (al-Ṭūsī, al-Zamakhsharī) read *faḍl* as God's favor (*luṭf*) by which He leads people toward belief and good deeds. Either way, the verse forbids the lover of God to take credit for his love. He did not manufacture it; it was given. This is the safeguard against the pride that would corrupt the very qualities described. The one who is humble toward the believers, firm against disbelief, and unmoved by blame might easily become proud of these virtues; the verse reminds him that they are a gift, and the giver may be thanked but the recipient may not boast.

**"And God Is All-Encompassing, Knowing"**

*Wa-Allāhu wāsiʿun ʿalīm* — "and God is Vast, Knowing." *Wāsiʿ* — whose bounty, mercy, and knowledge have no bounds; His *faḍl* is not a limited quantity that runs out. And *ʿalīm* — He knows to whom to give it: who will bear it, who will be faithful to it, who will use it for Him. The pairing answers the objection that would follow from "He gives it to whom He will": is the gift arbitrary? No — it is given by One whose generosity is boundless and whose knowledge is perfect.

**The Portrait as a Mirror**

The believer should hold this verse up as a mirror and ask five questions. Do I love God — not merely obey Him, but love Him, with the delight and longing the word implies? Am I tender toward my fellow believers — the ones nearest me, the ones easiest to be harsh with? Am I firm where the faith is opposed, or do I yield to pressure? Do I strive for God in some real way, outward or inward? And am I free of the fear of blame, or do the opinions of others still govern what I say and do? The verse promises that God will bring such people. It does not say from where. Every reader may aspire to be among them — and the verse's last phrases tell him how: not by his own manufacture, but by asking for God's bounty from One who is Vast and Knowing.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:55

> **Your protector is only God, and His Messenger, and those who believe, who perform the prayer and give alms while bowing down.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Positive Counterpart to Verse 51**

Verse 51 stated the prohibition: do not take Jews and Christians as *awliyāʾ*. Verse 55 states the alternative: *innamā waliyyukumu Allāhu wa-rasūluhu wa-lladhīna āmanū* — "Your *walī* is only God, and His Messenger, and those who believe." The particle *innamā*, "only," "none other than," is restrictive: it confines the believer's protective allegiance to exactly three — God, the Messenger, and the believers — and excludes every other. The source notes that the verse continues the discussion begun in verse 51 and reiterates its positive content (al-Ṭabarī). Where verse 51 told the believers where not to place their loyalty, verse 55 tells them where it belongs.

**The Order: God First, Then the Messenger, Then the Believers**

The source records al-Bayḍāwī's and al-Rāzī's observation about the structure. The word *walī* is in the singular, though three are named. The primary and essential *walī* is God — *al-Walī* is one of His Names (42:9, 28); He is "the *Walī* of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light" (2:257). The Messenger and the believers are *awliyāʾ* as an extension and corollary of one's *walāyah* toward God: one is bound to the Messenger because God sent him, and to the believers because they are bound to God. The singular *walī* thus expresses a single, unified allegiance flowing from God downward, not three competing loyalties. This is why the hypocrites' divided allegiance was so grave: it split what should be one.

The three named are the same three that ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit is reported to have named when he renounced his alliance with the Jews of Qaynuqāʿ: "I take as *walī* God, His Messenger, and the believers, and I am quit of the alliance of these disbelievers." The source records that some commentators saw this verse as an endorsement of ʿUbādah's declaration (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī). Others (al-Jalālayn, al-Wāḥidī) connected it to Companions who complained of being ostracized by the Qurayẓah and Naḍīr after the Muslims' break with them: the verse consoled them by naming the *walī* who would never abandon them.

**"Those Who Believe, Who Perform the Prayer and Give Alms"**

*Alladhīna yuqīmūna al-ṣalāta wa-yuʾtūna al-zakāta* — "who establish the prayer and give the *zakāh*." The believers who are the *awliyāʾ* of the faithful are identified by the two marks the Qur'an constantly pairs: establishing the prayer and giving the alms. The source offers two readings: a description of the believers in general (al-Ṭabarī), or of the sincere believers untainted by hypocrisy, in contrast to those described in verses 51–53 (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī; compare 9:71, "the believing men and believing women are *awliyāʾ* of one another; they enjoin right and forbid wrong, establish the prayer and give the alms"). The second reading fits the passage: the hypocrite also prays outwardly, but the verse's phrasing — *yuqīmūna*, "they establish," a word connoting steadfast and upright performance — points to genuine devotion. The believer's *awliyāʾ* are those whose faith is proved by worship and generosity, not by oaths.

**"While Bowing Down" — Wa-hum Rākiʿūn**

*Wa-hum rākiʿūn* — "and they are bowing." This final clause has generated one of the most discussed interpretive traditions in the Qur'an, and the source treats it fully. Grammatically it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and it can be read in more than one way.

The first reading takes it as descriptive of the believers' general state: they perform prayer and give alms *as people who bow* — that is, as people of humility and submission (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī). *Rukūʿ*, bowing, is the posture of humility, and the source cites 2:43, where prayer and alms are likewise joined with "bow with those who bow." On this reading the clause says: these are humble people, whose prayer and charity flow from lowliness before God — again in contrast to the hypocrites' pride and calculation.

The second reading, which the source records as widely reported in both Sunni and Shiite commentaries and attributed to early authorities including Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, takes the clause literally as describing a specific incident: a believer, while actually bowing in prayer, gave charity. The reports identify him as ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. A beggar entered the mosque asking for alms; no one gave; ʿAlī, who was bowing in prayer, extended his hand and the beggar took the ring from his finger; and this verse was revealed (al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Wāḥidī). Al-Zamakhsharī draws from it the lesson the source records: the verse encourages giving charity whenever it is requested, without delay, and commends ʿAlī's virtue in not postponing even until the end of his prayer. A minority tradition connects the verse to Abū Bakr instead (al-Rāzī).

**The Verse of Walāyah in Shiite and Sunni Understanding**

The source explains the significance of this verse for Shiite Islam, which calls it *āyat al-wilāyah*, "the verse of guardianship." For the Shīʿah, *walī* and *wilāyah* denote not merely protection or friendship but spiritual and political authority — the unique authority of ʿAlī and the Imams after him to lead the community as the Prophet's ﷺ rightful successors. Reading the verse as revealed about ʿAlī's giving of the ring, they take it as a clear textual proof that ʿAlī is the *walī* of the believers after God and the Prophet ﷺ, and hence their rightful leader (al-Ṭabrisī, al-Ṭūsī).

Sunni commentators, the source notes, generally respond in one of two ways. Some (Ibn Kathīr) hold that the traditions identifying the verse with ʿAlī's ring are not fully sound in their chains of transmission. Others accept the association but deny the legitimist inference: al-Rāzī argues that *walāyah* in this verse means what it means in verse 51 and in 9:71 — the bond of mutual support and protection among believers — and not a special spiritual authority; he notes that the verse's plural "those who believe" cannot naturally refer to one man; and he observes that ʿAlī did not adduce this verse at the *shūrā* convened after ʿUmar's death, where his right to the caliphate was at issue. The source's own judgment is balanced: the association of the verse with ʿAlī is so widespread, even in Sunni commentaries and among the earliest authorities, that it belongs authentically to the early exegetical tradition — whatever one concludes about the inferences drawn from it.

A believer of either tradition can hold the following without controversy: the verse binds the believers' allegiance to God, His Messenger, and the sincere faithful; it exalts humble prayer and prompt charity; and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, whom the Prophet ﷺ described as one "who loves God and His Messenger, and whom God and His Messenger love," was among the foremost exemplars of the qualities it names. Sunnis honor him as the fourth of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and one of the ten promised Paradise; the Prophet ﷺ said to him, "You are to me as Aaron was to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me" (al-Bukhārī 4416; Muslim 2404).

**Walāyah as the Bond of the Community**

The verse teaches that the community of faith is held together by a bond that begins in God. God is the believer's *walī*; the Messenger is his *walī* as God's envoy; the believers are his *awliyāʾ* as fellow servants of God. This bond is stronger than blood, tribe, nation, or interest, and it is the reason the hypocrites' alliances were so grave. To take God's enemies as protectors against God's community is to sever the bond at its root. Conversely, the believer who holds to this *walāyah* is never alone: he has God as Protector, the Sunnah of the Messenger as his guide, and every sincere believer as his ally. The Prophet ﷺ described the result: "The believers, in their mutual love, mercy, and compassion, are like one body; when one limb complains, the whole body responds with sleeplessness and fever" (al-Bukhārī 6011; Muslim 2586).

**The Verse for the Reader**

Whatever the reader's view on the historical occasion, the verse asks him three things. First, is God his *walī* in fact — the one to whom he turns first for protection, guidance, and support? Second, does he hold the Messenger and the sincere believers as his allies, standing with them in the decisive moment? And third, does he embody the marks named — steadfast prayer, ready charity, and the humility of one who bows — such that other believers can rightly count him among *their* *awliyāʾ*? The incident of the ring, whether or not one takes it as the verse's occasion, offers the standard: a charity so ready that it cannot wait even for the prayer to end.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:56

> **And whosoever takes as his protector God, and His Messenger, and those who believe—the party of God, they are the victorious!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Promise That Completes the Passage**

Verses 51–55 have set out the negative and positive commands concerning *walāyah*: do not take Jews and Christians as protectors (v. 51); your protector is only God, His Messenger, and the believers (v. 55). Verse 56 completes the passage with a promise: *wa-man yatawalla Allāha wa-rasūlahu wa-lladhīna āmanū fa-inna ḥizba Allāhi humu al-ghālibūn* — "and whoever takes as *walī* God and His Messenger and those who believe — indeed the party of God, they are the victors." The one who does what verse 55 commands is named a member of *ḥizb Allāh*, the party of God, and that party is declared victorious. The source notes that the verse describes those who follow the injunctions of verses 51 and 55 — they are the party of God.

The verse's structure is a conditional whose consequence is stated obliquely. One expects: "whoever takes God as *walī* — he will be victorious." Instead: "whoever takes God as *walī* — indeed *the party of God* are the victors." The substitution of the general noun for the pronoun is a rhetorical device (*al-iẓhār fī mawḍiʿ al-iḍmār*) that does two things at once: it names the person as belonging to God's party, and it grounds his victory in that membership rather than in himself. He does not win because of his own strength; he wins because he belongs to the party that always wins.

**Ḥizb Allāh: The Party of God**

*Ḥizb* is a group united by a common purpose, a faction, a company; the Qur'an uses the plural *aḥzāb* for the confederate tribes that besieged Madinah (33:20). *Ḥizb Allāh* is the company whose common purpose is God — bound together by *walāyah* toward Him. The source notes that the term occurs in 58:22 as well, where it is described in fuller terms, and that it is contrasted with *ḥizb al-shayṭān*, the party of Satan, in 58:19. The full passage of 58:22 deserves quoting, because it illuminates this verse:

> *"You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their kindred. Those — He has written faith upon their hearts and supported them with a spirit from Him. He will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein. God is well pleased with them, and they are well pleased with Him. Those are the party of God. Unquestionably, the party of God — they are the successful."*

The parallel is exact. In 58:22, the party of God are those who do not give their loving allegiance to God's opponents, even if those opponents are their own kin; God writes faith on their hearts, supports them with a spirit from Him, and is pleased with them; and they are *al-mufliḥūn*, the successful. In 5:56, the party of God are those who give their *walāyah* to God, His Messenger, and the believers rather than to the faith's enemies; and they are *al-ghālibūn*, the victors. Together the two verses define the party by its loyalty and promise it both victory and success. The contrasting party of Satan in 58:19 is defined by the opposite: Satan "has gained mastery over them and made them forget the remembrance of God; those are the party of Satan; unquestionably, the party of Satan — they are the losers." The hypocrites of verses 52–53, who "became losers," belong to that party; the lovers of God in verse 54 belong to this one.

The source observes that the term has been adopted by many groups in Islamic history, including the contemporary Lebanese movement whose name is the anglicized *Hezbollah*. The reader should distinguish the Qur'anic term from any organization that claims it. In the Qur'an, *ḥizb Allāh* is not a party in the political sense but the whole body of those whose allegiance is to God; no faction owns the title, and the criteria for membership are the spiritual ones the verse and 58:22 state — faith, loyalty to God over kin and interest, and God's good pleasure — not affiliation with any human institution.

**"They Are the Victorious" — Al-Ghālibūn**

*Ghālib* is from gh-l-b, to overcome, to prevail, to be dominant. The promise is stated in the strongest form: *humu al-ghālibūn*, "they, they are the victors" — with the emphatic pronoun and the definite article, as if to say, "victory is theirs and no one else's." The Qur'an makes the same promise repeatedly: "God has written: I shall surely prevail, I and My messengers" (58:21); "Our word has gone forth to Our servants the messengers: they will surely be helped, and Our host — they will surely be the victors" (37:171–173); "and the end is for the God-fearing" (7:128; 28:83).

What kind of victory is promised? The commentators understood it in layers. There is worldly victory: the party of God prevailed in Madinah, at Makkah, and over the apostate tribes, exactly as verses 52 and 54 foretold. But worldly victory is not guaranteed in every instance to every believer; prophets have been killed, and righteous communities have been overrun. The deeper victory is the one 58:22 names: God's pleasure and Paradise — *falāḥ*, ultimate success. And there is the victory of the truth itself, which prevails even when its bearers fall: the martyrs of Uḥud lost the battle and won everything. The Prophet ﷺ described a group of his community who would remain "manifest upon the truth, unharmed by those who forsake or oppose them, until God's command comes" (Muslim 1920) — a victory of steadfastness that does not depend on the fortunes of any single conflict. The believer who belongs to God's party may lose a battle; he cannot lose the war, because the outcome of the war was written before he was born.

**The Logic of the Passage: Fear and Security**

The passage 51–56 began with fear and ends with victory, and the movement is deliberate. The hypocrites sought protection from Jews and Christians because they feared "a change of fortune" (v. 52). They calculated that the Muslims might lose and hedged accordingly. Verse 56 answers the calculation at its root: the party of God does not lose. The believer who places his *walāyah* in God, His Messenger, and the believers has chosen the side whose victory is certain, and his security is greater than any alliance could give. The hypocrite's insurance was worthless, because the outcome it insured against — the defeat of God's party — is not possible; and the believer's apparent risk was no risk at all, because the party he joined cannot be overcome.

This reframing is the answer to every fear that leads a believer to compromise. Whenever he is tempted to seek security by softening his loyalty to God — to ally with what opposes the faith, to keep silent when truth is needed, to hedge his commitment against the possibility that God's promise fails — verse 56 reminds him that he is calculating wrongly. The side he is tempted to abandon is the only side that wins.

**Membership in the Party**

The verse defines membership simply: *man yatawalla Allāha wa-rasūlahu wa-lladhīna āmanū*, "whoever takes as *walī* God and His Messenger and those who believe." No lineage, no tribe, no nation, no organization confers it. It is available to anyone who directs his allegiance rightly. And it is verified, as 58:22 makes clear, by what one does when loyalty is tested — when loving God's opponents would be easier, more profitable, or more natural because they are one's own kin. ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, renouncing his lifelong allies for God's sake, is the model: he joined the party of God on the day he chose it over every other tie.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The believer should read verse 56 as both promise and question. The promise is that if he belongs to God's party, he is among the victors, whatever any given day may bring. The question is whether he does belong — whether his *walāyah* is, in fact, given to God, His Messenger, and the believers, or whether some part of it is held in reserve for other protectors, other loyalties, other calculations. The passage's whole argument is that the reserve is folly: it buys no real security and forfeits the only victory that lasts. The one who understands this places his whole allegiance where it belongs and finds, as the verse promises, that he is on the winning side.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:57

> **O you who believe! Take not as protectors those who take your religion in mockery and as play, from among those who were given the Book before you, or the disbelievers, and reverence God, if you are believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Prohibition with a Sharper Criterion**

Verse 51 prohibited taking Jews and Christians as *awliyāʾ*; verse 57 returns to the theme with a more precise identification of who is meant: *lā tattakhidhū alladhīna ittakhadhū dīnakum huzuwan wa-laʿiban* — "do not take as *awliyāʾ* those who take your religion in mockery and as play." Where verse 51 named communities, verse 57 names a *conduct*: mockery of the religion. And it applies the criterion across communities: *mina alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba min qablikum wa-l-kuffār* — "from among those who were given the Book before you, and the disbelievers." The verse thus clarifies verse 51's intent. The prohibited *walāyah* is not owed to any person because of his community but because of his hostility to the faith — and hostility includes not only fighting it but ridiculing it. The source states the principle: the enemies of the believers are not only those who fight the religion but those who mock it.

**Mockery and Play: Huzuw and Laʿib**

*Huzuw* is mockery, derision — the treatment of something serious as ridiculous. *Laʿib* is play, sport — the treatment of something serious as trivial. The two together describe a total refusal of seriousness: the one who mocks religion denies its truth; the one who plays with it denies its weight. The source traces the Qur'an's treatment of mockery of religion, of the prophets (15:11), of God's signs (30:10), and of His warnings (11:8), and its recurring judgment that the mockers will be "surrounded by that which they used to mock" (6:10; 16:34; 39:48; 40:83; 45:33; 46:26). To take religion as play, the source notes, is to engage in it vainly and without commitment (6:70; 7:51) — and the Qur'an condemns those who "took their religion as play and amusement, and whom the life of this world deluded" (7:51).

The Qur'an's severity about mockery is grounded in what mockery does. Argument against religion can be answered by argument; persecution can be endured; but mockery attacks not the content of the faith but its dignity, and it works on the mocked by shame rather than by reason. The believer who is laughed at is tempted to hide his faith or to soften it — not because he has been refuted but because he does not want to be ridiculous. Mockery is thus a peculiarly effective weapon against faith, and the Qur'an treats those who wield it as enemies in the full sense. It states elsewhere that mockery of God, His signs, and His Messenger is itself disbelief: "Was it God and His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking? Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief" (9:65–66).

**Who Was Meant**

The source records the reported occasions. One (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī) identifies the mockers as hypocrites whom some Muslims had befriended — men who professed Islam outwardly while ridiculing it privately; the verse warned the believers to discontinue their close relations with such people. This fits the verse's description of those who "take your religion in mockery" as coming from among the People of the Book: Jews who had feigned conversion (as verse 61 will describe, "they entered with disbelief and left with it") and mocked the faith they pretended to hold. Another occasion (al-Qurṭubī) identifies them as Jews and idolaters who mocked the Muslims when they prostrated in prayer — which verse 58 will specify as mockery of the call to prayer.
