The source also records al-Ṭabarī's reading of the two categories: "those given the Book" are the Jews and Christians who mock, and "the disbelievers" are a separate category, the idolaters. And it notes al-Shāfiʿī's legal inference (recorded by al-Qurṭubī): that Muslims should not take the People of the Book as military allies even against the idolaters. The source connects this to a reported incident in which the Prophet ﷺ declined the offer of some Madinan Jews to fight alongside him at Uḥud, and to a similar incident at the Trench (3:28). The commentary on verse 51 has already addressed the scope of these rulings: they pertain to the circumstances of the emergent community in Madinah, where the allegiance of such allies could not be relied upon, and later Islamic law permitted treaties and alliances with non-Muslim powers once the state was secure. The permanent principle is the verse's criterion: no protective alliance with those who hold the religion in contempt.

**The Reading of the Variant: Kuffār or Kuffāri**

A grammatical note the classical commentators discussed: the word *al-kuffār* may be read in the accusative (*al-kuffāra*), making the disbelievers a second object of "do not take" — "do not take as *awliyāʾ* those who mock ... nor the disbelievers" — or in the genitive (*al-kuffāri*), coordinating with "those given the Book" — "from among those given the Book and the disbelievers." Both readings are transmitted; both yield the same prohibition; and the second, adopted by most reciters, makes the verse's structure clearest: the mockers may come from either group, and the criterion applies to both.

**"And Reverence God, If You Are Believers"**

*Wa-ttaqū Allāha in kuntum muʾminīn* — "and be God-fearing, if you are believers." The conditional is the Qur'an's characteristic spur. It does not doubt the believers' faith; it appeals to it: your faith itself requires this of you. To take the mockers of one's religion as protectors is inconsistent with fearing God, for two reasons. First, it shows that one fears the mockers' power more than one fears God's displeasure — the same disorder of fear the sūrah has diagnosed repeatedly (vv. 3, 44, 52, 54). Second, it exposes one to the mockery's corrosive effect: a believer who keeps close company with those who ridicule his faith will, sooner or later, come to feel his faith as ridiculous. The Prophet ﷺ said: "A man is upon the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look to whom he befriends" (Abū Dāwūd 4833; al-Tirmidhī 2378). *Taqwā* here is self-protection as much as obedience.

**The Principle Beyond Its Occasion**

The verse's lasting teaching concerns the company a believer keeps and the loyalties he forms. It does not concern Jews or Christians or anyone else as such — the criterion is *conduct toward the religion*, and it applies equally to the nominal Muslim who ridicules Islam's practices, the secular acquaintance who treats faith as a joke, and the fellow professional whose banter about religion the believer laughs along with to fit in. The Qur'an elsewhere gives the practical rule: "When you hear God's signs being denied and mocked, do not sit with them until they enter into another conversation; otherwise you would be like them" (4:140). One need not be hostile; one must not be complicit. And one certainly must not make such people one's *awliyāʾ* — those to whom one turns for protection, whose approval one seeks, whose disapproval one fears.

The verse also has an inward application. The one who "takes religion as play" may be the believer himself, when he treats prayer as routine, the Qur'an as decoration, and the commandments as optional. The Qur'an's warning against taking the mockers as protectors is, at a deeper level, a warning against taking the mocker's attitude into one's own heart.

**The Verse in the Passage**

Verse 57 closes the group of verses on *walāyah* (51–57) by clarifying its principle, and opens onto the specific instance verse 58 will describe — the mockery of the call to prayer. The movement from "do not take as protectors those who mock your religion" to "when you call to prayer, they take it in mockery" gives the general command a concrete image: the *adhān* sounding over Madinah, and the mockers' laughter. The believer who has heard the command should be able to hear, in the next verse, exactly what it means.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:58

> **And when you call to prayer, they take it in mockery and as play. That is because they are a people who do not understand.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Only Verse on the Call to Prayer**

*Wa-idhā nādaytum ilā al-ṣalāti ittakhadhūhā huzuwan wa-laʿibā* — "And when you call to the prayer, they take it in mockery and as play." The source notes that this is the only verse in the Qur'an that refers directly to the call to prayer, and that it does so without the technical term *adhān*, using instead the verb *nādā*, to call out, to summon aloud. The commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī) took the verse as the scriptural basis for the *adhān* as an established institution: the Qur'an presupposes it — "when you call to prayer" — as an existing practice of the community, and Sūrat al-Jumuʿah refers to it again: "when the call is made for prayer on the day of assembly, hasten to the remembrance of God" (62:9).

**The Institution of the Adhān**

The source records the history. The call to prayer was instituted in the first or second year after the emigration to Madinah, when the community had grown and needed a public means of announcing the times of prayer. The Companions discussed options: a bell, as the Christians used; a horn, as the Jews used; a fire; a flag. None satisfied. Then ʿAbdullāh ibn Zayd ibn ʿAbd Rabbih dreamed of a man in green garments carrying a bell, whom he asked to sell it for the purpose of calling to prayer; the man said, "Shall I not guide you to something better?" and taught him the words of the *adhān*. Ibn Zayd reported the dream to the Prophet ﷺ, who said, "It is a true vision, God willing," and told him to teach the words to Bilāl, "for he has a stronger voice." When Bilāl gave the first call, ʿUmar came running, saying that he had seen the same dream (Abū Dāwūd 499; al-Tirmidhī 189; Ibn Mājah 706). Al-Qurṭubī records the report that the Prophet ﷺ had heard the call during the Night Journey; but the practice was instituted in Madinah, in the manner described.

The source gives the words of the Sunni *adhān*: *Allāhu akbar* (four times) — God is greatest; *ashhadu an lā ilāha illā Allāh* (twice) — I bear witness that there is no god but God; *ashhadu anna Muḥammadan rasūlu Allāh* (twice) — I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; *ḥayya ʿalā al-ṣalāh* (twice) — come to the prayer; *ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ* (twice) — come to success; *Allāhu akbar* (twice); *lā ilāha illā Allāh*. The dawn call adds *al-ṣalātu khayrun mina al-nawm*, "prayer is better than sleep." The Shiite *adhān*, as the source notes, adds a testimony that ʿAlī is the *walī* of God after the testimony to the Messenger, and *ḥayya ʿalā khayri al-ʿamal*, "come to the best of deeds," after the call to success.

The words of the *adhān* are a complete summary of the faith. They begin with God's greatness, proclaim His oneness and His Messenger, summon to the specific act of prayer and the general goal of success, and return to God's greatness and oneness. Five times a day, this summary is proclaimed aloud over every Muslim community. The Prophet ﷺ said: "When the call to prayer is made, Satan turns his back and flees, breaking wind, so as not to hear the *adhān*" (al-Bukhārī 608; Muslim 389) — the summons to God is unbearable to the enemy of God. And he promised the one who repeats the call after the caller, and then asks God's blessing on the Prophet and asks for him the *wasīlah*, that his intercession would be his (Muslim 384).

**The Mockery Described**

The source records the forms the mockery took. Some Christians or Jews of Madinah, on hearing the call, would ridicule the Prophet ﷺ or the believers and cast ill omens on them (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). Some disbelievers mocked the call as a religious innovation — an odd new practice unknown to earlier religions — or as having an ugly sound (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Wāḥidī). A report in al-Qurṭubī describes a Christian in Madinah who, whenever he heard "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," would say, "May the liar be burned" — and one night his servant entered his house with a fire, a spark fell, and he and his household were burned. Al-Qurṭubī also records that the verse's occasion involved the Jews' laughing and jeering when the *muʾadhdhin* called and the Muslims rose to pray.

The mockery of the *adhān* is a specific instance of the general conduct verse 57 named — "those who take your religion in mockery and as play" — and the placement of the verses shows what the abstract description means in practice: the sound of the call to God, and the derision of those who hear it as a joke.

**"That Is Because They Are a People Who Do Not Understand"**

*Dhālika bi-annahum qawmun lā yaʿqilūn* — "that is because they are a people who do not use reason." The verse diagnoses the mockery not as malice alone but as a failure of *ʿaql*, intellect, understanding. The source records al-Rāzī's explanation: those of real understanding know that prayer is the best of all human acts; and he quotes the saying, "The noblest movement is prayer, and the most beneficial stillness is fasting." The one who laughs at the call to prayer laughs at the summons to the one act that gives human life its meaning — the standing of a created being before its Creator. Only a mind that has not grasped what a human being *is* could find that ridiculous.

The diagnosis is precise and merciful at once. It is precise because mockery of worship is, in fact, an intellectual failure: the mocker has not thought about what he is mocking, or he has thought about it only in terms of surface and sound and strangeness, never in terms of what it means. It is merciful because it locates the fault in understanding, which can be corrected, rather than in nature, which cannot. Many who once mocked the *adhān* later wept at hearing it — including some of the fiercest opponents of the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah, who lived to give the call themselves.

**The Adhān as a Test of Hearts**

The Qur'an's placement of this verse among the verses on *walāyah* suggests that the call to prayer functions as a test of where people stand. When the *adhān* sounds, the believer's heart lifts; the hypocrite's heart sinks; the mocker laughs. The same sound produces opposite responses, and the responses reveal the hearts. The Prophet ﷺ described the believers' response: "If people knew what is in the call to prayer and the first row, and found no way to obtain it except by drawing lots, they would draw lots" (al-Bukhārī 615; Muslim 437). And he described the *muʾadhdhin*'s honor: "The *muʾadhdhins* will have the longest necks on the Day of Resurrection" (Muslim 387) — the most visible, the most honored, because they called others to God. Between the honor of the caller and the laughter of the mocker lies the whole distance between understanding and its absence.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The believer today hears the *adhān* — from a minaret, from a phone, from a voice in a small room — and this verse asks what he hears. Does he hear a routine sound, background noise to be tolerated? Then he is closer to the "play" the verse condemns than he would like. Does he hear a summons — "God is greatest; come to prayer; come to success" — that interrupts his affairs with the reminder of what matters most? Then he is among those who understand. And when he encounters those who mock — whether openly, as in Madinah, or subtly, in the small jokes and eye-rolls of a culture that finds public worship embarrassing — he should remember the verse's diagnosis and respond not with anger but with the confidence of one who knows what the mockers do not: that the call they find strange is the most reasonable sound in the world.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:59

> **Say, "O People of the Book! Are you vengeful toward us for no other reason than that we believe in God and in that which has been sent down unto us and in that which was sent down before, and because most of you are iniquitous?"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Believers' Question**

After the descriptions of verses 57–58 — the mockery of the religion and of the call to prayer — the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to put a question to the People of the Book: *qul yā ahla al-kitābi hal tanqimūna minnā illā an āmannā bi-Allāhi wa-mā unzila ilaynā wa-mā unzila min qablu wa-anna aktharakum fāsiqūn* — "Say: O People of the Book! Do you resent us for anything except that we believe in God, and in what was sent down to us, and in what was sent down before, and that most of you are iniquitous?" The question is rhetorical and its effect is to expose. It asks the mockers to state the grounds of their hostility, and it supplies the only grounds there are: the believers' faith — and the mockers' own corruption.

**"Do You Resent Us?" — Tanqimūna**

The verb *naqama* means to find fault with, to resent, to hold a grudge against, and by extension to take vengeance on. The source's translation, "vengeful," captures the sense of active hostility. The question *hal tanqimūna minnā illā ...*, "do you resent from us anything except ...," is a construction of restriction: there is no ground for your resentment except this. The source points to the parallel in 7:126, where Pharaoh's sorcerers, having believed in Moses and been threatened with death, say to Pharaoh: "You resent us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us" — the same verb, the same construction, the same situation of believers persecuted for nothing but belief. And to 85:8, where the People of the Trench "resented" the believers "only because they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praised." The Qur'an thus places the mockery of the Madinan People of the Book in a long line of hostility toward faith for its own sake — the hostility of Pharaoh, of the persecutors of the Trench, and of every age.

**The Three Objects of Faith**

The verse states what the believers believe in, and the statement is itself the argument. *Āmannā bi-Allāh* — "we believe in God": the God the People of the Book themselves profess. *Wa-mā unzila ilaynā* — "and in what was sent down to us": the Qur'an. *Wa-mā unzila min qablu* — "and in what was sent down before": the Torah, the Gospel, and all the prior revelations. Here is the irony the verse exposes. The Muslims believe in everything the People of the Book claim to believe in — God and His earlier scriptures — and in addition they believe in the final revelation. The Muslim faith is more inclusive than the faith of those who resent it: the Muslim honors Moses and Jesus; the Jew who resents him rejects Jesus, and the Christian rejects Muhammad ﷺ. What, then, is the ground of resentment? Not that the Muslims believe too little, but that they believe too much — that they include what the resenters exclude.

The source records a specific occasion connected to this point (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī): some Jews of Madinah broke with the Prophet ﷺ over his affirmation of the prophethood of Jesus, referenced in the phrase "what was sent down before." They came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked in whom he believed; he named the prophets, including Jesus; and they said, "We do not believe in Jesus or in anyone who believes in him." The resentment, in other words, was a resentment of the Muslims' *comprehensiveness* — their refusal to reject any of God's messengers. The Qur'an makes this comprehensiveness a defining mark of the believers: "We make no distinction between any of His messengers" (2:285).

**"And That Most of You Are Iniquitous"**

*Wa-anna aktharakum fāsiqūn* — "and that most of you are *fāsiqūn*." The final clause is the most cutting part of the question, and its grammar has been discussed. It is coordinated with the preceding clauses as an object of "except": "Do you resent us for anything except that we believe ... and that most of you are iniquitous?" The construction places the People of the Book's own *fisq* among the causes of their resentment — not as something the believers did but as something in the resenters themselves. The source explains: their rejection of the Prophet ﷺ had its roots in their own deviation from God's religion and law, which compelled them to harbor ill will toward the message. The person who has departed from God's law resents those who uphold it, because their fidelity is a standing rebuke to his infidelity.

This is one of the Qur'an's deepest observations about religious hostility. The mockers of verses 57–58 were not mocking because they had examined the Muslims' faith and found it unreasonable; they were mocking because the Muslims' seriousness exposed their own lack of it. A community that had covered the verse of stoning with its hand, taken bribes to soften rulings, and reverted to *jāhilī* standards of unequal blood could not look upon a community of fresh, earnest submission without discomfort — and discomfort turned to resentment, and resentment to mockery. The Qur'an says elsewhere: "Many of the People of the Book wish to turn you back to disbelief after your faith, out of envy from their own souls, after the truth has become clear to them" (2:109). *Ḥasad*, envy, is the psychological name for what this verse describes.

**"Most of You," Not "All of You"**

The verse says *aktharakum*, "most of you," and the qualification must not be overlooked. The Qur'an is scrupulous, throughout this sūrah and elsewhere, to distinguish. Verse 13 said "except a few of them"; verse 66 will describe "a moderate community among them"; 3:113 says "they are not all alike." The resentment described in this verse is the resentment of the corrupt majority of a particular time and place; the Qur'an does not ascribe it to every member of the People of the Book, and it will shortly (vv. 82–85) praise Christians whose eyes overflow with tears when they hear the Qur'an. The believer who reads this verse should hold the distinction firmly: the verse diagnoses a psychology, not a people.

**The Form of the Response: A Question, Not an Insult**

Note what the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to do in response to mockery. He is not told to mock back, to threaten, or to withdraw. He is told to *ask a question* — a question that places the burden on the mockers to justify themselves, and that, in the asking, states the believers' position with dignity. "What have we done, except believe in God, in our Book, and in yours?" The question cannot be answered without either conceding that the believers' faith is the grievance — which is shameful — or admitting the resenters' own corruption — which is more shameful. It is a model of how the believer meets derision: not with heat, but with a clear statement of what he actually believes and a calm invitation to the mocker to say what, exactly, he objects to.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The believer who is resented, mocked, or opposed for his faith — in a workplace, a family, a society — should learn from this verse to ask the diagnostic question: what, exactly, is the grievance? Often he will find, as the verse found, that the grievance is nothing but his belief and his seriousness — and that its root lies not in anything he has done wrong but in the discomfort his fidelity produces in those who have abandoned theirs. This knowledge should not make him proud, for his faith is God's gift (v. 54); but it should free him from the false guilt that mockery aims to produce. He believes in God, in what was sent down to him, and in what was sent down before. That is the whole of the charge against him. He should be content to plead guilty.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:60

> **Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that by way of recompense from God? Whomsoever God has cursed and upon whom is His Wrath, and among whom He has made some to be apes and swine, and who worship false deities, such are in a worse situation, and further astray from the right way."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counter-Question**

Verse 59 asked the People of the Book what ground they had for resenting the believers, and found none but the believers' faith and the resenters' own iniquity. Verse 60 presses the point with a second command to speak: *qul hal unabbiʾukum bi-sharrin min dhālika mathūbatan ʿinda Allāh* — "Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that, as recompense with God?" The "that" refers to what the mockers held in contempt — the believers' religion, which they considered a thing of ridicule. The Prophet ﷺ is told to answer: you consider our faith a bad thing? Let me tell you of something truly bad — the condition of those whom God has cursed. The structure is a reversal: the mockers had positioned themselves as judges of the believers' religion; the verse repositions them as the judged.

**The Irony of Mathūbah**

The source notes a deliberate irony in the word *mathūbatan*, translated "by way of recompense." *Mathūbah*, from th-w-b, to return, ordinarily denotes a positive return — a reward, what one receives back for good deeds (the same root gives *thawāb*, reward). To use it for divine punishment is sarcastic, in the manner of the Qur'an's "give them glad tidings of a painful punishment" (4:138; 9:34; 84:24). The mockers had treated the believers' religion as a joke; the verse answers in a register that matches: "shall I tell you of a *reward* worse than that?" — where the "reward" is curse, wrath, and transformation. Al-Zamakhsharī, as the source records, draws attention to this tone. It is the only mockery the Qur'an permits the believers: the turning of the mocker's frame back upon him.

**"Whomsoever God Has Cursed"**

*Man laʿanahu Allāh* — "whoever God has cursed." The source glosses the curse, following al-Ṭabarī, as exile from God's mercy — *laʿnah* being distance and expulsion from good. The Qur'an speaks of God's curse upon the Israelites who broke their covenant (v. 13; 2:88; 4:46–47), and 5:78 will say that "those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and of Jesus son of Mary." *Wa-ghaḍiba ʿalayh* — "and upon whom is His wrath": the Qur'an's most severe description, used in the Fātiḥah (1:7) for the path the believer asks to be spared, and in 2:61 and 3:112 for those "who used to disbelieve in God's signs and kill the prophets without right." To be cursed and under wrath is the opposite of being loved (v. 54): the mockers, who resented the believers for their faith, are shown the condition their own history had earned.

**"And Made Some of Them Apes and Swine"**

*Wa-jaʿala minhumu al-qiradata wa-l-khanāzīr* — "and made of them apes and swine." The source connects the apes to the account in 2:65 and 7:163–166 of the Sabbath-breakers of a coastal town, to whom God said, "Be apes, despised." The people had devised a trick to catch fish on the Sabbath while pretending to observe it — setting traps on Friday and collecting them on Sunday — and were transformed. The source records the readings of this transformation: it may be understood as a literal event, as most classical commentators held; or as a metaphor for the state, in this world or the next, of those who deliberately violate the Law while pretending to keep it — losing their humanity in the moral sense (see the commentary on 2:65); or, as Ibn ʿAjībah suggests, as a reference to God's changing and hardening their hearts (2:74; 5:13; 6:43) and making them prone to heedlessness (*ghaflah*). Mujāhid, among the early commentators, held that "their hearts were transformed, not their bodies."

The swine, the source notes, some commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī) connected to a different group — those among Jesus' followers who betrayed him, or who disbelieved after the table was sent down (5:115) — while the apes were the Sabbath-breakers. On this reading the verse refers to both communities: Jews and Christians alike had, in their histories, members who were transformed for their corruption. Whatever the precise reference, the verse's point is that the People of the Book who mock the Muslims have in their own past the record of those whom God so cursed — and it is they, not the believers, whose "recompense" should be a matter of concern.

The choice of animals is not arbitrary. The ape is the animal that imitates without understanding — an image of the Sabbath-breakers who imitated observance while violating its meaning. The swine is the animal of greed and uncleanness — an image of those who consumed the unlawful (v. 42's *suḥt*) and betrayed trust for gain. The transformation, literal or moral, fits the crime.

**"And Who Worshipped Ṭāghūt"**

*Wa-ʿabada al-ṭāghūt* — "and who worshipped *ṭāghūt*." *Ṭāghūt* is from ṭ-gh-y, to exceed bounds, to rebel; it names any object of worship or obedience other than God — idols, tyrants, Satan, false authorities (see 2:256; 4:51, 60, 76). The source notes the mention of the People of the Book's belief in *ṭāghūt* in 4:51, and al-Zamakhsharī's connection to the Israelites' worship of the golden calf (7:148–156; 20:86–97). The charge is pointed: the People of the Book resented the Muslims for believing in God; but their own history included the worship of a calf, and their present, as 9:31 will say, included taking "their rabbis and monks as lords besides God." Who, then, is in the worse position?

**"Those Are Worse in Position and Further Astray from the Even Path"**

*Ulāʾika sharrun makānan wa-aḍallu ʿan sawāʾi al-sabīl* — "those are worse in station and further astray from the even path." The verse concludes the comparison. *Makān*, place, station, standing: the mockers thought the believers' standing low; it is theirs that is low. *Sawāʾ al-sabīl*, the even path, the straight road — the phrase the sūrah used in verse 12 for what the covenant-breakers had lost, and will use again in verse 77. The mockers had strayed from it further than anyone they mocked.

The comparative forms — *sharr*, worse; *aḍall*, further astray — do not imply that the believers' position is bad and the mockers' merely worse. They are the Qur'an's way of adopting the mocker's premise for the sake of argument and then overturning it: "Even granting your view that our religion is a bad thing — which it is not — you should know of something worse, and it is your own condition."

**The Use and Misuse of the Verse**

This verse has been abused, in some times and places, as a term of contempt for Jews — "apes and swine" hurled as an insult. Such use is a betrayal of the verse. The verse does not say that Jews are apes and swine; it says that God *made some* (*minhum*) of a particular people, for a particular crime, into apes and swine — a historical judgment on the Sabbath-breakers, not a description of a people. The Qur'an itself, in the very passage where it recounts the Sabbath-breakers (7:163–166), describes the righteous among the same town who forbade the wrong and were saved. And the Prophet ﷺ, when asked whether the apes and swine of his time were the descendants of those transformed, said: "God did not destroy a people and then give them offspring; the apes and swine existed before that" (Muslim 2663) — closing the door to any notion that the transformation had descendants or that living animals or living people are its heirs. The verse is a warning about what deliberate violation of God's law does to a human being; the Muslim who uses it as an ethnic slur has himself violated the law of his Book, which commands justice even toward those one hates (v. 8).

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches the believer how to answer contempt: not by descending to abuse but by reminding the contemptuous that God's judgment is the only standard of high and low, and that by that standard the mocker of faith stands lower than the faithful he mocks. And it teaches him to fear for himself: the apes and swine were people who had God's Law and evaded it with a trick — traps set on Friday and collected on Sunday. The believer who finds clever ways around God's commands while keeping their outward form should read this verse with dread. Its warning is not about a people; it is about a practice — and the practice is available to anyone.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:61

> **When they come to you, they say, "We believe." But they certainly entered with disbelief and they have certainly left with it, and God knows best what they were concealing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Portrait of Feigned Belief**

*Wa-idhā jāʾūkum qālū āmannā wa-qad dakhalū bi-l-kufri wa-hum qad kharajū bih* — "And when they come to you, they say, 'We believe,' but they have certainly entered with disbelief and they have certainly left with it." The verse describes a specific and recognizable act: people who present themselves to the believers as fellow believers, whose profession is a mask, and who leave exactly as they came. The source records the occasion (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī): a group of Jews of Madinah came to the Prophet ﷺ professing belief in him and his message. Their profession was insincere, and God informed the Prophet ﷺ of it.

The passage from verse 57 onward has been building a picture of the mockers — those who take religion as play, who jeer at the call to prayer, who resent the believers for their faith — and verse 61 adds the final stroke: these same people, when it suits them, come and *say "we believe."* Mockery in private, profession in public. The Qur'an drew this portrait in its first Madinan sūrah: "When they meet those who believe, they say, 'We believe'; and when they are alone with their devils, they say, 'Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking'" (2:14). Verse 61 is the same figure, seen from the side of the believers who receive the profession.

**"They Entered with Disbelief and Left with It"**

The verse's central image is of a threshold crossed twice. *Dakhalū bi-l-kufr* — "they entered with disbelief": when they came into the Prophet's ﷺ presence, or into the community's gatherings, or into the mosque itself, they brought their disbelief in with them, hidden under the profession. *Kharajū bih* — "they left with it": nothing they heard or saw changed anything; the disbelief that entered is the disbelief that departed. The preposition *bi-*, "with," suggests accompaniment — as one enters *with* a companion or *with* a burden. Their disbelief was their constant companion, carried in and carried out.

The double *qad* — *wa-qad dakhalū ... wa-hum qad kharajū* — is emphatic: "they *certainly* entered ... they *certainly* left." The Qur'an insists on the completeness of the deception: not a partial faith that faltered, not a sincere inquiry that failed to convince, but disbelief unbroken from entry to exit, with a false profession in between.

The image is psychologically acute. There are people who sit among the believers, hear the Qur'an recited, watch the prayer, listen to the Prophet ﷺ himself — and are untouched, because they came not to receive but to observe, to gather information, to appear compliant, or to mock afterward. The source's context in verse 41 described the same type: "listeners for other people who have not come to you" — spies who attended in order to report. The heart that has decided not to believe can sit in the very presence of revelation and leave unchanged. The Qur'an says of such hearing: "Among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness" (6:25).

**"And God Knows Best What They Were Concealing"**

*Wa-Allāhu aʿlamu bi-mā kānū yaktumūn* — "and God knows best what they used to conceal." The verse ends where the Qur'an's treatment of hypocrisy always ends: with the divine knowledge that no mask can deceive. The believers might be fooled; the Prophet ﷺ himself, as a man, could not read hearts — "you would know them by the tone of their speech" (47:30) was the most he was promised, and God informed him of specific cases as here. But God knows *mā kānū yaktumūn*, what they were concealing — the imperfect tense indicating a habitual, continuous concealment. The concealment was their way of life; the knowledge is God's.

The verb *katama*, to conceal, is the same verb used in the Qur'an's charges against the People of the Book for concealing what God revealed (2:42, 140, 146, 159, 174; 3:71, 187). The connection is not accidental. Those who had concealed the Torah's ruling on stoning (v. 41) were practiced concealers; concealing their own disbelief under a false profession was one more exercise of a long-developed skill. And the same God who knew what they concealed of the Book knows what they concealed of their hearts.

**The Function of the Verse: Warning and Reassurance**

The verse serves two purposes at once. To the believers it is a warning: not every profession of faith is sincere; some who say "we believe" are exactly what they were before they said it; do not take them as *awliyāʾ* (v. 57) on the strength of words. The verse thus completes the practical instruction of the passage: the believers were told not to take the mockers as protectors, and now they are told how mockers present themselves — as believers. Discernment is required, and the criterion is conduct over time, not profession at the door.

To the Prophet ﷺ and the sincere, it is reassurance. The deceivers may deceive men, but they cannot deceive God, and their deception does not harm the deceived. The Prophet ﷺ was not required to unmask every hypocrite; he was required to convey the message, and he treated those who professed Islam according to their profession, leaving their secrets to God. He said, "I have not been commanded to search the hearts of people or to split open their bellies" (al-Bukhārī 4351; Muslim 1064). The believer who is deceived by a false profession has committed no fault; the fault is the deceiver's, and the Judge knows it.

**The Verse Turned Inward**

The Qur'an's portraits of hypocrisy are always mirrors as well as windows. The believer should ask whether he, too, ever enters and leaves unchanged. He comes to the Friday sermon, to the recitation, to the gathering of remembrance — and does he leave as he came? If so, he has, in a smaller way, "entered with" his state and "left with" it. The difference between him and the hypocrite is that his profession is sincere; but sincere profession that never issues in change is a lesser form of the same disease. The Qur'an asks: "Has not the time come for those who believe that their hearts should be humbled at the remembrance of God and what has come down of the truth?" (57:16). The heart that enters God's presence should not leave as it entered.

The Companions understood the verse as a standing exhortation to consistency between what one says at the threshold and what one carries across it. ʿUmar used to say, "Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account." The one who takes account will find, at the end of each gathering with the believers, whether he has left with more than he brought.

**The Verse in the Passage**

Verse 61 closes the portrait of the mockers that began at verse 57 and prepares the turn of verse 62, where the Qur'an will describe "many of them hastening to sin and enmity and devouring the unlawful" — the conduct that follows from concealed disbelief — and verse 63, where it will rebuke the religious authorities who failed to stop them. The sequence moves from the individual hypocrite who enters and leaves with his disbelief to the community whose leaders permit the corruption. The concealer at the door and the silent rabbi are two faces of one failure: the failure to let the truth in.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:62

> **Thou seest many of them hastening to sin and enmity, and consuming what is forbidden. Evil indeed is that which they were doing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Concealed Disbelief to Visible Conduct**

Verse 61 described those who entered and left with concealed disbelief, and ended with God's knowledge of what they hid. Verse 62 turns to what could not be hidden: *wa-tarā kathīran minhum yusāriʿūna fī al-ithmi wa-l-ʿudwāni wa-aklihimu al-suḥt* — "And you see many of them racing into sin and enmity and their devouring of the unlawful." The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and by extension to any observer: *tarā*, "you see." Concealed disbelief has a visible signature. The heart's condition may be hidden from men, but its fruits are not; and the fruits described here — sin, aggression, and illicit gain — were on open display.

The verse begins, as so often in this sūrah, with *kathīran minhum*, "many of them." Not all. The Qur'an's precision is unwavering; the next verses (65–66) will describe what the People of the Book could have received had they believed, and will name "a moderate community among them." The condemnation falls on the many, not on the whole.

**"Racing into Sin and Enmity"**

*Yusāriʿūna fī al-ithmi wa-l-ʿudwān* — "they race into sin and enmity." The verb is the third occurrence of *yusāriʿūna* in this sūrah: verse 41, racing into disbelief; verse 52, racing into the ranks of the faith's opponents; verse 62, racing into sin and aggression. In every case the word describes a perverse energy — eagerness directed toward what should repel. The Qur'an's ideal is the same verb pointed the other way: "they used to race to good deeds" (21:90). The sinner and the saint are both racers; the question is only the direction.

*Ithm* is sin in the broad sense — the source records that some glossed it here as lying (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī), fitting the "listeners to lies" of verses 41–42, and some as disbelief, while al-Ṭabarī takes it to cover all manner of sin. *ʿUdwān* is from ʿ-d-w, to pass beyond, to transgress — the same root as the "enmity" (*ʿadāwah*) God cast among them in verses 14 and 64 and as the "aggression" the sūrah forbade in verse 2 ("do not let hatred of a people lead you to aggress"). The source records al-Ṭabarī's and al-Zamakhsharī's identifications: hostility toward the Prophet ﷺ, wrongdoing in general, and transgression of God's limits. *Ithm* and *ʿudwān* together were paired in verse 2 as the things believers must *not* cooperate in: "do not help one another in sin and aggression." Here the many are described as racing into exactly those two things. The pairing distinguishes the sin against God (*ithm*) from the sin against people (*ʿudwān*) — the two axes along which every moral failure falls.

**"And Their Devouring of the Unlawful"**

*Wa-aklihimu al-suḥt* — "and their devouring of *suḥt*." The source directs the reader back to verse 42, where *suḥt* was explained: unlawful gain, specifically bribery — the payments taken by religious authorities to soften rulings for the powerful, as in the case of the two adulterers. The commentary there noted the root meaning: *saḥata*, to uproot, to destroy utterly; *suḥt* is gain that destroys its consumer. The verb here is *akl*, eating, devouring, and the Qur'an consistently uses it for illicit consumption of wealth — "do not devour one another's wealth wrongfully" (2:188; 4:29), "those who devour usury" (2:275), "those who devour the wealth of orphans" (4:10). The image is physical: the unlawful becomes part of the eater's body. The Prophet ﷺ described a man, disheveled from long travel, raising his hands to heaven and crying "O Lord, O Lord," "while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he has been nourished on the unlawful — so how can he be answered?" (Muslim 1015). The consumer of *suḥt* cuts himself off from God's response.

The third item is not merely one more sin in a list. Bribery is the specific mechanism by which the first two — sin and aggression — were institutionalized. The rabbis who took *suḥt* to alter the Torah's rulings made lying (*ithm*) into policy and injustice toward the weak (*ʿudwān*) into law. Verse 63 will name the leaders who permitted it.

**"Evil Indeed Is What They Were Doing"**

*La-biʾsa mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — "surely evil is what they used to do." *Biʾsa* is the verb of blame, the opposite of *niʿma*, the verb of praise. The phrase pronounces a verdict on conduct: what they were *doing* — the imperfect *kānū yaʿmalūn* indicating habitual, sustained action. The source draws attention to a subtle difference between this verse's ending and the next verse's, and the difference must be preserved: verse 62 ends with *yaʿmalūn*, "they were doing"; verse 63 ends with *yaṣnaʿūn*, "they were working," "fashioning." The commentary on verse 63 will explain the distinction, which al-Rāzī drew out: the common people are blamed for what they *did*; the leaders are blamed for what they *made* — the state of affairs their negligence produced.

**The Visibility of Corruption**

The verse's opening word, "you see," carries a lesson. The corruption of a religious community is not usually secret. Its sin, its aggression, its illicit money are visible to any honest observer — often most visible to outsiders, who have no interest in overlooking them. The Prophet ﷺ *saw* the condition of the many among the Jews of Madinah; it was not hidden. What the verse implies, and verse 63 will state, is that the community's own leaders also saw it and did nothing. Visibility without correction is the mark of a community whose guardians have failed.

The same is true of every community, including the Muslim one. When sin, aggression, and unlawful gain become visible features of a community's life — when they can be *seen* by any observer — the question the Qur'an will ask in the next verse becomes urgent: where are the scholars? Where are those who know better? The Prophet ﷺ foretold that his community would follow the ways of those before it, and this verse describes one of those ways: the normalization of the visible wrong.

**The Reflex of the Reader**

The believer should read the three charges of this verse as a self-examination before he reads them as an accusation of others. Does he race toward anything sinful with the eagerness the verb implies? Does he transgress against others — in speech, in business, in the small aggressions of daily life — and call it firmness or fairness? And does anything he consumes come from *suḥt* — from gain that involved deception, exploitation, or the sale of a principle? The Qur'an's portrait of the "many" is precise enough to serve as a mirror for the one. And the verse's final verdict, "evil is what they were doing," is the verdict the reader should fear for his own habitual conduct, not merely assign to the conduct of a people long dead.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:63

> **Why do the sages and the rabbis not forbid them from their sinful speech and their consuming what is forbidden? Evil indeed is that which they were working.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Turned on the Leaders**

Verse 62 described the many who raced into sin, aggression, and illicit gain. Verse 63 asks the question that follows inevitably: *law-lā yanhāhumu al-rabbāniyyūna wa-l-aḥbāru ʿan qawlihimu al-ithma wa-aklihimu al-suḥt* — "Why do the *rabbāniyyūn* and the *aḥbār* not forbid them from their sinful speech and their devouring of the unlawful?" The particle *law-lā*, "why not?", is a particle of rebuke and incitement (*taḥḍīḍ*); it expresses not curiosity but reproach: they should have, and they did not. The source states the shift precisely: verse 62 criticized the sinners; verse 63 criticizes the religious leaders who, knowing better, did nothing to stop them.

The two terms are those of verse 44: *rabbāniyyūn*, the devoted teachers and authorities, and *aḥbār*, the learned scholars. Verse 44 praised their predecessors: the prophets, the *rabbāniyyūn*, and the *aḥbār* who judged by the Torah "as they were entrusted to preserve it and were witnesses to it." Verse 63 indicts their successors. The same offices, the same titles — and the opposite conduct. The contrast is the sūrah's way of showing what religious leadership is for and what it becomes when it fails: the guardians of the Book who once upheld its rulings against kings now hold their tongues before the sinners of their own flock.

**The Duty Neglected: Forbidding Wrong**

The verse presupposes a duty: religious authorities are obliged to *forbid* (*nahā*) what is wrong. This is the second half of the pair that defines the Muslim community — "you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong" (3:110) — and the Qur'an makes its neglect by the Israelites' leaders a specific charge, repeated in verses 78–79 of this sūrah: "they used not to forbid one another from the wrong they did; evil indeed was what they used to do." The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Whoever among you sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart — and that is the weakest of faith."* (Muslim 49)

And he described the consequence of neglect with an image: people on a ship, some on the upper deck and some below; those below, wanting water, decide to bore a hole in the hull rather than trouble those above; "if they leave them to what they intend, they will all perish; and if they take hold of their hands, they will be saved, and all will be saved" (al-Bukhārī 2493). The religious leader who sees the hole being bored and says nothing is responsible for the sinking.

**"Their Sinful Speech" — Qawlihimu al-Ithm**

The verse names two things the leaders failed to forbid: *qawlihimu al-ithm*, "their speaking of sin," and *aklihimu al-suḥt*, "their devouring of the unlawful" — the latter repeated verbatim from verse 62. The first is specific: sinful *speech*. In the context of the passage, this is the lying of verses 41–42 ("listeners to lies"), the false claims about the Torah's rulings, the mockery of verses 57–58, the blasphemy of verse 64 ("God's hand is shackled"), and the false professions of verse 61. The leaders heard all of this and did not forbid it. The Qur'an treats speech as action: the tongue is the instrument by which most of the sins of a religious community are committed — lies about God, distortion of scripture, mockery, slander — and the leader who does not correct the tongue has abandoned the primary field of his duty.

**The Difference Between Yaʿmalūn and Yaṣnaʿūn**

The source draws careful attention to the endings of verses 62 and 63, and the distinction is one of the finest in the sūrah. Verse 62 ends: *la-biʾsa mā kānū yaʿmalūn*, "evil indeed is what they were *doing*." Verse 63 ends: *la-biʾsa mā kānū yaṣnaʿūn*, "evil indeed is what they were *working*" — *ṣanaʿa*, to make, to craft, to fashion, to manufacture. Al-Rāzī, as the source records, explains: of the common sinners, the Qur'an blames what they *did*; of the scholars, it blames what they *made* — the state of affairs they *produced* by their refusal to forbid, when they had the knowledge and standing to change it. The common man's sin is an act; the scholar's silence is a *manufacture*, because it creates the conditions under which the acts multiply. A society's sin is done by its members but *made* by its leaders.

*Ṣanaʿa* is also the more deliberate verb. One *does* a thing that may be careless or impulsive; one *makes* a thing with skill and intention. The scholars' silence was not inadvertent; it was a crafted policy — the product of calculation about what forbidding would cost them in position, income, and favor with the powerful. Their omission was an artifact, and the Qur'an judges it as such.

**"Among the Severest Verses of the Qur'an"**

The source records that early authorities — Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk among them — considered this among the most severe and frightening verses in the Qur'an (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said, "There is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in rebuke than this one," and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, "There is no verse in the Qur'an that I fear more than this." These were men of knowledge, and they understood that the verse, though addressed to the rabbis of Madinah, was addressed to *them* — to every person who possesses religious knowledge and therefore bears the duty to forbid what he sees. The verse's terror is that it makes knowledge a liability: the more one knows, the more one is responsible for, and the more one's silence "makes."

The Qur'an says elsewhere: "Why do you say what you do not do? Most hateful is it to God that you say what you do not do" (61:2–3). But this verse goes further: it condemns not the scholar who says one thing and does another, but the scholar who *says nothing* — who neither does the wrong nor forbids it, who keeps his own hands clean and lets the community rot. Neutrality, for the one who knows, is complicity.

**The Sin of Omission as the Root Sin of Leadership**

The source makes the essential point: the sin of omission on the part of the knowledgeable can be more serious and more deeply rooted than the sin of ordinary people. The ordinary sinner may not know better; the scholar does. The ordinary sinner harms himself and those near him; the scholar's silence licenses a community. And the ordinary sinner's act can be corrected by a scholar who speaks; but when the scholars themselves are silent, there is no one left to correct anyone. The Prophet ﷺ said: "God does not take away knowledge by snatching it from people, but by taking away the scholars, until when no scholar remains, the people take ignorant men as leaders, who are asked and give rulings without knowledge, and go astray and lead astray" (al-Bukhārī 100; Muslim 2673). A scholar who is present but silent has, in effect, taken himself away; the community is as leaderless as if he had died.

The historical case is exact. The *rabbāniyyūn* and *aḥbār* of Madinah had witnessed the abandonment of the stoning penalty, the unequal blood-money between Naḍīr and Qurayẓah, the bribery, the lying about the Torah's contents — and their silence had allowed all of it to become custom. When the Prophet ﷺ restored the Torah's ruling, he was doing what they should have done. His words, "I am the first to revive Your command after they had killed it," are an indictment of every rabbi who had let it die.

**The Verse for the Muslim Scholar**

The verse's warning passes to the Muslim *ʿulamāʾ* undiminished, for the Prophet ﷺ foretold that his community would follow the ways of those before it. Wherever Muslim scholars see sinful speech and unlawful gain among those who look to them, and remain silent — out of fear of rulers, fear of losing followers, fear of controversy, or the comfort of position — the *law-lā* of this verse is addressed to them: *why do you not forbid?* And the verse's ending will be their verdict: evil is what they *made*. Al-Ghazālī, in the *Iḥyāʾ*, wrote that the corruption of the common people follows from the corruption of rulers, and the corruption of rulers from the corruption of scholars — placing the scholars at the root of the whole chain. This verse is the Qur'anic ground of his observation.

**The Verse for Everyone Who Knows**

Nor is the verse confined to formal scholars. Every believer who knows a wrong to be wrong, and has the standing to say so — a parent, an elder, a teacher, a manager, a friend — falls under the verse's *law-lā* in proportion to his knowledge and his standing. The ḥadīth of the hand, the tongue, and the heart gives the gradations; but it does not permit the fourth option, which is to know, to be able, and to do nothing. That option is what the rabbis of Madinah chose, and it is what the Qur'an calls, with its most deliberate verb, an evil *manufacture*.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:64

> **The Jews say, "God's Hand is shackled." Shackled are their hands, and they are cursed for what they say. Nay, but His two Hands are outstretched, He bestows as He wills. Surely that which has been sent down unto thee from thy Lord will increase many of them in rebellion and disbelief. And We have cast enmity and hatred among them till the Day of Resurrection. As often as they ignite a flame for war, God extinguishes it. They endeavor to work corruption upon the earth. And God loves not the workers of corruption.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Example of the "Sinful Speech"**

Verse 63 rebuked the rabbis for not forbidding "their sinful speech." Verse 64 gives the most grievous example of that speech: *wa-qālati al-yahūdu yadu Allāhi maghlūlah* — "And the Jews say, 'God's hand is shackled.'" The verse then answers the blasphemy, describes its consequences, and widens into a statement about the fate of those who persist in it. It is one of the longest verses in the passage and among the most theologically significant, for it contains the Qur'an's affirmation of God's "two outstretched hands" — a phrase that has occupied theologians for fourteen centuries.

**"God's Hand Is Shackled": What Was Meant**

*Ghull* is a shackle or fetter binding the hand to the neck; the Qur'an uses the image for the helplessness of the damned (13:5; 34:33; 40:71). But the source identifies the sense here as the other use of the image: *miserliness*. In 17:29 God says to the Prophet ﷺ, "Do not make your hand shackled to your neck, nor extend it to its utmost" — that is, be neither miserly nor prodigal. To say "God's hand is shackled" is to say that God is stingy, that He withholds His bounty. The source records al-Ṭabarī's gloss: the speakers were claiming that God withholds His provision and bounty, at least from them.

The source presents al-Rāzī's careful discussion of why such a thing would be said. Al-Rāzī acknowledges that the Jews do not hold, as doctrine, that God is miserly or limited; they know His might and power. He proposes therefore that the statement was made not in earnest but in ridicule. When the Qur'an asked, "Who will lend God a goodly loan?" (2:245; 5:12; 57:11), some Jews affected to take it literally — God is in need of a loan! His hand must be shackled! — to make the Qur'anic call to charity seem absurd. Or, seeing the poverty of the early Muslim community in Madinah, they said mockingly that the hand of "Muhammad's God" was shackled, since He did not seem to enrich His followers. The source also records the reading of al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī that, when the Jews' own fortunes declined with the rise of Islam, they said it of themselves: God has closed His hand to us. And it notes the connection to their claim that God would punish them in the Fire only for a numbered few days (2:80; 3:24) — another assertion that placed a limit on God.

The report most often cited for the occasion names a Jew of Madinah, Finḥāṣ ibn ʿĀzūrāʾ, who said it — the same man reported to have said, "God is poor and we are rich" (3:181), when the Prophet ﷺ invited him to lend God a goodly loan. Whether earnest or mocking, the statement was blasphemy: to attribute miserliness to the One whose generosity is boundless.

**"Shackled Are Their Hands, and They Are Cursed for What They Say"**

*Ghullat aydīhim wa-luʿinū bi-mā qālū* — "shackled are their hands, and they are cursed for what they said." The source identifies the Qur'an's reflexive principle: the wrong one attributes to God or intends for others returns upon oneself, as in 2:9, "they would deceive God and the believers, but they deceive none but themselves." The Jews said God's hand was shackled; it is their hands that are shackled — from good, from generosity, from the ability to act, and, as many commentators noted, literally in the Hereafter, where the shackled hand is the image of the damned. The source records al-Ṭabarī's alternative reading of *ghullat* as an imprecation: "May their hands be shackled!" — from all good things. The miserliness that the Jews of Madinah were themselves known for — the withholding of what they owed the poor, the taking of interest, the refusal to spend in God's cause — was the real shackled hand; they projected onto God their own vice.

*Wa-luʿinū bi-mā qālū*: the curse, as the source notes following al-Ṭabarī, is exile from God's mercy — and it is incurred *bi-mā qālū*, by what they *said*. This is the "sinful speech" of verse 63 in its most extreme form, and its consequence.

**"Nay, His Two Hands Are Outstretched; He Bestows as He Wills"**

*Bal yadāhu mabsūṭatāni yunfiqu kayfa yashāʾ* — "Rather, His two hands are outstretched; He spends however He wills." The refutation is direct and abundant. Against the singular "hand ... shackled," the Qur'an sets the dual "two hands ... outstretched." *Mabsūṭ*, spread, open, extended — the open hand of the giver. The source connects this to the divine Name *al-Bāsiṭ*, "the Open-Handed, the Expander," and to the many verses in which God "expands and straitens provision for whom He wills" (13:26; 17:30; 28:82; 29:62; 30:37; 34:36, 39; 39:52; 42:12). God is not miserly; He gives without limit — but *kayfa yashāʾ*, however He wills. The last phrase answers the mockers' inference: that the Muslims' poverty proved God's stinginess. God's generosity is not measured by whether a given people is rich at a given moment; He expands and straitens in accordance with a wisdom the mockers did not see. The poverty of Madinah in the early years was not evidence of a closed hand but a stage in a plan that would, within a decade, place the wealth of Arabia and then of empires in the believers' hands.

**The Theology of God's "Hands"**

The source presents the debate this phrase occasioned, and the reader should understand its outlines. The Qur'an speaks of God's hand (48:10), His two hands (5:64; 38:75, where He created Adam "with My two hands"), and His hands in the plural (36:71). The commentators divided.

One approach, which the source records al-Ṭabarī as documenting, took all references to God's hand as metaphors — for His blessings, as here, or for His power and strength, as in 38:45, where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are "possessors of hands" (*ūlū al-aydī*), meaning possessors of strength. This was the approach of the Muʿtazilah and, in varying degrees, of the later Ashʿarī and Māturīdī theologians, who interpreted (*taʾwīl*) such expressions to avoid any suggestion of bodily form.

The other approach, which became the position of the early scholars (*salaf*) and was systematized by Ibn Taymiyyah and his school, holds that the expressions must be affirmed as God affirmed them — God has two hands, as He says — while denying any resemblance to created hands and refusing to specify their modality: "without asking how" (*bi-lā kayf*). Mālik's famous statement about God's "settling on the Throne" was applied to all such attributes: "The settling is known; its modality is unknown; belief in it is obligatory; and asking about it is innovation." On this view, to say "God has two hands" is simply to repeat what God said of Himself, in the manner that befits His majesty, "There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing" (42:11). The source notes that some scholars held that references to God's hand must be understood literally while rejecting anthropomorphism — this is that position.

The source also records a subsidiary debate: some (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī) proposed that the dual "two hands" simply signifies abundance — the utmost of generosity — as an Arab would say a man gives "with both hands." Al-Ṭabarī rejected this, arguing that the dual always denotes two specific things. Those who read "hand" as blessing proposed that the two hands are two kinds of blessing: this world and the next, outward and inward, or the granting of benefit and the prevention of harm (al-Rāzī).

What all positions share is the affirmation the verse is actually making: that God is boundlessly generous, that nothing constrains His giving, and that those who say otherwise have slandered Him. The believer may hold either theological approach in good conscience; he may not hold that God's hand is shackled.

**"What Has Been Sent Down to You Will Increase Many of Them in Rebellion and Disbelief"**

*Wa-la-yazīdanna kathīran minhum mā unzila ilayka min rabbika ṭughyānan wa-kufrā* — "and what has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief." The source identifies the paradox: revelation, sent to guide, increases some in error (3:19; 5:68; 8:2; 9:124; 17:41, 60, 82; 35:42; 71:6; 74:31). The Qur'an says of itself: "We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers, but it increases the wrongdoers only in loss" (17:82). The source explains through the Qur'an's name *al-Furqān*, the Criterion (2:53, 185; 3:4; 21:48; 25:1): part of revelation's function is to separate — to reveal who will accept and who will refuse. The same light that guides one who wants to see blinds one who has shut his eyes. The Qur'an's image for the refusers is unforgettable: "What is the matter with them that they turn away from the Reminder, as if they were frightened asses fleeing from a lion?" (74:49–51). Each new revelation confronted the obstinate with a new demand, and each refusal deepened the obstinacy. The verse says *kathīran minhum*, many — again, not all.

**"And We Have Cast Enmity and Hatred Among Them Until the Day of Resurrection"**

*Wa-alqaynā baynahumu al-ʿadāwata wa-l-baghḍāʾa ilā yawmi al-qiyāmah* — the same sentence the sūrah used of the Christians in verse 14, now applied to the Jews. The source records the readings: enmity among the Jews themselves, or among the People of the Book in general, or — al-Ṭabarī's suggestion — between the Jews and the Christians. Internal division is presented as a consequence of rejecting God's guidance: the community that will not be united by the truth is divided by everything else. The commentary on verse 14 made the point that this is a law, not an ethnic destiny, and applies to any community, including the Muslim one, that abandons what it was given.

**"Whenever They Kindle a Fire for War, God Extinguishes It"**

*Kullamā awqadū nāran li-l-ḥarbi aṭfaʾahā Allāh* — "whenever they light a fire for war, God puts it out." The source records al-Ṭabarī's reading — their repeated and unsuccessful hostility toward the Prophet's ﷺ mission: the plots, the alliances with the Makkans, the Trench, Khaybar, each ending in failure — and the broader reading that sees a pattern of military defeats from the Assyrian and Babylonian conquests onward (17:5). The image is of a fire that will not stay lit: kindled, extinguished, kindled again, extinguished again. The verse promises the believers that the schemes against them will fail, and it describes the schemers' futility — an energy endlessly spent on fires that God puts out.

**"They Strive to Work Corruption on the Earth, and God Loves Not the Corrupters"**

*Wa-yasʿawna fī al-arḍi fasādan wa-Allāhu lā yuḥibbu al-mufsidīn* — "and they strive in the earth for corruption, and God does not love the corrupters." The verse closes with the term the sūrah used in verses 32–33: *fasād fī al-arḍ*, corruption in the earth — the destruction of the order God established. Kindling wars, lying about God, taking bribes to twist the law, mocking the call to prayer: all of this is *fasād*. And the verse's ending, "God does not love the corrupters," is the negative image of verse 54's "a people whom He loves." The passage has moved from the beloved to the unloved, and the criterion is the same throughout: what one does with what God has given.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse warns against attributing to God any limitation born of one's own experience. The believer who is poor should not conclude that God's hand is closed to him; the believer whose prayers seem unanswered should not conclude that God withholds. God's two hands are outstretched, and He spends as He wills — which means that what is withheld now is held back by wisdom, not by stinginess, and what is given is given from an infinite store. The believer's own hands should imitate his Lord's: open, not shackled. And when he encounters mockery of God's generosity — in the cynicism of those who say religion asks for money because its God is poor, or in his own dark moments of suspecting that God is holding out on him — he should answer as the Qur'an answers: *bal*, "rather," "no" — His two hands are open.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:65

> **Had the People of the Book believed and been reverent, We would surely have absolved them of their evil deeds, and caused them to enter Gardens of bliss.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn from Condemnation to Invitation**

After the long indictment of verses 57–64 — the mockery, the concealed disbelief, the racing into sin, the silent scholars, the blasphemy of the shackled hand — verse 65 opens a door. *Wa-law anna ahla al-kitābi āmanū wa-ttaqaw la-kaffarnā ʿanhum sayyiʾātihim wa-la-adkhalnāhum jannāti al-naʿīm* — "And if only the People of the Book had believed and been God-fearing, We would surely have expiated their evil deeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss." The verse is a conditional, and its tone is that of a lament and an offer at once: all of this could have been otherwise; and, implicitly, it still can be. The Qur'an never condemns without pointing to the way out, and the way out is stated here in two words: *āmanū wa-ttaqaw*, believe and be God-fearing.

The address returns to the inclusive term *ahl al-kitāb*, "the People of the Book," after the specific "the Jews" of verse 64. The invitation is to Jews and Christians together.

**"Had They Believed"**

The source addresses the question that the verse raises: believed in what? The People of the Book already believed in God and the Last Day; the Qur'an does not deny it. The source records the majority view: "believed" here means believed in the Qur'an and the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. It acknowledges that "believe" is sometimes used in the Qur'an for the general act of faith in God and the Last Day among Jews and Christians as well as Muslims (2:62; 5:69), but notes that "believer" in the Qur'an most commonly denotes those who believe in all the prophets and all the Books — which necessarily includes the final Prophet ﷺ and the final Book — and thus a member of the community of Islam (see 4:136 and its commentary). The commentary on verse 59 observed that the Muslims believe in everything the People of the Book believe in *and more*; verse 65 asks the People of the Book to close the gap — to add to their faith in God and the earlier scriptures a faith in what came after, which their own scriptures foretold (7:157; 61:6).

The verse is thus the counterpart to verse 15's call: "O People of the Book, Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Book." Belief in this Messenger is what the sūrah asks. But the verse's second condition should not be forgotten.

**"And Been Reverent" — Wa-ttaqaw**

Faith alone is not the condition; the verse adds *taqwā*. The People of the Book's failure, as the preceding verses described it, was not merely a failure of belief but a failure of *conduct*: bribery, lying, mockery, the abandonment of God's law, the silence of the scholars. Belief in the Prophet ﷺ without a change in this conduct would not fulfill the verse's condition. *Taqwā* — the guarding of oneself against God's displeasure by obedience — is what the Jews of Madinah lacked even with respect to their own Torah, and what would be required of them under the Qur'an as well. The pairing of *īmān* and *taqwā* is the Qur'an's constant formula for the complete religious life: the right belief and the right fear. Neither substitutes for the other.

**"We Would Have Expiated Their Evil Deeds"**

*La-kaffarnā ʿanhum sayyiʾātihim* — "We would surely have covered over their evil deeds." The verb *kaffara*, from the root of *kufr* (covering), means to cover, to expiate, to blot out; a *kaffārah* is an expiation that covers a sin (the term will appear in verse 89 for the expiation of broken oaths, and appeared in verse 45 for the expiation earned by forgoing retribution). The promise is comprehensive: not some of their sins but *sayyiʾātihim*, their evil deeds — all of them. The Qur'an's teaching is that entry into Islam wipes out what preceded it: "Say to those who have disbelieved, if they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them" (8:38). The Prophet ﷺ said to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, who hesitated to pledge allegiance until his past sins were forgiven, "Do you not know that Islam demolishes what came before it?" (Muslim 121). Everything the passage has charged against the People of the Book — the concealment of the Torah, the bribery, the blasphemy — would be covered over by one sincere act of faith and reverence.

This is a staggering offer, and it is characteristic of the Qur'an's God, whose "two hands are outstretched" (v. 64). The verse that follows the refutation of God's supposed miserliness demonstrates His generosity in the most extravagant way: to those who slandered Him as stingy, He offers total forgiveness on the sole condition that they believe and fear Him.

**"And Admitted Them to Gardens of Bliss"**

*Wa-la-adkhalnāhum jannāti al-naʿīm* — "and We would surely have admitted them to the Gardens of Delight." The second promise follows the first: after the covering of sins, the entry into Paradise. *Jannāt al-naʿīm* — the Gardens of *naʿīm*, of bliss, ease, and delight — is one of the Qur'an's names for Paradise (10:9; 22:56; 31:8; 37:43; 56:12; 68:34). The double promise — forgiveness and Paradise — is the same the Qur'an makes to all who believe and do righteous deeds; the People of the Book are offered exactly what the Muslims are offered, on exactly the same terms.

**The Parallel Verses**

The source directs the reader to 2:103 and 7:96 for the same message. In 2:103, after the account of the Israelites' pursuit of sorcery: "And if they had believed and been God-fearing, a reward from God would have been better, if they only knew." In 7:96, after the account of the destroyed towns: "And if the people of the towns had believed and been God-fearing, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth." The formula *law āmanū wa-ttaqaw* — "had they believed and been God-fearing" — is the Qur'an's recurring statement of the path not taken, and of the door that remains open. Verse 66 will complete the thought in the terms of 7:96: worldly blessings from above and below, alongside the spiritual blessings of this verse.

**The Verse's Tenderness**

The verse should be read for its tone as well as its content. It comes after a sustained and severe indictment, and it is neither triumphant nor dismissive. It is regretful: *law anna*, "if only." The God who has just described their curse, their shackled hands, their kindled and extinguished fires, now says, in effect: none of this had to be. The Qur'an's severity toward the People of the Book in this passage is the severity of one who wants them saved and is grieved by their refusal — the same grief the Prophet ﷺ felt, which verse 41 addressed. The verse forbids the Muslim reader to take satisfaction in the condemnation of others; the proper response to another's error is the wish that he had believed, and the hope that he yet will.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The Muslim reading this verse should take three things from it. First, that the offer it makes is the offer he himself has accepted — and he should be grateful, not proud, that he stands inside the door the verse holds open. Second, that the conditions are two, not one: he has believed; has he been *reverent*? The People of the Book of this passage had scripture and profession and failed at *taqwā*; the Muslim who has scripture and profession and neglects *taqwā* is not safe merely because his profession is correct. And third, that the verse's tenderness toward the People of the Book should shape his own attitude toward them: not contempt, but the hope that they, too, will believe and be reverent, and enter the Gardens of Bliss.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:66

> **Had they observed the Torah and the Gospel and that which was sent down unto them from their Lord, they would surely have received nourishment from above them and from beneath their feet. There is a moderate community among them; but as for many of them, evil is that which they do!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Conditional**

Verse 65 promised spiritual reward — forgiveness and Paradise — had the People of the Book believed and been reverent. Verse 66 adds the worldly counterpart: *wa-law annahum aqāmū al-Tawrāta wa-l-Injīla wa-mā unzila ilayhim min rabbihim la-akalū min fawqihim wa-min taḥti arjulihim* — "And if only they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet." The verse is one of the most generous in the sūrah toward the earlier scriptures, and one of the most carefully qualified. It names three things to be upheld, promises a specific blessing, and ends by distinguishing a "moderate community" from the erring many.

**"Had They Upheld the Torah and the Gospel"**

The verb is *aqāmū*, "they established, upheld, made stand" — the same verb the Qur'an uses for prayer (*aqāma al-ṣalāh*). To *uphold* a scripture is more than to possess or recite it; it is to make it stand in one's life, to act on it, to keep it upright. The source places this verse among the several in the sūrah (vv. 44, 47, 68) that stress the importance of Jews and Christians following their own scriptures, and that indicate those scriptures remain a source of spiritual nourishment. The verse's logic is that the People of the Book had *not* upheld their own Books — they had covered the verse of stoning, abandoned equal retribution, taken bribes, and let their scholars fall silent — and that had they done so, blessing would have followed.

The source records two readings of what "upholding" requires. Al-Rāzī gives both: in the limited sense, it means upholding the covenant with God established in those scriptures in a general way — which would not preclude, and would indeed require, following the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, since the Torah and Gospel foretold him (7:157; 61:6); in the fuller sense, it means continuing to observe the rituals and laws prescribed in those scriptures, consistent with verse 48's statement that God appointed a law and a way for each community. Both readings agree that the scriptures were to be honored in practice, not merely in name.

**"And What Was Sent Down to Them from Their Lord"**

The third item is *mā unzila ilayhim min rabbihim*, "what was sent down to them from their Lord." The source records that most early commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) understood this as the Qur'an — sent down "to them" in the sense that its message is addressed to all humanity, including the People of the Book — while some proposed the other prophetic books of the Hebrew scriptures beyond the Torah narrowly defined, such as the book of Daniel (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī). On the majority reading, the verse's three items form a complete program: the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an — all three to be upheld, which is what a Jew or Christian who accepted the Prophet ﷺ would do. Al-Ṭabarī, as the source notes, drew the practical rule: the People of the Book should follow those teachings of the Torah and Gospel that the Qur'an endorses or at least does not declare false. This is the same principle as the Qur'an's role as *muhaymin*, guardian, in verse 48.

The three-fold naming also settles a question the passage has raised. The People of the Book had asked (v. 59) why the Muslims believe in "what was sent down before" — that is, in the earlier scriptures — as well as in the Qur'an. Verse 66 shows that this comprehensive faith is precisely what God asks of the People of the Book too: uphold *all* that was sent down.

**"They Would Have Eaten from Above Them and from Beneath Their Feet"**

The promised blessing is stated in a vivid image: *la-akalū min fawqihim wa-min taḥti arjulihim*, "they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet." The source records the majority reading (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī): an image of worldly prosperity — rain from the sky above, crops from the earth below. This matches 7:96, "We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth," and the source notes two connections within the passage: the verse is the worldly counterpart to verse 65's spiritual promise (al-Rāzī), and it is a direct answer to verse 64's slander that God's hand is shackled — the hand that was called miserly would have poured provision from above and below (al-Ṭabarī). The Qur'an's teaching that righteousness brings material blessing and corruption brings material want is stated repeatedly: Noah's people are promised that if they seek forgiveness, God "will send the sky upon you in abundance and aid you with wealth and sons" (71:10–12); the town that was ungrateful is "made to taste the garment of hunger and fear" (16:112).

The source offers a further reading, and it is a beautiful one. If the image is taken as spiritual allegory, "nourishment from beneath their feet" is the teaching of their own scriptures — the seed already planted in their ground — and "nourishment from above them" is the Qur'an, the rain sent down from heaven. Rain nourishes human beings directly, and it also nourishes the crops; so the Qur'an nourishes the People of the Book directly, and it also brings new life to their own scriptures — restoring the rulings they had abandoned, as the Prophet ﷺ restored the stoning verse, and clarifying what they had concealed (v. 15). On this reading, the verse describes exactly what the Qur'an claims to be for the People of the Book: not a replacement that renders their scriptures dead, but a rain that makes their scriptures live.

**"Among Them Is a Moderate Community"**

*Minhum ummatun muqtaṣidah* — "among them is a moderate community." The verse, having spoken of the People of the Book as a whole, pauses to make a distinction. *Muqtaṣid* is from q-ṣ-d, to aim, to go straight toward a goal; *iqtiṣād* is the middle course, moderation, balance between extremes (the modern word for "economy" comes from the same root). The source notes the difference from 2:143's description of the Muslim community as *ummatan wasaṭan*, "a middle community," and the Qur'an's consistent association of moderation with what is good (15:19; 17:29; 68:28).

Who is this moderate community? The source records the interpretations. Al-Ṭabarī: those People of the Book who take the middle course concerning Jesus — neither exaggerating his station by calling him the son of God, as many Christians do, nor denying his prophethood, as the Jews do — but regarding him as God's prophet, as the Qur'an presents him. This reading connects the verse to the sūrah's central doctrinal concern (vv. 17, 72–75, 116–117). Al-Rāzī connects it to 3:75, the People of the Book who are trustworthy in their dealings, and to 35:32's *muqtaṣid*, the one who takes a middle course between wronging himself and being foremost in good. Some (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī) took the moderate community to be those People of the Book who embraced Islam — ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and the Christians of Najāshī's court — though the source observes that this sits oddly with the description "moderate" and would not distinguish them from other converts.
