Whatever the precise reference, the verse affirms that among the People of the Book there exists a body of upright, balanced people, and it refuses to let the reader forget them.

**"But Many of Them — Evil Is What They Do"**

*Wa-kathīrun minhum sāʾa mā yaʿmalūn* — "but many of them, evil is what they do." The verse ends by restoring the proportion: the moderate community exists, but *many* — not all — act evilly. The Qur'an's arithmetic throughout this passage has been consistent: "many of them" (vv. 62, 64, 66), "most of you" (v. 59), "except a few" (v. 13). The verse thus holds two truths that are often held separately: that there is genuine goodness among the People of the Book, and that there was widespread corruption among those the Prophet ﷺ confronted. To emphasize either at the expense of the other is to misread the Qur'an. Verses 82–85 will describe the goodness at length; verses 57–64 have described the corruption. Verse 66 holds them in a single sentence.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches the believer three things. First, that scriptures are for *upholding* — *aqāmū* — not for possessing; the Muslim who has the Qur'an on his shelf and not in his conduct is in the position the verse laments. Second, that God's blessings, spiritual and material, follow faithfulness to what He has sent down — and that when a community finds itself in want, spiritual or material, it should look first to whether it has upheld its Book. And third, that fairness toward other communities requires the Qur'an's own proportion: acknowledging the moderate community wherever it exists, and naming the evil of the many without extending it to the all. The believer who can hold "among them is a moderate community" and "many of them do evil" in the same breath, as this verse does, has learned the Qur'an's way of speaking about others.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:67

> **O Messenger! Convey that which has been sent down unto thee from thy Lord, and if thou dost not, thou wilt not have conveyed His message. And God will protect thee from mankind. Surely God guides not disbelieving people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second "O Messenger"**

This is the second of the two verses in the Qur'an that address the Prophet ﷺ as *yā ayyuhā al-rasūl*, "O Messenger" — the first was verse 41 of this sūrah. The commentary there noted that the title emphasizes the office of conveying, and that both verses concern the burden of that office. Verse 41 consoled the Messenger for the rejection of his message; verse 67 commands him to deliver all of it regardless. *Balligh mā unzila ilayka min rabbik* — "Convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord." The verb *ballagha*, to cause to reach, to deliver, is the technical term for the prophetic function: *tablīgh*, the delivery of the message. The Prophet ﷺ would ask his Companions at the Farewell Pilgrimage, "Have I conveyed?" (*hal ballaghtu?*), and they would answer, "Yes," and he would say, "O God, bear witness" (al-Bukhārī 1741; Muslim 1218).

**"And If You Do Not, You Will Not Have Conveyed His Message"**

*Wa-in lam tafʿal fa-mā ballaghta risālatah* — "and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message." The sentence has a striking form: it appears almost tautological — if you do not convey, you have not conveyed — and the commentators drew from its form its meaning. The source records al-Zamakhsharī's reading: if the Prophet ﷺ were to conceal even the smallest part of what had been revealed, it would be as if he had not conveyed the message at all, as if he had concealed all of it. The message is a unity; its integrity depends on its completeness; a messenger who delivers nine-tenths and withholds one-tenth has not delivered *the message* but a different thing of his own selection. The verse thus makes the prophetic office an all-or-nothing trust. The source also records a report in which the Prophet ﷺ said that God had revealed to him that if he did not convey all that came to him, God would punish him.

**ʿĀʾishah's Use of the Verse**

The source records that ʿĀʾishah cited this verse as a sufficient refutation of anyone who claimed that the Prophet ﷺ had concealed any part of the revelation (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭabrisī). Her words, in al-Bukhārī and Muslim: "Whoever tells you that Muhammad concealed anything of what was sent down to him has lied, for God says, 'O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, you have not conveyed His message'" (al-Bukhārī 4612; Muslim 177). The argument is decisive within the tradition: the Qur'an itself commands complete delivery under the severest sanction, and the Prophet ﷺ obeyed the Qur'an; therefore nothing was withheld. What the community received is the whole of what was sent. This principle underlies the Muslim confidence in the Qur'an's completeness and closes the door to claims that any hidden revelation was reserved for an elect.

**"And God Will Protect You from Mankind"**

*Wa-Allāhu yaʿṣimuka mina al-nās* — "and God will protect you from the people." The verb *ʿaṣama* means to hold back, to guard, to preserve — the root of *ʿiṣmah*, the divine protection of the prophets. The promise is specific: God will protect the Messenger from the people while he conveys. The source observes that the assurance implies the Prophet ﷺ at times feared people's reaction to the message — not for his own life merely, but for the mission, which his death would have ended.

The source records several reports about the verse's effect. In Makkah, when the Muslims were in constant danger from Quraysh, the Prophet ﷺ was guarded by others (or his uncle Abū Ṭālib arranged guards). In Madinah too, in the early years, he was guarded at night. When this verse was revealed, he put his head out of his tent and said to his guards, "O people, go away, for God has protected me" (al-Tirmidhī 3046; al-Ḥākim). Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī record that fear left him completely; Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī, that he discontinued the guards. The source also records the report of the Bedouin who found the Prophet ﷺ alone and unarmed, raised his sword, and asked, "Who can protect you from me?" — to which the Prophet ﷺ answered, "God," and the man's hand trembled and the sword fell (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī; the story was also connected to verse 11, where it was recounted). And there is the report that after this verse, when the Prophet ﷺ was asked why he no longer took precautions, he said that God had guaranteed his protection.

The protection was fulfilled. The Prophet ﷺ faced assassination attempts, poisoning at Khaybar, the rock of the Naḍīr, the swords of Uḥud, and the plots of the hypocrites; he was wounded but never killed, and he died in his bed, his message complete. The verse's promise is bounded by its purpose — protection *until the message is conveyed* — and the Prophet ﷺ himself understood it so: after the Farewell Pilgrimage, when the message was complete, he began to speak of his departure.

**What Was the Prophet Hesitant to Convey?**

The verse's placement raises a question the source addresses: what was the Prophet ﷺ hesitant to deliver, such that this command was needed? Several answers are recorded, and they need not exclude one another.

The first (al-Ṭabarī) notes the verse's position in the middle of a long and critical discussion of the People of the Book, and suggests that the message the Prophet ﷺ hesitated over was this criticism itself — delivered to communities with whom the Muslims had treaties and among whom he had friends and neighbors. The next verse (68), which commands him to say to the People of the Book, "You stand on nothing until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to you," is read by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī as the specific message in question. A messenger hesitates to deliver hard words to people he does not wish to alienate; the verse tells him he must.

The second answer places the verse in the context of the Farewell Pilgrimage, at the end of the Prophet's ﷺ life. The source records that Ibn Kathīr connects it to the announcements made in the Farewell Sermon — the abolition of blood-feuds and usury, the rights of women, the sanctity of life and property, the completion of the religion — which the Prophet ﷺ delivered days before Ghadīr Khumm. This fits the sūrah's general dating as late Madinan, and the source judges the Farewell Pilgrimage context most plausible.

The third answer, which the source records from Twelver Shiite commentaries (al-ʿAyyāshī, al-Qummī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Ṭūsī) and from a small number of Sunni sources (al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ālūsī), connects the verse specifically to Ghadīr Khumm. On this reading, the Prophet ﷺ had received the instruction to declare ʿAlī's standing — "for whomever I am his *mawlā*, ʿAlī is his *mawlā*" — and hesitated, fearing the reaction of some Companions; this verse was revealed, commanding delivery and promising protection; and he then made the declaration before the assembled pilgrims at the pool of Khumm. The commentary on verse 3 has already treated the Ghadīr event and the ḥadīth (al-Tirmidhī 3713, among many transmissions), and the two ways the word *mawlā* is understood: by the Shīʿah, as designating ʿAlī the Prophet's ﷺ successor in authority; by the Sunnis, as "ally, beloved, one to whom loyalty is owed" — an affirmation of ʿAlī's honor, occasioned by complaints that had arisen against him after the Yemen expedition, but not a designation of succession.

A Muslim of either tradition can affirm what is certain: that the Prophet ﷺ declared at Ghadīr that whoever held him as *mawlā* should hold ʿAlī as *mawlā*; that he conveyed everything he was commanded to convey; and that the love of ʿAlī and of the Prophet's ﷺ household is part of the faith. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever loves ʿAlī loves me, and whoever loves me loves God" — and "None loves you but a believer, and none hates you but a hypocrite" (Muslim 78, from ʿAlī himself). The dispute concerns what the declaration implied for succession, and that dispute is not resolved by this verse, which commands delivery without specifying the content.

**"Surely God Guides Not Disbelieving People"**

*Inna Allāha lā yahdī al-qawma al-kāfirīn* — "indeed God does not guide the disbelieving people." The verse ends by returning the Messenger to his proper task and its limit. He must convey; he will be protected; and the result is God's. Those who disbelieve after the complete message has reached them will not be guided — not because the message failed but because they refused it. The Messenger is not responsible for the outcome, only for the delivery. This is the consistent Qur'anic distribution of responsibility: "Upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance" (24:54; 29:18).

**The Verse as the Charter of Tablīgh**

The verse is the charter of every believer who carries the message after the Prophet ﷺ. Its three principles are permanent. First, *completeness*: the message must be conveyed whole; the one who softens, omits, or edits it to suit his audience has not conveyed *it* but something of his own. The scholar who hides a ruling, the preacher who skips a hard verse, the parent who teaches the pleasant parts and omits the demanding ones — each falls under the verse's "you have not conveyed." Second, *courage*: the conveyer will fear people, and the answer to fear is not silence but trust in God's protection — which, for those after the Prophet ﷺ, is not a guarantee of physical safety but a guarantee that no one can harm them except by God's leave, and that what befalls them for His sake is reward. Third, *detachment from results*: the conveyer delivers; God guides. The one who measures his success by conversions will be tempted to compromise the message to increase them; the one who measures it by fidelity will deliver it whole and leave the rest to God.

The Prophet ﷺ fulfilled the verse to the letter. On the day of ʿArafah he asked, "Have I conveyed?" and a hundred thousand voices answered, "Yes." And he pointed to the sky and said, "O God, bear witness." That witness is the verse's fulfillment, and the standard for every messenger of the message after him.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:68

> **Say, "O People of the Book! You stand on naught till you observe the Torah and the Gospel, and that which has been sent down unto you from your Lord." Surely that which has been sent down unto thee from thy Lord will increase many of them in rebellion and disbelief. So grieve not for disbelieving people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Message That Had to Be Conveyed**

Verse 67 commanded the Messenger to convey what was sent down, whatever the reaction. Verse 68 gives the content: *qul yā ahla al-kitābi lastum ʿalā shayʾin ḥattā tuqīmū al-Tawrāta wa-l-Injīla wa-mā unzila ilaykum min rabbikum* — "Say: O People of the Book! You stand on nothing until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to you from your Lord." The source records the reading of al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī that this was the message the Prophet ﷺ had hesitated to convey — the hard word to the People of the Book that, for all their possession of scripture, they stood on nothing so long as they did not uphold it. The word is hard, and it is spoken by command.

**"You Stand on Nothing"**

*Lastum ʿalā shayʾ* — "you are not upon anything." The phrase is devastating in its simplicity. The People of the Book possessed the Torah and the Gospel; they had rabbis and priests, synagogues and churches, centuries of learning, and the pride of election. And the verse says: without upholding what you were given, all of this is *nothing* — you have no ground beneath you. To be "upon" something (*ʿalā shayʾ*) is to stand on a foundation; the Qur'an uses the phrase for those who are "upon guidance from their Lord" (2:5) and "upon a clear proof" (11:17). The People of the Book, the verse says, had no such footing, because their relationship to their scriptures had become one of possession without practice. The commentary on verse 66 explained the verb *aqāma*, to uphold, to make stand: a scripture that is not made to stand in one's life gives one nothing to stand on.

The verse is the mirror image of verse 66. There the Qur'an said: had they upheld the Torah, the Gospel, and what was sent down to them, they would have eaten from above and below. Here: until they uphold these, they stand on nothing. Verse 66 stated the blessing conditionally; verse 68 states the deficiency actually. The People of the Book had chosen the second condition.

**The Three Things to Be Upheld**

The three items are identical to those in verse 66: the Torah, the Gospel, and "what was sent down to you from your Lord." The source notes that most commentators understood the third as the Qur'anic message brought by the Prophet ﷺ. The verse thus makes the same demand as verse 66: comprehensive fidelity to God's revelation — the earlier Books and the final one — as the only foundation. It is not enough to hold the Torah and reject the Gospel, or to hold both and reject the Qur'an; the ground beneath one's feet is the *whole* of what God sent down, and the Qur'an is its completion and guardian (v. 48). The Prophet ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no one of this community, Jew or Christian, hears of me and then dies without believing in what I was sent with, but that he is among the people of the Fire" (Muslim 153).

Yet the verse's demand should also be read in its plainest sense. The People of the Book are told to uphold *the Torah and the Gospel*. The Qur'an does not say, "Abandon your Books and take ours"; it says, "Uphold your Books — and ours." The repeated insistence on the Torah and Gospel (vv. 43, 44, 47, 66, 68) shows that the Qur'an regards them as God's revelations, still binding on their communities, and that their faithful observance would lead — since they foretell the final Prophet ﷺ — to the acceptance of the Qur'an. A Jew who truly upheld the Torah, or a Christian who truly upheld the Gospel, would find in them the description of the one who was to come (7:157). The verse's demand is thus not to abandon but to *fulfill*.

**"What Has Been Sent Down to You Will Increase Many of Them in Rebellion and Disbelief"**

*Wa-la-yazīdanna kathīran minhum mā unzila ilayka min rabbika ṭughyānan wa-kufrā* — the sentence repeats verse 64 word for word. The source notes the echo. Its recurrence here has a particular force: the Prophet ﷺ has just been commanded to convey the hard message, and he is now told what its effect will be on many of them — not repentance but increased rebellion. The command to convey does not depend on the message's reception. The Prophet ﷺ is to deliver it knowing that it will harden many; the hardening is not a reason to withhold it, because the message is truth and the response to truth is the hearer's responsibility. The commentary on verse 64 explained the principle of the *Furqān*: revelation separates, and part of its function is to reveal the hearts of those who refuse it. *Ṭughyān* — overflowing the bounds, rebellion — is the same word the Qur'an uses of Pharaoh (20:24) and of the flood-waters (69:11): a transgression that swells beyond limits. The word for the sea's overflow is used for the soul's.

**"So Grieve Not for Disbelieving People"**

*Fa-lā taʾsa ʿalā al-qawmi al-kāfirīn* — "so do not grieve over the disbelieving people." The verse ends with a consolation. The verb *asiya*, to grieve, to sorrow, is the same verb Moses was told in verse 26: "so do not grieve over the iniquitous people," after the Israelites' refusal to enter the Holy Land. The source notes the parallel, and 27:70, "Do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress at what they plot." The Prophet ﷺ is placed in Moses' position: he has delivered God's command to a people who refuse it, and he is told, as Moses was told, that their refusal is not his burden. The sūrah began its account of Moses with grief over the Israelites' refusal and returns to grief now, over their descendants' refusal of the final Prophet ﷺ; and the divine answer is the same both times.

The consolation is not indifference. The Prophet ﷺ grieved deeply over the disbelief of those he called — the Qur'an says he almost "destroyed himself with grief" over them (18:6; 26:3). The command is not to cease caring but to cease being *consumed*: to deliver the message with full concern for its hearers and then to leave their choice to them and to God, without the grief that would paralyze him or tempt him to compromise. The messenger who cannot bear rejection will eventually soften the message to avoid it; the messenger who can bear it will deliver it whole. Verse 67 commanded wholeness; verse 68 supplies the emotional condition that makes wholeness possible.

**The Verse as a Standard for Every Community**

The verse's principle applies to every possessor of scripture, and the Muslim reader should apply it first to himself. "You stand on nothing until you uphold what was sent down to you." The Muslim who possesses the Qur'an, recites it, honors it, and does not uphold it — does not make it stand in his conduct, his dealings, his family, his community — stands on nothing, by the same measure the verse applied to the People of the Book. The Prophet ﷺ foretold that his community would inherit the ways of those before it, and the way of possessing without upholding is the very one this verse condemns. The verse is not a Muslim's boast against others; it is a standard that measures everyone who has been given a Book.

**The Verse for the One Who Conveys**

For the believer who carries the message, verse 68 completes the instruction of verse 67 with three practical truths. The message must sometimes be hard — "you stand on nothing" is not a diplomatic phrase, and the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say it. The message will sometimes harden its hearers — and this is not a failure of the message or the messenger. And the messenger must not grieve himself to death over the refusers — he must care, convey, and then commit them to God. The one who has learned these three has learned to carry the message the way the Prophet ﷺ carried it: whole, courageous, and free.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:69

> **Truly those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians—whosoever believes in God and the Last Day and works righteousness, no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verse of Hope in the Midst of Rebuke**

After verses 57–68 — the most sustained criticism of the People of the Book in the sūrah — verse 69 opens onto the widest horizon of hope. *Inna alladhīna āmanū wa-lladhīna hādū wa-l-ṣābiʾūna wa-l-naṣārā man āmana bi-Allāhi wa-l-yawmi al-ākhiri wa-ʿamila ṣāliḥan fa-lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn* — "Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians — whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteousness — no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve." The source notes that the verse is nearly identical to 2:62 and directs the reader to the commentary there; it also compares 22:17, where God will judge among believers, Jews, Sabeans, Christians, Magians, and idolaters on the Day of Resurrection. But the source rightly observes that the verse's placement here — within a sūrah largely devoted to the People of the Book, and directly after a long critical passage — gives it a particular weight: it is one of the most important Qur'anic affirmations that salvation is possible for those outside the Muslim community.

**The Four Groups Named**

*Alladhīna āmanū* — "those who believe": the Muslims, the followers of the final Prophet ﷺ. *Alladhīna hādū* — "those who are Jews." *Al-ṣābiʾūn* — "the Sabeans": a community mentioned three times in the Qur'an (2:62; 5:69; 22:17), whose identity the commentators debated — a monotheistic sect between Judaism and Christianity, or the star-venerating community of Ḥarrān, or the Mandaeans of Iraq who followed John the Baptist; the name is from ṣ-b-ʾ, to change one's religion, and the Makkans called the Prophet ﷺ himself a *ṣābiʾ* for leaving their religion. *Al-naṣārā* — "the Christians." The four groups span the religious landscape of the Qur'an's first hearers. And the verse's grammar, which the classical grammarians discussed at length (the nominative *al-ṣābiʾūna* where one expects the accusative), was explained by some as a device to emphasize the Sabeans — as if to say, even they, the least clearly defined of the groups, are included if they meet the condition.

**The Condition: Faith and Righteous Deeds**

The verse does not say that the four groups are saved as such. It says: *man āmana bi-Allāhi wa-l-yawmi al-ākhiri wa-ʿamila ṣāliḥan*, "whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteousness." The condition is the same for all four — including the Muslims, who are named first and are not exempted from it. Being called a Muslim, a Jew, a Sabean, or a Christian does not, by itself, secure anything; what secures salvation is *faith* — in God and the Last Day — and *righteous action*. The verse thus cuts through the confessional labels to the substance beneath them, and it does so in both directions: it denies that any label saves, and it affirms that the substance saves under any label.

The source draws the further inference: because the condition is stated in general terms, "whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteousness," it opens the possibility of salvation beyond the four named groups — to anyone, anywhere, who meets it. Together with verse 5 (intermarriage with the People of the Book) and verse 48 (God's appointment of a law and a way for each community), the source reads this verse as arguing for the continued validity of Judaism, Christianity, and by extension other divinely revealed religions, despite the Qur'an's strong criticism of specific doctrines and practices within them.

**How the Tradition Understood the Verse**

The classical commentators, aware of the verse's breadth, read it in the light of the whole Qur'an, and the reader should know the main positions. Some, following a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, held that the verse was abrogated or qualified by 3:85: "Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers" — so that after the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, the Jew, Sabean, or Christian who meets the verse's condition is the one who accepts him, since faith in God and the Last Day, sincerely held, leads to acceptance of God's final Messenger when his message reaches one. On this reading the verse describes the righteous of each community *before* the Prophet's ﷺ coming, and those who accept him after. Others, including al-Ṭabarī, read the verse as affirming that salvation depends on true faith and righteous deeds rather than on communal membership, while holding that true faith, once the Prophet ﷺ has been sent and his message truly reached a person, includes belief in him — as verse 65 said, "had the People of the Book believed and been God-fearing." Others held that the verse's promise extends to those of the earlier communities to whom the Prophet's ﷺ message has *not* reached in its truth — a position with support in the ḥadīth that those who did not hear the call will be tested on the Day of Resurrection, and in al-Ghazālī's argument in *Fayṣal al-Tafriqah* that God's mercy embraces those who never truly heard of the Prophet ﷺ or heard of him only in distorted form.

What the readings share is this: the verse's condition — faith in God and the Last Day and righteous action — is the real criterion, and God alone knows who meets it. The Qur'an says of the People of the Book in 3:113–115: "They are not all alike; among the People of the Book is an upright community reciting God's verses in the night hours and prostrating; they believe in God and the Last Day, enjoin right and forbid wrong, and hasten to good deeds; and those are among the righteous. And whatever good they do, they will never be denied it." The believer holds the Qur'an's universal call and its universal mercy together, and leaves the judgment of individuals to the Judge.

**"No Fear Shall Be upon Them, nor Shall They Grieve"**

*Fa-lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn* — the Qur'an's most frequent formula of salvation, occurring over a dozen times. The source records al-Rāzī's analysis: *khawf*, fear, concerns the future — dread of what is to come after resurrection; *ḥuzn*, grief, concerns the past — sorrow over what one has lost or left behind, including the earthly life. Those who are saved are freed from both. They have nothing to dread ahead, for what awaits them is better than anything behind; and they have nothing to mourn behind, for nothing they left compares with what they have found. The source draws the beautiful conclusion: freed from fear of the future and grief over the past, the saved live in an "eternal now" — the perpetual present of the paradisal state. This is what Paradise means psychologically: the end of the two temporal anxieties that shadow every human life on earth.

The formula also has a present application. The Qur'an promises the same freedom to the believer *in this life*, to the degree that his faith is real: "Indeed, the friends of God — no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve; those who believed and were God-fearing" (10:62–63). The one who truly believes in God and the Last Day has already, in part, been released from dread and regret: he knows Who governs the future and Who compensates the past.

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah**

The verse's placement is deliberate. The sūrah has criticized the People of the Book severely for specific failures: covering the Torah's rulings, taking bribes, mocking the call to prayer, slandering God, the silence of their scholars. Verse 69 ensures that the criticism is not mistaken for a blanket condemnation. The failures were real; but the door of salvation stands open to any Jew, Sabean, or Christian — and any human being — who believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds. The Qur'an's criticism is directed at conduct, and its mercy is directed at persons; verse 69 makes the distinction unmistakable.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The Muslim reading this verse should take from it, first, humility: he is named in the verse's first group, but he is not exempted from its condition; his label saves him no more than anyone else's saves them. Second, hope for others: he should wish salvation for every human being and should never presume to close a door that God has left open. Third, clarity about the criterion: faith in God and the Last Day, and righteous action — these are what count, and they are what he should cultivate in himself and hope for in others. And fourth, the promise itself, which he should hold as his own: that if he believes and does right, he will one day stand where no fear can reach him and no grief can follow.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:70

> **We indeed made a covenant with the Children of Israel, and sent messengers unto them. Whensoever a messenger brought them what their souls did not desire, some they would deny and some they would slay.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Return to the Covenant**

After the universal promise of verse 69, the sūrah returns to the specific history of the Children of Israel, and it does so by returning to the sūrah's opening theme: the covenant. *La-qad akhadhnā mīthāqa banī Isrāʾīla wa-arsalnā ilayhim rusulā* — "We indeed took the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We sent messengers to them." The sūrah began with "fulfill your pacts" (v. 1); verse 7 recalled God's covenant with the believers; verse 12 recounted the covenant with Israel and the twelve chiefs; verse 13 described its breaking; verse 14 the Christians' covenant and its neglect. Verse 70 resumes the thread. The source lists the Qur'an's references to the Israelite covenant (2:63, 83–84, 93; 4:154; 5:12; 7:134) and to the covenant with the People of the Book generally (3:187; 5:14; 7:169).

**Covenant and Messengers Together**

The verse pairs two divine acts: taking the covenant and sending messengers. The pairing is not incidental. A covenant is not a single moment but a relationship that must be renewed, and the messengers were the means of renewal: each prophet sent to Israel — after Moses, a long line through Joshua, Samuel, David, Solomon, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah, John, and Jesus — came to recall the people to the covenant they had made. The verb *arsalnā*, "We sent," with the emphatic plural *rusul*, stresses the abundance: not one reminder but many. The Qur'an says elsewhere: "We gave Moses the Book and followed him with messengers" (2:87). The Israelites were not left to forget; they were reminded again and again, and the verse's charge is that they refused the reminders.

The pairing also explains why the covenant's breaking was so grave. A people who broke a covenant made once and never recalled might plead forgetfulness. A people who broke it repeatedly, in the face of repeated messengers, could plead nothing. God's justice is that He does not punish before sending a messenger (17:15); His mercy is that He sends many; and the guilt of those who reject the many is proportionately greater.

**"Whenever a Messenger Brought Them What Their Souls Did Not Desire"**

*Kullamā jāʾahum rasūlun bi-mā lā tahwā anfusuhum* — "whenever a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire." The word *kullamā*, "whenever, each time," marks a pattern: this was not an occasional lapse but a repeated response. And the verse names the cause of the rejection with precision: the messenger brought *mā lā tahwā anfusuhum*, what their souls did not *desire*. The verb *hawiya*, from which comes *hawā*, caprice, desire, is the Qur'an's word for the inclination of the lower self. The messengers were rejected not because their message was unclear, or unproven, or unreasonable, but because it opposed *desire*. They came with commands that restrained appetite, demands that cost comfort, truths that wounded pride, and the soul that preferred its desires rejected them.

This is the Qur'an's diagnosis of the rejection of prophets in every age. Prophets are not rejected on the merits; they are rejected because they demand what people do not want to give. The Qur'an says of the Makkans: "If the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted" (23:71). And of the Israelites specifically, in the verse's parallel: "Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you were arrogant? Some you denied, and some you killed" (2:87). The mechanism is arrogance — *istakbartum* — the refusal to be told.

The verse's phrasing is a mirror for every reader. The test of one's relationship to revelation is not how one responds to the parts one already likes; it is how one responds to *mā lā tahwā anfusuhum* — the commands that oppose one's desires. The person who accepts the Qur'an's comforts and rejects its demands has the Israelite response in miniature.

**"Some They Denied, and Some They Slew"**

*Farīqan kadhdhabū wa-farīqan yaqtulūn* — "a group they denied, and a group they slay." The two verbs describe the two degrees of rejection. *Kadhdhabū*, they called liars — the rejection of the message by denying the messenger's truthfulness. *Yaqtulūn*, they kill — the rejection of the messenger by destroying him. The source lists the Qur'an's references to the Israelites' rejection and killing of prophets (2:87, 91; 3:183–184; 4:155), and the biblical record confirms the pattern: Zechariah son of Jehoiada stoned in the temple court, Isaiah sawn asunder by tradition, Jeremiah imprisoned and, by tradition, stoned in Egypt, John the Baptist beheaded, and Jesus, whom they sought to kill — though the Qur'an says they did not, "but it was made to appear so to them" (4:157). Jesus himself said: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee" (Matthew 23:37).

The change of tense is noticed by the grammarians: *kadhdhabū*, perfect, "they denied"; *yaqtulūn*, imperfect, "they kill" — the present tense conveying the vividness of the act, as if it were happening before the reader's eyes, and its continuation as a disposition. The killing of the prophets is not a closed chapter but a standing tendency of the soul that prefers its desires: it will silence the messenger by any means, and the ultimate means is death.

**The Verse in Its Context**

The verse's placement after verse 69 balances the balance. Verse 69 opened the door of salvation to all who believe and do right; verse 70 returns to the historical record of a people who, as a community, repeatedly refused. The two are not in tension. Verse 69 concerns individuals and their faith; verse 70 concerns a communal pattern of rejecting prophets. The individual Jew who believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds is embraced by verse 69; the collective history of denying and killing prophets is indicted by verse 70. And the indictment leads directly to verse 71, which will describe the spiritual blindness that the pattern produced — and to verses 72–77, which will turn from the Jews to the Christians and their exaggeration of Jesus, the last of the messengers to Israel.

**The Lesson for the Community of Muhammad ﷺ**

The Prophet ﷺ foretold that his community would follow the ways of those before it, and the specific way of verse 70 — rejecting what the soul does not desire — is among the most easily inherited. The Muslim community does not kill its prophets, for the last Prophet ﷺ has come; but it can "kill" his inheritors. The scholars who convey what the soul does not desire — the unwelcome ruling, the uncomfortable truth, the rebuke of the powerful — have been denied, imprisoned, exiled, and killed in Muslim history, and the pattern is the one this verse describes. The believer who reads it should ask how he receives the messenger of an unwelcome truth in his own life: with the openness of the covenant, or with the denial — and, in his heart, the wish to silence — of the soul that prefers its desires.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks one question of everyone who reads it: what do you do when God's message opposes your desire? The Children of Israel had a covenant and many messengers, and each time the message crossed their desires they denied it or killed its bearer. The reader has the Qur'an, and it will cross his desires — that is what revelation does. The covenant is fulfilled by those who, at that crossing, choose the message over the desire. It is broken by those who, at that crossing, do what the verse describes. There is no third response.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:71

> **And they supposed that there would be no trial, and so became blind and deaf. Then God relented unto them; then [again] many of them became blind and deaf. And God sees whatsoever they do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Root of the Rejection**

Verse 70 described the pattern: whenever a messenger brought what their souls did not desire, they denied or killed him. Verse 71 identifies what lay beneath the pattern: *wa-ḥasibū allā takūna fitnatun* — "and they supposed that there would be no trial." The word *fitnah* here carries its sense of trial and testing — the smelting that separates metal from dross — and, by extension, the consequence or punishment that follows failure of the test. They supposed that nothing would come of it: that they could deny and kill God's messengers and suffer no trial, no reckoning, no consequence. This supposition was the root of the whole history. A people who believe they will not be tested behave as though they will not be tested.

The supposition had a source, which the Qur'an names elsewhere: the belief in a special immunity. "The Fire will not touch us except for a numbered few days" (2:80; 3:24). "We are the children of God and His beloved ones" (5:18). The election of Israel, which was real — "I favored you above the worlds" (2:47) — had been converted in their minds from a responsibility into a guarantee: God had chosen them, therefore God would not punish them, therefore they could do as they pleased. The verse's *ḥasibū*, "they supposed," marks it as a false calculation. The favored are tested more, not less: "We will surely test you" (2:155) is addressed to the community God loves most.

**"And So Became Blind and Deaf"**

*Fa-ʿamū wa-ṣammū* — "so they became blind and deaf." The verse describes the consequence of the false supposition as a loss of the spiritual senses. The source traces the Qur'an's use of blindness and deafness for insensitivity to the prophetic message (2:171; 6:104; 7:64; 10:43; 11:28; 13:19; 27:4, 66, 81; 30:53; 41:17, 44; 43:36–37, 40), and cites the key verse: "It is not the eyes that go blind, but the hearts within the breasts that go blind" (22:46). The blindness is of the heart; the deafness is of the heart. The Israelites who denied and killed prophets were not stupid or uninformed — they had the Torah and its scholars; they *could not see* what the prophets showed and *could not hear* what the prophets said, because the organ of seeing and hearing spiritual truth had been disabled.

The sequence matters: the supposition came first (*ḥasibū*), then the blindness (*fa-ʿamū*, with the *fāʾ* of consequence). The source raises the Qur'an's dual teaching on this point. On the one hand, a preexisting moral blindness can impede a person's ability to be moved by the message (2:6–7); on the other, it is willful mocking, rejection, and transgression that *produce* the blindness (2:14–18). The source resolves the apparent tension through the doctrine of *fiṭrah*: every human being is born with a pure primordial nature (30:30) and an innate awareness of God's lordship (7:172); blindness is therefore not original but *acquired* — the result of moral deformity brought about by sin and repeated transgression, or of a divine curse as punishment for sin (47:23: "Those are the ones God has cursed, so He deafened them and blinded their eyes"). The Israelites' blindness was the fruit of their supposition and their sins; they blinded themselves, and God sealed what they had chosen.

**"Then God Turned to Them"**

*Thumma tāba Allāhu ʿalayhim* — "then God relented toward them." Here the verse turns, and the turn is mercy. Despite the blindness and deafness, despite the denial and killing of messengers, God *turned* to them — *tāba ʿalayhim*, the phrase used for God's acceptance of repentance and His restoration of favor. The commentators understood this as the periods of restoration in Israelite history: the return from the Babylonian captivity, the rebuilding of the Temple, the sending of new prophets, the renewal of the covenant. God did not abandon them to the blindness they had chosen. He opened their eyes again, and for a time they saw.

The clause is essential to the verse's theology. The Qur'an's account of Israel is not a story of a people rejected once and forever; it is a story of repeated rejection met by repeated mercy. God's turning toward them shows that the blindness was not permanent or irreversible — it was a condition that God could and did lift when they turned back. This is the same truth stated in verse 54: God's turning precedes the servant's turning; "He turned to them so that they might turn" (9:118).

**"Then Many of Them Became Blind and Deaf Again"**

*Thumma ʿamū wa-ṣammū kathīrun minhum* — "then many of them became blind and deaf." The cycle repeats. Having been restored, *many* — the Qur'an's careful quantifier again, not all — relapsed into the same blindness. The verse's structure is a compressed history: false supposition → blindness → divine mercy → renewed blindness. And the final relapse, in the context of this sūrah, is the rejection of the last two messengers to Israel: Jesus, whom they sought to kill, and Muhammad ﷺ, whom the Jews of Madinah, in the very passage the sūrah has just concluded, mocked, resisted, and plotted against.

The word *kathīr*, "many," placed after the verbs, is emphatic by its position and merciful by its content: even in the final relapse, not all were blind. The "moderate community" of verse 66 and the upright of 3:113 remained. And the door of verse 69 remained open.

**"And God Sees What They Do"**

*Wa-Allāhu baṣīrun bi-mā yaʿmalūn* — "and God is Seeing of what they do." The verse ends with an exquisite irony. They became *blind* — and God is *Seeing*. They lost the capacity to see the truth; God never loses sight of them. The Name *al-Baṣīr*, the All-Seeing, set against the double *ʿamū*, "they became blind," is the verse's judgment in a single word: the blindness they chose does not blind Him to what they do. The supposition that there would be no trial — that no one was watching, that no reckoning would come — is answered by the last phrase: He sees. Everything they did in their blindness was done before an eye that does not close.

**The Cycle as a Universal Pattern**

The verse's compressed history is not only Israel's. Every community — and every soul — is capable of the cycle: the assumption of immunity, the resulting blindness, God's merciful restoration, and the relapse. The Muslim community has passed through it more than once in its history, and the individual believer passes through it in small: the period of confidence that becomes complacency, the dullness of heart that follows, the moment of mercy that awakens him, and the drift back. The verse teaches what breaks the cycle: not supposing that there will be no *fitnah*. The believer who remembers that he will be tested — that God sees, that reckoning comes, that election is responsibility — keeps his eyes and ears open. The one who supposes himself safe closes them.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse's first word for the human error is *ḥasibū*, "they supposed." The believer should examine his suppositions. Does he suppose, in some corner of his heart, that his membership in the Muslim community, his lineage, his knowledge, or his past good deeds exempt him from trial? That supposition is the seed of blindness. And does he remember, when he finds himself dull to the Qur'an and deaf to reminder, that God turned to Israel in its blindness and can turn to him — that the blindness is not final if he turns? The verse holds both the warning and the hope, and it ends with the fact that makes both urgent: God sees what he does.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:72

> **They certainly disbelieve, those who say, "Truly God is the Messiah, son of Mary." But the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel! Worship God, my Lord and your Lord." Surely whosoever ascribes partners unto God, God has forbidden him the Garden, and his refuge shall be the Fire. And the wrongdoers shall have no helpers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn to Christian Doctrine**

Verses 70–71 concluded the sūrah's account of the Children of Israel's rejection of their messengers, ending with the last two — Jesus and Muhammad ﷺ. Verses 72–77 now turn to the opposite error: not the rejection of Jesus but his exaltation beyond what he was. The sūrah thus presents the two deviations from the truth about Jesus as a pair: the Jews who denied him, and the Christians who deified him; and it will describe the "moderate community" (v. 66) and the true religion as the middle between them. Verse 72 opens with the same words as verse 17: *la-qad kafara alladhīna qālū inna Allāha huwa al-Masīḥu ibnu Maryam* — "They have certainly disbelieved who say, 'God is the Messiah, son of Mary.'" The source directs the reader to verse 17 and to the other verses that refute Jesus' divinity directly or indirectly (3:59; 4:171–172; 5:75, 116–117; 9:31). The commentary on verse 17 treated the name *al-Masīḥ* and the doctrinal issues at length; this verse adds a new element — Jesus' own words.

**The Exact Claim Refuted**

The claim named is precise: *inna Allāha huwa al-Masīḥ*, "God is the Messiah" — with the emphatic pronoun *huwa*, "He is," making the identity complete. This is not merely "the Messiah is divine" but "God *is* the Messiah" — the full identification of God with Jesus. The source records the observation of al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī that this explicit formulation was characteristic of certain Christian sects in particular — they name the Jacobites, the Syrian Miaphysites, who rejected the doctrine of two natures in Christ and asserted a single, unified divine-human nature, which their opponents read as a collapse of the distinction between God and the man Jesus. Orthodox Chalcedonian Christianity, with its careful formula of two natures in one person, would not say "God is the Messiah" without qualification; but the Qur'an addresses the claim as it was made by those who made it, and the underlying issue — the ascription of divinity to Jesus — is common to all forms of Christian doctrine. Whatever the theological refinements, the Qur'an's position is that Jesus is a man and a messenger, and that to worship him is to worship a creature.

**"But the Messiah Said: Worship God, My Lord and Your Lord"**

*Wa-qāla al-Masīḥu yā banī Isrāʾīla uʿbudū Allāha rabbī wa-rabbakum* — "And the Messiah said, 'O Children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord.'" The verse's argument is to set the words of Jesus himself against the claim made about him. Jesus is quoted addressing his own people, the Children of Israel, and commanding them to worship *God* — not himself — and describing God as *my* Lord and *your* Lord. The source notes that this phrase occurs in Jesus' mouth in 3:51; 5:117; 19:36; 43:64, and explains its force: it asserts Jesus' full humanity and servanthood. The one who says "my Lord" has a Lord; the one who has a Lord is a servant; and a servant is not God. Jesus places himself in exactly the same relationship to God as his hearers: God is his Lord as He is theirs.

The source observes that the closest Gospel parallel is John 20:17, where the risen Jesus says to Mary Magdalene, "I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God." The structure is the same — my X and your X — and the second half, "my God and your God," is precisely the Qur'anic point: Jesus calls God *his God*. The source notes that the term "Father" is problematic from a Qur'anic perspective (see v. 18, where the claim to be God's children is rebuked), and that the Gospel saying is not in the context of a command to worship. But the Gospels record such commands elsewhere: "Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve" (Matthew 4:10; Luke 4:8), and Jesus' affirmation of the Shema: "Hear, O Israel; the Lord our God is one Lord" (Mark 12:29). The Qur'an's claim is that Jesus taught what these passages record — the worship of the one God — and that the deification of Jesus was a later development that Jesus himself will disavow (vv. 116–117).

**"Whoever Ascribes Partners to God, God Has Forbidden Him the Garden"**

*Innahu man yushrik bi-Allāhi fa-qad ḥarrama Allāhu ʿalayhi al-jannata wa-maʾwāhu al-nār* — "Indeed, whoever associates partners with God, God has forbidden him the Garden, and his refuge is the Fire." The verse continues Jesus' speech — many commentators read this sentence as still his words — and states the consequence of *shirk*, the association of anything with God in His divinity. The source notes that the criticism of Jesus' divinity here and in 9:31 is followed by the warning against *shirk*, leading al-Zamakhsharī and others to classify the claim that Jesus is God as a form of *shirk*, and to read the warning as directed at those who make it.

*Shirk* is, in Islamic teaching, the one sin that God does not forgive if a person dies upon it: "Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" (4:48, 116). The reason is not arbitrary. Every other sin is a failure within the relationship of servant to Lord; *shirk* is the destruction of the relationship itself — the giving of what belongs to God alone to something that is not God. The verse states its consequence with the strongest verb: *ḥarrama*, God has *forbidden* him the Garden — as one forbids a place to a trespasser. And *maʾwāhu al-nār* — "his refuge is the Fire": the one who sought refuge in a false god finds his only refuge in the Fire.

The Qur'an's teaching that *shirk* is unforgivable if one dies upon it does not close the door of repentance — verse 74 will open it explicitly: "Will they not turn to God in repentance and seek His forgiveness?" The sentence is against the one who *persists* in *shirk* to death, not the one who turns.

**"And the Wrongdoers Shall Have No Helpers"**

*Wa-mā li-l-ẓālimīna min anṣār* — "and the wrongdoers shall have no helpers." The verse ends with the term *ẓālimūn*, wrongdoers — and the Qur'an calls *shirk* "a tremendous wrong" (*ẓulm ʿaẓīm*, 31:13), because it places worship where it does not belong. The word *anṣār*, helpers, is pointed: it is the word from which *naṣārā*, Christians, may derive (see v. 14) — the "helpers" of Jesus. The verse's ending thus carries an implicit warning: those who called themselves the helpers of the Messiah, if they deified him, will find on that Day no helper — not even the Messiah, who will disavow their claim (v. 117). The intercession of Jesus, on which many hoped, is not available to those who worshipped him instead of God.

**The Balance of the Verse**

The verse must be read with the balance the Qur'an itself maintains. It condemns a specific claim — that God is the Messiah — and it describes the consequence of *shirk* for those who persist in it. It does not condemn Christians as such, and it does not pass judgment on every individual Christian; the sūrah's verse 69 and verses 82–85 forbid that reading. What it does is state, with total clarity, that Jesus was a servant of God who commanded the worship of God, and that to worship Jesus is to do what Jesus himself forbade. The Muslim holds this position not from hostility to Jesus — the sūrah has honored him and his Gospel (v. 46) — but from loyalty to what Jesus taught. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising the son of Mary; I am only His servant, so say, 'the servant of God and His messenger'" (al-Bukhārī 3445). The warning was directed at the Muslims, lest they do to Muhammad ﷺ what had been done to Jesus.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse's lesson is not confined to Christology. It is about the human tendency to exalt the beloved beyond his station — to make of a prophet, a saint, a scholar, a leader, or an ancestor something more than a servant of God. The Christians' deification of Jesus was the extreme case; the Prophet ﷺ warned that his community would be tempted toward the same. The believer's safeguard is Jesus' own words in this verse: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord." The greatest of God's servants is still a servant, and the relationship the greatest have to God is the relationship the least have: He is Lord of them both. Whoever remembers this cannot fall into *shirk*, however much he loves the beloved — and he loves rightly only when he loves them as servants of the One they served.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:73

> **They certainly disbelieve, those who say, "Truly God is the third of three," while there is no god save the one God. If they refrain not from what they say, a painful punishment will befall those among them who disbelieved.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Divinity of Jesus to the Trinity**

Verse 72 addressed the claim that God is the Messiah. Verse 73 addresses a distinct but related doctrine: *la-qad kafara alladhīna qālū inna Allāha thālithu thalāthah* — "They have certainly disbelieved who say, 'God is the third of three.'" The source explains the distinction: the previous verse criticized belief in the divinity of Jesus; this one criticizes the doctrine of the Trinity — or at least, the source is careful to say, an exaggerated form of that doctrine in which God is one of three separate entities to be worshipped. The phrase *thālithu thalāthah*, "third of three," means one of three, a member of a triad — as the Qur'an elsewhere says of the Companions of the Cave that some said "they were three, the fourth of them their dog" (18:22). To say that God is "the third of three" is to make Him one member of a set of three — to place Him alongside two others in a plurality of deities.

**"While There Is No God but One God"**

*Wa-mā min ilāhin illā ilāhun wāḥid* — "and there is no god except one God." The refutation is immediate and consists of the simple assertion of *tawḥīd*. The construction is emphatic: *mā min ilāhin*, "there is no god at all" (the *min* of comprehensive negation), *illā ilāhun wāḥid*, "except one God." Against the arithmetic of three, the Qur'an sets the arithmetic of one — and it does not argue the point at length, because *tawḥīd* is for the Qur'an the self-evident foundation of all religion, taught by every prophet including Jesus (v. 72: "worship God, my Lord and your Lord"), witnessed by the Torah's Shema, and confirmed by reason: "If there had been in them gods other than God, they would both have been ruined" (21:22).

**What Trinity Is Meant?**

The source presents the commentators' discussion with care, and the reader should follow it. Some commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī) understood the "three" of this verse to be God, Jesus, and Mary — three distinct deities — on the basis of verse 75, which stresses the humanity of both Jesus and his mother, and verse 116, where Jesus is asked whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods besides God. There is historical evidence for the veneration of Mary reaching quasi-divine proportions in some circles of the late antique East; the sect known as the Collyridians, described by Epiphanius in the fourth century, offered cakes to Mary as to a goddess, and popular devotion in Arabia and Syria may have gone further than the official doctrine.

The source is equally clear that the commentators were generally aware that the orthodox Christian doctrine of the Trinity comprises Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — not Mary — as three persons in one divinity (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī), and that some argued that only certain sects, such as the Jacobites and Nestorians, held a belief in three distinct deities (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī). Al-Rāzī, as the source records, understood the three persons of the orthodox doctrine to represent for Christians three aspects of God — His Essence, His Word (the Logos), and His Life (the Spirit) — and observed that this formulation bears some analogy to the Islamic doctrine of God's Essence and Attributes. But the analogy did not persuade him: he judged the doctrine clear error, because it hypostatizes the attributes into persons, each of whom is called God, and because it attaches one of them to a human being who was born, ate, and was crucified (in Christian belief). The Islamic doctrine holds that God's attributes — His Word, His Life, His Knowledge — are neither identical with His Essence nor other than it, but they are not *persons* and are not to be worshipped, and none of them became a man.

**The Qur'an's Objection Stated Precisely**

Whatever formulation of the Trinity is in view, the Qur'an's objection is the same and can be stated precisely. The Qur'an rejects any doctrine in which (1) a plurality is predicated of God's divinity, such that He is "one of three"; (2) a created being — Jesus, or Mary, or anyone — is included in that divinity; or (3) worship is directed to anyone other than the one God. The sophisticated formulations of Trinitarian theology were devised to avoid the charge of tritheism — to affirm one God in three persons, not three gods. The Qur'an's response, in 4:171, is to command: "Do not say 'three'; desist — it is better for you; God is only one God; exalted is He above having a son." The Qur'an judges that however the doctrine is refined, the affirmation of three "persons" each of whom is God, and the identification of one of them with a man, compromises the oneness that every prophet taught. Al-Rāzī's engagement shows that Muslim theologians understood the doctrine as its adherents stated it, and rejected it on its merits.

**"If They Do Not Desist from What They Say"**

*Wa-in lam yantahū ʿammā yaqūlūna* — "and if they do not desist from what they say." The source connects this to 4:171, where the People of the Book were told to "desist" (*intahū*) from saying "three." That verse commanded; this verse states the consequence of not obeying: *la-yamassanna alladhīna kafarū minhum ʿadhābun alīm*, "a painful punishment will surely touch those among them who disbelieved." The threat is real and severe. But its phrasing is exact, and the source draws out its significance.

**"Those Among Them Who Disbelieved"**

The punishment is threatened not for "them" but for *alladhīna kafarū minhum*, "those among them who disbelieved." The source records the debate. Some commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) held that the threat is for Christians in general, since the Qur'an identifies certain common Christian doctrines as disbelief, or at least for those who persist in the doctrine and do not repent as verse 74 urges (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī). But the source argues — and the text supports — that the partitive *minhum*, "among them," restricts the threat: it falls on those among the Christians who *disbelieve*, implying that not all do. And it notes that a reading which barred all Christians from Paradise would contradict verse 69 and 2:62 — which promise that whoever among the Christians believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds shall have no fear — and 3:113, and would be inconsistent with the description of Christian virtue in verses 82–85.

The verse's precision thus preserves two things. It preserves the gravity of the doctrine: to say "God is the third of three" is *kufr*, and persisting in it brings painful punishment. And it preserves the distinction among persons: not everyone who bears the name Christian is guilty of the *kufr* the verse names; some among them believe in the one God and do right, and the Qur'an's promises reach them. God alone knows which is which — who says "three" out of ignorance, inherited habit, or a sincere but mistaken attempt to honor God's Word, and who says it in willful rejection of the truth once known. The verse condemns the doctrine and threatens the disbelievers; it does not authorize the believer to pronounce on the eternal fate of any individual.

**The Structure of Verses 72–74**

The three verses form a unit. Verse 72: the divinity of Jesus — refuted by Jesus' own words. Verse 73: the Trinity — refuted by the assertion of *tawḥīd* — and the threat for those who persist. Verse 74: the call to repentance — "Will they not turn to God in repentance and seek His forgiveness?" The movement is from error, to consequence, to the open door. The Qur'an never states a threat without stating the way to escape it, and the way is always the same: *tawbah*, turning back to God. The Christian who hears verses 72–73 is not being told that he is lost; he is being told what he must leave, and that God is "Forgiving, Merciful" toward the one who leaves it.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The Muslim reading this verse should take from it, first, the absolute clarity of *tawḥīd*: God is one, not one of three, not one of any number, and nothing created shares in His divinity. Second, the seriousness with which the Qur'an treats doctrine about God: what one *says* about God — *ʿammā yaqūlūn*, "what they say" — is not a matter of indifference; false speech about God is *kufr*, and the verse threatens it. Third, the Qur'an's precision in condemning a doctrine while distinguishing among those who hold it. And fourth, the verse's implicit invitation, made explicit in the next: for every error about God, there is repentance; and the God who is one is also the God who forgives.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:74

> **Will they not turn to God in repentance and seek His forgiveness? And God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Door After the Threat**

Verses 72 and 73 stated the errors — that God is the Messiah, that God is the third of three — and threatened painful punishment for those who persist. Verse 74 follows immediately with a question that is an invitation: *a-fa-lā yatūbūna ilā Allāhi wa-yastaghfirūnahu wa-Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm* — "Will they not, then, turn to God in repentance and seek His forgiveness? And God is Forgiving, Merciful." The source states the verse's function simply: those who hold doctrines about Jesus' nature and the Trinity that contradict *tawḥīd* are urged to repent. The brevity of the verse is part of its force. After the long doctrinal statements, the Qur'an says only this: turn back; ask forgiveness; He forgives.

**The Rhetorical Form: A Question of Astonishment and Invitation**

The construction *a-fa-lā*, "will they not, then?", combines the interrogative, the *fāʾ* of consequence, and the negative. It expresses gentle astonishment — given what has just been said, given the punishment threatened and the forgiveness available, how can they *not* turn? — and it functions as an encouragement (*taḥḍīḍ*), urging the action it asks about. The Qur'an uses this form when the answer should be obvious and the action easy: "Will they not, then, reflect on the Qur'an?" (4:82; 47:24). The question assumes the hearer's good sense and appeals to it: the way out is open, the cost is nothing but the abandonment of an error, and the reward is the forgiveness of the Forgiving. What could hold anyone back?

**Tawbah and Istighfār: Two Movements**

The verse names two acts. *Yatūbūna ilā Allāh* — "they turn to God": *tawbah*, repentance, is from t-w-b, to return; it is the turning of the whole person away from the error and back toward God. *Yastaghfirūnahu* — "they seek His forgiveness": *istighfār*, from gh-f-r, to cover, to protect; it is the asking that the past be covered over. The two are distinct and complementary. *Tawbah* is the change of direction; *istighfār* is the request that the distance already traveled in the wrong direction be forgiven. One may seek forgiveness without truly turning — the lips ask while the heart remains where it was — and the Qur'an pairs the two here to make clear that both are required. The Prophet ﷺ described the conditions of true repentance as ceasing the sin, regretting it, and resolving not to return to it; where the sin involved wronging another, restoring the right. For an error of doctrine, *tawbah* means abandoning the false belief and affirming the true one — for the Christian addressed here, ceasing to say "three" and affirming that God is one and Jesus His servant and messenger.

**The Object: "To God"**

The turning is *ilā Allāh*, "to God" — and the specification is pointed in this context. The error being addressed was the direction of worship toward Jesus or toward a triad; the repentance is a turning of the face back toward the one God from whom it had been diverted. There is no intermediary in the verse: not the Church, not a priest, not Jesus himself as a mediator, but the direct turning of the creature to the Creator. This is the Qur'an's constant teaching: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of God's mercy; indeed, God forgives all sins; indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful" (39:53). The repentant soul goes to God directly, and God receives it directly.

**"And God Is Forgiving, Merciful"**

*Wa-Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm* — the verse's closing pair of Names is the guarantee of its invitation. *Ghafūr* is the intensive form: not merely one who forgives but one who forgives abundantly, repeatedly, completely — whose forgiveness covers the gravest sins. *Raḥīm* is the mercy that flows to the one who turns. The commentary on verse 34 noted the gradation the tradition observed between *ghafūr* and *raḥīm*: forgiveness removes the punishment; mercy adds the gift. The one who turns from *shirk* is not merely spared the Fire; he is welcomed into a mercy that the Qur'an describes as encompassing all things (7:156).

The placement of these Names after verses 72–73 is itself an argument. The error named in those verses — *shirk* — is the one sin the Qur'an says God does not forgive *if one dies upon it* (4:48). And yet the verse that follows says God is *Ghafūr*, all-forgiving. The reconciliation is in the verb of this verse: *yatūbūna*, "they turn." *Shirk* is unforgivable *unrepented*; repented, it is forgiven like any other sin — indeed, the Qur'an says that God converts the past evil of the one who repents into good (25:70), and the Prophet ﷺ said, "Islam demolishes what came before it" (Muslim 121). The greatest sin and the widest forgiveness meet in the single act of turning.

**The Verse as a Model of Divine Address**

The verse teaches how God speaks to those in error, and therefore how believers should. After a clear statement of the error and its consequence — with no softening of either — comes an immediate, tender, and hopeful appeal to turn. There is no gloating, no dwelling on the threat, no delight in the punishment. The threat is stated once; the invitation follows at once. The Qur'an's God is not eager to punish: "What would God do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?" (4:147). He states the truth because the truth must be stated, and then He asks — *asks*, in the form of a question — why they will not come back.

The Muslim who engages Christians, or anyone in error, should learn from the verse's proportion. The truth must be stated plainly; verses 72–73 do not equivocate. But the statement must be followed, as verse 74 follows, by the open hand. The one who states the error and stops has done half the Qur'an's work; the one who softens the error to avoid offense has done none of it. The Qur'an does both halves: it names the error without compromise, and it invites without reservation.

**The Verse Turned Toward the Reader**

Though addressed to Christians who hold the doctrines of verses 72–73, the verse's question is asked of every soul that has drifted from *tawḥīd* in any degree. Few Muslims say "God is the third of three"; many give to created things — wealth, status, the approval of others, their own desires — a devotion that belongs to God alone. The Qur'an calls this the hidden *shirk*, and the Prophet ﷺ feared it for his community more than the open kind: "The thing I fear most for you is the lesser *shirk*" — and when asked what it was, he said, "Showing off" (Aḥmad 23630). To all such drift the verse's question applies: *will you not turn to God and seek His forgiveness?* And the answer the verse supplies is the same for the Christian and the Muslim, the great sinner and the small: He is Forgiving, Merciful.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:75

> **The Messiah, son of Mary, was naught but a messenger—messengers have passed away before him. And his mother was truthful. Both of them ate food. Behold how We make the signs clear unto them; yet behold how they are perverted!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Positive Statement of Who Jesus Was**

Verses 72–73 stated what Jesus was *not* — not God, not one of three. Verse 75 states what he *was*: *mā al-Masīḥu ibnu Maryama illā rasūl* — "The Messiah, son of Mary, is nothing but a messenger." The construction *mā ... illā*, "nothing but," is restrictive: it confines Jesus' status to the category of *rasūl*, messenger, and excludes every higher category. The source notes that Jesus is described as a messenger throughout the Qur'an, and that 4:171 uses the same restrictive formula — "the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only a messenger of God" — while adding there that he was "His Word which He cast to Mary, and a Spirit from Him." These additional titles, which the Qur'an gives to no other prophet, mark Jesus' unique origin (created by God's word "Be," without a father, and animated by a spirit from God, as Adam was); but they do not raise him above the category of messenger, and 4:171 immediately adds: "So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say 'three.'"

**"Messengers Have Passed Away Before Him"**

*Qad khalat min qablihi al-rusul* — "messengers have passed away before him." The clause places Jesus in a series. He was not unprecedented in kind; he was one of many whom God sent, and, like them, he was a human being with a beginning and, as the Qur'an says of the others, an end in this world. The source makes the striking observation that an identical statement is made about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in 3:144: "Muhammad is nothing but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?" That verse was recited by Abū Bakr on the day of the Prophet's ﷺ death, when ʿUmar, in grief, refused to believe he had died; Abū Bakr said, "Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; and whoever worshipped God, God is Living and does not die," and recited 3:144, and the Companions said it was as if they had never heard the verse before (al-Bukhārī 3667–3668).

The parallel between 5:75 and 3:144 is deliberate and decisive. The Qur'an applies to Jesus the very same description it applies to Muhammad ﷺ: nothing but a messenger, one of a line, mortal like those before him. The Muslim who insists on Jesus' humanity is not diminishing Jesus; he is placing him where the Qur'an places its own Prophet ﷺ. And the Muslim who is tempted to exalt Muhammad ﷺ beyond servanthood is warned by the same formula that warns the Christians.

**"And His Mother Was Truthful" — Ṣiddīqah**

*Wa-ummuhu ṣiddīqah* — "and his mother was a *ṣiddīqah*." Mary is described with the feminine of *ṣiddīq*, a term of the highest honor. The source explains its range: the Qur'an uses *ṣiddīq* of prophets — Abraham (19:41) and Idrīs (19:56) — and of the highest rank of the saintly, who in 4:69 are placed immediately after the prophets: "those whom God has blessed among the prophets, the *ṣiddīqūn*, the martyrs, and the righteous." A *ṣiddīq* is one who is utterly truthful and who utterly affirms the truth — the intensive form conveying both constant truthfulness and complete confirmation. The source records two connections: al-Zamakhsharī links Mary's title to her affirmation of Jesus' prophethood, as Abū Bakr received the title *al-Ṣiddīq* for affirming the Prophet's ﷺ Night Journey when others doubted; al-Rāzī links it to 66:12, where Mary "confirmed (*ṣaddaqat*) the words of her Lord and His Books, and was among the devoutly obedient."

The title's placement in this verse does two things at once. It honors Mary in the highest terms the Qur'an gives to any non-prophet — and the Qur'an elsewhere says that God "chose her and purified her and chose her above the women of the worlds" (3:42), and the Prophet ﷺ named her among the four perfect women (al-Bukhārī 3411). And, in the same breath, it *limits* her: she was a *ṣiddīqah*, a truthful servant — not a goddess, not the mother of God in any sense that would make her divine. The verse answers the veneration of Mary that verse 73's commentary described, by giving her exactly her due: the highest human honor, and nothing more.

**"Both of Them Ate Food"**

*Kānā yaʾkulāni al-ṭaʿām* — "they both used to eat food." The argument is stated in the simplest possible terms. God does not eat; the one who eats is a creature with needs; Jesus and Mary ate; therefore they were creatures. The source explains the purpose: to affirm their full humanity and refute those who see them as divine. The argument's plainness is its strength. It requires no theology; it is an appeal to fact. Whoever eats has a body that hungers, digests, and excretes — the commentators did not shy from the last implication — and such a body is not God's. The Qur'an makes the same argument about all messengers: "We did not make them bodies that did not eat food, nor were they immortal" (21:8), and about Muhammad ﷺ: "This messenger eats food and walks in the markets" (25:7 — the objection of the Makkans, which the Qur'an accepts as a description).

The source acknowledges what a fair reading requires: Christian theology also holds Jesus to be "fully human" — the Chalcedonian formula is "truly God and truly man" — and the New Testament stresses his humanity in passages such as Luke 18:19 ("Why callest thou me good? none is good, save one, that is, God") and Philippians 2:6–8 (he "took upon him the form of a servant"). The Qur'an's argument is that the humanity the Christians affirm is *all* there was: the one who ate food was a man, and the divinity added to him is the exaggeration the next verses will name.

**"Behold How We Make the Signs Clear to Them; Then Behold How They Are Turned Away"**

*Unẓur kayfa nubayyinu lahumu al-āyāti thumma unẓur annā yuʾfakūn* — "Look how We make the signs clear to them; then look how they are deluded away." The verse ends with a double *unẓur*, "look," addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and to every reader. Look, first, at the clarity of the signs: the argument just given is as clear as an argument can be — messengers before him, a truthful mother, eating food. Look, second, at the response: *annā yuʾfakūn*, "how they are turned away" — the passive of *afaka*, to turn something from its proper course, to delude; *ifk* is a lie that turns the truth upside down. The passive form is significant: they *are turned*, as if by a force acting on them — the force of inherited belief, of institutional authority, of the desire to have a God who is also a man. The two "looks" measure the gap between the clarity of the truth and the perversity of its rejection, and they invite wonder at it.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse gives the believer the complete Qur'anic position on Jesus and Mary in a single sentence, and it should be memorized as such: a messenger, in a line of messengers; a mother who was a *ṣiddīqah*; two human beings who ate. Everything the Qur'an says about them elsewhere — the virgin birth, the miracles, the Word and Spirit, the raising to God, the return at the end of time — sits within this frame and does not break it. The verse also gives the believer a method: to argue for *tawḥīd* not with abstractions but with facts as plain as eating. And it gives him a warning in its last clause: clarity of signs does not guarantee acceptance; people *are turned away* from what is obvious, by forces the verse leaves unnamed but every honest person can identify in himself. The reader should look, as the verse commands, at both — and then look at his own heart, to see which of the two it resembles.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:76

> **Say, "Do you worship, apart from God, that which has no power to benefit or harm you, when it is God Who is the Hearing, the Knowing?"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Argument from Powerlessness**

After the factual argument of verse 75 — Jesus and Mary ate food — verse 76 adds the argument from power. *Qul a-taʿbudūna min dūni Allāhi mā lā yamliku lakum ḍarran wa-lā nafʿan* — "Say: Do you worship, besides God, what possesses for you neither harm nor benefit?" The source notes that the Qur'an poses this rhetorical question frequently, directly or through the prophets, as an argument against worshipping anything other than God (10:18, 106; 13:16; 20:88–89; 21:62–66; 22:12; 25:55; 26:71–73). Abraham asks his people whether their idols hear when they call, or benefit or harm them (26:72–73); Moses' people are asked whether the calf could answer them or possess harm or benefit for them (20:89); the Makkans are asked whether they worship, besides God, what neither harms nor benefits (10:18). The question is the Qur'an's standard test for any object of worship: *can it do anything for you?*

**Worship and Power**

The argument rests on a definition of worship. To worship (*ʿabada*) is to direct one's ultimate devotion, hope, and fear toward something — to serve it as the one who can grant what one needs and avert what one dreads. Worship therefore presupposes power in its object: one worships what one believes can benefit or harm. The verse's argument is that Jesus and Mary — for all their honor — *lā yamliku*, "do not possess," "do not control," any harm or benefit for those who worship them. The verb *malaka*, to own, to have in one's power, is precise: whatever benefit came through Jesus — his healing of the sick, his raising of the dead — came, as the Qur'an insists, "by God's leave" (3:49; 5:110); he did not *own* the power; he was its channel. And now, raised to God, he can neither answer prayers directed to him nor avert any harm from those who pray. The one who directs worship to him directs it to one who cannot, of himself, respond.

The Christian will object that he does not worship Jesus as a powerless man but as God incarnate, whose power is God's. The Qur'an's reply is verse 75: the one who ate food was a man; and a man, however honored, possesses nothing of himself — "Say: I do not possess for myself harm or benefit, except as God wills" (7:188; 10:49), which is the very thing God commanded Muhammad ﷺ to say of *himself*. If the final Prophet ﷺ possesses no harm or benefit of his own, neither did Jesus; and what possesses no harm or benefit is not to be worshipped.

**The Order: Harm Before Benefit**
