The verse names *ḍarr*, harm, before *nafʿ*, benefit — as does 10:106, 13:16, and 25:55 — though in some verses the order is reversed (10:18; 20:89). The commentators observed that when harm is mentioned first, it stresses the more urgent concern: people turn to false objects of worship above all out of fear — to be protected from harm — and the verse strips the false object of that primary function first. What cannot protect you cannot be worth your worship; and only then, what cannot benefit you cannot be worth it either.

**"When It Is God Who Is the Hearing, the Knowing"**

*Wa-Allāhu huwa al-samīʿu al-ʿalīm* — "and God — He is the Hearing, the Knowing." The verse closes by naming the One who *does* possess power, and it names Him with two attributes chosen for the context. *Al-Samīʿ*, the Hearing: God hears the prayer of every worshipper, wherever and whenever it is offered; the false object of worship does not hear, or hearing, cannot respond. *Al-ʿAlīm*, the Knowing: God knows the need before it is spoken and the worshipper's state before he knows it himself. The emphatic *huwa*, "He," makes the contrast complete: *He* is the one who hears and knows — not the Messiah, not his mother, not any created thing. The one who prays should pray to the One who hears; the one who needs should ask the One who knows.

The two Names also answer an implicit objection. Someone might say: we do not expect Jesus to act by his own power; we pray to him so that he may intercede with God. The Qur'an's answer is that God hears directly and knows directly; He needs no intermediary to inform Him of His servants' needs, and He has authorized no one to be prayed *to*. Intercession in the Qur'an is real but is granted by God's leave to whom He wills, on the Day of Judgment, for whom He is pleased (2:255; 21:28); it is never a reason to direct worship or prayer to the intercessor in this life. "And your Lord says: Call upon Me; I will respond to you" (40:60). The line is direct.

**The Verse in the Sequence**

Verses 72–77 form a compact argument, and verse 76 is its fourth step. Verse 72: the claim that God is the Messiah is disbelief, refuted by the Messiah's own command to worship God. Verse 73: the claim that God is one of three is disbelief, refuted by *tawḥīd*. Verse 74: turn to God, who forgives. Verse 75: the Messiah was a messenger, his mother a *ṣiddīqah*, both ate food. Verse 76: what you worship besides God has no power over you; God alone hears and knows. Verse 77 will conclude: do not exaggerate in your religion. The sequence moves from the statement of error, through consequence and invitation, to two rational arguments — from humanity and from powerlessness — and ends with the diagnosis of the error's cause: *ghuluww*, exaggeration.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse's question — do you worship what possesses neither harm nor benefit for you? — is a question the believer should ask of every object of his devotion. The Muslim does not worship Jesus; but he may give the devotion that belongs to God to things that possess no harm or benefit of themselves: to wealth, as though it could secure him; to people, as though their approval could save him or their disapproval destroy him; to his own plans, as though they controlled outcomes. The Prophet ﷺ taught Ibn ʿAbbās: "Know that if the whole nation gathered to benefit you with something, they could not benefit you except with what God has written for you; and if they gathered to harm you with something, they could not harm you except with what God has written against you" (al-Tirmidhī 2516). The one who has absorbed this teaching has absorbed verse 76: nothing besides God possesses harm or benefit; therefore nothing besides God deserves the heart's worship, and the heart that gives its worship to God alone is free of every other fear and every other hope. He hears; He knows; He is enough.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:77

> **Say, "O People of the Book! Do not exaggerate in your religion beyond the truth, and follow not the caprices of a people who went astray before, and led many astray, and strayed from the right way."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Diagnosis: Ghuluww**

The passage on Christian doctrine (vv. 72–77) closes with a command that names the root of the error: *qul yā ahla al-kitābi lā taghlū fī dīnikum ghayra al-ḥaqq* — "Say: O People of the Book! Do not exaggerate in your religion beyond the truth." The verb *ghalā* means to exceed the proper limit, to overflow — used of a pot boiling over and of a price rising too high; *ghuluww* is excess, extremism, exaggeration. The source notes that the same command occurs in 4:171, and that in both places it is addressed primarily to Christians in relation to the claims of divinity for Jesus. The Qur'an's diagnosis of the deification of Jesus is thus not that the Christians loved him too little but that they honored him *too much* — beyond the truth of what he was. Their error was an error of excess in devotion, and the Qur'an treats it as such.

**"In Your Religion" — The Location of the Excess**

The excess is *fī dīnikum*, "in your religion." This is a specific and penetrating observation. There is an excess in worldly matters — greed, ambition, indulgence — that religion is meant to restrain. But there is also an excess *within religion itself*: the tendency of the devout to go beyond what God revealed, to add to the truth in the name of honoring it, to make of the prophet more than a prophet and of the law more than the law. This excess is more dangerous than the worldly kind because it wears the dress of piety and is defended as devotion. The Christians who deified Jesus did so out of love for him; the *ghuluww* was an overflow of reverence. The Qur'an's warning is that reverence, uncontrolled by truth, becomes its opposite: the highest honor one can give a servant of God is to obey him, and Jesus commanded the worship of God alone (v. 72).

**"Beyond the Truth" — Ghayra al-Ḥaqq**

The qualification *ghayra al-ḥaqq*, "other than the truth," "beyond the truth," is the measure. It implies that there is a *right* degree of devotion — the truth — and that exaggeration is the passing beyond it. Jesus is to be honored as a messenger, God's Word and Spirit, born of a virgin, worker of miracles by God's leave, raised to God: this is the truth, and it is a very high honor. To go beyond it — to call him God, or God's son, or one of three — is *ghuluww*. The verse does not ask the Christians to honor Jesus less than the truth; it asks them to honor him *no more* than the truth. And the truth, as verse 75 stated, is that he was a messenger who ate food.

**"And Follow Not the Caprices of a People Who Went Astray Before"**

*Wa-lā tattabiʿū ahwāʾa qawmin qad ḍallū min qablu wa-aḍallū kathīran wa-ḍallū ʿan sawāʾi al-sabīl* — "and do not follow the caprices of a people who went astray before, and led many astray, and strayed from the even path." The verse traces the *ghuluww* to a source: it was not the Christians' own invention but the following of earlier people's *ahwāʾ*, their caprices and desires. The source records the identifications. Al-Ṭabarī: the Jews, who went astray before by rejecting Jesus entirely — so that the verse warns Christians against the *opposite* extreme, and the two errors, deficiency and excess, are both departures from the even path. Ibn Kathīr and al-Zamakhsharī: the early leaders and authorities of the Christian community who established the Christological and Trinitarian doctrines, and who, through those doctrines and later through their rejection of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, led many astray. Al-Qurṭubī: both Jews and Christians, urged to accept the truth about Jesus — a major prophet whose message and signs are to be believed — without exaggeration into divinity or sonship. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabrisī: a general warning against the various errors of their predecessors and religious leaders, as discussed throughout the section from verse 41.

The reading of Ibn Kathīr and al-Zamakhsharī fits the history most exactly. The doctrines of the Trinity and the two natures were not taught by Jesus but formulated over centuries by councils and theologians — at Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381), Ephesus (431), and Chalcedon (451) — often under imperial pressure and amid bitter division. The Christians of the Prophet's ﷺ time inherited these formulations as "the faith," but the Qur'an describes them as the *ahwāʾ* of people who came before — the products of human reasoning and desire, not of revelation. And the influence of pre-Christian religious ideas — divine sonship, dying and rising gods, triads of deities — on these formulations is a matter the Qur'an's phrasing seems to anticipate: the people "who went astray before" may include those whose ideas the early Christian theologians absorbed.

**The Triple Ḍalāl**

The verse describes the earlier people with three verbs from the root ḍ-l-l, to stray: *ḍallū*, they went astray; *aḍallū kathīran*, they led many astray; *ḍallū ʿan sawāʾi al-sabīl*, they strayed from the even path. The repetition is not redundant. The first *ḍallū* describes their own initial error. *Aḍallū kathīran* describes its propagation: the error of a leader becomes the error of a multitude, and the leader bears the sin of all who follow him — the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever calls to misguidance bears a sin like the sins of all who follow him, without their sins being diminished (Muslim 2674). The final *ḍallū ʿan sawāʾi al-sabīl* describes the result: a settled departure from the straight road, now institutionalized and inherited. The phrase *sawāʾ al-sabīl*, the even path, was used in verse 12 for what the Israelite covenant-breakers lost and in verse 60 for what the cursed had strayed from; the sūrah's repeated use of it marks the single standard from which all the deviations it describes — Jewish and Christian alike — are departures.

**Ghuluww as a Universal Danger**

The verse is addressed to the People of the Book, but the Prophet ﷺ applied its principle to his own community with the utmost seriousness. "Beware of *ghuluww* in religion," he said at the Pilgrimage, when handing pebbles for the stoning and specifying that they be small, "for those before you were destroyed only by *ghuluww* in religion" (al-Nasāʾī 3057; Ibn Mājah 3029). And he said: "Do not exaggerate in praising me as the Christians exaggerated in praising the son of Mary; I am only His servant, so say, 'the servant of God and His messenger'" (al-Bukhārī 3445). The warning was needed. Muslim history has seen *ghuluww* toward the Prophet ﷺ, toward ʿAlī and the Imams, toward Sufi masters, toward scholars and founders of schools — the raising of the honored beyond the truth, the attribution to them of knowledge of the unseen, of control over harm and benefit, of a status that shades toward the divine. Every such exaggeration is what this verse forbids, and every one has the same structure as the Christian one: love that overflows the bounds of truth and ends by dishonoring the beloved, who wanted only to be a servant of God.

The verse also names the mechanism by which *ghuluww* spreads: following the *ahwāʾ* of predecessors. Exaggeration is rarely invented fresh; it is inherited, defended as tradition, and reinforced by the authority of those who taught it. The Muslim who inherits an exaggeration from his teachers or his culture is in the position of the Christians of this verse: following the caprices of a people who went astray before. The remedy is the same the verse implies — return to *al-ḥaqq*, the truth as revealed, and measure every inherited devotion against it.

**The Verse as the Close of the Passage**

Verse 77 completes the movement that began at verse 72. The passage stated the errors, threatened their consequence, invited repentance, argued from humanity and powerlessness, and now diagnoses the cause and warns against its source. It is a complete treatment: doctrinal, rational, pastoral, and historical. Verses 78–81 will turn back to the Children of Israel, and the sūrah's handling of the two communities will then converge in verses 82–85, where the Christians who "do not exaggerate" — the monks and priests who weep at the truth — are praised as nearest in affection to the believers. The praise of verse 82 is the reward of heeding verse 77: those who kept their religion within the truth are the ones whose eyes overflow at recognizing it.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The believer should read this verse as a plumb line. Wherever his devotion — to the Prophet ﷺ, to the righteous, to his school or teacher or community — has risen beyond what God revealed, he is in *ghuluww*, and the Prophet ﷺ said that *ghuluww* destroyed those before him. The measure is *al-ḥaqq*, the truth: honor everything exactly as much as God honored it, and no more. And wherever he finds himself defending an inherited excess with the words "this is what we were taught," he should hear the verse's warning about following the caprices of those who went astray before. The straight road is *sawāʾ al-sabīl*, the even path — neither the deficiency that denies God's messengers nor the excess that deifies them — and the whole sūrah has been calling its readers to walk it.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:78

> **Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and Jesus son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Return to the Children of Israel**

After the address to the Christians in verses 72–77, the sūrah turns back to the Children of Israel: *luʿina alladhīna kafarū min banī Isrāʾīla ʿalā lisāni Dāwūda wa-ʿĪsā ibni Maryam* — "Cursed were those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel by the tongue of David and of Jesus son of Mary." The verse's opening qualification must be read with care: *alladhīna kafarū min banī Isrāʾīl*, "those who disbelieved *among* the Children of Israel" — the partitive *min* marking, as always in this sūrah, a portion and not the whole. The curse falls on the disbelievers among them, not on the people as such. The Qur'an's precision here is the same as in verse 73's "those among them who disbelieved" and verse 66's "a moderate community among them."

**The Meaning of "Cursed"**

The source records the majority reading of *laʿn*, cursing, here and throughout the Qur'an: exile from divine mercy — distance from God's favor and protection. The Arabic *laʿana* originally means to drive away, to banish; a *laʿīn* is one banished from his people. To be cursed by God is to be driven from the nearness that is the whole good of the creature. The curse is not an arbitrary malediction; it is the natural consequence of the conduct the verse's end will name — disobedience and transgression — pronounced by those authorized to pronounce it.

**"By the Tongue of David and of Jesus"**

The remarkable feature of the verse is that the curse is pronounced not directly by God but *ʿalā lisāni*, "by the tongue of," two prophets: David and Jesus. The source records the early commentators' explanation: the curse refers to statements about the disbelieving Israelites in the Psalms of David and the Gospel of Jesus — and some add that they were cursed also in the Torah of Moses and in the Qur'an of Muhammad ﷺ (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The prophets' tongues are the instrument of God's judgment; what they pronounced under inspiration was His verdict.

The choice of David and Jesus — rather than Moses, the giver of the Law — is significant. David and Jesus stand at two later points in Israel's history, and both were rejected by portions of their people: David faced rebellion and betrayal, and Jesus was rejected by the leaders who sought his death. Their curses mark the two great crises of Israel's fidelity after the Torah. The Psalms contain David's imprecations against the wicked among his people — "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous" (Psalm 69:28) — and the Gospels record Jesus' woes against the scribes and Pharisees: "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! ... Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?" (Matthew 23). The Qur'an's statement that the disbelievers were cursed "by the tongue of David and Jesus" corresponds to what the Jewish and Christian scriptures themselves record.

**The Specific Occasions**

The source records the more specific identifications that the commentators made. Many linked David's curse to the Sabbath-breakers of 7:163–166 — the people of Eilat (Aylah) on the coast, who devised the trick with fish-traps and were transformed into apes (al-Jalālayn, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī); David, on this account, was the prophet through whose tongue the curse was pronounced upon them. And they linked Jesus' curse to those who disbelieved after the miraculous table was sent down (vv. 112–115), some of whom, by report, were transformed into swine — connecting this verse to verse 60's "He made of them apes and swine" (al-Ṭabarī). On this reading the two curses correspond to the two transformations: David's to the apes, Jesus' to the swine. Whether or not the specific correspondences are accepted, the verse's structure presents two moments in Israel's history at which a prophet pronounced God's curse on the disbelievers among his people, and the two transformations of verse 60 as their signs.

**"That Was Because They Disobeyed and Used to Transgress"**

*Dhālika bi-mā ʿaṣaw wa-kānū yaʿtadūn* — "that was because they disobeyed and were transgressing." The verse gives the cause, and the cause is conduct. Two verbs: *ʿaṣaw*, they disobeyed — the refusal of a specific command; and *kānū yaʿtadūn*, they used to transgress — the habitual crossing of limits, the imperfect tense indicating a settled practice. The curse was not for their lineage, their identity, or their name; it was for what they did. This is the Qur'an's consistent moral logic: consequence follows conduct, and the divine curse is earned. The verse's *dhālika bi-mā*, "that was because of," is the causal formula the Qur'an uses whenever it wants to make clear that a judgment is deserved.

The word *iʿtidāʾ*, transgression, is from the same root as the *ʿudwān* the sūrah forbade in verse 2 ("do not help one another in sin and transgression") and described in verse 62 ("racing into sin and transgression"). The Sabbath-breakers transgressed the limit of the Sabbath; the deniers of the table transgressed the limit of the covenant they had made with Jesus when they asked for the sign. Transgression is the crossing of a boundary God set, and it is the specific thing that the sūrah — which opened with "God decrees what He wills" and the setting of boundaries — has been warning against throughout.

**The Verse and the Following Verse**

Verse 78 states that the disbelievers were cursed and why; verse 79 will specify the particular form of the disobedience: "they would not forbid one another the wrong they committed." The connection is important. The verse does not say they were cursed only for committing wrongs but — as the next verse will make explicit — for *failing to forbid* the wrongs among them. The curse pronounced by David and Jesus fell upon a community whose members tolerated one another's transgressions. The Prophet ﷺ made this connection in a famous ḥadīth, which the commentary on verse 79 will present in full: "The first deficiency that entered the Children of Israel was that a man would meet another and say, 'Fear God and leave what you are doing,' and the next day he would meet him again, and it would not prevent him from eating and drinking and sitting with him" — and he recited this verse (Abū Dāwūd 4336; al-Tirmidhī 3047).

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches that God's curse is a consequence, not a caprice; that it falls on disbelievers among a people, not on the people as such; that it may be pronounced through the tongues of His prophets, whose scriptures record it; and that its cause is disobedience and habitual transgression. The believer should take from it a warning about his own community: the Muslim community has the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ, as Israel had David and Jesus, and the Prophet's ﷺ tongue also pronounced curses — on the one who takes usury, on the one who alters land-boundaries, on the one who curses his parents, on the woman who tattoos and the woman who is tattooed (Muslim 1978, 2125). The condition that makes such curses fall is the same as in this verse: disobedience and habitual transgression, tolerated by a community that will not forbid it. The verse's warning to Israel is the Muslim's warning too.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:79

> **They would not forbid one another from the wrong they committed. Evil indeed is that which they used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Specific Sin Behind the Curse**

Verse 78 said the disbelievers among the Children of Israel were cursed "because they disobeyed and used to transgress." Verse 79 names the particular form of that transgression: *kānū lā yatanāhawna ʿan munkarin faʿalūh* — "they used not to forbid one another the wrong they did." The verb *yatanāhawna* is the sixth form of n-h-y, to forbid — the reciprocal form: *they did not forbid one another*. The wrong was not merely committed; it was committed *in community*, and no one in the community forbade it. The Qur'an locates the root of the curse not in the individual acts but in the collective silence that permitted them.

**Munkar: The Wrong That Should Be Rejected**

*Munkar* is from n-k-r, to not know, to reject as unfamiliar; a *munkar* is what sound nature and sound religion *disown* — the wrong that any healthy conscience should recognize as alien and reject. Its opposite is *maʿrūf*, from ʿ-r-f, to know — the right that sound nature recognizes as familiar and good. The pair "enjoining *maʿrūf* and forbidding *munkar*" defines the mission of the Muslim community (3:104, 110), and the source lists the Qur'an's repeated insistence on it (3:114; 9:112; 22:41; 31:17). The verse says the Israelites failed at the second half: they did not forbid the *munkar*. And the wrong in question was *faʿalūh*, "which they did" — their own wrong, committed among themselves, by their own people. The source specifies this: they failed to forbid wrongs committed among themselves or by their own community. The failure was internal: a people who would not police themselves.

**The Ḥadīth of the First Deficiency**

The commentary on verse 78 promised the full text of the Prophet's ﷺ ḥadīth on this verse, and it is the indispensable key to its meaning:

> *The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The first deficiency that entered the Children of Israel was that a man would meet another man and say, 'O so-and-so, fear God and leave what you are doing, for it is not lawful for you.' Then he would meet him the next day, and it would not prevent him from being his companion at food and drink and in his sitting. When they did that, God struck the hearts of some of them against others." Then he recited: "Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and Jesus son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress. They would not forbid one another the wrong they committed. Evil indeed is that which they used to do" — through to "many of them are iniquitous." Then he said: "No, by God! You shall surely enjoin right, and forbid wrong, and take hold of the hand of the wrongdoer, and bend him to the truth, and restrain him to the truth — or else God will strike the hearts of some of you against others, and then curse you as He cursed them."* (Abū Dāwūd 4336; al-Tirmidhī 3047; Ibn Mājah 4006)

The ḥadīth describes the exact mechanism of the failure. It was not that no one ever spoke; the man *did* say, "Fear God and leave what you are doing." The failure was in what followed: the next day, the reprover sat with the wrongdoer as before, ate with him, drank with him, as if nothing had been said. The word of rebuke was spoken once and then cancelled by conduct. The wrongdoer learned that the rebuke cost him nothing — his companion's friendship, table, and company were unaffected — and so the rebuke had no force. This is *lā yatanāhawna*: a forbidding that is not a forbidding, because it has no consequence. The Prophet ﷺ describes the result: "God struck the hearts of some of them against others" — the community's hearts became alike in corruption, the reprover's heart taking on the color of the wrongdoer's through his continued intimacy with him. And the Prophet's ﷺ warning to his own community is unmistakable: do the same, and you will be cursed as they were cursed.

**The Duty of Forbidding Wrong**

The source states the position of Islamic law: enjoining right and forbidding wrong among one's own community is an obligatory religious duty — a central moral responsibility of the individual and a foundation of the moral society (see 3:104). The obligation is *farḍ kifāyah*, collective: if enough people discharge it, the rest are excused; if no one does, all are guilty. Its gradations are those of the ḥadīth cited at verse 63: with the hand for those with authority, with the tongue for those with knowledge and standing, and with the heart — the inner rejection of the wrong — as the minimum below which there is no faith (Muslim 49). The source cites, from al-Thaʿlabī, the ḥadīth, "The best striving is a word of truth" — and the fuller form specifies "before a tyrannical ruler" (Abū Dāwūd 4344; al-Tirmidhī 2174). The jurists set conditions on the duty — that the wrong be known to be wrong, that it be visible, that forbidding not produce a greater wrong — but they never permitted the abandonment of the duty itself, and they held that its abandonment is what brings communities to ruin.

The ḥadīth of the ship, cited at verse 63, describes why: the ones on the lower deck who bore a hole in the hull will sink everyone unless the ones above take hold of their hands. A community is one vessel; a wrong tolerated in one part is a hole in the hull. And the Prophet ﷺ described the alternative: "When people see a wrongdoer and do not take hold of his hands, God is about to encompass them all with punishment from Him" (Abū Dāwūd 4338; al-Tirmidhī 2168).

**The Connection to Verse 63**

The source directs the reader to verse 63, where the rabbis and scholars were rebuked for not forbidding their followers' sinful speech and devouring of the unlawful. The two verses describe the same failure at two levels. Verse 63 was about the *leaders*: the *rabbāniyyūn* and *aḥbār* who had the knowledge and authority and did not use them. Verse 79 is about the *whole community*: they did not forbid *one another* — the reciprocal verb includes everyone. The leaders' silence licensed the people's; the people's mutual tolerance made the leaders' silence comfortable. The community that was cursed by David and Jesus was one in which no one — neither scholar nor layman — held anyone else to God's law. The curse of verse 78 was the curse of a society that had dissolved the bonds of mutual accountability.

**"Evil Indeed Is What They Used to Do"**

*La-biʾsa mā kānū yafʿalūn* — "surely evil is what they used to do." The verse ends with the verb *yafʿalūn*, "they do" — the third variation in the sūrah's refrain (verse 62 had *yaʿmalūn*, verse 63 *yaṣnaʿūn*). The choice of *faʿala* — the most general verb of action — matches the verse's content: the *munkar* is described as *faʿalūh*, "which they did," and the verdict uses the same verb. Their doing was evil, and their not-forbidding of the doing was part of the doing. The silence is counted among the deeds.

**The Psychology of Mutual Tolerance**

The verse and its ḥadīth describe a social psychology that every community knows. The reprover who rebukes and then resumes intimacy does so for understandable reasons: he does not want to lose a friend, disrupt a family, or be thought self-righteous; he tells himself that he has "said his piece" and that further pressure would be harsh. But the effect of his conduct is to signal that the wrong is, after all, tolerable — that one can do it and keep every social good. The wrongdoer is confirmed; the community's standard drops; and the reprover himself, sitting daily with the wrong, gradually ceases to feel it as wrong. This is what "God struck the hearts of some of them against others" means: hearts become alike through proximity. The ḥadīth's remedy is not cruelty but *consequence*: "take hold of the hand of the wrongdoer, bend him to the truth" — make the wrong cost something, so that the forbidding is real.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The believer should measure his own conduct against the ḥadīth's picture. When he sees wrong among his family, his friends, his community — does he forbid it? And when he has forbidden it, does his subsequent conduct confirm the rebuke or cancel it? The Prophet's ﷺ oath — "No, by God! You shall surely enjoin right and forbid wrong" — is addressed to him, and its alternative is the curse of this verse. The verse does not ask him to be harsh, intrusive, or self-righteous; it asks him not to be complicit. The community that forbids one another's wrongs, with love and with consequence, is the community God does not curse. The community that "would not forbid one another" was cursed by the tongues of two prophets — and the third Prophet ﷺ swore that his own would be cursed likewise if it did the same.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:80

> **Thou seest many of them allying with those who have disbelieved. Evil indeed is that which they have sent forth for their souls: the anger of God is upon them, and in punishment shall they abide.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Visible Alliance**

Verses 78–79 described the historical curse upon the disbelievers among the Children of Israel and its cause — their failure to forbid one another's wrongs. Verse 80 returns to the present of the Prophet's ﷺ Madinah: *tarā kathīran minhum yatawallawna alladhīna kafarū* — "You see many of them taking as allies those who have disbelieved." The verb *tarā*, "you see," addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, marks the conduct as observable and contemporary, as in verse 62. And the verb *yatawallawna* is the key term of verses 51–57: to take as *awliyāʾ*, protectors, allies. The Jews of Madinah — many of them, not all — were allying with the *kāfirūn*, the disbelievers, meaning the idolaters of Makkah and the pagan tribes, against the Muslims.

**Who Are "Those Who Have Disbelieved"?**

The source makes an important observation about this verse's vocabulary. The People of the Book are sometimes described as disbelievers in the Qur'an — not absolutely, but insofar as they do not meet its requirement of believing in all prophets and scriptures including Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. But verses 80–81 draw a clear *distinction* between the People of the Book and "those who have disbelieved," since the former are criticized for allying with the latter. The disbelievers of this verse are the idolaters (*mushrikūn*) — the source records al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Zamakhsharī identifying the alliance as that of certain Jews of Madinah, or hypocrites among them, with the Makkan idolaters against the Muslims. The source directs the reader to 4:51–52, where the Qur'an describes People of the Book who "believe in sorcery and *ṭāghūt* and say of those who disbelieve, 'These are better guided in the way than those who believe'" — the report being that Jewish leaders, visiting Makkah to forge the alliance that produced the Battle of the Trench, were asked by Quraysh whether their idolatry or Muhammad's ﷺ religion was better, and answered, to please their hosts, that Quraysh's was.

That is the alliance this verse condemns: a monotheistic people, possessors of the Torah, allying with worshippers of idols against worshippers of the one God — and declaring, for political advantage, that idolatry was better guided than *tawḥīd*. The source draws out the significance: the rise of Muhammad ﷺ confronted the Jews of Arabia with a choice between allying with him, whose message affirmed their God and their prophets while challenging their practice, or allying with the idolaters, whose religion was anathema to their own. Many chose the idolaters. The choice reveals the priority: the preservation of position over the defense of *tawḥīd*.

**The Mirror of Verse 51**

The verse is the mirror image of verse 51, and the correspondence is deliberate. Verse 51 forbade the *Muslims* from taking Jews and Christians as *awliyāʾ*; verse 80 condemns the *Jews* for taking the idolaters as *awliyāʾ*. The source notes the Qur'an's parallel prohibitions on Muslims seeking protectors among disbelievers and wrongdoers (8:73; 45:19). The principle is one and applies to all: a community of faith should not place its protective allegiance with the enemies of faith. The Jews of Madinah, in allying with idolaters against the Muslims, violated a principle their own scripture upheld — the Torah's absolute hostility to idolatry — and did so for the same reason the hypocrites of verse 52 did: fear of "a change of fortune," and the calculation that the idolaters might win.

**"Evil Indeed Is What They Have Sent Forth for Their Souls"**

*La-biʾsa mā qaddamat lahum anfusuhum* — "surely evil is what their souls have sent forward for them." The verb *qaddama*, to send forward, to send ahead, is the Qur'an's term for deeds done in this life that precede a person to the next, where they await him (the source directs to 75:13: "Man will be informed that Day of what he sent forward and what he held back"). The image is of a traveler who sends his baggage ahead to his destination: what he will find on arrival is what he sent. The Jews of Madinah, in allying with the idolaters, sent forward something evil — and the verse's phrase "their souls sent forward for them" places the responsibility squarely on themselves: it was their own choice, dispatched by their own hands, to await them.

**"The Anger of God Is upon Them"**

*An sakhiṭa Allāhu ʿalayhim* — "that God is angered with them." The word *sakhaṭ*, displeasure, indignation, is stronger than the ordinary word for anger and is the opposite of *riḍā*, good pleasure. God's *riḍā* is the highest reward — "God is well pleased with them and they with Him" (5:119; 58:22; 98:8); His *sakhaṭ* is the corresponding punishment. The verse explains what the "evil they sent forward" was: it was that God's displeasure came upon them. The construction *an sakhiṭa* — "namely, that God was angered" — makes the divine anger the content of what they earned. The alliance with idolatry was not merely a political error; it was the purchase of God's displeasure with their own deeds.

**"And in Punishment Shall They Abide"**

*Wa-fī al-ʿadhābi hum khālidūn* — "and in the punishment they will abide." The verse ends with permanence — *khālidūn*, abiding, eternal. The commentary on verse 37 discussed the principle: permanence in punishment is the consequence of disbelief persisted in to death; the believer who sins exits the Fire. The verse's *khulūd* is therefore the fate of those who, in allying with idolatry against God's religion, disbelieved and died so. It is not a sentence on every Jew of Madinah — the verse said "many of them," and verse 69 remains open — but on those whose alliance was an expression of settled rejection.

**The Deeper Failure**

The verse describes a failure of *loyalty to God* in the deepest sense. The Jews of Madinah had the truth of God's oneness; they had the prophets, the Torah, the covenant. When a Prophet ﷺ arose proclaiming exactly that oneness, they could have recognized in him an ally in the oldest cause of their own faith — the cause of Abraham against the idols. Instead, they allied with the idols' worshippers against him. Whatever their grievances — his challenge to their authority, his exposure of their concealments — the choice to stand with *shirk* against *tawḥīd* was a betrayal of everything their own scripture stood for. This is why the Qur'an treats it as *kufr* in the fullest sense: not the disbelief of one who never knew, but of one who knew and chose the other side.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse's warning passes to the Muslim community in the form the sūrah has already given it: verses 51–57. The believer who allies with the enemies of faith against the community of faith — for advantage, for security, for fear of a change of fortune — is doing what this verse condemns, and the sūrah has warned that such alliance can amount to leaving the religion (v. 54). But the verse also teaches a subtler lesson: that a person can possess the truth and betray it in the moment of decision. The Jews of Madinah did not renounce the Torah; they simply, when the choice came, preferred their position to its principle. Every believer faces smaller versions of the same choice — moments when standing with the truth costs something and standing with its opponents pays — and the verse tells him what is being sent forward, in that moment, for his soul.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:81

> **And had they believed in God and the Prophet, and that which was sent down unto him, they would not have taken them as protectors, but many of them are iniquitous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Root of the Alliance**

Verse 80 described the alliance of many of the Jews of Madinah with the idolaters; verse 81 gives its root: *wa-law kānū yuʾminūna bi-Allāhi wa-l-nabiyyi wa-mā unzila ilayhi mā ittakhadhūhum awliyāʾ* — "And had they believed in God and the Prophet and what was sent down to him, they would not have taken them as *awliyāʾ*." The verse is a counterfactual conditional, like verses 65 and 66: had they believed, this would not have happened. The alliance with idolatry is thus presented not as a political misjudgment but as a *symptom* — the outward evidence of an inward absence of faith. Faith, had it been present, would have made the alliance impossible.

**Three Objects of Faith**

The verse names three things they should have believed in: *Allāh*, God; *al-nabī*, the Prophet; and *mā unzila ilayhi*, what was sent down to him. The source records two readings of the second and third. Al-Ṭabarī: the Prophet is Muhammad ﷺ and what was sent down to him is the Qur'an — had the Jews believed in the final Prophet and the final Book, they would not have allied with the idolaters against him. Al-Rāzī offers an alternative: the Prophet is *their own* prophet, Moses, and what was sent down to him is the Torah — had they truly believed in Moses and the Torah, whose first and greatest commandment is the rejection of idolatry, they could never have allied with idol-worshippers against a monotheist.

The source observes that both readings lead to the same conclusion, and they are in fact complementary. On al-Rāzī's reading, the alliance betrayed the Torah; on al-Ṭabarī's, it betrayed the Qur'an; and the Qur'an's position is that the Torah, truly believed, leads to the Qur'an (7:157; 61:6). The Jew who believed in Moses would have recognized the one whom Moses foretold, and the Jew who recognized him would not have stood with the idolaters against him. The failure was one failure, describable from either end.

**Faith as the Ground of Loyalty**

The verse's logic rests on a principle stated throughout verses 51–57: *walāyah* — protective allegiance — flows from faith. One's *awliyāʾ* are determined by what one believes. The believer's *walī* is God, His Messenger, and the believers (v. 55), *because* he believes in them; the one who takes God's enemies as *awliyāʾ* shows, by that act, where his faith actually lies. Verse 81 applies this principle diagnostically to the Jews of Madinah: their alliance revealed their unbelief. And it applies, by the same logic, to anyone: show me whom you take as protector, and I will show you what you believe.

The Qur'an makes the point positively in 58:22: "You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or sons or brothers or kindred." Faith and loyalty to faith's enemies cannot coexist; where the second is present, the first is absent. This is not a rule imposed from outside but a description of how the heart works: it cannot give its allegiance to two opposed things at once, and the one it chooses reveals the one it loves.

**"But Many of Them Are Iniquitous"**

*Wa-lākinna kathīran minhum fāsiqūn* — "but many of them are *fāsiqūn*." The verse ends with the sūrah's careful arithmetic once more: *many*, not all. And with the word *fāsiq* — the one who has broken out of the bounds of obedience, who has left the path while perhaps still claiming to walk it. The word was the third verdict in the refrain of verses 44–47 and closed verse 49 ("many of mankind are iniquitous") and verse 59 ("most of you are iniquitous"). Its use here diagnoses the alliance as *fisq*: a breach of the bounds — a departure from what their own religion and their own scripture required. They were not iniquitous because they were Jews; they were iniquitous because, being Jews, possessors of the Torah, they allied with idolatry against *tawḥīd*.

The word also leaves room. *Fisq* is not *kufr* in the absolute sense; the *fāsiq* is one who has strayed but may return. The verse's *kathīr*, "many," together with its *fāsiqūn*, "iniquitous," describes a large body of people who had broken the bounds — not a whole people eternally condemned. Verse 82 will immediately go on to describe the Christians who are nearest in affection to the believers, and verse 69 remains the standing promise for any Jew who believes and does right.

**The Verse's Completion of the Passage**

Verses 78–81 form a unit that answers the Christian passage of verses 72–77. The Christians erred by excess — exaggerating Jesus into God. The disbelieving Israelites erred by defect — rejecting the prophets, failing to forbid wrong, and, in the Prophet's ﷺ own time, allying with idolatry against the last of God's messengers. Both are departures from *sawāʾ al-sabīl*, the even path (v. 77). And in both cases the sūrah's diagnosis is the same: a failure of faith. The Christians' *ghuluww* came from following the *ahwāʾ*, caprices, of predecessors rather than the truth; the Jews' alliance came from the absence of true belief in God, His Prophet, and His Book. The remedy for both is the same: *īmān* — real faith in God, in all His messengers, and in all His Books, which would have kept the Christians from exaggerating Jesus and the Jews from betraying Moses.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches the believer to read his own alliances as evidence of his own faith. The principle is uncomfortable but exact: *had they believed, they would not have taken them as protectors*. The reader may apply it in reverse: where he finds his allegiance given to what opposes God — in the company he keeps, the causes he serves, the authorities he defers to, the approval he seeks — he should ask whether the cause is a deficiency of faith that he has not acknowledged. The verse does not permit the comfortable separation of "what I believe" from "whom I stand with." They are one thing, seen from two sides. And the verse's final word, *fāsiqūn*, is both a warning and a mercy: it names the breach, and it leaves the way back open — for the *fāsiq* is one who has left the bounds, and the bounds are still there to return to.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:82

> **Thou wilt surely find the most hostile of men toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who ascribe partners unto God. And thou wilt find the nearest of them in affection toward those who believe to be those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verse of Comparison**

After the long critical treatment of both Jews and Christians, the sūrah pauses to compare their attitudes toward the Muslim believers. *La-tajidanna ashadda al-nāsi ʿadāwatan li-lladhīna āmanū al-yahūda wa-lladhīna ashrakū* — "You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God." *Wa-la-tajidanna aqrabahum mawaddatan li-lladhīna āmanū alladhīna qālū innā naṣārā* — "And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward those who believe to be those who say, 'We are Christians.'" The verse then gives the reason for the Christians' nearness: the presence among them of priests and monks, and their freedom from arrogance. Verses 83–85 will describe the fruit of that nearness — tears at the recitation of the Qur'an, and the reward of Paradise.

**The Two Statements and Their Scope**

The source addresses directly the question of whether these statements are absolute — true of Jews and Christians as such, in all times — or descriptive of a historical situation. Some commentators (al-Thaʿlabī) took them as absolute. The source argues, persuasively, that this reading is belied by history: at many points Muslims had far better relations with Jews than with Christians — the Crusades and the Spanish Reconquista being clear examples, and one might add the flourishing of Jewish communities under Muslim rule in Baghdad, Córdoba, and Istanbul, often as refugees from Christian persecution. The verse is therefore best read in the context of the Prophet's ﷺ life and the early community. The Jews of Madinah and its region presented a continual challenge to the Prophet's ﷺ authority, and some colluded with the Makkan idolaters against him — the alliance verse 80 has just described. The Christians, by contrast, had played positive and even pivotal roles in the Prophet's ﷺ life and mission.

The verse's own language supports the contextual reading. It says *la-tajidanna*, "you will surely find" — addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, describing what *he* would find in *his* experience. It describes the Christians not as "the Christians" but as *alladhīna qālū innā naṣārā*, "those who say, 'We are Christians'" — a phrase that, as verse 14 showed, can carry a note of qualification: those who claim the name. And it grounds the Christians' nearness in specific qualities — priests, monks, absence of arrogance — which are qualities of *some* Christians in *some* times, not permanent attributes of a community. Where those qualities are present, the nearness follows; where they are absent, so is the nearness. The verse thus describes a disposition and its causes, not an unchangeable ethnic or confessional fact. Al-Zamakhsharī, as the source records, observed that the Jews' hostility made it particularly hard for them to accept the Qur'an, while the Christians' affection made it comparatively easier — a psychological observation about how enmity and affection condition receptivity to truth.

**The Christians Who Helped the Prophet ﷺ**

The source names the Christians whose conduct lies behind the verse. The monk Baḥīrā, who recognized the young Muhammad ﷺ as a future prophet when the Makkan caravan passed his cell in Syria, and warned Abū Ṭālib to guard him. Waraqah ibn Nawfal, the Christian cousin of Khadījah, who, when the Prophet ﷺ came trembling from the cave of Ḥirāʾ after the first revelation, identified what had come to him as "the *Nāmūs* that came to Moses" and said, "Would that I were young and could live to the day your people drive you out" (al-Bukhārī 3; Muslim 160). And the Negus (al-Najāshī), the Christian king of Abyssinia, who sheltered the first Muslim emigrants for years, refused Quraysh's demand to surrender them, and, when Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib recited Sūrat Maryam before him, wept until his beard was wet and said, drawing a line on the ground with his staff, "By God, this and what Jesus brought come from the same niche" (Ibn Hishām; Aḥmad 1740). When the Negus died, the Prophet ﷺ performed the funeral prayer for him in absentia (al-Bukhārī 1245; Muslim 951) — the only such prayer he is recorded to have performed, and a testimony to his regard.

**The Occasion of Revelation**

The source records the reports. One early commentator connected the verse to the Muslims' first encounter with the Negus, but the source notes that this is chronologically impossible, since the sūrah is Madinan and that encounter was Makkan (Ibn Kathīr). Most commentators connect the verse to a later event: the Negus sent a delegation of his people — reports say seventy, or twenty, or thirty men — to the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah; when the Qur'an was recited to them, they wept and believed (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Zamakhsharī). Some accounts add that the delegation returned and recited the Qur'an to the Negus, who believed as well (al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī). The source is careful to note that there is no historical evidence that the Negus formally became Muslim, and that the verse attributes positive qualities to Christians generally — describing them as "nearest in affection to those who believe," not as believers themselves (al-Thaʿlabī). Ibn Kathīr records the view that the verse refers to Christians who believed in the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood while continuing to live by the way of the Gospel, remaining "Christian" in the confessional sense. The source's conclusion is judicious: whatever the precise occasion, the report of the Negus illustrates the good relations between the Prophet's ﷺ community and an important Christian kingdom, and points to a spiritual affinity between Christians and Muslims as the basis of those relations.

**"Because Among Them Are Priests and Monks"**

*Dhālika bi-anna minhum qissīsīna wa-ruhbānan* — "that is because among them are *qissīsūn* and *ruhbān*." The verse's first reason for the Christians' nearness is the presence of religious exemplars. *Qissīs* (from Syriac *qashīshā*, elder) is a priest or presbyter; the source records that some commentators (Ibn Kathīr, al-Zamakhsharī) took it to mean the religious scholars of the Christians, and that Salmān al-Fārsī — who had been a Christian before Islam and had served several monks — reported that the Prophet ﷺ glossed the word as *ṣiddīqūn*, the truthful or saintly ones (Ibn Kathīr). *Ruhbān*, plural of *rāhib*, from r-h-b, to fear: the monks, those who withdrew from the world out of fear of God. The verse credits the priests and monks with shaping their community's character — learned men and devout men whose example kept the Christians humble and God-fearing, in contrast to the *aḥbār* of verse 63, whose silence corrupted theirs.

The source is careful about the Qur'an's attitude toward monasticism, and the reader should hold its balance. The verse praises the monks' effect on their community. But the Qur'an also blames "many of the rabbis and monks" for devouring people's wealth and barring from God's way (9:34), criticizes their followers for taking them as lords (9:31), and says that monasticism itself "they invented; We did not prescribe it for them, but only the seeking of God's pleasure — yet they did not observe it as it should be observed" (57:27). The Prophet ﷺ forbade his Companions the celibacy and extreme asceticism of monks: "There is no monasticism in Islam"; "the monasticism of my community is *jihād*"; and to ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn, who wished to renounce marriage, he said, "Do you turn away from my Sunnah? I pray and I sleep, I fast and I break the fast, and I marry women" (al-Bukhārī 5063). The Islamic ideal is the balance the Prophet ﷺ embodied: devotion within the world, not withdrawal from it. The verse honors what was genuine in the monks — their humility, their fear of God, their receptivity to truth — without endorsing the institution as such. The source directs also to 3:113: "Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite God's signs in the night hours while they prostrate."

**"And Because They Are Not Arrogant"**

*Wa-annahum lā yastakbirūn* — "and because they are not arrogant." The second reason is the decisive one. *Istikbār*, arrogance — the claiming of greatness (*kibr*) for oneself — is, in the Qur'an, the root of the rejection of God's signs. The source lists the Qur'an's repeated connection of arrogance to spiritual blindness (2:87; 6:93; 7:75–76, 146; 10:75; 23:67; 31:7; 35:42–43; 39:59, 72; 41:15; 45:8, 31; 46:10; 63:5; 71:7) and its contrast with the humility that prostrates (4:172–173; 16:49; 21:19; 32:15; 40:60; 41:37–38). Iblīs's sin was *istikbār* (2:34); Pharaoh's was *istikbār* (28:39); and the Israelites' rejection of their prophets was, in 2:87, *istakbartum*, "you were arrogant." The verse says the Christians it describes lacked this vice — and therefore, as the next verse will show, could weep at the truth when they heard it. The one who is not arrogant can be taught; the one who is arrogant cannot, however learned. The verse locates the whole difference between hostility and affection, between rejection and recognition, in this single quality.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches the believer, first, to read the Qur'an's descriptions of communities in context and to recognize that the qualities it praises or blames are qualities of conduct that any community may have or lose. Second, it teaches him what makes a people receptive to truth: the presence of genuine exemplars of learning and devotion, and the absence of arrogance. He should ask whether his own community has the first and lacks the second — for the verse's logic applies to Muslims too: a community with corrupt scholars and arrogant hearts will be hostile to truth however Muslim its name. And third, it teaches him to honor what is honorable in others. The Negus was a Christian king who wept at Sūrat Maryam and sheltered the persecuted; the Prophet ﷺ prayed for him when he died. The verse asks the believer to see such people as the Prophet ﷺ saw them: nearest in affection, and, as the next verses will say, rewarded by God for what they said.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:83

> **And when they hear that which was sent down unto the Messenger, thou seest their eyes overflow with tears because of the truth they recognize. They say, "Our Lord, we believe, so inscribe us among the witnesses.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Scene**

Verse 82 described the Christians who are nearest in affection to the believers, and named the causes: priests and monks among them, and freedom from arrogance. Verse 83 shows the effect in a single scene: *wa-idhā samiʿū mā unzila ilā al-rasūli tarā aʿyunahum tafīḍu mina al-damʿi mimmā ʿarafū mina al-ḥaqq* — "And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflow with tears because of what they recognize of the truth." The source connects the scene to the delegation of the Negus, who wept when the Qur'an was recited to them in Madinah, and to the Negus himself, whose beard was wet with tears at Jaʿfar's recitation of Sūrat Maryam. The verse is one of the most tender in the Qur'an, and it stands as the culmination of everything the sūrah has said about the People of the Book: after the covenant-breakers, the concealers, the mockers, and the exaggerators, here are the ones who hear and weep.

**"Their Eyes Overflow with Tears"**

*Tafīḍu mina al-damʿ* — "overflow with tears." The verb *fāḍa* is used of a vessel filled beyond its capacity, of a river overflowing its banks. The image is not of a tear escaping but of eyes so full that they spill — an involuntary overflow, the body's response to something too great for it to contain. The Qur'an does not say "they wept"; it says their eyes *overflowed*, as if the tears came of themselves, from a fullness within. And the phrase *mimmā ʿarafū mina al-ḥaqq*, "from what they recognized of the truth," names the source of the fullness.

**Recognition: ʿArafū**

The verb is *ʿarafū*, "they recognized" — not "they learned" or "they were persuaded." *Maʿrifah* is the knowledge of something already known, the recognition of a familiar face. The Christians wept not because they heard something new but because they heard something they *knew* — the truth that their own scripture had taught them, the God their monks had worshipped, the Jesus their priests had honored, now spoken with a clarity and authority that confirmed everything true they had held. The Qur'an describes the same recognition in 2:146: "Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their own sons." The truth is one; those who have lived with a portion of it recognize the whole when it comes. This is why the verse credits their tears to recognition: the Qur'an did not convert them from something alien but completed something familiar.

The source directs the reader to 17:107–109: "Those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down on their faces in prostration, and say, 'Glory be to our Lord; the promise of our Lord has indeed been fulfilled.' And they fall on their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility." And to 28:52–53: "Those to whom We gave the Book before it — they believe in it; and when it is recited to them they say, 'We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord; indeed we were, even before it, submitters.'" The pattern is consistent: the sincere among the People of the Book, hearing the Qur'an, recognize, weep, prostrate, and say "we believe" — and they say that they were *already* submitters, because what they submitted to before was the same truth.

**Tears as the Sign of a Living Heart**

The tears are the verse's evidence of the quality verse 82 named: *lā yastakbirūn*, they are not arrogant. The arrogant heart does not weep at truth; it argues, resists, or mocks. The humble heart is moved. The Qur'an praises those "whose skins shiver" at the Qur'an, "then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of God" (39:23), and describes the believers as those whose "hearts tremble when God is mentioned" (8:2). The source records the ḥadīth cited by al-Thaʿlabī: "Recite the Qur'an and weep, and if you do not weep, then make yourself weep" (Ibn Mājah 1337) — that is, if the tears do not come naturally, seek the state that produces them, for the absence of any response to God's word is a symptom of hardness. The Prophet ﷺ himself wept at the Qur'an: when Ibn Masʿūd recited Sūrat al-Nisāʾ to him and reached "how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness over these?" (4:41), he said, "Enough," and Ibn Masʿūd turned and saw his eyes flowing (al-Bukhārī 4582; Muslim 800). And Abū Bakr could not recite the Qur'an in prayer without weeping (al-Bukhārī 682). The Christians of this verse wept as the Prophet ﷺ and his closest Companion wept — and the Qur'an records their tears as a mark of honor.

**"They Say: Our Lord, We Believe"**

*Yaqūlūna rabbanā āmannā* — "they say, 'Our Lord, we believe.'" The tears issue in words, and the words are a profession of faith addressed to God: not "we are convinced" but "*our Lord*, we believe." The source records al-Ṭabarī's gloss: they believe in Muhammad ﷺ as a divinely sent prophet and in the Qur'an as truth from God — even if, as Ibn Kathīr's reading at verse 82 allowed, some remained Christian in confession, living by the way of the Gospel. The profession is addressed to God because it is God who is being trusted; and it uses *rabbanā*, "our Lord," the address of the servant who knows himself as such — the very relationship the sūrah has insisted upon against those who called Jesus God.

**"So Inscribe Us Among the Witnesses"**

*Fa-ktubnā maʿa al-shāhidīn* — "so write us down with the witnesses." The petition is precise and beautiful. They ask to be *written* — inscribed in God's record — among *al-shāhidīn*, the witnesses. The source records the interpretations: those who witness to the truth and to God's oneness, or specifically the community of Muhammad ﷺ (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The second reading has strong Qur'anic support: the Muslim community is described as "witnesses over mankind" (2:143; 22:78), and the Prophet ﷺ will be a witness over them (4:41). To ask to be inscribed among the witnesses is to ask to be counted with those who bear testimony to the truth on the Day when testimony is taken — to stand, on that Day, not among the accused but among those who testify. The Christians who wept at the Qur'an asked for nothing less than membership in the community of witnesses, and verse 85 will record that God granted it.

The word *shāhid* also echoes Jesus' own words at the end of the sūrah, where he says to God, "I was a witness (*shahīd*) over them while I was among them" (v. 117). The Christians who asked to be inscribed among the witnesses were asking to be joined to their own prophet's role — to witness to the truth as he witnessed to it.

**The Verse in the Structure of the Sūrah**

The verse fulfills the promise made in verse 14's commentary — that the sūrah would praise Christians at 82–85 — and it balances the sūrah's severity. The same sūrah that said "they have disbelieved who say God is the Messiah" (vv. 17, 72) and threatened painful punishment for those who say "God is the third of three" (v. 73) now shows Christians whose eyes overflow at the Qur'an and who beg to be written among the witnesses. The Qur'an's criticism was of doctrines and conduct; its praise is of persons who, hearing the truth, recognize it. The two are not in tension. The Christians of verse 83 are precisely those who, hearing "Jesus said: worship God, my Lord and your Lord" (v. 72), recognized in it the voice of their own prophet and wept.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The Muslim reader should measure himself against these Christians. They heard the Qur'an once and wept; he hears it daily — does he weep? They recognized the truth from a portion of it; he possesses the whole — does he recognize it, or has familiarity dulled him to what moved strangers to tears? The verse is a rebuke to the believer whose heart has grown hard to what he hears every day, and an invitation to recover the first hearing. And it is an instruction in how to regard those outside the community who are moved by the truth: as the Qur'an regards them — with honor, with the record of their tears, and with the hope that God will grant their petition as He granted this one. The believer who cannot honor a Christian weeping at the Qur'an has not understood the Book that recorded the tears.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:84

> **And how should we not believe in God and the truth that has come unto us, when we desire that our Lord should cause us to enter among the righteous people?"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Continuation of the Christians' Speech**

Verse 83 recorded the Christians' profession — "Our Lord, we believe, so inscribe us among the witnesses" — and verse 84 continues their words: *wa-mā lanā lā nuʾminu bi-Allāhi wa-mā jāʾanā mina al-ḥaqqi wa-naṭmaʿu an yudkhilanā rabbunā maʿa al-qawmi al-ṣāliḥīn* — "And what is it with us that we should not believe in God and what has come to us of the truth, when we long that our Lord should admit us among the righteous people?" The verse is a rhetorical question put by the Christians themselves, and it has the character of a self-justification offered to those who might question their belief — their own co-religionists, perhaps, or the community they had left behind, or their own hesitations. It is the speech of people who have found the truth and cannot understand why anyone would ask them to deny it.

**"What Is It with Us That We Should Not Believe?"**

*Wa-mā lanā lā nuʾminu* — "and what is with us, that we do not believe?" The construction *mā lanā*, "what is with us?", expresses astonishment at the suggestion of an alternative: what reason could we possibly have not to believe? The source records al-Ṭabarī's gloss of the objects of belief: in God — that is, in His oneness — and in the truth that has come to us through His revelations. The question implies that unbelief, given what they have recognized, would be irrational: they have heard the truth, recognized it as truth, wept at it; what possible ground could there be for refusing it? The verse thus presents faith not as a leap but as the *obvious* response to recognized truth, and unbelief as the thing requiring explanation.

The form mirrors the Qur'an's own rhetorical questions to the unbelievers — "What is the matter with you, how do you judge?" (10:35; 37:154; 68:36) — but here the question is asked by believers about themselves, from the inside. The one who has recognized the truth finds that the burden of proof has shifted: it is no longer "why should I believe?" but "what is wrong with me if I do not?"

**The Case Against Hesitation**

The verse may also be heard as an answer to a specific pressure. Some accounts of the Negus's delegation report that when they returned to Abyssinia and professed faith, others rebuked them: "May God disgrace you — you left your religion for that of a people you met on a journey." The Christians' reply in this verse answers exactly such a rebuke: what reason do we have not to believe? The pressure to remain within an inherited faith against recognized truth — the pressure of family, community, identity, and the shame of having "changed" — is among the strongest human forces, and the verse records people who overcame it by a simple appeal to reason: the truth came to us; we recognized it; why would we refuse it? The Qur'an honors this reasoning by recording it, and verse 85 will show God rewarding it.

**"And We Long That Our Lord Should Admit Us Among the Righteous People"**

*Wa-naṭmaʿu an yudkhilanā rabbunā maʿa al-qawmi al-ṣāliḥīn* — "and we long that our Lord should enter us among the righteous people." The verb *ṭamiʿa* is to hope eagerly, to covet, to long for; the source records al-Zamakhsharī's observation that the Christians' desire to be among the righteous is itself a sign of their belief, since disbelievers desire no such thing. What one longs for reveals what one is. The Christians did not long for the approval of their former community, or for safety, or for the preservation of their identity; they longed to be admitted among *al-qawm al-ṣāliḥīn*, the righteous — and this longing is the second half of their argument: not only is there no reason *not* to believe, there is every reason *to* believe, because belief is the way to what we most desire.

The source records the identifications of "the righteous people": the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, or simply those who affirm God's oneness (al-Ṭabarī). And it records al-Rāzī's inference that the Christians' response indicates a new awareness of the need to abandon their trinitarian beliefs — for to long to be among those who affirm God's oneness is to accept that oneness as the standard. The petition thus goes further than verse 83's "inscribe us among the witnesses": there they asked to be counted among those who testify; here they express longing to be *admitted*, entered, brought in — the verb of entering Paradise (*adkhala*) — among the righteous. They are asking for the company of the saved.

**The Word "Ṣāliḥīn"**

*Ṣāliḥ*, righteous, from ṣ-l-ḥ, to be sound, whole, fit for purpose — the opposite of *fasād*, corruption, which the sūrah has condemned repeatedly (vv. 32, 33, 64). The *ṣāliḥūn* are the last of the four ranks named in 4:69 — "the prophets, the *ṣiddīqūn*, the martyrs, and the righteous" — and the company of the righteous is what the prophets themselves prayed for: Joseph asked God to "join me with the righteous" (12:101), Abraham asked to be "joined with the righteous" (26:83), and Solomon asked to be admitted "by Your mercy among Your righteous servants" (27:19). The Christians of this verse use the prayer of the prophets. Their longing places them in a line that runs from Abraham through Joseph and Solomon to the delegation weeping in Madinah: the longing to be among the sound, the whole, the fit — the people who are what God made human beings to be.

**The Verse as the Model of Sincere Conversion**

Verses 83–84 together describe the anatomy of a sincere turning to the truth, and its elements deserve to be named. First, *hearing*: they heard what was sent down. Second, *recognition*: they knew it as truth, from what they already possessed of truth. Third, *emotion*: their eyes overflowed — the heart moved before the tongue spoke. Fourth, *profession*: "Our Lord, we believe." Fifth, *petition*: "inscribe us among the witnesses." Sixth, *reason*: "what is with us that we should not believe?" And seventh, *longing*: "we long that our Lord should admit us among the righteous." Hearing, recognition, emotion, profession, petition, reason, longing — the whole person is engaged: ears, mind, heart, tongue, will. This is what faith looks like when it is real, and the Qur'an records it in strangers so that the believers may know it in themselves.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse's question is one the believer should ask himself in his own hesitations. When he knows a truth and delays acting on it; when he recognizes what God requires and finds reasons to postpone; when the pressure of others makes him quiet about what he believes — the Christians' question is his: *what is with me, that I do not believe and act, when I long to be among the righteous?* The verse suggests that most hesitation, examined honestly, has no reason behind it — only pressure, habit, and fear. And it suggests the cure: to remember what one longs for. The one who keeps before him the desire to be admitted among the righteous people will find the reasons for hesitation dissolving, as they dissolved for the strangers who wept at the Qur'an and asked, with astonishment, how they could possibly not believe.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:85

> **So God rewarded them for what they said with Gardens that have rivers running below, to abide therein, and that is the recompense of the virtuous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Divine Response**

Verses 83–84 recorded the Christians' tears, their profession of faith, their petition to be inscribed among the witnesses, and their longing to be admitted among the righteous. Verse 85 records God's answer: *fa-athābahumu Allāhu bi-mā qālū jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhāru khālidīna fīhā wa-dhālika jazāʾu al-muḥsinīn* — "So God rewarded them, for what they said, with Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and that is the recompense of the doers of good." The *fāʾ* of consequence links the reward directly to what preceded: *because* they said what they said, God rewarded them. The petition was granted. They asked to be admitted among the righteous, and God admitted them to the Gardens where the righteous dwell.

**"For What They Said"**

*Bi-mā qālū* — "for what they said." The verse specifies that the reward was for their *speech*: the profession "Our Lord, we believe," the petition "inscribe us among the witnesses," the reasoning "what is with us that we should not believe?", the longing "we long that our Lord should admit us among the righteous." The commentators noted the significance. Speech in the Qur'an is not cheap: the sūrah has condemned "sinful speech" (v. 63), the slander "God's hand is shackled" (v. 64), the saying "God is the Messiah" (v. 72) and "God is the third of three" (v. 73) — and in each case the *saying* was the sin. Here, correspondingly, the *saying* is the merit. What one says about God and to God is weighed. The word *qālū* also implies, as the commentators understood, the sincerity behind it — for the same words spoken by the hypocrites of verse 61 ("we believe") earned nothing. The Christians' words were the overflow of hearts that had recognized the truth, and God rewards the word that comes from such a heart.

The word *athāba*, "He rewarded," is the positive counterpart to the ironic *mathūbah* of verse 60. There, the Prophet ﷺ was told to inform the mockers of a worse "recompense" — curse, wrath, transformation. Here, the true *thawāb*, the true recompense, is given to those who wept at the truth. The sūrah's vocabulary of reward has been restored to its proper meaning.

**"Gardens Beneath Which Rivers Flow, Abiding Therein"**

The reward is described with the Qur'an's most frequent image of Paradise: *jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār*, "Gardens beneath which rivers flow." The source directs the reader to 2:25 for the image's first appearance and its discussion. To the Arab of the desert, the garden with running water beneath its trees was the summit of earthly delight; the Qur'an uses it as the sensible image of a bliss that "no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived" (al-Bukhārī 3244; Muslim 2824). *Khālidīna fīhā*, "abiding therein forever": the permanence that the sūrah has attached to punishment for the disbelievers (vv. 37, 80) is here attached to reward. The Christians who asked to be *admitted* (*yudkhilanā*, v. 84) are admitted to a place they will never leave.

**"And That Is the Recompense of the Doers of Good"**

*Wa-dhālika jazāʾu al-muḥsinīn* — "and that is the recompense of the *muḥsinūn*." The verse ends by classifying the Christians of verses 82–84 among the *muḥsinūn* — those who practice *iḥsān*, excellence, doing what is beautiful. *Iḥsān* is the highest of the three degrees the Prophet ﷺ described in the ḥadīth of Gabriel: *islām* (outward submission), *īmān* (inward faith), and *iḥsān* — "to worship God as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you" (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8). The Qur'an says, "God loves the *muḥsinīn*" (2:195; 3:134, 148; 5:13, 93), and this sūrah used the word in verse 13, where the Prophet ﷺ was told to pardon the covenant-breakers, "for God loves the doers of good." That the Christians who wept at the Qur'an are placed in this category — the category of those whom God loves — is the sūrah's final word on the "nearest in affection" of verse 82: their affection was requited by God's love.

**The Question of Their Confession**

The commentary on verse 82 recorded the discussion of whether these Christians became Muslims in the full sense or believed in the Prophet ﷺ while remaining Christian in confession. The verse's reward does not settle the question by itself, but the surrounding verses do much to clarify it. They believed in "what was sent down to the Messenger" (v. 83); they asked to be inscribed among the witnesses, which most commentators took to mean the community of Muhammad ﷺ; they longed to be among "the righteous people," whom al-Ṭabarī identified with the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions; and al-Rāzī saw in their words a turning from trinitarian belief. The picture is of people who accepted the Prophet ﷺ and his Book — who *believed*, in the Qur'an's full sense. Whether they then adopted every outward practice of the Muslim community or continued, for a time or for life, in the forms of their previous worship, is a matter the sources leave open, and the Qur'an's reward is for what they *said* from the heart. The verse does not authorize the conclusion that Trinitarian belief is rewarded with Paradise — verses 72–73 have said the opposite — but it does establish that the Christian who recognizes the truth of the Qur'an and turns to God in faith and longing is rewarded as a *muḥsin*, whatever the stage of his outward transition.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Argument**

Verse 85 completes the sūrah's account of the People of the Book with a reward, not a punishment. The long section that began at verse 41 has moved through covenant-breaking, concealment, bribery, mockery, blasphemy, the silence of scholars, alliance with idolatry, and exaggeration of Jesus — and it ends with Gardens beneath which rivers flow, given to Christians who wept. The placement is not accidental. The Qur'an closes the section by showing that the door it held open throughout — verse 65's "had they believed," verse 69's "whoever believes in God and the Last Day" — is a real door through which real people passed, and that God's response to those who pass through it is not grudging admission but the recompense of the *muḥsinūn*. The severity of the section was never an end in itself; it was the clearing of the ground for this.

Verse 86 will state the other side — those who disbelieved and denied the signs are the companions of the Fire — so that the section ends, as the Qur'an always ends such sections, with the two destinations set side by side. But the order matters: the Gardens come first.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches that God rewards *speech* that flows from a recognizing heart — and the believer should ask what his own speech about God and to God is earning. It teaches that the *muḥsinūn* are not defined by their origin: Christians who had never heard the Qur'an until a delegation's visit were placed in that rank on the day they wept and spoke. And it teaches the believer to hope for others as generously as God does: the same Book that condemned the doctrine of the Trinity rewarded Trinitarians who turned, with the highest reward it has. The Muslim who reads verses 82–85 and comes away with anything other than a widened heart toward those who sincerely seek God has read them wrongly. The Prophet ﷺ prayed the funeral prayer for the Negus; the Qur'an promised Gardens to his delegation. That is the standard.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:86

> **As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs—such shall be the inhabitants of Hellfire!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Other Destination**

Verse 85 gave the reward of those who recognized the truth and said, "Our Lord, we believe": Gardens beneath which rivers flow. Verse 86 gives, in a single sentence, the fate of the opposite response: *wa-lladhīna kafarū wa-kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā ulāʾika aṣḥābu al-jaḥīm* — "And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of the Blaze." The source notes that the pairing is the Qur'an's constant pattern: the image of Gardens for the believers and the virtuous (2:25) set beside the punishment of the Fire for the disbelievers and deniers (2:39; 5:10; 7:36; 22:51; 57:19; 64:10). The two verses together close the long section on the People of the Book (vv. 41–86) with the two destinations side by side, and the brevity of verse 86 after the fullness of verses 82–85 is itself a statement: the reward is described at length; the punishment is stated and left.

**The Exact Parallel with Verse 10**

The verse repeats, nearly word for word, verse 10 of this sūrah: "And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of Hellfire." Verse 10 followed verse 9's promise of forgiveness and great reward for those who believe and do righteous deeds; verse 86 follows verse 85's reward for those who said, "we believe." The sūrah has thus framed its central section with the same pair of verses: promise and threat at verses 9–10, promise and threat at verses 85–86. What lies between — the covenants, the Israelites, Cain and Abel, the *ḥudūd*, the judgment by revelation, the alliances, the People of the Book — is bracketed by the two possible ends of every human story. The repetition tells the reader that everything in between is, finally, about which of these two verses will describe him.

**Two Acts: Disbelief and Denial**

The verse names two things: *kafarū*, they disbelieved, and *kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā*, they denied Our signs.
