The commentary on verse 10 explained the distinction, and it applies here with particular force after verses 82–85. *Kufr* is the inward state — the covering of the truth, the refusal to acknowledge it. *Takdhīb* is the outward act — calling the signs lies. The Christians of verses 82–85 did the opposite of both: they *recognized* the truth (the opposite of covering it) and *affirmed* it with their tongues (the opposite of calling it a lie). The two groups are exact inverses, and the verse's placement makes the contrast unmistakable: the same signs were presented to both; one wept and believed; the other disbelieved and denied.

*Āyātinā*, "Our signs": the word covers the verses of the Qur'an, the miracles of the prophets, and the evidences in creation. In the context of verses 82–85, the signs are what was "sent down to the Messenger" (v. 83) — the Qur'an that the Christians heard and recognized. Those who heard the same Qur'an and called it a lie are the subject of this verse. The Qur'an's principle is that the sign that guides one blinds another (v. 64's "will increase many of them in rebellion and disbelief"); the difference lies not in the sign but in the heart that receives it.

**"Companions of the Blaze"**

*Aṣḥābu al-jaḥīm* — "the companions of *al-jaḥīm*." *Jaḥīm* is one of the Qur'an's names for Hell, from j-ḥ-m, to blaze fiercely; it is the Fire in its intensity. The word *aṣḥāb*, companions, is used for both destinations — "companions of the Garden" (*aṣḥāb al-jannah*) and "companions of the Fire" (*aṣḥāb al-nār*) — and it conveys belonging, permanent association: they are the Fire's people, as one is the people of a town. The commentary on verse 37 established the principle that permanence in the Fire is the consequence of disbelief persisted in to death, and this verse's subjects — those who *disbelieved and denied* — are exactly those to whom that principle applies.

**The Function of the Brief Verse**

Why does the Qur'an state the threat so briefly after describing the reward so fully? The pattern serves several purposes. It maintains the balance the Qur'an never abandons: hope is never offered without fear, nor fear without hope, lest the reader presume or despair. It preserves proportion: God's mercy "precedes His wrath" (al-Bukhārī 7404; Muslim 2751), and the Qur'an's descriptions of reward are characteristically longer and more loving than its descriptions of punishment. And it gives the threat the force of finality: after the tears, the profession, the petition, and the Gardens, the single sentence about the Blaze lands like a closing door.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Movement**

Verse 86 closes the section on the People of the Book, and verse 87 will turn abruptly to the Muslim community: "O you who believe! Do not forbid the good things God has made lawful for you." The transition is significant. Having shown the two destinations for those who received the earlier revelations, the sūrah turns to those who received the final one, and its first instruction to them is a warning against *ghuluww* of a different kind — the forbidding of what God made lawful, the excess of self-imposed austerity. The Christians' monks were praised in verse 82 for their humility, but their monasticism was "invented" (57:27); and the Muslims are now warned not to imitate the invention. The sūrah moves from the fate of the earlier communities to the guidance of the last, and the thread that connects them is the sūrah's constant theme: staying within the bounds God set — neither breaking them by transgression nor adding to them by exaggeration.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to hold both verses 85 and 86 in view at once and to know that he stands between them. He has heard the signs; his response to them is being recorded; and the two verses describe the only two outcomes. The believer should not read verse 86 as a description of others alone — the People of the Book who denied — but as the warning it is for anyone who hears God's signs and covers them or calls them lies, in whatever form: the Muslim who hears a verse he dislikes and explains it away, who knows a ruling and denies its authority, who treats the Qur'an's promises and threats as metaphors that bind no one. The Christians of verses 82–85 heard the Qur'an once and wept; verse 86 warns those who hear it often and remain unmoved. The two responses are always available; the verse tells the reader what each one leads to.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:87

> **O you who believe! Do not forbid the good things that God has made lawful unto you, and do not transgress. Surely God loves not transgressors.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn to the Believers**

After the long section on the People of the Book (vv. 41–86), the sūrah returns to the Muslim community with an address that has occurred throughout: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū*, "O you who believe!" And its first instruction is unexpected. One might expect, after the praise of Christian monks and the condemnation of Christian exaggeration, a call to greater devotion. Instead: *lā tuḥarrimū ṭayyibāti mā aḥalla Allāhu lakum* — "Do not forbid the good things that God has made lawful for you." The sūrah, which opened by legislating what is lawful and unlawful (vv. 1–5) and which has just condemned *ghuluww*, exaggeration in religion (v. 77), now warns the believers against their own form of *ghuluww*: making unlawful what God made lawful, out of a misplaced zeal for austerity.

**The Occasion of Revelation**

The reports of the verse's occasion, preserved by al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, and others, describe a moment in the early community when a group of Companions, moved by a sermon of the Prophet ﷺ on the Hereafter that had stirred their hearts, resolved to renounce the world. ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, al-Miqdād, Sālim the client of Abū Ḥudhayfah, and others gathered in ʿUthmān's house and agreed among themselves: to fast every day, to pray all night, to abstain from meat and fat, to wear coarse garments, to renounce women and perfume, and, some said, to castrate themselves. When the Prophet ﷺ heard of it, he went to them and said:

> *"Have I not been told that you agreed to such-and-such? ... By God, I am the most God-fearing of you and the most conscious of Him; yet I fast and I break the fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me."* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401)

This verse was revealed in confirmation. The commentators also record the case of ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn specifically, who asked the Prophet's ﷺ permission to be castrated and to withdraw into a life of wandering devotion, and was refused: "Do you turn away from my Sunnah?" And they record that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, who had vowed to fast every day and pray all night, was told by the Prophet ﷺ: "Your body has a right over you, your eye has a right over you, your wife has a right over you, and your guest has a right over you" (al-Bukhārī 1975; Muslim 1159).

**"The Good Things" — Ṭayyibāt**

The verse does not say "do not forbid what God has made lawful" but "do not forbid the *ṭayyibāt* of what God has made lawful." *Ṭayyib* — good, pure, wholesome, pleasing — was the key word of verse 4 ("Say: the good things are made lawful for you") and verse 5 ("Today the good things are made lawful for you"). The word insists on the positive value of what is permitted: it is not merely "allowed" but *good*, made lawful because it is good. Food, marriage, rest, adornment, the enjoyment of God's creation — these are *ṭayyibāt*, and God made them lawful as a gift. To forbid them is not merely to exceed one's authority; it is to refuse a gift and to imply that the Giver erred in giving it.

**"That God Has Made Lawful for You"**

The phrase *mā aḥalla Allāhu lakum*, "what God has made lawful for you," states the ground of the prohibition. The authority to make lawful and unlawful belongs to God alone. The Qur'an condemns those who "forbid what God has not forbidden" as sharply as those who permit what He has forbidden: "Say: Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision, and you have made of it unlawful and lawful? Say: Has God permitted you, or do you fabricate against God?" (10:59). And 16:116: "Do not say, about what your tongues falsely describe, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful,' to fabricate a lie against God." The source lists the Qur'an's criticism of arbitrary prohibitions — the pagan Arabs' taboos on certain animals (6:138–145, 150–151), and the forbidding of adornment (7:32: "Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?"). The believer who forbids himself what God made lawful, *as a matter of religion*, has done what the pagans did: legislated in God's place. This is the specific sin the verse forbids — not the choice to abstain from a permitted thing for a good reason (which is allowed), but the treating of a lawful thing as *ḥarām*, as though God had forbidden it.

**"And Do Not Transgress"**

*Wa-lā taʿtadū* — "and do not transgress." The verb *iʿtadā*, to cross a limit, has been the sūrah's word for the crossing of God's bounds from verse 2 onward ("do not transgress" in the matter of hunting during pilgrimage). Here it is placed alongside the forbidding of lawful things, and the commentators read it in two complementary ways. First, as the *opposite* excess: do not forbid the lawful, and do not transgress into the unlawful — the verse forbids both directions of departure from God's bounds, the ascetic's and the libertine's. Second, as a description of the *same* act: to forbid what God made lawful *is* transgression — a crossing of the limit of one's authority, an intrusion into God's exclusive right to legislate. Both readings are true, and together they express the verse's principle: God's bounds are to be kept exactly, neither narrowed nor widened.

**"Surely God Loves Not the Transgressors"**

*Inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu al-muʿtadīn* — the phrase occurs also in 2:190 and 7:55, as the source notes, and 10:74 says God seals the hearts of the transgressors. Its appearance here is pointed. The Companions who resolved on extreme austerity did so out of love for God and desire for His pleasure; the verse tells them that the transgression they were about to commit is not loved by God. This is the paradox of religious excess: it is undertaken to please God and displeases Him. The one who forbids himself the lawful believes he is drawing nearer; the Qur'an says he is crossing a limit, and God does not love those who cross limits — even in His direction.

**The Islamic Middle Way**

The verse is the Qur'anic charter of the balance the Prophet ﷺ embodied. Islam has no monasticism (57:27); its ideal is not withdrawal from the world but devotion within it. The Prophet ﷺ married, ate meat and sweets, wore good clothes on Friday and the festivals, used perfume, laughed with his Companions, raced with his wife, and said, "Beloved to me of your world are women and perfume, and the coolness of my eye is in prayer" (al-Nasāʾī 3939). He said, "The religion is ease; no one makes the religion hard but that it overcomes him" (al-Bukhārī 39). And he said of the two ways of error: "Beware of *ghuluww* in religion, for those before you were destroyed by *ghuluww* in religion" (al-Nasāʾī 3057). The Christians' monks, praised in verse 82 for their humility, had invented an austerity God did not prescribe; the Muslim community is warned in verse 87 not to imitate the invention. The Qur'an's description of the community as *ummatan wasaṭan*, a middle nation (2:143), includes this: the middle between the pagan who forbids arbitrarily and the ascetic who forbids excessively, and the middle between indulgence and denial.

**The Psychology of Self-Imposed Prohibition**

Why do devout people forbid themselves the lawful? The verse's occasion suggests the answers. Sometimes from a sudden intensity of feeling — the Companions had been moved by a sermon — that seeks an outlet in drastic renunciation. Sometimes from a suspicion of pleasure as such, as though God's gifts were traps. Sometimes from a desire to *exceed* — to be more devout than the norm, and to be seen to be. And sometimes from a real misjudgment of what God wants: the belief that He is pleased by suffering for its own sake. The Prophet's ﷺ response addresses each: he is the most God-fearing of them, and he enjoys the lawful; God is not pleased by self-denial He did not command; the body, the wife, the eye, and the guest have *rights*; and turning from his Sunnah is turning from *him*. The religion he taught is one in which gratitude for the *ṭayyibāt* is itself worship — "eat of the good things We have provided you, and give thanks to God" (2:172) — and in which the pious enjoy God's gifts precisely because they know Whom to thank for them.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to examine his prohibitions. Has he made *ḥarām* — in his own mind, or in his teaching to others — anything God made lawful? Has he treated marriage, enjoyment, rest, beauty, or good food as suspect, or as obstacles to piety, when God called them *ṭayyibāt*? Has he admired forms of austerity that the Prophet ﷺ explicitly refused? The verse's two commands are the measure: do not forbid the good things God made lawful, and do not transgress. Between them lies the Sunnah — the way of the one who fasted and broke his fast, prayed and slept, and married — and the believer's task is to walk it, neither adding to God's law in the name of zeal nor subtracting from it in the name of ease. "God loves not the transgressors" — in either direction.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:88

> **Eat of that which God has provided you that is lawful and good, and reverence God, in Whom you are believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Positive Command After the Prohibition**

Verse 87 forbade the believers to forbid what God made lawful. Verse 88 turns the prohibition into a positive command: *wa-kulū mimmā razaqakumu Allāhu ḥalālan ṭayyiban* — "And eat of what God has provided you, lawful and good." The imperative *kulū*, "eat," is the Qur'an's characteristic way of affirming the goodness of creation and the legitimacy of enjoying it. The source notes the parallels: 2:168 ("O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan"), 2:172 ("O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you, and give thanks to God"), and 16:114 ("So eat of what God has provided you, lawful and good, and be grateful for God's favor"). In each, the command to eat is joined to a further command — gratitude, avoidance of Satan's footsteps, or, as here, *taqwā*. Eating is never merely eating; it is the occasion of a relationship.

**"Of What God Has Provided You" — Rizq**

*Mimmā razaqakumu Allāh* — "of what God has provided you." The word is *rizq*, provision — the sustenance that God allots to every creature. The phrasing places every lawful meal within the frame of divine provision: what the believer eats is not simply what he earned or found but what God *gave*. This reframing is the ground of the whole verse. If food is God's provision, then to eat it is to receive a gift, to refuse it (as verse 87's ascetics wished) is to refuse a gift, and to eat it with *taqwā* — with consciousness of the Giver — is to complete the gift's purpose. The source's observation about verses 87–88 together is apt: the Qur'an's stipulations on food are few, and the range of lawful foods is wide; the believers are to eat and enjoy freely. The commentators drew from the two verses the principle that the default status of food — and of things generally — is permissibility (*al-aṣl fī al-ashyāʾ al-ibāḥah*): whatever God has not forbidden is lawful, and the burden of proof lies on the one who would forbid.

**"Lawful and Good" — Ḥalālan Ṭayyiban**

The two qualifiers are the Qur'an's standard pair for permitted food, and they are not redundant. *Ḥalāl* is the legal category: what God has permitted, as opposed to what He has forbidden in verse 3 and elsewhere. *Ṭayyib* is the qualitative category: good, wholesome, pure, pleasing — as opposed to *khabīth*, foul. The Qur'an says of the Prophet ﷺ that "he makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the foul things" (7:157), which suggests that the lawful and the good coincide: God forbids only what is foul and permits only what is good. But the commentators also noted a further sense of *ṭayyib*: lawfully *acquired*. Food that is lawful in kind but obtained by theft, fraud, usury, or bribery is not *ṭayyib*, and the believer is commanded to eat only what is both lawful in itself and clean in its acquisition. The sūrah has condemned *suḥt*, unlawful gain, at verses 42, 62, and 63; verse 88's *ṭayyib* is the positive counterpart: eat what is clean, in nature and in source. The Prophet ﷺ said: "God is *ṭayyib* and accepts only the *ṭayyib*" (Muslim 1015) — and went on to describe the traveler whose prayer is not answered because his food, drink, and clothing are unlawful.

**"And Reverence God" — Wa-ttaqū Allāh**

The command to eat is immediately followed by the command to fear God: *wa-ttaqū Allāha alladhī antum bihi muʾminūn*, "and be conscious of God, in whom you believe." The juxtaposition is the verse's teaching. The permission to enjoy is not a permission to forget. The believer eats — freely, gratefully, from the wide field of the lawful — and he eats *as one conscious of God*: mindful of the Giver, careful of the limits, aware that he will be asked about the blessing. The Qur'an says: "Then you will surely be asked that Day about the delights" (102:8). *Taqwā* in the context of eating means several things: eating only the lawful and good; not exceeding into waste — "eat and drink, but do not be excessive; indeed He does not love the excessive" (7:31); remembering God's name over the food and thanking Him after it; and sharing it with those who lack.

The pairing of enjoyment and *taqwā* is the resolution of the tension that produced verse 87's ascetics. They feared that enjoyment would lead to heedlessness, and so they resolved to renounce enjoyment. The Qur'an's answer is not renunciation but *taqwā* within enjoyment: eat, and fear God. The two are not opposed; the second sanctifies the first. The believer who eats with the name of God on his lips, gratitude in his heart, and moderation in his hand has turned a meal into worship — and has done what the ascetic sought to do by renunciation, without refusing God's gift.

**"In Whom You Are Believers"**

*Alladhī antum bihi muʾminūn* — "in whom you believe." The verse ends by grounding *taqwā* in faith: fear God, whom you *believe in*. The clause is an argument: your faith itself requires this consciousness. To believe in God is to believe that He provides, that He sets limits, that He watches, and that He will ask. The one who believes these things and eats heedlessly has a faith that has not reached his table. The verse's final phrase asks the believer to bring his creed to his meals — to let what he professes about God govern what he does with God's provision.

**Eating as a Field of Faith**

The Qur'an devotes a surprising amount of attention to food — what may be eaten, how, with what consciousness — and verses 87–88 show why. Food is the most basic and constant of human needs, the point at which the body's demands and God's provision meet several times a day. It is therefore the most constant field in which faith is either practiced or neglected. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to say *bismillāh* before eating and *al-ḥamdu li-llāh* after, to eat with the right hand, to eat from what is nearest, to sit rather than recline, to not criticize food, to share it — "the food of one suffices two, and the food of two suffices four" (al-Bukhārī 5392; Muslim 2058) — and to leave a third of the stomach for breath. Each of these turns the necessity of eating into an occasion of remembrance. The verse's command — eat, and fear God — is fulfilled in these small acts, which make the believer's table a place where God is present.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse gives the believer permission and responsibility in one breath. Permission: eat what God has provided, lawful and good, without the guilt or suspicion that verse 87's ascetics felt; God's gifts are to be received. Responsibility: eat as one who believes in God — from lawful sources, in moderation, with gratitude, and with awareness that the blessing will be asked about. The believer who has absorbed the verse neither renounces the world nor is enslaved by it; he receives it from God's hand and returns it to God's service. That is the *taqwā* of the table, and it is the same *taqwā* that governs everything else.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:89

> **God will not take you to task for that which is frivolous in your oaths, but He will take you to task for the oaths you have pledged in earnest. The expiation thereof is the feeding of ten indigent people with the equivalent of that which you feed your own family, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. And whosoever finds not [the means], let him fast for three days. That is the expiation for your oaths when you have sworn [them]. But keep your oaths. Thus does God make clear unto you His signs, that haply you may give thanks.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Connection to Verses 87–88**

Verse 87 forbade the believers to forbid what God made lawful; verse 88 commanded them to eat of it. Verse 89 addresses the practical problem that follows: what of the one who has *sworn* to abstain from a lawful thing? The Companions who resolved on renunciation had, some of them, bound themselves by oath — to never eat meat, never sleep on a bed, never approach women. Verse 87 told them the renunciation was wrong; verse 89 tells them what to do about the oath. The source records al-Ṭabarī's observation that "what is frivolous in your oaths" relates most specifically to oaths taken to avoid lawful foods, following verses 87–88, while having a general application. And it records al-Qurṭubī's principle, drawn from the verse: swearing to abstain from a lawful thing does not make it forbidden in God's sight. The oath is broken, the expiation paid, and the lawful thing remains lawful.

**Two Kinds of Oath**

The verse distinguishes: *lā yuʾākhidhukumu Allāhu bi-l-laghwi fī aymānikum wa-lākin yuʾākhidhukum bi-mā ʿaqqadtumu al-aymān* — "God will not take you to task for the *laghw* in your oaths, but He will take you to task for what you have bound by oaths." *Laghw* is idle, unintentional speech — the "by God" that Arabs (and others) let slip in conversation without meaning to swear: "No, by God," "Yes, by God." The source directs the reader to 2:225, which states the same principle: "God will not take you to task for the *laghw* in your oaths, but He will take you to task for what your hearts have earned." ʿĀʾishah explained *laghw* as "a man's saying, 'No, by God,' and 'Yes, by God'" (al-Bukhārī 6663). Such speech carries no accountability and requires no expiation; God does not hold a person to what he never intended to bind himself by.

*Mā ʿaqqadtumu al-aymān* — "what you have tied by oaths": the verb *ʿaqqada*, to knot, to tie firmly, from the same root as *ʿuqūd*, the "pacts" of verse 1 with which the sūrah opened. The deliberate oath is a knot tied with intention — a binding of oneself before God to do or not do something. This oath *is* accountable, and if broken requires expiation. The source records the commentators' discussion of exactly which oaths require expiation: al-Ṭabarī reports the views that it is the frivolous oaths (meaning that God does not hold one accountable for frivolous oaths *once expiated*), the earnest oaths made with sinful intent, or the earnest oaths made and not fulfilled. The mainstream position is the last: the deliberate oath to do or refrain from something in the future, which is then broken, requires the expiation the verse describes. The source also records the important exclusion (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī): for the *yamīn ghamūs*, the "plunging" oath — a deliberate lie sworn by God about a past fact, to deceive — there is no expiation, because it is a major sin that expiation cannot cover; it "plunges" its swearer into sin and then into the Fire, and only repentance avails. The Prophet ﷺ counted "the plunging oath" among the greatest sins (al-Bukhārī 6675).

**What an Oath Is**

The source notes that an oath is swearing by God's Name — or, according to some, by the Qur'an, since swearing by anything else is not legitimate (al-Qurṭubī). The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever swears, let him swear by God or keep silent" (al-Bukhārī 6108; Muslim 1646), and "Whoever swears by other than God has committed *shirk*" (al-Tirmidhī 1535; Abū Dāwūd 3251). The reason is that an oath invokes the one sworn by as witness and guarantor; to invoke a creature in that role is to give it a status that belongs to God. The seriousness of the oath derives from this: the one who swears by God has called God to witness his word, and to break the word is to treat God's witness lightly. The source lists the Qur'an's insistence on fidelity to oaths (3:77; 38:44), its warnings against using them disingenuously (2:224; 16:91–92, 94), and its criticism of disbelievers and hypocrites who break them or use them deceptively (5:53; 6:109; 16:38; 24:53; 35:42).

**The Expiation: Three Options and a Fallback**

The verse prescribes *kaffārah* — expiation, from k-f-r, to cover — for the broken deliberate oath. The word was explained at verse 45 (the forgiver's expiation) and verse 65 (God's covering of sins); here it is a specific act that covers the breach of an oath. Three options are given, at the swearer's choice, and a fallback for the one who cannot afford them.

*Iṭʿāmu ʿasharati masākīna min awsaṭi mā tuṭʿimūna ahlīkum* — "feeding ten poor persons from the average of what you feed your families." The number is fixed at ten; the quality is fixed at the *awsaṭ*, the middle, the average — not the worst one eats nor the best, but what one's own household ordinarily eats. The source records the discussions: bread with dates and oil, or meat as the best; or a fixed measure of wheat or grain (a *mudd* per person in the Shāfiʿī and Mālikī schools, half a *ṣāʿ* in the Ḥanafī); or a full lunch and supper (al-Ṭabarī). The phrase "the average of what you feed your families" is both a standard and an ethic: the poor are to be fed as one's own family is fed, not with scraps.

*Aw kiswatuhum* — "or clothing them": one or two garments per person, some specifying a garment sufficient for prayer, some including a head covering (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī).

*Aw taḥrīru raqabah* — "or freeing a slave": literally "the liberation of a neck." The source notes the condition that the slave be sound, without physical deficiency (al-Ṭabarī). This option appears repeatedly in the Qur'an's expiations (4:92; 58:3), and it is one of the many mechanisms by which the Law worked to dissolve slavery from within: every broken oath, every accidental killing, every *ẓihār* divorce became an occasion to free a human being. In a world without slavery, this option lapses, and the other two remain.

*Fa-man lam yajid fa-ṣiyāmu thalāthati ayyām* — "and whoever does not find [the means], then fasting three days." The source records the disagreement over whether the days must be consecutive: some required it (following Ibn Masʿūd's reading, which added "consecutive"), others did not, since the verse does not stipulate it as 58:4 does for the two months of *ẓihār* (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). Fasting is available only to one who cannot afford the other three (al-Ṭabarī); it is the fallback, not an alternative.

The source records further details: that the recipients must be truly poor and not one's own dependents (al-Qurṭubī); that they should be free persons, since slaves are their masters' responsibility; and the disagreement over whether they must be Muslims — the Ḥanafī school permitting expiatory food and clothing to be given to the poor of other religious communities (al-Qurṭubī; see 2:272 and 60:8 on charity to non-Muslims). The source lists the Qur'an's other expiations for comparison: 2:184 (fasting), 4:92 (accidental killing), 5:95 (hunting during pilgrimage), 58:2–4 (*ẓihār*).

**"That Is the Expiation for Your Oaths When You Have Sworn — But Keep Your Oaths"**

*Dhālika kaffāratu aymānikum idhā ḥalaftum wa-ḥfaẓū aymānakum* — "that is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn; and guard your oaths." Two clauses that must be held together. The first establishes that the expiation *is available*: the broken oath can be repaired. The second commands: *guard* your oaths — do not swear lightly, do not break what you swore without cause, and do not treat the expiation as a license. The commentators read "guard your oaths" in three senses: be sparing in swearing; fulfill what you swear; and, if you must break an oath, pay the expiation. The Prophet ﷺ gave the governing rule:

> *"Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him do what is better and expiate his oath."* (Muslim 1650; al-Bukhārī 6622)

This ḥadīth, which the jurists applied universally, is the reconciliation of the two clauses. An oath does not bind one to a wrong or a lesser good; the one who has sworn to abstain from a lawful thing (the case of verse 87), or to do something harmful, or to withhold a kindness (the case of 2:224), should break the oath, do the better thing, and expiate. Abū Bakr had sworn not to support his relative Misṭaḥ after Misṭaḥ's part in the slander of ʿĀʾishah; when 24:22 was revealed — "let them pardon and overlook; would you not love that God should forgive you?" — he said, "Yes, by God, I love that God should forgive me," resumed his support, and expiated his oath (al-Bukhārī 4750). An oath is a knot tied before God; it may be untied before God, at the price God set, when God's own purposes require it.

**"Thus Does God Make Clear to You His Signs, That You May Give Thanks"**

*Ka-dhālika yubayyinu Allāhu lakum āyātihi laʿallakum tashkurūn* — "thus God makes clear to you His signs, that perhaps you may be grateful." The verse ends with gratitude as the fitting response to legislation — a striking pairing. Why should the law of oaths produce thanks? Because it is a *mercy*: it relieves the believer of accountability for idle speech; it provides a way out of oaths that would bind him to harm; it fixes a clear and affordable price; and it protects the sanctity of God's Name while keeping the believer from being trapped by his own tongue. The ascetics of verse 87 had bound themselves by oath to a life the Prophet ﷺ rejected; verse 89 unbinds them at the cost of feeding ten poor — and turns their misguided zeal into a meal for the hungry. A law that does this deserves gratitude.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches the believer, first, to take his oaths seriously: to swear by God alone, sparingly, and with intent to fulfill. Second, to know that a deliberate oath, once broken, requires expiation — feeding, clothing, freeing, or fasting — and to pay it. Third, to know that an oath never binds him to the worse: if he has sworn to something that God's law or God's mercy calls him to abandon, he should abandon it, do the better, and expiate. And fourth, to be grateful for a Law that neither ignores the sanctity of the oath nor makes it a trap — that guards God's Name and guards the believer's freedom at once, and turns even his mistakes into charity.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:90

> **O you who believe! Wine, and gambling, and idols, and divining arrows are but a means of defilement, of Satan's doing. So avoid it, that haply you may prosper.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Verse on Intoxicants**

This is the verse by which wine and all intoxicants were finally and completely forbidden to the Muslim community. The source situates it in the chronological sequence of the Qur'an's treatment of the subject, and the sequence should be understood, because it is a model of how the Qur'an legislates. First, in Makkah, 16:67 mentioned "the fruits of the date-palm and the vine, from which you derive strong drink and good provision" — a neutral acknowledgment of the practice as part of the description of God's bounties. Second, in Madinah, 2:219 answered a question: "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit" — a moral judgment without a prohibition, which led some Companions to abandon wine. Third, 4:43 forbade approaching prayer while intoxicated — which, given five daily prayers, restricted drinking to narrow windows and further weaned the community. Fourth, this verse: complete prohibition. The gradual approach reflects the Qur'an's understanding of human habit. ʿĀʾishah said: "Had the first thing revealed been 'Do not drink wine,' they would have said, 'We will never leave wine'" (al-Bukhārī 4993). The community was prepared, step by step, until the final command could be received — and when it came, it was obeyed instantly.

**The Occasion of Revelation**

The source records that the verse came after some Companions became drunk and fought until one was seriously injured (al-Ṭabarī). The fuller accounts describe a gathering at which, after drinking, an Anṣārī and a Muhājir quarreled; one struck the other with a camel's jawbone and split his face. In another account, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ was the one struck, and he prayed, "O God, make clear to us concerning wine," and ʿUmar prayed the same. ʿUmar's prayer is recorded as recurring: after 2:219 was revealed, he said, "O God, give us a clear statement concerning wine," and again after 4:43, and when this verse was revealed and recited to him — "will you then desist?" — he said, "We have desisted, we have desisted" (Abū Dāwūd 3670; al-Tirmidhī 3049). Another report connects the verse to an occasion when a Companion, leading the prayer while drunk, recited Sūrat al-Kāfirūn wrongly — "I worship what you worship" — which produced 4:43.

The immediate effect of the verse is among the most remarkable events in the history of the community. Anas ibn Mālik reported that he was serving wine to a gathering of Companions in Abū Ṭalḥah's house when a crier announced that wine had been forbidden. Abū Ṭalḥah said, "Go out and pour it away," and Anas poured it out, and "it flowed in the streets of Madinah" (al-Bukhārī 2464; Muslim 1980). No one finished his cup; no one asked for a grace period; the jars were broken and the wine ran in the lanes. A habit that had been woven into Arab life and poetry for centuries was abandoned in an afternoon by a community whose hearts had been prepared to obey.

**The Four Things Named**

*Al-khamr* — wine. The word is from kh-m-r, to cover, to veil (a *khimār* is a head-covering); wine is so named, as ʿUmar explained in the sermon the source cites, because it *covers* the intellect: "*Khamr* is what clouds (*khāmara*) the mind" (al-Bukhārī 4619; Muslim 3032). The source notes the legal consequence: though *khamr* technically denotes grape wine, the prohibition extends to all intoxicating beverages, by ʿUmar's definition and by the Prophet's ﷺ explicit statement: "Every intoxicant is *khamr*, and every intoxicant is forbidden" (Muslim 2003), and "Whatever intoxicates in large quantity, a small quantity of it is forbidden" (Abū Dāwūd 3681; al-Tirmidhī 1865). The source also notes, from Ibn Kathīr, that the ban covers not only consumption but sale and profit: the Prophet ﷺ said, "God has cursed wine, its drinker, its server, its seller, its buyer, its presser, the one for whom it is pressed, its carrier, and the one to whom it is carried" (Abū Dāwūd 3674). By analogy, the jurists extended the ruling to every substance that clouds the mind — the narcotics and drugs of later ages fall under the same prohibition.

*Al-maysir* — gambling. The source explains that *maysir* was a specific pre-Islamic game of chance in which arrows were drawn to divide a slaughtered camel, the losers paying for the animal, and directs the reader to 2:219. The prohibition is understood to cover all forms of gambling — every transaction in which wealth changes hands on the basis of chance, with gain for one meaning loss for another. The source notes Ibn Kathīr's report that some extended the ban to games that squander time, such as chess and backgammon, but that these were never banned in Islamic law as such (though the Shāfiʿī school disapproved of chess and the majority forbade backgammon on the basis of a ḥadīth) and remained popular among Muslims. The line the Law drew is between the game played for stakes — forbidden — and the game played without them, which is judged by whether it distracts from obligations.

*Al-anṣāb* — idols, or more precisely, as the source notes, the stone altars (*nuṣub*) on which the pagans sacrificed to their gods, mentioned in verse 3 as rendering meat unlawful. The word includes the standing stones themselves as objects of veneration.

*Al-azlām* — the divining arrows, also from verse 3: the headless arrows marked "do" and "do not" that the pagans drew at the Kaʿbah to decide their affairs — a practice of seeking guidance from chance in place of God.

**The Grouping and Its Meaning**

The verse places wine and gambling alongside idols and divining arrows — two social vices alongside two forms of *shirk* — and calls them all *rijsun min ʿamali al-shayṭān*, "defilement, of Satan's work." The grouping is instructive. Wine and gambling are not merely bad habits; they are placed in the same category as idolatry and divination, as things that belong to the pagan order Islam came to abolish. What links them? Each is a surrender of the human being's God-given faculties to something other than God: wine surrenders the intellect; gambling surrenders wealth and judgment to chance; the altars surrender worship to stone; the arrows surrender decision to fortune. All four are forms of *rijs* — filth, defilement, the impurity that clings — and all four are Satan's *work*, the means by which he draws people from God.

**"So Avoid It" — Ijtanibūhu**

The command is *fa-jtanibūhu*, "so avoid it," "keep to the side of it." The verb *ijtanaba*, from *janb*, side, means to stay away from, to shun — a stronger prohibition than "do not do it," since it forbids not only the act but its vicinity. The commentators noted that the Qur'an uses *ijtanibū* for the gravest matters: "avoid the filth of idols" (22:30), "avoid *ṭāghūt*" (16:36), "avoid much suspicion" (49:12). The command to *avoid* wine — rather than merely "do not drink" — is the basis of the Law's prohibition of sitting where wine is served, trading in it, and approaching it in any way. The singular pronoun *-hu*, "it," referring to the four things collectively as one *rijs*, treats them as a single category of defilement to be shunned as a whole.

**"That You May Prosper" — Laʿallakum Tufliḥūn**

The verse ends with *falāḥ*, success, prosperity, the word explained at verse 35: the farmer's word for the seed that splits the ground and grows. The prohibition is presented not as a deprivation but as the condition of flourishing. Wine and gambling promise pleasure and gain; the verse says that avoiding them is the way to real success — in this world, where the drinker and the gambler destroy their health, wealth, families, and reason, and in the next, where the *rijs* they carried is weighed. The call to prayer says *ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ*, "come to success," five times a day; verse 90 says that success requires leaving the cup and the dice.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer, first, to know the scope of the prohibition: every intoxicant, in every quantity, in every form of involvement — drinking, serving, selling, sitting with; and every form of gambling, however dressed — lotteries, betting, the speculative games of modern finance that are chance in a suit. Second, to understand *why*: not because pleasure is evil, but because these things are Satan's tools for clouding the mind, wasting wealth, and — as the next verse will say — sowing enmity and blocking the remembrance of God. And third, to imitate the response of the Companions: the wine flowed in the streets of Madinah the hour the verse was heard. That immediacy of obedience — no bargaining, no delay, no "one last time" — is the mark of a heart prepared, as theirs had been, to hear "will you then desist?" and answer, "We have desisted."

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:91

> **Satan desires only to sow enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of God, and from prayer. Will you, then, refrain?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason Behind the Prohibition**

Verse 90 named wine and gambling as Satan's work and commanded their avoidance. Verse 91 explains why — and the explanation is not medical or economic but spiritual and social: *innamā yurīdu al-shayṭānu an yūqiʿa baynakumu al-ʿadāwata wa-l-baghḍāʾa fī al-khamri wa-l-maysiri wa-yaṣuddakum ʿan dhikri Allāhi wa-ʿani al-ṣalāh* — "Satan only desires to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to bar you from the remembrance of God and from prayer." The restrictive *innamā*, "only," focuses the whole matter: whatever pleasures wine and gambling seem to offer, Satan's *purpose* in them is exactly two things — division among the believers, and distance from God. The verse thus gives the Qur'an's own account of the harm, and it identifies the harm at the level of the community's bonds and the soul's connection to its Lord.

**The Reasoning of the Law**

The verse is a rare and important instance of the Qur'an stating the rationale (*ʿillah*) of a prohibition explicitly. The jurists drew on it to establish that the prohibition of intoxicants is not arbitrary but grounded in identifiable harms, and that anything producing the same harms falls under the same ruling — which is the basis of the extension to all intoxicants and all forms of gambling. But the verse also teaches something about how the Qur'an wants its commands understood: not as bare decrees but as protections. God forbids wine *because* it does this to you. The believer who understands the reason obeys not from fear alone but from agreement — he sees what the prohibition protects and wants it protected.

**"Enmity and Hatred Among You"**

The first harm is *al-ʿadāwah wa-l-baghḍāʾ*, enmity and hatred — the exact pair the sūrah said God cast among the Christians (v. 14) and the Jews (v. 64) as a consequence of their neglect of His covenant. The repetition is deliberate and alarming: what befell the earlier communities as a *punishment*, Satan seeks to produce among the Muslims *through wine and gambling*. The occasion of verse 90 illustrated the mechanism: Companions who loved one another drank, quarreled, and split one another's faces with camel-bones. Wine loosens the restraints that keep enmity in check — the tongue says what it should not, the hand strikes what it should not, and the morning finds friendships broken. Gambling produces enmity by its structure: every gain is another's loss; the loser resents the winner; the winner suspects the loser; and money that should have bound them in trade or charity is instead the object of a contest that leaves one of them despoiled. The community that verse 55 described as bound by *walāyah* — mutual protection and love — is dissolved by these two things into resentment.

The verse's *baynakum*, "among you," should be noticed. Satan's target is not merely the individual drinker or gambler but the *relations* between believers. The harm is social before it is personal. A community is held together by trust, restraint, and goodwill; wine destroys restraint, gambling destroys trust, and both destroy goodwill.

**"And Bar You from the Remembrance of God and from Prayer"**

The second harm is *yaṣuddakum ʿan dhikri Allāhi wa-ʿani al-ṣalāh* — "he bars you from the remembrance of God and from prayer." *Ṣadda*, to turn away, to block, to bar — the verb the Qur'an uses of those who "bar from the way of God." Wine bars from remembrance because the clouded mind cannot remember; the drunk forgets God as he forgets everything, and the habitual drinker forgets Him even when sober, because his heart has been trained toward the cup. Gambling bars from remembrance because it consumes the attention utterly — the gambler thinks of nothing but the game, the odds, the next stake; his heart is in the dice, not with God.

And both bar from *prayer* specifically. The verse names *al-ṣalāh* separately after *dhikr*, though prayer is the greatest remembrance, to stress the point: these two things cause the believer to miss the prayer — the drunk who cannot stand for it or recites it wrongly (the occasion of 4:43), the gambler who cannot leave the game when the call is heard. Prayer is the believer's connection to God five times a day; anything that severs it severs the lifeline. The commentators observed that the two harms are related: enmity among the believers and neglect of prayer feed each other, for the prayer in congregation is the daily renewal of brotherhood, and the one who misses it loses both God and his brothers.

**Satan's Method: The Small Door**

The verse reveals Satan's method, and the revelation is applicable far beyond wine and gambling. He does not approach the believer with an invitation to hate his brothers or abandon his prayer — such an invitation would be refused. He approaches with a *cup* — a pleasant thing, a social thing, a thing that seems harmless — and through the cup he obtains the hatred and the abandoned prayer. The verse names the *means* (wine and gambling) and the *end* (enmity and distance from God), and it teaches the believer to judge the means by the end. Whatever in his life produces enmity among believers and bars him from remembrance and prayer — whatever it is, however it is dressed — is Satan's work in the sense of this verse, and the ruling on it follows. The scholars applied this to everything from excessive entertainment to obsessive commerce: the test is what it does to one's brothers and one's prayer.

**"Will You, Then, Refrain?"**

*Fa-hal antum muntahūn* — "so are you going to desist?" The verse ends not with a command but with a question, and the form is significant. After naming the four defilements, commanding their avoidance, and explaining the harm, the Qur'an asks: *well, will you stop?* The question is a rhetorical demand — stronger than an imperative, because it places the burden on the hearer to answer. It implies that the case has been made in full and that no reasonable person, having heard it, could answer anything but yes. The source records ʿUmar's answer, and it is the answer of the whole community: *intahaynā, intahaynā* — "We have desisted, we have desisted" (Abū Dāwūd 3670). The question was asked once; the answer was given at once; and the wine ran in the streets.

The question also carries a note of expectation and even of tenderness. God does not say "stop or else"; He asks, as one asks a person whom one trusts to do the right thing once he understands: *now that you know, will you stop?* The believer's honor is engaged; his understanding is credited; and his answer is awaited.

**Enmity and Hatred: The Sūrah's Recurring Concern**

The source notes that intra-communal enmity and hatred are described elsewhere in the sūrah as the fate of the Christians (v. 14) and the Jews (v. 64) for their forgetfulness and disobedience. Verse 91's warning that Satan seeks the same for the Muslims through wine and gambling closes a circle. The earlier communities were divided as a punishment for abandoning God's remembrance; the Muslims are warned that wine and gambling are Satan's tools to produce both the abandonment and the division. The sūrah's teaching is consistent: a community stays united by staying with God, and whatever separates it from God separates its members from one another.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to see wine and gambling — and everything like them — as Satan sees them: not as pleasures but as instruments, whose purpose is to set him against his brothers and cut him off from his Lord. It asks him to judge every habit by the two tests the verse supplies: does it breed enmity among the believers? does it bar me from remembrance and prayer? And it asks him, having understood, the question it asked the Companions: *will you desist?* The Companions answered with their jars broken and the wine in the lanes. The verse awaits every reader's answer — and the answer is given not in words but in what he does with the cup, the dice, and every other small door through which the enemy seeks the two great harms.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:92

> **Obey God and obey the Messenger, and be wary. But if you turn away, then know that only the clear proclamation is incumbent upon Our Messenger.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Seal on the Prohibition**

Verses 90–91 forbade wine and gambling, explained the harm, and asked, "Will you then desist?" Verse 92 follows with a general command that seals the prohibition and lifts it into the wider frame of obedience: *wa-aṭīʿū Allāha wa-aṭīʿū al-rasūla wa-ḥdharū* — "And obey God and obey the Messenger, and be on your guard." The source records the reading of al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī that the command, though general in form, is meant here to encourage obedience specifically to the prohibitions of verses 90–91. The structure is characteristic of the Qur'an: a specific ruling is given, its reason explained, and then the believer is reminded that the ruling rests on the authority of God and His Messenger and must be obeyed on that basis — not only because he agrees with the reason, but because God commanded it.

**"Obey God and Obey the Messenger"**

The source lists the many places where the paired command occurs (3:32, 132; 4:59; 8:1, 20, 46; 24:54; 33:33; 47:33; 58:13; 64:12; and see 7:156–157; 59:7). The repetition of the verb — *aṭīʿū Allāha wa-aṭīʿū al-rasūla*, "obey God and obey the Messenger," rather than "obey God and the Messenger" — was noted by the commentators as significant. It establishes the Messenger's commands as an independent source of obligation: the believer obeys the Messenger not only when he transmits the Qur'an but in everything he commands, because "whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God" (4:80), and "what the Messenger gives you, take; and what he forbids you, refrain from" (59:7). The prohibition of wine is a case in point. The Qur'an forbade *khamr*; the Messenger ﷺ specified that every intoxicant is *khamr*, that a small amount of what intoxicates in large amount is forbidden, that the sale and carriage of wine are forbidden, and that the drinker is to be punished. These specifications are binding by the authority of this verse's second *aṭīʿū*.

The doubled command is also the Qur'anic foundation of the Sunnah's authority in general — the principle that Islam is not the Qur'an alone but the Qur'an as taught, explained, and applied by the Prophet ﷺ. The one who says "I follow only the Qur'an" has disobeyed the Qur'an's own command to obey the Messenger, and has left himself without the guidance by which the Qur'an's commands become livable: the details of the prayer, the measures of *zakāh*, the rites of pilgrimage, and the definitions of *khamr* are all in the Sunnah.

**"And Be Wary" — Wa-ḥdharū**

*Iḥdharū*, "be on your guard, beware," from ḥ-dh-r, caution, vigilance. The word was used in verse 41 ("if you are not given it, *beware*") and verse 49 ("*beware* of them lest they tempt you"). Here it is absolute — beware — without a stated object, and the commentators supplied it from context: beware of disobedience; beware of Satan's tricks described in verse 91; beware of returning to what you have been commanded to leave. The verb's placement after the double command to obey suggests that obedience requires vigilance: the prohibited thing does not disappear when it is prohibited; it remains available, attractive, and defended by Satan's whispering, and the believer must guard himself against it actively. The wine that ran in the streets of Madinah could be pressed again; the command to beware is the guard set against the return.

**"But If You Turn Away"**

*Fa-in tawallaytum* — "but if you turn away." The verse contemplates the possibility of disobedience and states its consequence — not, as one might expect, punishment, but a clarification of responsibility: *fa-ʿlamū annamā ʿalā rasūlinā al-balāghu al-mubīn*, "then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear proclamation." The source lists the parallel verses in which the Prophet ﷺ is reminded that his only duty is to deliver the message clearly (3:20; 5:99; 13:40; 16:82; 29:18; 36:17; 42:48; 64:12) and that he has no control over others' response and is not responsible for those who remain unmoved (4:80; 6:107; 42:6, 48).

The statement does two things at once. To the Prophet ﷺ, it is consolation and release: he has conveyed the prohibition clearly; if they turn away, the failure is theirs, not his. To the believers, it is a warning with a subtle edge: if you turn away, do not imagine that the Messenger's task was to make you obey — his task was to make the command *clear*, and that has been done; the clarity of the proclamation removes every excuse. The word *mubīn*, clear, manifest, is the key. A command that was obscure might excuse disobedience; a command that is *clear* — as the prohibition of wine was made clear, after ʿUmar's repeated prayer for exactly that clarity — leaves the one who turns away with nothing to plead. The Prophet ﷺ said at the Farewell Pilgrimage, "Have I conveyed?" — and the community's "Yes" was the acknowledgment that the *balāgh mubīn* had been delivered and that responsibility now rested with them.

**The Division of Responsibility**

The verse states a principle of great importance for the believer's understanding of religion: the Messenger conveys; the hearer chooses; God judges. The Messenger is not a policeman charged with enforcing compliance, nor a magician charged with producing faith; he is a *conveyor* (*muballigh*), and his responsibility ends with clear delivery. The hearer is not a passive recipient whose faith is manufactured for him; he is a moral agent who, having received a clear message, chooses to obey or to turn away — and bears the consequence. And God, who sent the Messenger and gave the hearer his freedom, judges the choice. This distribution protects the Messenger from the crushing burden of others' souls (which verse 68 addressed: "grieve not for the disbelieving people") and protects the hearer from the illusion that someone else's clarity can substitute for his own obedience.

**The Verse in the Passage**

Verse 92 closes the unit that began at verse 87. The unit moved from the prohibition of forbidding lawful things (87), to the command to eat and fear God (88), to the law of oaths (89), to the prohibition of wine and gambling and its rationale (90–91), and now to the general command of obedience and the statement of the Messenger's responsibility (92). Verse 93 will address a question the prohibition raised — what of those who drank before it was revealed, and those who died having drunk? — and will answer with the assurance that there is no blame on those who believed and did right in what they consumed before the prohibition. The passage as a whole is a lesson in how divine law works: God legislates through His Messenger; the Messenger conveys clearly; the believer obeys, guards himself, and bears responsibility; and God, in His mercy, does not hold anyone to a law before it was revealed.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks three things of the believer. First, obedience — to God, and to the Messenger as an independent authority whose Sunnah binds; the one who accepts the Qur'an's prohibition of wine and rejects the Sunnah's definition of it has obeyed half the verse. Second, vigilance — *iḥdharū* — the active guarding of oneself against the return of what was forbidden, because prohibition removes the permission but not the temptation. And third, the acceptance of responsibility: the message has been made clear; the Messenger has done his part; there is no one left to blame. The believer who turns away turns away from a *balāgh mubīn*, and the verse asks him to *know* this — to have no illusion, on the Day the accounts are taken, that the clarity was lacking.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:93

> **There is no blame upon those who believe and perform righteous deeds for that which they have eaten, so long as they are reverent, and believe, and perform righteous deeds, then are reverent and believe, and then are reverent and virtuous. And God loves the virtuous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question That Prompted the Verse**

When wine was forbidden by verses 90–91, the Companions faced a painful question. The prohibition came late in the Madinan period — well after Badr and Uḥud — and many good Muslims had drunk wine throughout their lives and died before the prohibition. Some had fallen as martyrs at Badr and Uḥud with wine in their bodies. What of them? Had they died in sin? The source records that this verse was revealed in answer to the Companions' concern (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī). The reports name those who asked: some said, "What of our brothers who died drinking it?"; others, "What of those who were killed at Badr and Uḥud?" The verse's answer is a complete reassurance: *laysa ʿalā alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti junāḥun fī-mā ṭaʿimū* — "There is no blame on those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they consumed" — before the prohibition, so long as they were God-fearing believers who did right.

**The Principle: No Law Before Its Revelation**

The verse states a foundational principle of divine justice: God does not hold people accountable for a prohibition before it is revealed. The source cites the parallels. In 2:275, those who practiced usury before its prohibition were permitted to keep what they had gained: "whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists may have what is past." In 2:143, after the change of the *qiblah*, the Companions worried about those who had died praying toward Jerusalem, and the verse answered: "God would not let your faith go to waste." The principle is stated generally in 17:15 — "We never punish until We have sent a messenger" — and 4:22–23, which forbid marriages the pagans had permitted, "except what has already passed." God's law binds from the moment it is made known; what preceded is covered by His mercy. This principle protects the believer from a crushing retroactive guilt and reflects the nature of the Law as *guidance*, not as a trap.

For the Companions who had died, the answer was complete: they had believed, done righteous deeds, feared God, and obeyed every command they had received; the wine they drank was lawful when they drank it; and they died as *muḥsinūn*, whom God loves.

**The Misreading the Verse Invited**

The source records an episode that shows how a verse of mercy can be twisted. Some reasoned as follows: the verse says there is no blame on believers for what they consumed "so long as they fear God and believe and do righteous deeds"; and verse 91 forbade wine because it produces enmity and neglect of prayer; therefore a believer who can drink without these effects — who remains God-fearing, believing, and righteous — incurs no blame. This argument was actually made in the first century. Qudāmah ibn Maẓʿūn, a Companion, was brought before ʿUmar for drinking, and defended himself with this verse. ʿUmar answered: "You have misread it. Had you feared God, you would have avoided what God forbade" — and had him flogged (ʿAbd al-Razzāq; al-Bayhaqī). Later, in the time of ʿAlī, a group in Kūfah declared wine lawful on the same reasoning; ʿAlī consulted the Companions, and ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās concluded that whoever held wine lawful after the prohibition should be asked to repent, and if he refused, executed as an apostate — for he had denied a ruling established by clear text and consensus.

The source's judgment is exact: the misreading is contradicted by the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ, by the consensus (*ijmāʿ*) of the community on the absolute prohibition of wine, and by the universally accepted interpretation of the verse as concerning those who drank *before* the prohibition (al-Rāzī). The verse's own words defeat the misreading: it exempts those who "fear God" — and, as ʿUmar said, the God-fearing do not drink what God forbade. The one who drinks after the prohibition has, by that act, failed the verse's first condition. The episode is a lasting warning about the method of reading scripture: a verse of mercy is not a license to violate a verse of command; the two are read together, and the Sunnah and consensus fix the meaning.

**The Threefold Structure of the Verse**

The verse's most striking feature is its triple repetition of *taqwā*, each time paired with something: *idhā mā ttaqaw wa-āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti* — "when they fear God and believe and do righteous deeds"; *thumma ttaqaw wa-āmanū* — "then fear God and believe"; *thumma ttaqaw wa-aḥsanū* — "then fear God and do good." The source presents the interpretations, and they deserve to be set out.

The first and most illuminating reading connects the three pairings to the three degrees of the ḥadīth of Gabriel (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8): *īmān* (right belief), *islām* (submission in the obligatory acts, which most understand by "righteous deeds"), and *iḥsān* (excellence — "to worship God as if you see Him"). The verse names all three: belief, righteous deeds, and *iḥsān*, each grounded in *taqwā*. Some commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) specify: "righteous deeds" is the observance of all obligations and prohibitions; "doing good" (*iḥsān*) is the performance of supererogatory acts by which one draws nearer to God — echoing the ḥadīth qudsī cited at verse 35:

> *"My servant draws near to Me with nothing more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him; and My servant continues to draw near to Me with supererogatory works until I love him."* (al-Bukhārī 6502)

On this reading, the verse describes an ascent: from *taqwā* with faith and obligatory works, to *taqwā* with confirmed faith, to *taqwā* with excellence — and it ends where the ḥadīth qudsī ends: "God loves the *muḥsinīn*." The source notes al-Rāzī's judgment that to have earned God's love in this way is the highest spiritual degree and the noblest station.

A second reading (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī) takes the three *taqwā*s temporally: mindfulness of what was prohibited in the past (the wine they drank before the ban — they were not blameworthy, for it was not yet forbidden), what is prohibited in the present (they must now avoid it), and what will be prohibited in the future (they must be ready to obey whatever comes). A third reading takes them by gravity: fear of disbelief, fear of major sins, fear of minor sins. A fourth takes the repetition as emphasis — the Qur'an's way of stressing that *taqwā* is the condition of everything.

These readings converge on a single point: the exemption for past consumption is granted to people whose lives are defined by *taqwā* — the continuous, deepening, all-encompassing consciousness of God that made them obey every command as it came. The verse describes not a loophole but a character.

**"And God Loves the Virtuous"**

*Wa-Allāhu yuḥibbu al-muḥsinīn* — the verse ends, as verses 13 and 85 ended, with God's love for those who do what is beautiful. The source notes the other places where God is said to love the *muḥsinīn* (2:195; 3:134, 148; 5:13). Here the phrase is the verse's climax and its deepest reassurance. The Companions had asked whether their dead brothers were blamed; the verse answers not only "no blame" but "God *loves* them." The martyrs of Badr who had drunk wine when it was lawful had believed, feared God, obeyed, and given their lives; they were *muḥsinūn*, and the wine in their bodies did not diminish God's love by an atom.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches three lessons. First, the mercy of God's law: it does not reach backward to condemn what was done in obedience before the command came; the believer is judged by his response to what he knew. Second, the danger of misreading mercy as license: the one who uses a verse of exemption to justify what a clear command forbids has, as ʿUmar told Qudāmah, misread it — and has failed the verse's own condition of *taqwā*. Third, the shape of the religious life the verse describes: *taqwā* joined to faith, to obedience, and finally to *iḥsān*, in an ascent that ends in God's love. The believer should ask where he stands on that ascent — and should take heart that the verse's structure is a ladder, and that every rung of it is *taqwā*, which is available to anyone who chooses it.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:94

> **O you who believe! God will surely try you with something of the game you obtain with your hands and your spears, so that God may know the one who fears Him unseen. So whosoever transgresses after that, his shall be a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Return to the Pilgrimage**

The sūrah opened with the sanctities of the pilgrimage — the forbidding of hunting while in *iḥrām* (v. 1), the sacred month, the offerings, the garlands, the sanctuary (v. 2) — and now, after its long central section, it returns to the same theme with a new emphasis. Verses 94–96 treat the prohibition of hunting during pilgrim sanctity in detail; verse 97 the Kaʿbah as a support for mankind. Verse 94 introduces the subject with a striking announcement: *la-yabluwannakumu Allāhu bi-shayʾin mina al-ṣaydi tanāluhu aydīkum wa-rimāḥukum* — "God will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach." The prohibition of hunting in *iḥrām* is presented not merely as a rule but as a *test* — a deliberately designed trial of the believers' fear of God.

**The Occasion**

The commentators place the verse in the context of the pilgrimage of al-Ḥudaybiyah (6/628) or the ʿUmrah of the following year, when the Muslims, in *iḥrām*, found the region around Makkah teeming with game — so abundant, the reports say, that wild animals and birds came close enough to be taken by hand, and the pilgrims could have caught them without effort or pursuit. The abundance was itself the test: game that must be hunted at a distance requires resolve to pursue, and its prohibition is easy; game that walks up to one's tent and can be seized by hand requires only the absence of restraint, and its prohibition tests restraint at its most basic. The source explains the phrase "with your hands and your spears" accordingly (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī): game obtained by hand refers to small game — birds, eggs, young animals that cannot escape; game obtained by spears refers to larger animals. The verse names both extremes: the trivial catch that takes no effort and the substantial catch that takes skill, and it forbids the pilgrim both.

**The Nature of the Test**

The verse uses the verb *balā*, to test, the root of *balāʾ*, trial — the same word used in verse 48 ("that He might test you in what He has given you"). The Qur'an's tests are of many kinds: with fear, hunger, and loss (2:155); with good and evil (21:35); with wealth and children (8:28). This test is of a distinctive kind: a test by *abundance of the easily available forbidden thing*. The believer is placed in a situation where the forbidden is at hand, effortless, unobserved, and attractive — and the only barrier is his fear of God. The commentators compared it to the test of the Sabbath-breakers in 7:163, whose fish "came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come" — a test designed so that the forbidden was most abundant exactly when it was forbidden. The Israelites failed that test by their trick with the traps; the Muslims in *iḥrām* were being given its counterpart.

**"So That God May Know Who Fears Him Unseen"**

*Li-yaʿlama Allāhu man yakhāfuhu bi-l-ghayb* — "so that God may know who fears Him in the unseen." The purpose of the test is stated, and it contains two points that need explanation.

First, "so that God may know." God's knowledge is eternal and complete; He does not learn by testing. The commentators explained the phrase, as they explained its parallels (2:143; 3:142; 47:31), in one of two ways: God's knowledge here means His knowledge of the thing *as it actually occurs* — the knowledge that establishes the reality of the deed and forms the basis of reward and punishment, so that no one is judged on what God knew he *would* do but on what he *did*; or "that God may know" means "that God may make known" — to the person himself, to others, and as evidence on the Day of Judgment — who fears Him. Either way, the test's function is to *manifest* the fear of God in action, so that it becomes a reality in the world and a witness in the record.

Second, "who fears Him *bi-l-ghayb*" — in the unseen, unobserved, in private. The source notes this precisely (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī): the pilgrim is to observe the prohibition even when out of sight of others, thus demonstrating that he fears God even when no human eye is on him. This is the heart of the verse and the definition of *taqwā*. The fear of God that operates only when observed is fear of people, not of God; the fear that operates in solitude — when the bird is in reach, the tent is empty, and no one would ever know — is the real thing. The Qur'an praises those "who fear their Lord in the unseen" (21:49; 35:18; 36:11; 50:33; 67:12), and the Prophet ﷺ named among the seven whom God shades on the Day when there is no shade but His "a man who remembers God in solitude and his eyes overflow" (al-Bukhārī 660; Muslim 1031). The abundant game around the pilgrims' tents was a laboratory for exactly this quality.

**The Method of Divine Testing**

The verse teaches something about how God tests. He does not always test by making the forbidden hard to reach; sometimes He tests by making it easy. The Companions had left their homes, taken on *iḥrām*, and journeyed toward the Kaʿbah with hearts full of devotion; and God surrounded them with game they could take by hand. The test was not whether they *could* resist — of course they could — but whether they *would*, when resistance was the only thing standing between them and the easy catch. This is the shape of most of the believer's tests in ordinary life: the forbidden is rarely hard to obtain; it is easy, available, and private, and the whole test lies in whether the fear of God operates when nothing else does.

**"Whosoever Transgresses After That, His Is a Painful Punishment"**

*Fa-mani ʿtadā baʿda dhālika fa-lahu ʿadhābun alīm* — "so whoever transgresses after that, for him is a painful punishment." The verb *iʿtadā*, transgress, cross the limit, is the sūrah's word once more. "After that" — after the announcement that this is a test, after the clarity of the prohibition, after the statement of its purpose. The one who hunts in *iḥrām* after this verse does so knowing that he is failing a test God announced in advance. That knowledge aggravates the transgression: he was told what the test was, and he failed it anyway. Verse 95 will give the expiation for the one who does so; but the expiation covers the legal consequence, and this verse's "painful punishment" awaits the one whose transgression expressed a real contempt for God's limits.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to recognize the tests of easy availability in his own life and to understand what they are for. The unobserved opportunity — the private access to what is forbidden, the moment when no one would know — is not an accident; it is the situation in which the quality God is looking for can appear. The verse names that quality: fearing Him *in the unseen*. Every such moment is a small *iḥrām* with game walking up to the tent. The believer who restrains his hand in that moment has done what the pilgrims of al-Ḥudaybiyah were asked to do, and has shown — to God, to himself, and to the record — that his fear of God is real. And the verse's warning stands for the one who reaches out: "after that" — after knowing — the transgression is a failure of the one test that matters.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:95

> **O you who believe! Slaughter not any game while you are in a state of pilgrim sanctity. And [for] the one among you who slaughters it intentionally, a recompense of cattle, the like of that which he slaughtered, as judged by two just men among you, as an offering brought to the Kaʿbah, or the expiation of feeding the indigent, or the equivalent of this in fasting, that he may taste the evil consequences of his affair. God has forgiven that which is past, but whosoever relapses, God will take vengeance upon him, and God is Mighty, Possessor of Vengeance.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Explicit Prohibition and Its Expiation**

Verse 94 announced the test; verse 95 states the rule and its remedy. *Lā taqtulū al-ṣayda wa-antum ḥurum* — "Do not kill game while you are in *iḥrām*." The prohibition, which verse 1 had stated in passing ("game not being lawful to you while you are in pilgrim sanctity"), is now given in full legal form, with the penalty for violation and the conditions of its application. The source notes that the ban applies to those performing either the major or the minor pilgrimage (*ḥajj* or *ʿumrah*) — to anyone in the state of *iḥrām*.

**What Is Prohibited: The Killing**

The verb is *lā taqtulū*, "do not kill." The source draws the legal consequence (al-Qurṭubī): it is the taking of the animal's life that is prohibited, not the eating as such; if other pilgrims eat from game killed by someone else, no expiation is due from them — though verse 96 will complicate this question, as the commentary there will show. The prohibition covers wild land animals that are hunted for food; it does not cover domestic animals, which may be slaughtered and eaten in *iḥrām*, nor — as the source notes — animals that threaten human life. The Prophet ﷺ named five (in some versions six) creatures that may be killed even in *iḥrām* and even in the sanctuary: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse, and the rabid dog (al-Bukhārī 1829; Muslim 1198) — with the snake and, by analogy, the lion, wolf, and other predators added. The jurists derived the principle: what is harmful by nature may be killed; what is hunted for food or sport may not.

**The Occasion**

The source records that the verse was revealed after one of the Anṣār, performing *ʿumrah* in 628, killed a wild donkey (al-Qurṭubī). Other reports connect the general rule to the well-known incident of Abū Qatādah, who, not being in *iḥrām* while his companions were, hunted a wild donkey and brought it to them; they hesitated to eat it and asked the Prophet ﷺ, who asked whether any of them had pointed to it or helped in the hunt; when they said no, he said, "Then eat what remains of its meat" (al-Bukhārī 1824; Muslim 1196) — a ḥadīth that will bear on verse 96.

**"Intentionally" — Mutaʿammidan**

The expiation is prescribed for *man qatalahu minkum mutaʿammidan*, "whoever of you kills it intentionally." The source notes the implication: the expiation is required from the one who violates the ban deliberately, as opposed to accidentally or having forgotten that he is in *iḥrām*. The commentators divided on the case of the accidental or forgetful killer. The majority (Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah) held that the expiation is due even for accidental killing — by analogy to the blood-money for accidental homicide (4:92), and because the verse's "intentionally" describes the usual case without excluding the others, and the sanctity of the game is violated regardless of intent. Others (Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭāwūs, Aḥmad in one report, and the Ẓāhirīs) held to the verse's letter: expiation is for the deliberate killer only, and the accidental killer owes nothing but repentance. Both positions have strong support; the majority view prevailed in practice as the more cautious.

**The Recompense: Three Options**

The verse prescribes *jazāʾ*, recompense, in three forms.

First, *mithlu mā qatala mina al-naʿam*, "the like of what he killed, from cattle" — a domestic animal equivalent to the game killed, offered as a sacrifice at the Kaʿbah. The source records that the equivalence was understood either as an animal of similar size and kind (an ostrich for a camel, a wild donkey or cow for a cow, a gazelle for a goat, a rabbit for a young goat, as the Companions ruled in recorded cases) or as the monetary equivalent (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). The animal is *hadyan bāligha al-kaʿbah*, "an offering reaching the Kaʿbah" — brought to the Makkan sanctuary, slaughtered there, and distributed among its poor (al-Jalālayn, al-Qurṭubī).

Second, *aw kaffāratun ṭaʿāmu masākīn*, "or an expiation of feeding the poor" — the value of the equivalent animal spent on food for the needy.

Third, *aw ʿadlu dhālika ṣiyāman*, "or the equivalent of that in fasting" — one day's fast for each measure (*mudd*, about half a liter) of food that the equivalent would have provided (al-Qurṭubī).

The verse's *aw*, "or," gives the killer a choice among the three, according to most jurists, though some ordered them by priority. The source notes that feeding and fasting are also expiations for broken oaths (v. 89), but that here, because the context is the pilgrimage, the primary expiation is the offering at the Kaʿbah.

**"As Judged by Two Just Men Among You"**

*Yaḥkumu bihi dhawā ʿadlin minkum* — "two possessors of justice among you shall judge it." The equivalence of the game and the domestic animal is not left to the killer's own assessment but is determined by two just men — persons of known probity and, the jurists added, knowledge of animals. The source notes that their estimation is also the basis of the other two options: the value they set determines how much food is given or how many days are fasted. The requirement is a small model of Islamic judicial procedure: an interested party does not judge his own case; the judgment is entrusted to the just; and two are required, not one, for the same reason two witnesses are required in most matters. ʿUmar, asked by a man who had killed a gazelle in *iḥrām* what he owed, called ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf and judged with him that he owed a goat — and when the man went away saying that the Commander of the Faithful could not decide by himself, ʿUmar called him back and recited this verse: "two just men" — and said, "I am ʿUmar and this is ʿAbd al-Raḥmān" (al-Bayhaqī). The caliph submitted to the verse's procedure.

**"That He May Taste the Evil Consequence of His Affair"**

*Li-yadhūqa wabāla amrih* — "that he may taste the *wabāl* of his affair." *Wabāl* is the heavy, harmful consequence of an act — from *wābil*, a heavy downpour. The expiation is not merely restitution; it is designed to make the transgressor *feel* the weight of what he did. The animal he must offer, the poor he must feed, or the days he must fast are the taste of his transgression's consequence — a lesson written into the remedy so that the remedy corrects as well as covers.
