## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:103

> **God has not established baḥīrah, or sāʾibah, or waṣīlah, or ḥām. But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God, and most of them do not understand.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Repudiation of Pagan Consecrations**

The verse names four Arabic terms — *baḥīrah*, *sāʾibah*, *waṣīlah*, *ḥām* — and declares that God did not institute any of them: *mā jaʿala Allāhu min baḥīratin wa-lā sāʾibatin wa-lā waṣīlatin wa-lā ḥām*. The terms refer, the source explains, to kinds of camels (and in some cases sheep) that the pre-Islamic Arabs regarded as sacred and dedicated to their gods. Such animals could not be ridden, milked, slaughtered, or burdened; they were released to wander and graze freely, and anyone who came upon them was to leave them alone. The verse repudiates the whole institution in a single sentence, and then diagnoses it: it is a lie fabricated against God by people who do not understand.

**The Four Categories**

The source records the commentators' definitions, noting that they differ and overlap — the customs varied by tribe, and the Muslim scholars of the second century were already reconstructing a vanished practice. The *baḥīrah* (from b-ḥ-r, to slit, split open) was a she-camel that had borne a certain number of offspring — five, according to al-Qurṭubī, the fifth being male according to al-Rāzī — whose ear was then slit as a mark of consecration; she was released, her milk was reserved for the idols (or for men only, forbidden to women), and no one might ride her or shear her. The *sāʾibah* (from s-y-b, to let loose, to flow) was a she-camel released by her owner as a votive offering — in thanks for recovery from illness, for safe return from a journey, or for some good fortune (al-Rāzī); the source also records the report that *sāʾibah* could refer to a slave freed completely, with all ties to the former master severed. The *waṣīlah* (from w-ṣ-l, to join, connect) was a ewe or she-camel that bore female offspring in succession, or a female and a male together (al-Jalālayn, al-Rāzī) — the female "joined" to her brother and so exempted him from being sacrificed to the gods, or the female herself consecrated for her valuable milk. The *ḥām* (from ḥ-m-y, to protect) was the only male of the four: a stud camel who had sired a certain number of offspring (al-Jalālayn), or whose offspring had themselves sired (al-Rāzī); his back was declared "protected," and he could not be ridden, loaded, or barred from pasture or water.

The source notes that these animals were marked by slit ears so that people would recognize their status, and points to 4:119, where Satan vows: "I will command them, and they will slit the ears of cattle; and I will command them, and they will alter God's creation." The verse in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ names the practice as Satan's project; verse 103 names it as a lie against God.

**Why the Qur'an Objects**

The customs might seem harmless — even pious, since they express gratitude and release animals from labor. The source identifies the three grounds on which the Qur'an condemns them.

First, they were *idolatrous in orientation*: the animals were consecrated to the gods, their milk and use dedicated to the idols. The source records al-Ṭabarī's report that these practices were among the first ways the Arabs deviated from the religion of Abraham. The Prophet ﷺ said, "I saw ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy al-Khuzāʿī dragging his intestines in the Fire; he was the first to release the *sāʾibah*" (al-Bukhārī 3521; Muslim 2856) — for ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy was, in the Arab memory, the man who brought idols to Makkah and instituted the customs of their worship. The consecrated camel was the first crack in Abraham's monotheism, and the verse closes it.

Second, they *arbitrarily restricted the good things God had provided*. The source connects the verse to 5:87–88 and their commentary — the prohibition of forbidding what God has made lawful — and to the parallel critiques in 6:136–139, 143–145 and 10:59: "Say: Have you considered what provision God has sent down for you, and you have made some of it unlawful and some lawful? Say: Did God permit you, or do you fabricate against God?" A camel is a *ṭayyib*, a good thing God created for riding, milk, meat, and burden; to declare it untouchable by human decree is to forbid what God permitted, which the sūrah has treated as a sin in its own right.

Third — and this is the verse's own charge — the pagans *represented their own inventions as divine law*. The source records Ibn Kathīr's point: they claimed that these consecrations were required by God or were means of drawing near to Him. This is what the verse calls *yaftarūna ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhib*, "they fabricate the lie against God" — the sin of attributing to God what He did not say. The source lists the Qur'an's many condemnations of this sin (3:24, 93–94; 6:21, 93, 137–140, 144; 7:37, 152; 10:17–18, 59–60, 69; 16:56, 116), and notes that it is often connected with the religious innovations of earlier communities. The Qur'an regards it as among the gravest of sins: "Who does greater wrong than one who fabricates a lie against God?" (6:21, 93, 144; 7:37; 10:17; 11:18; 18:15; 29:68; 61:7).

**"God Has Not Established"**

The verse's phrasing — *mā jaʿala Allāhu*, "God did not make, did not institute" — is precisely aimed at the third charge. It does not say "these animals are not sacred" but "God did not make them so." The point is the *source* of the ruling. Only God legislates the sacred; the pagans had usurped that prerogative, inventing sanctities and then attributing them to God to give them force. The sūrah has treated this usurpation from its first verses — "God decrees whatsoever He desires" (v. 1) — and has condemned it in the People of the Book who "take their rabbis and monks as lords" by accepting their permissions and prohibitions (9:31, as the Prophet ﷺ explained to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim; al-Tirmidhī 3095). Verse 103 condemns it in the Arabs. The principle is the same: the boundary between *ḥalāl* and *ḥarām* is God's to draw, and whoever draws it himself and signs God's name to it has told a lie against God.

**"But Those Who Disbelieve Fabricate Lies Against God"**

*Wa-lākinna alladhīna kafarū yaftarūna ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhib* — the *lākinna*, "but rather," marks the true origin of the customs: not God, but the disbelievers' fabrication. The verb *iftarā* (from f-r-y, to cut, to cut out) means to invent, to cut out a falsehood from whole cloth. The customs were tailored by men and labeled as God's. The verse's attribution of the fabrication to "those who disbelieve" is significant: the inventors were the leaders of *kufr* — ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy and his successors, the guardians of the idols — who devised the customs and profited from them.

**"And Most of Them Do Not Understand"**

*Wa-aktharuhum lā yaʿqilūn* — "and most of them do not use reason." The verse distinguishes between the few who fabricated and the many who followed. The inventors lied knowingly; the mass of the people followed without thinking — inheriting the customs, practicing them out of habit, and never asking whether God had actually commanded them. The verb *ʿaqala*, to use the intellect, to bind (the *ʿiqāl* is the cord that hobbles a camel), names what they failed to do: they did not restrain their inherited practice with thought. The phrase prepares for verse 104, where these same people will say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers practicing," and be asked, "Even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?" The failure of the many is not fabrication but *taqlīd* — unthinking imitation — and the verse names it as a failure of *ʿaql*.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to test every religious practice by a single question: *did God establish this?* The pre-Islamic Arabs had a rich religious life — sanctuaries, consecrated animals, votive offerings, gestures of gratitude — much of it sincere and some of it inherited from Abraham; and the Qur'an cut through it with the question of source. What God did not institute is not religion, however pious it looks and however long it has been practiced; and to present it as God's law is to lie against Him. The believer's own religion is not immune to the same drift: customs accumulate, pious inventions attach themselves to worship, and people forget that God did not command them. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever introduces into this affair of ours what is not of it, it is rejected" (al-Bukhārī 2697; Muslim 1718). The verse's "God has not established" is the measure; the verse's "most of them do not understand" is the warning against inheriting without thinking; and the verse's "fabricate lies against God" is the name of the sin that the thoughtless inheritance ends in.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:104

> **And when it is said unto them, "Come unto that which God has sent down, and unto the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is that which we have found our fathers practicing." What! Even if their fathers knew naught and were not rightly guided?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Excuse of the Fathers**

Verse 103 repudiated the pagan consecrations of camels; verse 104 records how their practitioners defended them when called to the revelation: *wa-idhā qīla lahum taʿālaw ilā mā anzala Allāhu wa-ilā al-rasūli qālū ḥasbunā mā wajadnā ʿalayhi ābāʾanā* — "And when it is said to them, 'Come to what God has sent down and to the Messenger,' they say, 'Enough for us is what we found our fathers upon.'" The source notes that 2:170 is nearly identical, and that the theme runs through the whole Qur'an. The verse then answers the excuse with a single devastating question: *a-wa-law kāna ābāʾuhum lā yaʿlamūna shayʾan wa-lā yahtadūn* — "What! Even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?"

**"Come to What God Has Sent Down, and to the Messenger"**

The call is doubled — to the revelation and to the Messenger — in the same pairing that verse 92 used ("obey God and obey the Messenger"). The revelation is the text; the Messenger is its living exposition. To come to both is to accept the Qur'an and the Sunnah together as the source of guidance. The call's verb, *taʿālaw*, "come up," is from ʿ-l-w, to be high; it is an invitation to ascend — the same word the sūrah used in 3:64, "Come to a word common between us and you." The one who calls says, in effect: rise from where you are to where God has placed His guidance.

**"Sufficient for Us Is What We Found Our Fathers Upon"**

The answer is *ḥasbunā*, "our sufficiency, enough for us." The word is one the Qur'an elsewhere uses of God — *ḥasbunā Allāh*, "God is sufficient for us" (3:173); *ḥasbiya Allāh*, "God is my sufficiency" (9:129; 39:38). The pagans apply it to their fathers' custom: what the fathers did is *enough*; nothing more is needed; the revelation is superfluous. The choice of word exposes the substitution at the heart of *taqlīd*: the ancestors have taken the place that belongs to God. And the phrase *mā wajadnā ʿalayhi ābāʾanā*, "what we found our fathers upon," is honest in its own way — it does not claim that the fathers were right, or that the practice is reasonable, or that God commanded it; it claims only that the fathers *did* it and the sons *found* them doing it. The whole argument is inheritance.

**The Pattern in the Qur'an's Narratives**

The source shows that this is the standard defense of every people who rejected a prophet. It lists the verses in which peoples invoke their fathers against the messenger: 2:170; 7:70 (the people of Hūd: "Have you come to us that we should worship God alone and forsake what our fathers worshipped?"); 10:78 (Pharaoh's people to Moses: "Have you come to turn us from what we found our fathers upon?"); 11:62 (Thamūd to Ṣāliḥ: "Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?"); 11:87 (Midian to Shuʿayb: "Does your prayer command you that we should leave what our fathers worshipped?"); 14:10; 23:24; 28:36; 31:21; 43:22–23 ("We found our fathers upon a way, and we are guided by their footsteps"). And it quotes 34:43, where the outrage is explicit: "This is nothing but a man who wishes to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship." The source notes two uses of the excuse. Sometimes it is offered as grounds for *rejecting* the prophet — the fathers' way is the standard, and the prophet contradicts it. Sometimes it is offered to *deflect blame* for immoral practice, as in 7:28: "When they commit an indecency, they say, 'We found our fathers doing it, and God has commanded us thus.' Say: 'Truly God does not command indecency. Do you say of God what you do not know?'" — where the fathers' custom is compounded with the lie against God that verse 103 condemned.

The source also points to Abraham, the father of the monotheists, who confronted the excuse in his own people. In 21:51–54 he asks them what the images are that they are devoted to; they answer, "We found our fathers worshipping them"; and he replies, "You and your fathers have been in manifest error." In 26:69–76 he asks whether their idols hear or help, and when they say, "We found our fathers doing thus," he declares that their idols are his enemies. Abraham's answer to the fathers' custom is the model of the answer verse 104 gives — and it is pointed, since the Arabs who invoked their fathers were themselves descended from Abraham and claimed him as the source of their customs. Their true father had rejected their argument before they made it.

**"What! Even If Their Fathers Knew Nothing and Were Not Guided?"**

The verse's reply is a rhetorical question of a form the Qur'an uses to expose an absurdity: *a-wa-law*, "even if?" The question grants, for argument's sake, that the pagans are following their fathers — and asks whether that is a sufficient reason *if the fathers themselves were ignorant and unguided*. The answer is obviously no: following a guide is reasonable only if the guide knows the way. The pagans' argument had a hidden premise — that the fathers knew — and the verse drags the premise into the light and asks them to defend it. They cannot; the fathers knew nothing of God's law and were guided by nothing but their own invention.

The verse names two deficiencies: *lā yaʿlamūna shayʾan*, they knew nothing, and *lā yahtadūn*, they were not guided. The first is a lack of knowledge; the second is a lack of direction. A person might know much and still be misguided, or be guided by God's mercy without much learning; the fathers had neither. To follow such fathers is to follow the blind — and the Qur'an's image for *taqlīd* is exactly this: "the likeness of those who disbelieve is that of one who shouts at what hears nothing but a call and a cry: deaf, dumb, blind, they do not use reason" (2:171, immediately after 2:170's version of this verse).

**Taqlīd and Personal Responsibility**

The source draws the principle that the Islamic tradition drew from the verse: it is a strong basis for resisting *taqlīd* — blind imitation of purported authorities in matters of religious doctrine, without inquiry (al-Rāzī). The verse does not condemn following as such; the Qur'an commands following the Messenger, and it commands the unlearned to ask the learned (16:43). What it condemns is following *without regard to whether the one followed knows and is guided* — following on the ground of inheritance alone. The source draws the minimal conclusion (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī): one is responsible for finding *worthy* sources of instruction. The believer who follows a scholar because the scholar knows and is guided is doing what the verse permits; the one who follows his fathers' customs because they are his fathers' is doing what the verse condemns. The difference is whether the follower has asked the question the verse asks: does this guide know? is he guided?

The source connects this to the Qur'an's doctrine of the primordial covenant (7:172), in which every human soul testified to the lordship of God before time: "Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we testify." Because of that testimony, the source explains, individuals are personally responsible for their religious choices; no one can plead his fathers' custom against the knowledge his own soul carries. The Prophet ﷺ said that every child is born on the *fiṭrah*, the primordial nature, "and it is his parents who make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian" (al-Bukhārī 1385; Muslim 2658) — the parents' custom overlays the primordial knowledge, but does not erase it, and the person remains answerable for what he does with what he knows.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to examine the ground of his religion. Much of what anyone believes and practices was received from parents, community, and culture, and there is nothing wrong with inheriting the truth; the Companions' children inherited Islam from them. What is wrong is to make inheritance itself the reason — to say *ḥasbunā*, "it is enough for us," of custom, and to close one's ears to the call, "Come to what God has sent down." The believer should be able to answer the verse's question about his own guides: do they know? are they guided? If yes, he follows them with a clear conscience; if he does not know, he must find out; and if the answer is no, no length of ancestry can justify following them. And he should remember that the fathers whom the pagans invoked were themselves descendants of Abraham, who had told his own people, "You and your fathers have been in manifest error" — the truest inheritance from the fathers is the courage to test what the fathers did.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:105

> **O you who believe! You have charge of your own souls. He who is astray cannot harm you if you are rightly guided. Unto God shall be your return all together, and He shall inform you of what you used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Individual Before God**

After the repudiation of the pagans who hid behind their fathers' customs (vv. 103–104), the verse turns to the believers with a principle that answers the pagan excuse: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū ʿalaykum anfusakum* — "O you who believe, upon you are your own souls." The source reads the connection: if the disbelievers wrongly claimed that their fathers' example excused them, the believers are told the truth that the excuse denied — every human being bears responsibility for the fate of his own soul. No one's father can save him, and no one's father can condemn him. The verse then adds its second clause: *lā yaḍurrukum man ḍalla idhā ihtadaytum* — "the one who goes astray cannot harm you if you are guided" — and closes with the reminder of the return and the reckoning.

**"Upon You Are Your Own Souls"**

The phrase *ʿalaykum anfusakum* is, grammatically, an imperative construction: *ʿalaykum* followed by an accusative means "take charge of," "hold to," "attend to" — as in *ʿalaykum bi-sunnatī*, "hold to my Sunnah." The source records both readings. As a statement, it means "you are responsible for your own souls"; as a command, it means "Take charge of your souls! Guard them!" — which some commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī) understood as an admonition to preserve one's own soul from disobedience. The two readings converge: the believer is told that his soul is his charge, and commanded to discharge it.

**"He Who Is Astray Cannot Harm You If You Are Guided"**

The source records several identifications of "the one who is astray." It may be the fathers of verse 104, whose misguidance does not harm the son who leaves it; or other disbelievers generally, whose rejection of the message does not diminish the believer; or Satan, whom the Qur'an repeatedly declares to have no independent authority over souls: "I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me" (14:22); "You have no authority over My servants" (15:42; 17:65); "He has no authority over those who believe and trust in their Lord" (16:99); "He had no authority over them except that We might know who believes in the Hereafter" (34:21). In every case the principle is the same: the misguidance of another, whether ancestor, neighbor, or devil, cannot enter the believer's soul without his consent, and cannot be charged to his account if he did not consent. "No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another" (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38).

**The Central Question: Does This Cancel Commanding Right and Forbidding Wrong?**

The source identifies the commentators' primary concern with the verse. Read carelessly, "you have charge of your own souls; the one astray cannot harm you" could seem to license withdrawal — a private piety that minds its own soul and leaves others to theirs. But the Qur'an has made enjoining right and forbidding wrong a defining mark of the believing community (3:104, 110, 114; 7:157, 199; 9:67), and this very sūrah has just cursed the Israelites for failing to do it (vv. 78–79). Does verse 105 nullify that obligation?

The source records that most commentators (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) answered decisively: no. The verse does not cancel the duty of admonition; it clarifies its *limit*. The believer is obliged to enjoin and forbid; he is not obliged to *succeed*. If he has done his duty and the other person persists in error, that error does not harm him — he is not responsible for what he could not effect. The verse's condition, "if you are guided," includes, in the majority reading, *being guided to enjoin right and forbid wrong*; the one who abandons that duty is not "guided" in the verse's sense, and the misguided *do* harm him — by his complicity in their misguidance. The commentators read the verse alongside the ḥadīth of the ship, in which the Prophet ﷺ described people on the lower deck boring a hole to get water: "If they leave them to what they intend, they will all perish; if they seize their hands, they will be saved, all of them" (al-Bukhārī 2493) — and alongside the ḥadīth that "if people see an oppressor and do not restrain him, God is about to send His punishment upon them all" (Abū Dāwūd 4338; al-Tirmidhī 2168).

The decisive report comes from Abū Bakr himself. He stood on the pulpit and said: "O people, you recite this verse — 'O you who believe, upon you are your own souls; the one astray cannot harm you if you are guided' — and you put it in the wrong place. I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: 'When people see wrong and do not change it, God is about to envelop them all in His punishment'" (Abū Dāwūd 4338; al-Tirmidhī 2168; Ibn Mājah 4005). The first caliph anticipated the misreading and corrected it from the Prophet's own mouth: the verse is not a license for silence.

**Other Readings**

The source records further interpretations. Some (al-Rāzī) read "upon you are your own" as "upon you are your own *people*" — that is, the believer is responsible for guiding the members of his own community, not those outside it who reject the call. Others (al-Rāzī) read the verse as consolation: do not be grieved by the recalcitrance of those who refuse your admonition — for even the Prophet ﷺ was told that he had no control over acceptance of the message (vv. 92, 99). This reading fits the verse's placement after the pagans' refusal in verse 104: the believers, having called them to what God sent down and been answered with "enough for us is our fathers' way," are told not to be harmed in heart by the refusal.

**The Deferred-Application View and Its Weakness**

The source records a reading attributed to some Companions — Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī — that the time for the verse's application had not yet come, and that it would apply only in a future age when people would be so impervious to guidance and the world so filled with wrong that the believer's only remaining duty would be to protect his own soul (al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī). The report from Abū Thaʿlabah is explicit: he asked about the verse and was told that the Prophet ﷺ had said, "Enjoin right and forbid wrong, until you see greed obeyed, desire followed, the world preferred, and every opinionated man admiring his own opinion — then upon you is your own soul, and leave the common people" (Abū Dāwūd 4341; al-Tirmidhī 3058). The source judges this a weak reading of the verse as a whole, since it would restrict the verse's relevance to a distant future; but the ḥadīth itself is sound in its own terms, and the commentators harmonized it: the duty to enjoin and forbid remains, but its *form* changes when admonition becomes futile or dangerous — from active correction to guarding one's own soul and disapproving in the heart, the "weakest of faith" (Muslim 49). The verse, on this harmonization, is always in force; what shifts with the times is how much a believer can do beyond his own soul.

**"Unto God Is Your Return All Together"**

*Ilā Allāhi marjiʿukum jamīʿan* — "to God is your return, all together." The word *jamīʿan*, all together, is pointed: the guided and the misguided, the believer who admonished and the pagan who refused, the son who left his fathers' way and the fathers who never left it — all return to the same Judge. The verse's first clause separated their responsibilities; this clause reunites them before God, where each will answer for his own.

**"And He Will Inform You of What You Used to Do"**

*Fa-yunabbiʾukum bi-mā kuntum taʿmalūn* — "and He will inform you of what you used to do." The source lists the Qur'an's repetitions of this phrase (5:48; 6:60; 9:94, 105; 10:23; 29:8; 31:15; 39:7; 62:8). The verse ends by confirming the individuality of judgment: God informs each of *what he did* — not what his fathers did, not what his neighbors did, not what the misguided around him did. The believer will be told his own record; the pagan will be told his. This is why the misguided cannot harm the guided: each account is separate, and God reads each to its owner.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse gives the believer a balance he must not tip in either direction. On one side: his soul is his own charge; no one else's error condemns him; he must not be crushed by the refusal of those he calls, nor drawn after them, nor made to feel that their misguidance is his failure. On the other side: "if you are guided" includes the duty to speak — Abū Bakr's warning stands against the one who reads the verse as permission to be silent. The believer who holds both walks the path the sūrah has traced from verse 2 ("help one another in righteousness") through verses 78–79 (the curse of the silent) to this verse: he does what he can for others, guards what he must in himself, and leaves the result to the One to whom all return together, who will inform each soul of what it did.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:106

> **O you who believe! The witness between you, when death approaches one of you, at the time of the bequest, shall be two just men among you, or two from among other than yourselves if you are traveling upon the earth when death befalls you. Detain the two of them after the prayer, and let them both swear by God, if you doubt [them], "We will not sell it for any price, though he were a kinsman, nor will we conceal the witness of God, for then we would surely be among the sinners."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Longest Legal Verse of the Sūrah**

Verses 106–108 form a single legal unit on the witnessing of deathbed bequests, and verse 106 is the most detailed of them. The passage seems, at first, an abrupt turn from the preceding themes; but its placement is coherent. Verse 105 established that each soul answers for itself before God; verses 106–108 apply that accountability to a situation in which one person's rights depend entirely on another's honesty — the dying traveler whose property is in the hands of witnesses no court can check. The passage's concern, as the source notes, is the religious duty of truthful witness (4:135; 5:8) and faithful discharge of trusts (2:283; 4:58; 8:27; 23:8–11; 70:32–35). And it culminates, in verse 108, with the sūrah's refrain: "reverence God and listen."

**The Legal Background: Bequests**

The source summarizes the law of the bequest (*waṣiyyah*). A person may bequeath up to one-third of his property to anyone who is not already an heir with a fixed share under 4:11–12. The Qur'an first enjoined bequests generally for parents and relatives (2:180) and widows (2:240); after 4:11–12 assigned fixed shares to parents, spouses, and close relatives, most schools held that the fixed heirs may not also receive bequests — the Prophet ﷺ said, "God has given every possessor of a right his right, so there is no bequest to an heir" (Abū Dāwūd 2870; al-Tirmidhī 2120). And 4:11–12 stipulates that bequests and debts are settled *before* the estate is divided among the heirs. The bequest, therefore, must be reliably known — which requires witnesses.

**"The Witness Between You ... Two Just Men Among You"**

*Shahādatu baynikum idhā ḥaḍara aḥadakumu al-mawtu ḥīna al-waṣiyyati ithnāni dhawā ʿadlin minkum* — "the witnessing among you, when death approaches one of you, at the time of the bequest, is two possessors of justice from among you." The source notes the alternative reading "the witness to what is with you." The verse requires two witnesses of established probity (*dhawā ʿadl*, the same phrase used for the assessors of game in verse 95), and the source records that most understood *minkum*, "from among you," as "from among the Muslims" (al-Ṭabarī). The source also notes a minority reading (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī): "from among you" = from your own kin or neighborhood, and "other than yourselves" = outsiders to that circle. The requirement of two witnesses matches the Qur'an's general rule for property transactions — debts (2:282) and the return of orphans' property (4:6) — and the source notes that the dual masculine form *dhawā ʿadl* was understood as requiring two men (al-Qurṭubī).

**"Or Two from Other Than Yourselves If You Are Traveling"**

*Aw ākharāni min ghayrikum in antum ḍarabtum fī al-arḍi fa-aṣābatkum muṣībatu al-mawt* — "or two others from other than you, if you are traveling in the land and the calamity of death befalls you." Here the verse makes an accommodation of great significance. The traveler who falls ill and dies far from home, among strangers, may have no Muslims at hand to witness his bequest; the verse permits him to take witnesses from *other than yourselves* — which most commentators (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) understood as non-Muslims. The source records that some held the non-Muslim witnesses may be of any religion, since the verse does not specify, while others restricted them to Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians; that the testimony of members of these communities has been accepted in Islamic courts; and that in Islamic courts in India, Hindu testimony was also accepted in some cases. The verse is thus a foundation for the admissibility of non-Muslim testimony in Islamic law — at least in necessity — and a mark of the Qur'an's practical realism: the law is made for people who travel, trade, and die among those of other faiths, and it does not leave them without recourse.

**The Occasion: The Silver Cup**

The source relates the incident. A Muslim — Budayl ibn Abī Maryam, a client of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ — traveled to Syria on trade with two Christians, Tamīm al-Dārī and ʿAdī ibn Baddāʾ (Tamīm later became a Muslim and a noted Companion). Budayl fell ill and, nearing death, wrote an inventory of his goods, hid it among them, and entrusted the goods to his two companions to deliver to his family. When they returned, they delivered the goods; but the family, finding the inventory, noticed that a silver cup inlaid with gold was missing. The two were brought to the Prophet ﷺ, who made them swear by God that they had held nothing back, and let them go. Later the cup was found in Makkah, and its purchasers said they had bought it from Tamīm and ʿAdī. Two of the deceased's heirs then swore that the cup was Budayl's and that their testimony was truer than the Christians' — and took the cup (al-Bukhārī 2780; al-Tirmidhī 3060; al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The verse, and the two that follow, codify the procedure the case revealed: the witnesses' oath, the discovery of their perjury, and the counter-oath of the heirs.

**"Detain Them After the Prayer"**

*Taḥbisūnahumā min baʿdi al-ṣalāh* — "you shall hold the two of them after the prayer." The witnesses are to be detained — kept back, made to stand — after the prayer, and put on oath. The source records that the commentators generally held the detention and oath to be required only when the witnesses' honesty is suspect (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī), as the verse's *in irtabtum*, "if you doubt," makes explicit. "The prayer" was widely understood as the afternoon (*ʿaṣr*) prayer, since the Prophet's ﷺ practice was to exact oaths at that hour (al-Ṭabarī) — the hour when, as a ḥadīth says, the angels of the day and night gather, and when a false oath is most terrible (al-Bukhārī 2369; Muslim 108, on the man who swears falsely "after ʿaṣr" to sell his goods). The source notes that some held "the prayer" need not mean the Islamic prayer, since the witnesses might be non-Muslims, in which case they are detained after their own prayer (al-Ṭabarī) — on the principle that a person who has just prayed is more likely to fear God and less likely to perjure himself. The timing is psychological as well as ceremonial: the oath is administered when the conscience is most awake.

**The Oath**

The witnesses swear: *lā nashtarī bihi thamanan wa-law kāna dhā qurbā* — "we will not sell it for any price, even if he were a relative" — that is, we will not exchange our testimony, or God's name, for any worldly gain, nor bend it in favor of a kinsman; *wa-lā naktumu shahādata Allāhi* — "and we will not conceal the testimony of God" — the testimony God has commanded and will judge; *innā idhan la-mina al-āthimīn* — "for then we would be among the sinners." The source notes that "we will not sell it" is a promise not to profit from the witnessing in any way (al-Ṭabarī). The oath's two clauses cover the two ways a witness fails: by *altering* testimony for gain or kinship, and by *concealing* it. The Qur'an elsewhere calls concealment of testimony a sin of the heart: "Do not conceal testimony; whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful" (2:283). And the phrase "the testimony of God" elevates the matter: the witness does not merely report a fact between men; he discharges a trust that God has placed on him.

**Swearing by God**

The source notes that the verse is evidence that solemn oaths are to be sworn by God — the same principle established at verse 89 with the ḥadīth, "Whoever swears, let him swear by God or be silent" (al-Bukhārī 6108; Muslim 1646; al-Qurṭubī) — and records that al-Shāfiʿī also permitted swearing on a written copy of the Qur'an (al-Qurṭubī). The commentary on verse 89 treated the theology of the oath; here the point is procedural: the oath by God is the instrument by which a court that cannot see into hearts binds the conscience of a witness it cannot otherwise check.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse is a portrait of trust at its most vulnerable. A dying man, far from home, places everything he owns in the hands of two companions and dies; no one saw what he had; no court can reconstruct it; his family depends entirely on the honesty of two strangers. The Law does what it can — it requires two witnesses, it makes them swear after prayer, it puts the dread of God's name between them and the silver cup — but in the end, the matter rests on conscience. The verse teaches the believer that when he is entrusted with what no one can check, he is standing exactly where the verse places the witnesses: before God, whose testimony he must not conceal and whose name he must not sell for any price. And it teaches him that the Law's procedures — oaths, timing, detention, counter-oaths — are not empty forms but the scaffolding of a society in which people can die among strangers and trust that their families will receive what is theirs.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:107

> **But if it is discovered that the two of them are guilty of sin, then two others shall stand in their place, from those most entitled as claimants, and swear by God, "Indeed, our witness is truer than their witness, and we have not transgressed, for then we would surely be among the wrongdoers."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Remedy for Perjured Witnesses**

Verse 106 laid out the primary procedure: two witnesses, an oath after the prayer. Verse 107 provides for its failure: *fa-in ʿuthira ʿalā annahumā istaḥaqqā ithman* — "but if it is discovered that the two of them have incurred sin." The verb *ʿuthira* (from ʿ-th-r, to stumble upon, to come across) is exact: the discovery is accidental, as in the occasion of revelation — the silver cup turned up in Makkah, and its buyers named the sellers. The Law does not expect to catch every perjurer; but it provides for the case in which one is caught.

**"Guilty of Sin"**

The source explains the sin: the betrayal of the specific trust the witnesses undertook toward the deceased's bequest (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) — by concealing part of it, appropriating it, or testifying falsely about it. The phrase *istaḥaqqā ithman*, literally "the two deserved sin," "became liable for sin," implies that the sin has been *established* against them — not merely suspected but discovered by evidence, as the cup was.

**"Then Two Others Shall Stand in Their Place"**

*Fa-ākharāni yaqūmāni maqāmahumā* — "then two others shall stand in their standing-place." The two who now stand are described as *mina alladhīna istaḥaqqa ʿalayhimu al-awlayān* — a phrase of notorious grammatical difficulty, read in several ways by the early reciters, which the source renders "from those most entitled as claimants." The most common understanding is: two of the heirs — those against whom the sin was committed, the ones nearest to the deceased and most entitled to his estate (al-Ṭabarī). The source records al-Zamakhsharī's reading of "those nearest to it" as embracing both those most entitled to the bequest and those closest to the deceased's affairs, who therefore know his situation best. In the occasion of revelation, these were the deceased's relatives — ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and al-Muṭṭalib ibn Abī Wadāʿah, in some accounts — who swore and took the cup.

**Why the Heirs Must Swear**

The source notes the reason for the second oath: the heirs are not disinterested witnesses; they are claimants to the very property in dispute, and so their word alone cannot decide the matter. The Law makes them swear, as it made the original witnesses swear, because the oath by God is the only instrument that can bind a party whose interest is engaged. The principle appears throughout Islamic procedure: "The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies" (al-Bayhaqī; al-Tirmidhī 1341), and in cases where proof is unavailable on either side, oaths decide. Verse 107 is a particular application: when the first oath (of the witnesses) is shown to have been false, the second oath (of the heirs) replaces it — and the fact that the heirs have an interest is offset by the fact that the witnesses have been proven liars.

**The Heirs' Oath**

The heirs swear: *la-shahādatunā aḥaqqu min shahādatihimā* — "surely our testimony is more deserving [of acceptance] than their testimony" — because theirs has been exposed as false and ours is truthful; *wa-mā iʿtadaynā* — "and we have not transgressed" — the sūrah's verb once more; the source explains it as "we have not exceeded the limits in what we testify concerning the bequest" (al-Ṭabarī) — we claim only what was his, not more; *innā idhan la-mina al-ẓālimīn* — "for then we would be among the wrongdoers." The oath's structure mirrors the witnesses' oath in verse 106: an affirmation, a disavowal of excess, and a self-curse. Where the witnesses said "we would be among the *sinners*" (*āthimīn*), the heirs say "we would be among the *wrongdoers*" (*ẓālimīn*) — because the heirs' false oath would not merely be a sin against God but a wrong against the witnesses, whose property (or reputation) their oath takes.

**The Balance of the Procedure**

The two verses together construct a balanced procedure. The witnesses are trusted first, and their oath is taken; if evidence of their perjury emerges, the heirs' oath displaces it. Neither side is allowed to decide by bare assertion; each is bound by God's name; and the evidence that surfaces decides which oath prevails. The commentators observed that the procedure honors both parties: it does not presume the witnesses guilty — they are sworn and released — nor does it leave the heirs without remedy when guilt is discovered. And it places at every step the fear of God, since the false oath in either mouth is, by the swearer's own words, sin and wrong.

**A Note on Abrogation**

The commentators discussed whether this procedure — in particular, the admission of non-Muslim witnesses and the oath of the claimants — was abrogated by later rules of evidence, and some held that it was. But the source's presentation, following al-Ṭabarī and the majority of early authorities, treats the verses as operative: Ibn ʿAbbās said, "This verse is firm; it is not abrogated," and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal ruled by it. The procedure remains a model of how the Law handles the failure of trust where ordinary proof is unavailable.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse teaches the believer that the Law is not naïve. It trusts witnesses, but it prepares for their betrayal; it binds the honest by oath and exposes the dishonest by evidence; and it does not allow the proven liar's word to stand over the truthful claimant's. For the believer who is ever a witness, an executor, a trustee, or an heir, the two verses are a warning and a comfort: a warning that God's procedures, even in this world, are designed to bring the concealed cup to light — and a comfort that the one wronged by a false witness is not without recourse. Behind both stands the sūrah's constant reminder: every oath is sworn before God, who knows what is disclosed and what is concealed (v. 99), and who will inform each soul of what it did (v. 105).

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:108

> **Thus it is more likely that they will bear true witness, or fear that their oaths will be countered by oaths thereafter. And reverence God and listen. God guides not iniquitous people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Purpose of the Procedure**

The third verse of the passage states the rationale of the first two: *dhālika adnā an yaʾtū bi-l-shahādati ʿalā wajhihā aw yakhāfū an turadda aymānun baʿda aymānihim* — "That is more likely that they bring the testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths." The source explains: the procedures of verses 106–107 are designed to make it *likely* that witnesses execute a bequest faithfully, and to increase public trust in such matters. The verse is, in effect, the Law explaining itself — one of the places where the Qur'an gives not only the rule but the *wisdom* of the rule, and thereby teaches the believer how to think about law.

**Two Motives: Conscience and Consequence**

The verse names two mechanisms by which the procedure secures truthful witness. The first, *an yaʾtū bi-l-shahādati ʿalā wajhihā*, "that they bring the testimony on its face" — as it actually is, without alteration or concealment — appeals to *conscience*: the solemn oath by God, sworn after prayer, in the formula "we would be among the sinners," awakens the fear of God in a witness who has any, and moves him to tell the truth for God's sake. The second, *aw yakhāfū an turadda aymānun baʿda aymānihim*, "or that they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths" — that is, that the heirs' counter-oath (v. 107) will displace theirs and expose them — appeals to *consequence*: even the witness whose conscience is weak may be restrained by the knowledge that his perjury can be discovered and overturned, and that he will then stand disgraced as a proven liar. The verb *turadda*, "be returned, be turned back," pictures the false oath rebounding on the one who swore it.

The pairing is a small lesson in moral psychology. The Law does not rely on conscience alone, because not everyone has one; nor on consequence alone, because not every lie is caught. It arranges both — the oath before God for the fearing, and the counter-oath for the calculating — so that the honest are confirmed and the dishonest are deterred by whichever motive reaches them. The source notes that some commentators (al-Qurṭubī) saw in the verses a general aim: to impress upon all people the solemnity of oaths and of serving as witnesses. The elaborate procedure — detention, the hour after prayer, the formula, the counter-oath — is itself a teaching: it tells everyone who watches it that testimony is a grave thing.

**"And Reverence God and Listen"**

*Wa-ttaqū Allāha wa-smaʿū* — "and be conscious of God, and listen." The passage closes with the sūrah's most frequent command, *taqwā*, joined to *ismaʿū*, "hear" — the verb that verse 7 used for the covenant ("we hear and we obey") and that verse 71 negated in the "deaf and blind." To *listen*, in the Qur'an's usage, is not merely to receive sound but to heed: "Listen and obey" (64:16). The command tells the believers that the procedure they have just been given is to be *heeded* — put into practice as given — and that their *taqwā*, their consciousness of God, is the ultimate guarantee that the procedure will work. No court can force a witness to be honest; only his fear of God can. The verse therefore ends the law with the disposition that makes law effective.

**"God Guides Not Iniquitous People"**

*Wa-Allāhu lā yahdī al-qawma al-fāsiqīn* — "and God does not guide the corrupt people." The phrase has closed several verses of the sūrah (vv. 25, 26, 59, 81), and here it has a pointed application: the witness who perjures himself, the executor who conceals the cup, the claimant who swears to more than his due — these are *fāsiqūn*, people who have broken out of the bounds of obedience; and God does not guide such people. The clause is both a warning and a diagnosis. The warning: the one who lies under oath cuts himself off from God's guidance. The diagnosis: the one who could betray a dying man's trust was already outside the bounds, and his perjury is the fruit of a *fisq* that preceded it. The verse's placement after the command to listen is a caution: the one who *does not* listen — who takes the oath lightly, who treats the procedure as a formality — is on the road to the *fisq* that God does not guide.

**The Passage as a Whole**

Verses 106–108 belong, as the source observes, to the Qur'an's insistence on two duties: truthful witness (4:135, "be upholders of justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves"; 5:8, "be witnesses for God in justice") and faithful discharge of trusts (2:283, "let the one entrusted discharge his trust and fear God"; 4:58, "God commands you to render trusts to their owners"; 8:27, "do not betray God and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts knowingly"; 23:8, "those who keep their trusts and their covenant"; 70:32). The passage places these duties at their most testing point — the deathbed of a traveler, far from any court — and shows how the Law surrounds them with procedure while resting them finally on *taqwā*.

The passage also completes a thread that the sūrah began at its first word. The sūrah opened with "fulfill your contracts" (v. 1); it commanded the believers to "be witnesses for God in justice" (v. 8); it required expiation for broken oaths (v. 89); and it now ends its legal content with the oath of witnesses and the procedure that protects the bequest of the dying. The chapter's legislation, from the food on the table to the words at the deathbed, is one continuous teaching about *ʿaqd*, the binding word, and *amānah*, the trust. After verse 108, the sūrah turns to its final subject: the Day when God will gather the messengers, and Jesus will render his account.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to understand the Law as God presents it here: a wise arrangement of motives that makes truthfulness likely and falsehood dangerous, resting on a foundation that no arrangement can replace — the fear of God. The believer should honor the procedures of justice — oaths, witnesses, evidence — not as bureaucratic forms but as the means by which trust is protected among people who cannot see one another's hearts. He should be the kind of witness who needs no counter-oath to keep him honest, because "reverence God and listen" is already written on his conscience. And he should take the closing clause as a personal caution: the road to becoming one whom God does not guide begins with the small betrayal, the concealed cup, the oath taken lightly. The one who guards the small trust guards his guidance.

## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:109

> **The day when God will gather the messengers and say, "What response did you receive?" they will say, "We have no knowledge. Truly it is Thou Who knowest best the things unseen."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn to the Final Scene**

With verse 109 the sūrah leaves legislation and enters its closing movement: a scene of the Day of Judgment that will run, with the long address to Jesus, to the end of the chapter. *Yawma yajmaʿu Allāhu al-rusula fa-yaqūlu mādhā ujibtum* — "On the day when God gathers the messengers and says, 'What were you answered?'" The verse opens in the accusative, *yawma*, "on the day," without a governing verb — and the source records the commentators' explanations of the grammar, each of which affects the sense. Some (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Zamakhsharī) supply an implicit "beware of" or "remember," so that the verse is a warning: "[Beware] the Day when God will gather the messengers"; others connect it to the preceding command, "reverence God and listen ... [on] the Day"; still others (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī) connect it to the preceding clause, "God does not guide the corrupt people [on] the Day when He gathers the messengers" — that is, on that Day the corrupt will find no guidance. In every reading, the effect is the same: the legal verses on witness and oath are suddenly placed against the backdrop of the ultimate hearing, where the witnesses will be the messengers themselves.

**"What Response Did You Receive?"**

God's question to the messengers, *mādhā ujibtum*, "what were you answered?" — literally, "with what were you responded to?" — asks each messenger about the reception his message met. The source records the commentators' understanding of its purpose: the question is not for God's information, since He knows, but is a *rebuke to the peoples* (al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ṭabarī). It is addressed to the messengers because they are the leaders of their communities (al-Thaʿlabī), and it is asked in the hearing of those communities, so that each people will hear its own prophet asked, "How did they answer you?" — and know what the answer must be. The scene resembles the questioning of the buried girl in 81:8–9, "when the girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed" — where the question is put not to the guilty but to the victim, so that the guilty hear their crime named by the one they wronged. The messengers were the ones the peoples rejected, mocked, expelled, and killed; God asks *them* how they were received.

**"We Have No Knowledge"**

The messengers' reply is the verse's puzzle: *lā ʿilma lanā* — "we have no knowledge." The source lays out the difficulty. The messengers are, by the Qur'an's repeated testimony, witnesses for and against their communities on the Day of Judgment: "How will it be when We bring from every community a witness, and bring you as a witness against these?" (4:41); "We made you a middle community, that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger a witness over you" (2:143); also 4:69; 16:89; 22:78; 57:19. They surely *know* how they were received. Why, then, do they say they have no knowledge?

The source presents the commentators' answers and weighs them.

The first explanation (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī): the terror of the Day will so overwhelm even the messengers that they will be unable to answer at first; later, when their composure returns, they will testify. The source notes the objection (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī): the Qur'an states that the believers will have no fear on that Day (2:62; 21:103), and the messengers are the foremost of the believers.

The second explanation (al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī): the messengers mean that they do not know what their communities did *after their deaths*, nor the secret intentions of those who followed them. This connects the verse to Jesus' words in verse 117: "I was a witness over them while I was among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them." A messenger knows the response he received in his lifetime; he does not know the whole history of his community or the hearts of those who professed to follow him. The source notes the difficulty: the Qur'an still says the prophets will testify concerning their communities.

The third explanation, which the source judges the best (al-Zamakhsharī; also al-Bayḍāwī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī): the reply is an expression of *humility before God's knowledge*. It means either "we have no knowledge save what You have taught us" — the very words the angels spoke when God asked them the names of things: "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us" (2:32) — or "we have no knowledge compared with Yours," since God's knowledge of the matter is complete and theirs is partial. In this reading, the messengers do not deny that they know; they deny that their knowledge counts beside God's. The source adds al-Rāzī's refinement: the messengers know the *outward* of their peoples' response — who professed and who refused — but God alone knows the *inward*, the sincerity or hypocrisy behind the profession; and since judgment is upon the inward, they defer the judgment to Him. And al-Zamakhsharī's summary: the messengers, though aware of their communities' deeds, *prefer to entrust the matter of their judgment to God*.

**"Truly It Is Thou Who Knowest Best the Things Unseen"**

*Innaka anta ʿallāmu al-ghuyūb* — "truly You, You are the Knower of the unseen things." The intensive *ʿallām*, the all-knowing, the one who knows utterly; the plural *ghuyūb*, the hidden things, all the unseen realms. The source cross-references verse 116, where Jesus will close his own disavowal with the same words: "You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your Soul; truly You are the Knower of the unseen things." The phrase is the key to the messengers' reply. They are the greatest of created knowers, and yet before *ʿallām al-ghuyūb* they say, "we have no knowledge." Their humility is not false modesty but accurate perception: beside the One who knows every hidden thing — the concealed response, the secret rejection, the inward faith — the knowledge of the greatest prophet is as nothing.

**The Adab of the Messengers**

The scene teaches the *adab*, the right conduct, of the servant before God. The messengers could have answered, "We were rejected, mocked, and killed" — and every word would have been true. Instead they answer, "You know best." They do not accuse; they do not complain; they do not press their case; they lay the matter before the Judge who needs no testimony. Their reply is the model of the believer's posture in every wrong he has suffered: he knows what was done to him, but he leaves the judgment to the One who knows better. And it is the model of the believer's posture toward his own knowledge: however much he knows, he says with the angels and the prophets, "we have no knowledge except what You have taught us."

**The Connection to the Sūrah's Themes**

The verse gathers up the chapter's concerns. The sūrah has repeatedly reminded the Prophet ﷺ that his duty is only to convey (vv. 67, 92, 99) and that God knows what people disclose and conceal (v. 99); verse 109 shows the Day on which that division of labor is completed: the messengers report that they conveyed, and God, who alone knows the response in its fullness, judges. The sūrah has just legislated the oath of witnesses (vv. 106–108); verse 109 shows the ultimate witnesses — the messengers — declining to testify beyond what they know and deferring to the Knower of the unseen. And the verse prepares the ground for the sūrah's climax: God will turn from the messengers in general to one messenger in particular, Jesus son of Mary, and ask him not "what response did you receive?" but "did you say to people: take me and my mother as gods?" — and Jesus' answer will be the fullest example of what verse 109 describes.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to picture the Day when the messengers will be gathered and asked how humanity answered them, and to hear the question as addressed to himself: how did *he* answer the Messenger sent to him? The messengers will not accuse; they will say, "You know best." But God does know best — He knows the reader's response, outward and inward, as He knows the response of every people to every prophet. The believer should ensure that when his Prophet ﷺ is asked, "What response did you receive?" his own name is among those the answer need not conceal. And he should learn, from the messengers' humility, the posture of every knower before God: "We have no knowledge; truly You are the Knower of the unseen."

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:110

> **Then God will say, "O Jesus son of Mary! Remember My Blessing upon thee, and upon thy mother, when I strengthened thee with the Holy Spirit, that thou mightest speak to people in the cradle and in maturity; and when I taught thee the Book, Wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel; and how thou wouldst create out of clay the shape of a bird, by My Leave, and thou wouldst breathe into it, and it would become a bird, by My Leave; and thou wouldst heal the blind and the leper, by My Leave; and thou wouldst bring forth the dead, by My Leave; and how I restrained the Children of Israel from thee, when thou didst bring them clear proofs, and those who disbelieved among them said, 'This is naught but manifest sorcery.'"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Messengers to One Messenger**

Verse 109 showed God gathering all the messengers and asking what response they received. Verse 110 narrows the scene to one of them: *idh qāla Allāhu yā ʿĪsā ibna Maryam* — "when God says, 'O Jesus, son of Mary.'" From here to verse 118, the source notes, God addresses Jesus specifically about his mission and about what his followers did with it. The sūrah that has treated Christians more extensively than any other chapter — their covenant (v. 14), their doctrines (vv. 17, 72–77), their best and worst (vv. 82–85) — closes by letting Jesus himself speak before God, and by having God first recount, in a single long verse, everything He gave him. The verse is a catalogue of the blessings of Jesus, and its refrain is *bi-idhnī*, "by My leave," four times.

**"O Jesus Son of Mary"**

The address itself is a doctrine. God calls him *ibn Maryam*, son of Mary — the name the Qur'an uses for Jesus more than any other, twenty-three times, and always with the same force: he is the son of a woman, born of a mother, a human being. The Christians called him "Son of God"; God calls him "son of Mary." In a verse that will go on to recount his miracles — powers that seem divine — the address fixes at the outset who is performing them: the son of a woman, by the leave of God.

**"Remember My Blessing upon You and upon Your Mother"**

*Udhkur niʿmatī ʿalayka wa-ʿalā wālidatik* — "remember My favor upon you and upon your mother." The word *niʿmah*, blessing, favor, is the sūrah's word from its opening verses (vv. 3, 6, 7, 11, 20). God does not say "remember your powers" or "remember your works"; He says "remember My favor" — placing every extraordinary thing about Jesus under the heading of *gift*. And He includes the mother: Mary, whom verse 75 called *ṣiddīqah*, whom God chose above the women of the worlds (3:42), who received the Spirit and bore the Word. The pairing of son and mother anticipates verse 116, where the two will be named together as the objects of the false worship Jesus will disavow. God blessed them both; people deified them both; and the verse's "remember My blessing" is the corrective before the disavowal.

**"When I Strengthened You with the Holy Spirit"**

*Idh ayyadtuka bi-rūḥi al-qudus* — "when I supported you with the Spirit of Holiness." The source explains the phrase thoroughly. The strengthening of Jesus with the Holy Spirit is mentioned in 2:87 and 2:253, and the Spirit's role in his very conception in 4:171 ("a Spirit from Him"), 19:17 (the Spirit sent to Mary in the form of a man), 21:91 and 66:12 ("We breathed into her of Our Spirit"). *Rūḥ al-qudus* is understood in the Qur'anic context and the commentary tradition as the archangel Gabriel, the angel of revelation (al-Ṭabarī) — who is "the Spirit" in 16:102 ("the Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord"), 26:193 ("the Faithful Spirit"), 42:52, 97:4. The source also records the identification with the Spirit as such, "of the Command of my Lord" (17:85), and al-Rāzī's observation that the construction *rūḥ al-qudus* — "Spirit of the Holy" — relates to the divine name *al-Quddūs*, the Holy (59:23; 62:1), and could be rendered "Spirit of God." From this connection, the source notes, Jesus' title in Islam is *Rūḥ Allāh*, the Spirit of God, which serves as a proper name for him. The support of the Spirit was, for Jesus, both origin and companion: he was conceived by the Spirit's breath and accompanied by the Spirit's strengthening throughout his mission.

**"That You Might Speak to People in the Cradle and in Maturity"**

*Tukallimu al-nāsa fī al-mahdi wa-kahlan* — "you speak to people in the cradle and as a mature man." The source notes that Jesus' speech in infancy — found also in 3:46 and 19:29–30, where the infant says, "I am the servant of God; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet" — is an exclusively Qur'anic attribute, absent from the Bible. Its purpose in the Qur'an's narrative is twofold: to vindicate Mary against the accusation of unchastity by the testimony of the newborn himself, and to establish, from Jesus' first words, his identity: *ʿabd Allāh*, servant of God. The pairing with "in maturity" (*kahlan*, the age of full manhood, thirty to fifty) tells us that the infant and the man spoke the same message — the miracle of the cradle was not a childish wonder but the first prophetic speech.

**"And When I Taught You the Book, Wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel"**

*Wa-idh ʿallamtuka al-kitāba wa-l-ḥikmata wa-l-tawrāta wa-l-injīl* — "and when I taught you the Book and Wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel." The source explains that Jesus is described here as a bearer of revelation in the same terms the Qur'an uses for the other prophets: "the Book and Wisdom" (3:81; 4:54, 113; also 2:129, 151, 231; 3:164; 62:2) refers to the scriptures given to the prophets and to their knowledge of the scriptures' meaning (al-Ṭabarī). The Torah is named because Jesus was sent to the Children of Israel to confirm and partially amend it (3:50; 5:46); the Gospel because it was his own revelation, "wherein is guidance and light" (v. 46). Jesus was thus a scholar of the Torah and the recipient of the Gospel — a link in the chain of prophets, not a break in it.

**The Four Miracles, "By My Leave"**

The verse then recounts four miracles, and attaches to each — three times explicitly, and to the first twice — the qualifier *bi-idhnī*, "by My leave." The source identifies the significance: these particular miracles suggest powers that the Qur'an reserves for God. The creation of a bird from clay and its animation by breath is *exactly parallel* to God's creation of the human being: "I am creating a human from clay ... when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My Spirit" (15:26–29; 32:7–9; 38:71–72). Healing is God's: "and when I am ill, it is He who heals me" (26:80). Raising the dead is God's throughout the Qur'an — "God gives life to the dead" (2:73; 22:6; 30:50; 41:39). Jesus did all three. The Qur'an does not diminish the miracles; it states them plainly — he *did* create the bird's form, breathe into it, and it *became* a bird; he *did* heal the born-blind and the leper; he *did* bring out the dead. But every one of them was *bi-idhnī*. The repetition is the verse's theology: the acts are Jesus'; the power is God's; Jesus is the instrument, God the agent. The commentary on verse 17 argued that God's power over the Messiah proves the Messiah is not God; verse 110 gives the positive side: the Messiah's power is God's power lent to him — which is why he could say, as the Gospel also has him say, "I can do nothing of myself."

The source notes the relation to Christian sources. Jesus' healings and raisings of the dead are found in the canonical Gospels; the creation of birds from clay is found in the non-canonical Infancy Gospel of Thomas. The Qur'an confirms what it confirms on its own authority, not on the authority of any text; and it confirms these miracles in order to make its own point about them — that they were by God's leave.

**"And How I Restrained the Children of Israel from You"**

*Wa-idh kafaftu Banī Isrāʾīla ʿanka idh jiʾtahum bi-l-bayyināti* — "and when I held back the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs." The source records the majority understanding: God thwarted their attempt to kill him — for the Qur'an asserts that "they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them" (4:157). The verb *kafaftu*, I restrained, held back, is the same the Qur'an uses of God restraining hands from the believers (5:11; 48:20, 24). The one who could raise the dead by God's leave was himself preserved from death by God's hand — a final demonstration that the power in his life was never his own. The source notes that "clear proofs" (*bayyināt*) is said of Jesus in 2:87 and 2:253 and is the Qur'an's general term for divine revelation in all its forms.

**"This Is Nothing but Manifest Sorcery"**

*Fa-qāla alladhīna kafarū minhum in hādhā illā siḥrun mubīn* — "and those who disbelieved among them said, 'This is nothing but manifest sorcery.'" The source notes that the same charge was made against Jesus in 61:6, against Moses (10:76; 20:57; 27:13; 28:36), against Muḥammad ﷺ (6:7; 10:2; 21:3; 43:30; 46:7; 74:24; and 54:2 for the splitting of the moon), and against the messengers in general (11:7; 34:43; 37:15). The accusation is the last refuge of the one who cannot deny the miracle and will not accept its meaning. The blind man sees; the leper is clean; the dead man walks; and the disbeliever says, "sorcery" — because the alternative is submission. The verse's *minhum*, "among them," is the sūrah's usual care: not all the Children of Israel, but those among them who disbelieved.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to hold two truths together, as the Qur'an holds them. Jesus was extraordinary — supported by the Spirit, speaking in the cradle, taught the Torah and the Gospel, creating, healing, raising the dead, preserved from his enemies. And every extraordinary thing about him was God's *niʿmah*, God's blessing, done by God's *idhn*, God's leave. The Christians who deified him saw the first truth and lost the second; the Jews who called him a sorcerer denied the first to escape the second; the Qur'an affirms both and asks the believer to do the same. And in the verse's form — God reminding Jesus of His blessings, and Jesus listening — the believer sees the posture of every creature before its Creator: whatever he has done, he did by leave; whatever he is, he is by favor; and on the Day the messengers are gathered, the greatest of them will be told, "Remember My blessing upon you," and will answer, as the next verses show, with nothing but acknowledgment.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:111

> **And when I inspired the apostles to believe in Me and in My messenger, they said, "We believe. Bear witness that we are submitters."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Blessing Continued: Faithful Followers**

God's recital of His blessings upon Jesus (v. 110) continues with one more: *wa-idh awḥaytu ilā al-ḥawāriyyīna an āminū bī wa-bi-rasūlī* — "and when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and in My messenger." After the Spirit, the speech in the cradle, the Book and Wisdom, the four miracles, and the protection from his enemies, God names the gift of *disciples who believed*. It is a gift a prophet does not take for granted; Noah preached nine hundred and fifty years and gained few; Lot found not a single house of believers besides his own (51:36). Jesus was given the *ḥawāriyyūn*, and the verse counts them among God's blessings upon him. The verse also opens the passage (111–115) from which, as the source notes, the sūrah takes its name: the account of the table, *al-māʾidah*, that the disciples asked to be sent down from heaven.

**The Ḥawāriyyūn**

The word *ḥawāriyyūn*, the disciples or apostles of Jesus, is from ḥ-w-r, whose root sense is whiteness and purity — the *ḥawāriyyāt* are women of pure complexion; *ḥawwara* is to whiten cloth. The commentators explained the name variously: that the disciples were bleachers of cloth by trade; that they were pure of heart; or that their souls were cleansed of every stain, as white cloth is cleansed. The Qur'an uses the word only of Jesus' followers (3:52; 61:14), and the Prophet ﷺ borrowed it for al-Zubayr: "Every prophet has a *ḥawārī*, and my *ḥawārī* is al-Zubayr" (al-Bukhārī 2846; Muslim 2415) — where the sense is a close, devoted, trusted companion.

**"When I Inspired the Apostles"**

The verb is *awḥaytu*, "I inspired," from the root of *waḥy*, which usually denotes prophetic revelation. The source addresses the difficulty: the disciples were not prophets, so what does it mean that God "revealed" to them? The commentators glossed the word here as *ilhām*, a casting into the heart — a less direct form of inspiration than what the prophets received (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī). The Qur'an uses *awḥā* in this broader sense elsewhere: God "inspired" the mother of Moses to cast him into the river (28:7), "inspired" the bee to build its hives (16:68), and "inspired" the earth on the Last Day (99:5). None of these is prophetic revelation; each is a divine prompting placed within the recipient. The disciples' faith, the verse says, was such a prompting: God moved their hearts to believe. This is the sūrah's doctrine of verse 54 again — God's love precedes; His action in the heart is the source of the heart's response — and the doctrine of verse 83, where the Christians' tears flowed "from what they recognized of the truth." The disciples believed because God inspired them to; and the verse credits their belief to Him as a blessing upon Jesus.

**"To Believe in Me and in My Messenger"**

The content of the inspiration is faith in *God and His messenger* — the two objects that the Qur'an always joins, and that the *shahādah* joins. The disciples' faith was in God first and in Jesus as *rasūlī*, "My messenger" — a title that defines Jesus, in God's own words, as one sent by God, not as God. The verse's placement is deliberate: immediately before the account of the table and the disavowal of verse 116, God states that the faith He inspired in Jesus' disciples was faith in Him and in Jesus *as messenger*. Whatever later Christians came to believe about Jesus, the faith of his first followers, as God Himself inspired it, was the faith of the *shahādah*.

**"We Believe. Bear Witness That We Are Submitters"**

*Qālū āmannā wa-shhad bi-annanā muslimūn* — "They said, 'We believe; and bear witness that we are *muslimūn*.'" The source cross-references 3:52–53, where the disciples answer Jesus' call, "Who are my helpers unto God?" with "We are the helpers of God; we believe in God; bear witness that we are submitters" — though 3:54 then adds "and they plotted," referring to the Israelites who opposed him, not to the disciples. The disciples' self-description as *muslimūn* — those who have surrendered to God — is the Qur'an's standing claim: the true followers of every prophet were *muslimūn*, submitters to God, whatever name they bore (Abraham in 2:131; Jacob's sons in 2:133; Joseph in 12:101; the magicians of Pharaoh in 7:126; the Queen of Sheba in 27:44; Jesus' disciples here and in 3:52). Islam is not a new religion begun in the seventh century but the primordial submission that every prophet taught and every true disciple embraced. The disciples of Jesus were Muslims in this sense — and the Qur'an, addressing the Christians of Arabia, reminds them of it: your first fathers in faith said, "bear witness that we are submitters."

The disciples' "bear witness" is addressed to Jesus, or, in the reading of some commentators, to God. In either case it is a request for testimony: they want their submission recorded, attested, made a matter of witness — the same desire that verse 83 described in the Christians who wept: "write us among the witnesses." The theme of witnessing that runs through the sūrah (vv. 8, 83, 106–108, 113, 117) appears here in the mouths of Jesus' disciples: they want to be witnessed as submitters.

**Belief Before Submission: The Order of Faith**

The source records al-Rāzī's observation on the verse's sequence. The disciples say first "we believe" (*āmannā*) and then "we are submitters" (*muslimūn*); inward belief precedes outward submission — the conforming of action to God's will. The source connects this to the classical Sunni definition of faith: "knowledge in the heart, affirmation with the tongue, and action with the limbs" (*maʿrifah bi-l-qalb, iqrār bi-l-lisān, ʿamal bi-l-arkān*). The heart believes; the tongue confesses; the limbs submit — and the order matters. Submission without belief is the *islām* of the Bedouins whom the Qur'an corrected: "The Bedouins say, 'We believe.' Say: You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts" (49:14). Belief without submission is the "faith" of the one who knows the truth and does not act on it — the failure the sūrah has condemned in the People of the Book who "recognize" and yet reject (v. 83 versus v. 41). The disciples had both in the right order: they believed, and their belief expressed itself in surrender, and they asked to be witnessed as having done so.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Portrait of Christianity**

The verse is a key to the sūrah's whole treatment of the Christians. The chapter has condemned the doctrines of divine sonship (v. 18), the identification of God with the Messiah (vv. 17, 72), and the "third of three" (v. 73); it has praised the Christians who are humble, who weep at the truth, and who are "nearest in love to the believers" (vv. 82–85). Verse 111 shows the *origin* of the Christian community as the Qur'an understands it: a group of disciples whom God inspired to believe in Him and in His messenger, who declared themselves submitters. This is what Christianity was at its source — and this is what the sūrah calls the Christians back to. The doctrines the sūrah condemns are, in its view, later accretions (*ghuluww*, v. 77) upon a faith that began as the *islām* of the *ḥawāriyyūn*. The verse is not a polemic against Christians but an appeal to their own beginnings.

**The Verse for the Reader**

The verse asks the believer to see his faith as God's gift before it is his achievement. God *inspired* the disciples to believe; their "we believe" was the echo of His prompting. The believer who finds faith in his heart should know where it came from, and thank the One who cast it there, as God counted the disciples' faith among His blessings on Jesus. And he should learn from their order: belief first, then submission, then the request to be witnessed — a faith that goes from the heart to the tongue to the limbs and asks God to record it. The disciples wanted to be known as *muslimūn*. The believer who says the same words in his prayers should say them as they did: as the full surrender of one whom God has inspired to believe in Him and in His messenger.

---
## Sūrah al-Māʾidah 5:112

> **When the apostles said, "O Jesus son of Mary! Is thy Lord able to send down to us from Heaven a table spread with food?" He said, "Reverence God, if you are believers."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Request That Named the Sūrah**

The verse begins the account from which Sūrat al-Māʾidah takes its name: *idh qāla al-ḥawāriyyūna yā ʿĪsā ibna Maryama hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka an yunazzila ʿalaynā māʾidatan mina al-samāʾ* — "When the disciples said, 'O Jesus son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?'" The word *māʾidah* denotes a table laid with food — from m-y-d, to sway, to move, said of a table because the food on it sways, or because it is brought to and fro; a bare table is not a *māʾidah*. The disciples ask for a laden table from the sky, and Jesus' answer is a call to *taqwā*. The verse raises three questions the commentators addressed: what exactly did the disciples ask, why did they ask it, and why did Jesus answer as he did.

**"Is Your Lord Able?" — The Problem of the Question**

The source notes the difficulty. As it stands, the question — *hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka*, "is your Lord able?" — seems to express doubt about God's omnipotence, which would be astonishing from disciples who had just been described as inspired by God to believe (v. 111) and who had witnessed Jesus raising the dead (v. 110). The commentators offered several resolutions.

First, a variant reading. Some of the Companions and early reciters — ʿAlī, ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and the reading of al-Kisāʾī — read *hal tastaṭīʿu rabbaka*, "can you ask your Lord?" — with "you" (Jesus) as the subject and "your Lord" as the object of an implied asking. On this reading, recorded in the source (al-Ṭabarī), the disciples do not question God's ability at all; they ask whether Jesus can petition God on their behalf. ʿĀʾishah said: "The disciples knew better than to ask whether God was able; they asked, 'Can you ask your Lord?'"

Second, on the standard reading *hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka*, "is your Lord able," the commentators understood the question as idiomatic — as when one says to a friend, "can you come with me?" meaning "will you?" — so that the disciples asked whether God *would* do it, not whether He *could*. Al-Zamakhsharī compared it to asking a generous man, "can you give me this?" without any doubt of his means.

Third, some (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) took the question as revealing a real deficiency — not disbelief, but a lack of the certainty proper to their station; they asked for a sign because, despite their profession in verse 111, their faith in Jesus' prophethood was not yet settled. The source notes the Qur'an's other accounts of people demanding signs from their prophets out of weak faith (4:153; 6:37, 109; 7:203). On this reading Jesus' answer is a rebuke.

**Why Did They Ask?**

The source records the possible motives.
